label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Pharmacare after two years: what the 2024 Act has delivered, who is covered, and what the full program would cost

report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually committed Canada to — the legal architecture, the first-phase drug list, the conditions attached to provincial money, and the deadlines

The Pharmacare Act (S.C. 2024, c. 24) received Royal Assent and came into force on 10 October 2024. It is a short statute — eleven sections — and the most important thing about it is what it does not do. It creates no national drug plan, no entitlement, and no federal formulary. It sets out a purpose, four principles the Minister of Health "is to consider," and a conditional payment power. Everything that has actually reached patients flows from that payment power and from agreements signed under it.

### The four principles, and what they bind

Section 4 lists the principles the Minister must consider when collaborating toward national universal pharmacare: improving accessibility of pharmaceutical products "in a manner that is more consistent across Canada"; improving affordability "including by reducing financial barriers for Canadians"; supporting appropriate use; and "provide universal coverage of pharmaceutical products across Canada" [2]. The verb matters. The Minister "is to consider" these principles; he is not obliged to achieve them, and no province is obliged to meet them. The Act's purpose clause (section 3) is similarly aspirational — to "guide efforts" toward implementation and to support the development of a national formulary and bulk purchasing strategy [2].

### The payment provision is conditional, and narrow

The operative funding clause is section 6:

> 6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes. [2]

Two things follow. First, the obligation to pay is triggered only by an agreement; without a signature, there is no federal money and no federal coverage obligation. Second, the statutory scope of that money is contraception and diabetes only. The Act names no other therapeutic area. Section 6(2) adds a clarification that any such agreement "is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" — meaning no deductible or copayment at the point of sale for the listed products [2].

This is why the program is described as a "first phase." The Act was designed as a down payment: fund a narrow list now, legislate the machinery for a broader plan, and leave the expansion to future funding decisions. Section 5 commits the government to "maintaining long-term funding" beginning with drugs for rare diseases, but attaches no amounts and no schedule [2].

### The machinery: formulary, bulk buying, expert committee

The Act set four deliverables, each with a statutory deadline tied to the first anniversary of Royal Assent, 10 October 2025:

- **An essential drugs list.** Section 8(1) required the Minister, after talks with provinces and territories, to ask the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform a national formulary that would set the scope of what Canadians should get under universal pharmacare, due no later than 10 October 2025. Section 8(2) then required the Minister to open discussions based on that list [2].
- **A national bulk purchasing strategy.** Section 9 required the same request to CDA, also by the first anniversary [2].
- **An appropriate-use strategy.** Section 10(1) required the Minister to publish a pan-Canadian strategy on appropriate use of prescription drugs by the first anniversary [2].
- **A committee of experts on financing.** Section 11 required the Minister to establish a committee of experts within 30 days of Royal Assent, and required the committee to report within one year on options for operating and financing a national, universal, single-payer pharmacare plan, with the report tabled in both Houses [2].

The financing question was therefore explicitly deferred by the statute itself: Parliament did not decide in 2024 how a national plan would be paid for or split between orders of government. It commissioned advice. The committee's final report was published in 2025.

### What the Act did not settle

Three absences explain most of what followed. There is no per-capita entitlement formula in the Act, so the size of each province's offer was negotiated deal by deal. There is no penalties or conditionality mechanism beyond the terms written into each bilateral agreement. And there is no expansion timetable: the Act's second phase — the national formulary and the broader drug list — depends entirely on future appropriations, which is precisely where the program stalled in 2026 (see section 6).

The design also explains the shape of the federalism problem. Because provinces administer drug plans and the federal government can only pay, a province that declines to sign loses nothing it already had; it simply does not gain the federal transfer. The Act creates an opt-in, not a national standard.

### 2. Which provinces and territories signed funding agreements, when coverage actually began in each, and why the other nine have not signed

Four jurisdictions signed. Nine did not, and two of those said so formally. The four agreements were all signed within six weeks of each other in early 2025, under a Liberal government that was about to face an election; nothing has been signed since.

### The four agreements, in the order they were signed

**Manitoba — 27 February 2025, the first.** The federal government committed "more than $219 million over four years" for universal coverage of a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications [3]. Coverage began 15 April 2025 under the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program. Health Canada's announcement framed the population served as nearly 350,000 Manitobans of reproductive age and more than 149,000 people with diabetes [3].

**British Columbia — 6 March 2025, the largest.** Federal funding of "more than $670 million over four years" for contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies [4]. BC's own program page describes the same agreement as "up to $670 million in funding over three years" [9]. The agreement text resolves the apparent contradiction: it runs four fiscal years but pays only three at the full rate — $17,406,567 in 2025-26, then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29 for Stream 1, plus a one-time $37,839,549 for devices and supplies in 2026-27 [37]. Adding those four amounts plus the one-time device payment adds up to just over $670 million — my own arithmetic — and matches the "more than $670 million" in both announcements; the three full-rate years are what BC means by "three years." The agreement fixes the implementation date at 1 March 2026 and ends 31 March 2029 [37], so BC's program has a three-year funded life. The federal announcement cited 1.3 million British Columbians of reproductive age and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [4].

**Prince Edward Island — 7 March 2025, the smallest per capita and the most generous relative to size.** More than $30 million over four years, with coverage starting 1 May 2025 [5]. Health Canada cited 41,000 Islanders of reproductive age and 16,000 with diabetes [5]. PEI's deal also covers blood glucose test strips.

**Yukon — 20 March 2025, the smallest in dollars.** $9.5 million, with coverage originally promised "not later than January 2026" and actually launched 15 April 2026 [27][16]. The territory's agreement was projected to support more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and more than 3,000 for diabetes [16]. Yukon's program is administered by Pacific Blue Cross with automatic enrolment and real-time adjudication at the pharmacy, and pharmacare pays first even for residents who hold private insurance [16].

### What the four add up to

The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives and the Canadian Health Coalition calculated in July 2025 that the four agreements total $928 million over four years beginning in 2026, covering nearly 7.5 million people, with per-capita funding varying "from $117 per resident for British Columbia to $198 per resident for Yukon" — an average of $156 [8]. Their conclusion was blunt: four out of five Canadians live outside the program.

The CCPA also costed what the non-signing provinces are forgoing, using the same per-capita method: "New Brunswick would likely receive $136 million through a bilateral pharmacare agreement over four years. Nova Scotia would receive $171 million, and Ontario would receive an estimated $2.5 billion over four years" [8]. Those are advocacy-organisation estimates, not federal offers, and should be read as orders of magnitude.

The funding envelope explains the arithmetic of why the program stopped where it did. Budget 2024 allocated $1.5 billion over five years. The four agreements committed $928.5 million — "62% of the total funding envelope" — for jurisdictions holding only 18% of the population [24]. On the original per-capita formula there was never enough money in the envelope to sign the remaining provinces at the same rate. Either the formula had to fall for later joiners, or Parliament had to appropriate more.

### Why the other nine did not sign

The reasons differ by province and are documented unevenly.

**Alberta** was the most explicit. Its health minister said the province wanted the ability to opt out of a national plan and instead take a per-capita share to enhance what she called an already robust provincial program [28]. Alberta also told CBC it had "serious concerns" about long-term sustainability and wanted to decide which medications were covered, and that it had not received details on Ottawa's long-term plan or how it would be financed. CIHI's November 2025 national health expenditure report states flatly that "Quebec and Alberta have formally opted out, preferring to maintain their own pharmacare programs" [22]. Quebec's position is structural: it runs its own mandatory drug insurance scheme and has consistently sought compensation with no conditions.

**Ontario, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Nunavut and the Northwest Territories** never signed. The public record of their reasons is thinner and mostly consists of provincial statements about the shortness of the funding, the absence of a long-term federal commitment, and a mismatch between the federal design and existing provincial programs. New Brunswick's premier and Ontario's premier both said in February 2025 that they were interested but that Ottawa was not recognising their provinces' needs. Nova Scotia's health department said five months before the 2026 budget that it wanted to restart talks.

**The 2025 election and the change of government** is the proximate reason the queue stopped moving. Former health minister Mark Holland said in February 2025 that there was not enough time to negotiate further deals before the election [19]. His successor, Marjorie Michel, said in July 2025 that Canada had "a new government" in "a new context," and that some provinces had not wanted the two coverages on offer at the time, and still did not. By 2026 the answer was clearer still: Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said after PEI raised its funding concerns publicly that "The door was closed on our province" [18].

Ontario put the position on the record in its own legislature. Asked at the Standing Committee on Social Policy on 28 September 2026 to confirm that Ontario would receive zero federal pharmacare dollars because it had not signed, Health Minister Sylvia Jones did not dispute it and said: "the federal government has paused all negotiations, conversations and any interest in expanding the program" [35]. She pointed to Ontario's existing drug programs for people under 25, over 65, and on ODSP or Ontario Works as the reason the province did not need a deal. The same exchange produced the only public figure for what a signed province draws in a year: MPP Robin Lennox stated that BC "this year, will receive $250 million" [35], which is consistent with the $204,948,289 annual Stream 1 amount in BC's agreement plus the $37,839,549 device payment landing in 2026-27 [37].

**The federal design itself is a cause.** The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts noted that the four agreements fund an average of about 70% of total spending on the included medicines, that only four of 13 jurisdictions had signed, and that the drug lists were inconsistent between them — which is why the committee recommended abandoning the bilateral model altogether in favour of direct federal funding of a single national list [13]. That recommendation was not adopted.

Health Canada's 2026-27 departmental plan confirms the position: it describes providing pharmacare funding to "residents of British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island, and Yukon" and names no other jurisdiction and no planned expansion [26].

### One number worth keeping separate

The 7.5 million figure above is the population of the four jurisdictions, not the number of users. The federal government has never published a count of people who have actually received a pharmacare-covered prescription. Section 4 sets out what the provinces have reported.

### 3. What is covered in practice — the drugs and devices on each list, what changed for patients (deductibles, copays, devices and supplies), and what is still excluded

The first phase covers a narrow, defined basket: contraception, diabetes medications, and the devices and supplies used to administer and monitor diabetes. Within that basket the coverage is genuinely first-dollar — no deductible, no copayment on the listed product. Outside it, nothing changed.

### What is on the federal list

Health Canada's own description of the basket is specific. For contraception: oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants, and injections [15]. For diabetes: metformin, insulin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors, plus supplies to administer medication (insulin pumps, syringes) and to monitor the condition (glucose monitors, test strips) [15].

The department attaches indicative costs to those drugs: metformin "about $100 per year," insulin "between $900 and $1,700 per year," sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors "from $100 to over $1,000 per year" [15]. Those figures are useful because they set the scale of what a patient saves. They are also modest next to the total cost of the disease: Diabetes Canada estimates up to $18,300 a year for Type 1 and up to $10,000 a year for Type 2 [25].

The diabetes burden Health Canada is aiming at: "About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes. In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028" [15].

### What is not covered

Three exclusions matter more than the inclusions for understanding the program's limits.

**Fees beyond the product.** Health Canada's coverage page states that pharmacare "**only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" and excludes delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees [14]. The about page adds the same caveat: "You may still have to pay other fees, like delivery fees or prescribing fees" [15]. In practice this means a patient in a rural area receiving a delivery, or paying a pharmacist to prescribe a contraceptive under expanded scope of practice, can still face a charge for a "free" product.

**GLP-1 drugs.** Semaglutide is not in the basket. In BC, "National pharmacare does not cover semaglutides so deductibles would apply" [25] — Ozempic remains available only under Special Authority for diabetes when other therapies have failed, and Wegovy is listed for weight management but not at 100% coverage. This exclusion is the single largest clinical gap in a diabetes program: the newest and most-prescribed class of diabetes drugs is outside it.

**Everything else.** The federal page is explicit that "Private and public drug plans will still cover a range of products outside the contraceptives and diabetes medications included in pharmacare bilateral agreements" [15]. Asthma inhalers, blood pressure medication, antibiotics, antidepressants, cancer drugs taken at home — none of it is touched.

### What actually changed for patients

The change is not "drugs became free" in the abstract; it is that income-based deductibles stopped applying to a specific list. This is clearest in BC, where Fair PharmaCare's income-tested deductible is the mechanism that left people paying out of pocket before coverage began — for a family earning $100,000, roughly $3,000 in prescriptions before the plan pays anything and $4,000 before full coverage. Plan NP sits outside that: "Plan NP covers many diabetes medications, menopause hormone therapy medications and contraceptives for all B.C. residents enrolled in MSP. Coverage is automatic at the pharmacy" — no registration and no receipts [9]. BC's February 2026 launch release described the effect as ending the deductibles that applied to its existing diabetes and menopause coverage [11].

The scale BC is claiming: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [11].

### Where provinces went beyond the federal list

The agreements are not identical, and two provinces used federal money to fund more than the federal scope.

**BC added menopausal hormone therapy.** MHT is not contraception and not diabetes. BC included it in Plan NP, covering oral micronized progesterone, vaginal and topical estrogen, estrogen/progesterone gels and patches, oral estradiol, oral conjugated estrogen and oral medroxyprogesterone at 100% with no income test — therapies that cost $240 to $1,800 a year uninsured [25]. This is a provincial policy choice layered onto the federal transfer, and it means "national pharmacare" delivers a materially different benefit in BC than in Manitoba.

**BC expanded devices and supplies.** "On April 1, 2026, BC PharmaCare expanded coverage of certain diabetes-related devices and supplies, made possible by federal national pharmacare funding" [10] — including alcohol wipes, lancets and ketone strips, plus insulin pumps (the mylife Ypsopump in December 2025, the Omnipod 5 in April 2026) [10].

**Manitoba added HIV drugs and hormone replacement therapy.** MEPP, effective 15 April 2025, provides no-cost coverage for birth control, diabetes medications, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy, with no Pharmacare deductible, reimbursing up to the lowest-cost interchangeable product plus a professional fee up to $14 [12]. It excludes people who already have 100% coverage under another public program, such as Non-Insured Health Benefits, and requires a Manitoba Health card [12].

**PEI added blood glucose test strips** as part of its program.

### The private-insurance question, which is not settled

Because the listed products are single-payer and first-dollar, the public plan displaces private coverage for those products. Health Canada's framing is that patients "won't need to coordinate benefits for covered products with private insurance plans" [15].

The insurance industry's reading is narrower than some provinces feared. The Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association has said "The Pharmacare Act is clear that insurers cannot cover any drugs that are covered by single-payer government pharmacare" — but because GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic are not in the pharmacare basket, private plans continue to cover them in all provinces including those with agreements. That directly rebuts the argument New Brunswick advanced for not signing: that joining would shift roughly $60 million of Ozempic cost onto its public plan [20].

What no government has published is how much of the new public spending substitutes for private coverage that already existed versus extending coverage to people who had none. Global Public Affairs put the question precisely in June 2025 and noted that no level of government had provided the data to answer it [24]. That gap persists.

### The basket the Act promised but has not delivered

Separately from the contraception and diabetes list, the Act required Canada's Drug Agency to prepare a list of essential prescription drugs to inform a national formulary. The agency's June 2025 consultation document set out the method: screen 655 drugs across 14 ATC groups plus 9 related products, starting from the CLEAN Meds list of 128 medications and aligning with the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines, and include a product if it is on CLEAN Meds or the WHO list, or is first-line per a health technology assessment and listed on at least seven public drug plans [29]. The list was delivered to the Minister. It has not been funded. No jurisdiction covers any drug because of it.

### 4. How many people are actually using it — enrolment, registration and claims figures, and how much federal money has flowed

This is the weakest part of the public record, and the weakness is structural rather than accidental. No government publishes a count of people who have received a pharmacare-covered prescription. What exists is a patchwork: two provinces have released uptake figures, one has released a projection, one has released nothing specific, and the federal government measures its own success by counting jurisdictions rather than patients.

### What the federal government measures

Health Canada's transfer-payment description for the program states its expected results plainly. In the short term, it expects "an increase in residents accessing a range of diabetes and contraception drugs and devices through provincial and territorial public drug plans is expected" The indicator it chooses is that "The number of jurisdictions implementing universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage for a range of contraception and diabetes prescription drugs and related products will indicate where and how much access has increased" [31].

That is a count of governments — four — presented as a proxy for access. The medium-term measure is better designed but slower: an increase in the number of Canadians taking their contraception and diabetes medications as prescribed, "measured using Statistics Canada data on reporting cost-related non-adherence" [31]. That data is collected by the Canadian Community Health Survey every two years. Health Canada's own performance table reports the national cost-related non-adherence rate at 5.1% in 2023-24 and 5.1% in 2024-25 [26] — unchanged across the period in which the first agreements were signed and two programs launched. The indicator cannot yet show an effect, and no jurisdiction-specific breakdown has been published.

There is no federal indicator, target, or published dataset for the number of individuals receiving a covered product. That is the central measurement gap in the program.

### The money, which is better documented than the people

The federal spending profile is available in the transfer-payment tables and it tells its own story. The Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications Initiative is a statutory-authority transfer running from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2029, with forecast and planned spending of:

- 2024-25 (forecast): $59,254,126
- 2025-26 (planned): $100,939,163
- 2026-27 (planned): $320,066,361
- 2027-28 (planned): $477,227,188 [31]

A separate Diabetes Devices and Supplies Fund, also running to 31 March 2029, adds $20,487,407 planned in 2025-26 and $37,839,549 in 2026-27, with nothing scheduled in 2027-28 [31].

Those figures are the real answer to "how much has flowed." In the first full year of operation — 2025-26 — the federal government planned to spend about $101 million on contraception and diabetes medications plus about $20 million on devices and supplies. That is roughly $121 million against total Canadian prescription drug spending of well over $30 billion. The ramp to $477 million in 2027-28 reflects British Columbia's March 2026 start and Yukon's April 2026 start, not an expansion to new jurisdictions: my own arithmetic from the four annual figures gives a cumulative total of about $957 million over the four years, which is consistent with the $928.5 million in signed agreements plus the device fund [31][24]. The CCPA's independently derived figure of $88.1 million in federal pharmacare contributions for 2025-26 [7] is lower than the planned figure of $100,939,163 for that year [31], which is normal for a forecast-to-actual gap but is the only independent check available.

### What the provinces report

**Prince Edward Island** has the most complete public accounting, and it covers both halves of the basket. As of October 2026, more than a year and a half into its program, PEI's Department of Health and Wellness reported that "Over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [20].

Two things about those numbers deserve attention. First, the diabetes figure (over 20,000) exceeds the pre-launch projection of about 16,000 people with diabetes on the Island [20] — plausibly because the program covers supplies and devices that people with diabetes use whether or not they previously had drug coverage. Second, the contraception figure (over 5,000) is far below the pre-launch projection of about 41,000 Islanders of reproductive age. Some of that gap is definitional: 41,000 is the population of reproductive age, not the number who use prescription contraception, and many use methods not requiring a prescription. But the gap is large enough that it is the single best available signal that take-up among the eligible population is partial. The dollar figures give the scale: about $500,000 in out-of-pocket savings across 5,000 contraception users implies an average saving of roughly $100 per person — my own division, and a reminder that contraception is a low-cost basket item compared with insulin.

**Manitoba** reports on contraception but not, in any figure I could find, on diabetes. Between 2 October 2024 and 21 October 2025, "more than 53,000 people got free birth control through the program," with 190,000 prescriptions dispensed across all contraceptive types and nearly nine in ten of those for oral contraceptives [30]. A provincial spokesperson gave those figures to CBC. Important caveat: Manitoba's free contraception program began in October 2024 under the province's own authority, before the federal MEPP took effect in April 2025, so the 53,000 figure measures a provincial program that the federal money now partly funds rather than the federal agreement's own effect.

The Manitoba numbers also expose a design problem. To get free contraception, a patient needed a prescription from a doctor or nurse practitioner — pharmacists could not prescribe contraceptives as of December 2025, despite a government promise in May and a throne speech commitment in November. In a province where "More than 150,000 Manitobans don't have a family doctor" [30], that requirement is a direct barrier to the program's reach.

**British Columbia** has published eligible population figures rather than user counts: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [11]. Those are projections of who is eligible, published two days before the 1 March 2026 launch.

I looked for a claims count in the obvious places and did not find one. The Ministry of Health's 2025/26 Annual Service Plan Report, published August 2026, reports no Plan NP user or claim figures; its only pharmacare references are the 1 March 2026 MHT launch and a separate pharmacist-prescribing program [34]. The report does show PharmaCare's actual operating expense at $1,470,532 thousand against an estimate of $1,787,903 thousand — an underspend of $317,371 thousand and the largest variance in the ministry's financial summary [34]. That underspend is suggestive but not probative: it could reflect lower-than-expected Plan NP costs, or unrelated PharmaCare forecasting, and the report does not attribute it. I would not read it as a take-up measure.

The structural reason no count exists is that BC's coverage has no enrolment step. Plan NP covers "all B.C. residents enrolled in MSP" automatically at the pharmacy [9], and Health Canada's eligibility rules are residency-based with no registration — coverage applies "no matter your" age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [36]. The eligible and enrolled populations are identical by construction, so only a claims-based count would show actual use, and none has been published.

The BC agreement also explains why: it requires no results reporting until fiscal 2027-28. "Beginning in Fiscal Year 2027-28, as a condition of annual funding under this Agreement, by October 1 of each Fiscal Year, British Columbia agrees to report to Canada the amount of Savings delivered to British Columbia Residents" for device and supply coverage, along with an attested financial statement [37]. The first such report is therefore due 1 October 2027 — after the program's first full year, and two and a half years after signing. Nothing in the agreement requires a count of patients, and nothing was due before then.

**Yukon** reported the projected population at signing — more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and more than 3,000 for diabetes [16] — and launched on 15 April 2026 with automatic enrolment and real-time adjudication, again with no published claims data.

### Why "how many people are using it" has no clean answer

Three separate things are being counted and conflated in public discussion:

1. **Population covered by an agreement** — about 7.5 million people, per the CCPA/CHC calculation [8]. This is the number most often quoted, and it is not usage. It counts everyone who lives in a jurisdiction where the benefit exists, including people who need neither contraception nor diabetes medication.
2. **Eligible population** — the subset who might use it, such as BC's nearly 570,000 with diabetes plus 160,000 with menopausal symptoms, or Manitoba's 350,000 of reproductive age and 149,000 with diabetes. Still a projection.
3. **Actual users** — the only real usage measure, and available for exactly one jurisdiction in one half of the basket: PEI's 5,000 contraception users and 20,000-plus diabetes beneficiaries, and Manitoba's 53,000 contraception users.

The distinction matters because it is the difference between a program that has extended a benefit to millions of people and a program that has demonstrably changed medication use for tens of thousands. Both statements can be true at once, and only the second is evidence of the program working.

The federal government has the data to close this gap. Provincial drug plans adjudicate these claims and report to CIHI's National Prescription Drug Utilization Information System, and the committee of experts noted that provinces running bilateral agreements "have not had challenges administering free access using their existing systems and provincial health cards" [13]. What has not happened is publication. CIHI's NPDUIS holds claims data through fiscal 2025-26, but no pharmacare-specific public reporting has been issued, and the 2026 calendar-year data will not be available until June 2027.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost, and how those estimates differ and why

There are five credible estimates in circulation, and the most important thing to say about them is that they are not measuring the same thing. Two measure the *total* public cost of funding a drug list. Two measure the *incremental* cost above what governments already spend. One measures only the first phase. Comparing them directly — as most commentary does — produces apparent contradictions that are not real.

### The baseline the estimates start from

PBO's 2023 report establishes the arithmetic everything else works from. In 2021-22, total prescription drug spending in Canada was $36.6 billion. Of that, "About 46 per cent ($16.9 billion) of total prescription drug expenditure was covered by public sources; 40 per cent ($14.7 billion) by private insurance; and the remaining 14 per cent ($4.9 billion) was paid for out-of-pocket" [23]. PBO notes that the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association estimated roughly 25 million Canadians — 73% — had private drug insurance in 2021 [23].

For scale in 2025: CIHI reports drug expenditures at 13.3% of total health spending, with total health spending forecast at $399 billion, and drug spending growing 3.3% in 2025 after 4.4% in 2024 and 5.2% in 2023.

### Estimate 1: PBO's full single-payer plan (October 2023)

This is the number most often cited as "the cost of pharmacare." PBO modelled a national application of Quebec's RAMQ formulary with universal access and a copayment scheme — a $5 copayment on brand-name prescriptions, with exemptions for under-16s, students aged 16–18, those over 65, pregnant women, people with disabilities, and EI and welfare recipients [23]. The model assumes 20% confidential rebates on brand-name drugs and 25% on new drugs, and a 13.5% increase in utilization [23].

The results, over 2023-24 to 2027-28:

- **Total drug expenditure** under pharmacare: $33.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [23].
- **Gross incremental cost to public drug plans:** $14.8 billion in 2024-25, rising to $17.3 billion in 2027-28 [23].
- **Net incremental cost to the public sector** (federal and provincial combined, after copayment revenue and savings on direct federal spending): $11.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 [1].
- **Economy-wide savings:** $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28 [1].

The gap between the $14.8 billion gross and the $11.2 billion net is the copayments plus the reduction in federal direct spending, chiefly the Medical Expense Tax Credit. The gap between "incremental public cost" and "total expenditure" is existing public spending: pharmacare replaces $16.9 billion of public drug spending as well as expanding it. This is why the $33.2 billion and $11.2 billion figures both appear in coverage of the same report and appear to contradict each other. They do not.

PBO also modelled alternative formularies, and the results are the most policy-relevant part of the report. A **catastrophic** drug plan — covering only very high costs — would cost the public sector just $1.8 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.0 billion in 2027-28. An **essential medicines** formulary is stranger: it raises total drug expenditure by $0.4 billion in 2024-25, because "The list of essential medicines consists primarily of generic drugs, the prices for which are already sufficiently low that little additional savings can be achieved with a single-payer plan" [23]. The 13.5% increase in utilization is not offset by price savings on drugs that are already cheap. This finding matters for the current program: the first-phase basket is largely generics, so the savings case for it is weaker than the savings case for a brand-heavy formulary.

### Estimate 2: PBO's costing of the actual first phase (May 2024)

When PBO costed Bill C-64 as drafted, the number was very different because the question was different. "The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [6]. Not per year — over five years. The difference between this and the $11.2 billion annual figure is that the first phase covers only contraception and diabetes, and it is layered on existing coverage rather than replacing it.

The assumptions are explicit and they matter: the program "will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons" — the latter assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions — and "will also cover the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage" [33]. PBO assumed no additional federal confidential rebates, no behavioural substitution from unlisted to listed drugs, and no Medical Expense Tax Credit savings [33]. It rated its own confidence low: "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage" [6].

The Fraser Institute noted that the government's own Budget 2024 figure was $1.5 billion over five years, so PBO's $1.9 billion exceeded it by about $400 million before a single agreement was signed [32].

### Estimate 3: The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts (2025)

The committee appointed under section 11 of the Act produced the estimate closest to a policy design rather than a hypothetical. Its headline: "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars" [13]. Again, note the wording — *total* cost of *publicly funding* a list, not incremental cost.

The committee built its range from two directions.

**The $6.0 billion lower bound** is the more original work. It took the 185 medicines on Canada's Drug Agency's essential list — all multi-source and unpatented — and used IQVIA CompuScript 2024 data: "In 2024, total spending on these 185 medicines was $12.6 billion" [13]. It then adjusted that figure in six steps: up 2% for jurisdictions missing from the data, up 4% for volume growth, up 5% for induced use; down 14% for brand-to-generic pricing, down 17% for lower public markups and fees, and down 40% for competitive pricing [13]. The result is $6.0 billion.

**The $10 billion upper bound** is taken from PBO. The committee reports that PBO's estimate for a RAMQ-length list was $35 billion in total cost for 2025-26, with an incremental public cost of $11.9 billion [13][23]. "For a shorter list of essential medicines, the estimated cost in 2025 to 26 was $9.8 billion" [13] — and the committee adopted $9.8 billion as its upper bound, noting that PBO assumed a 13.5% increase in use.

The committee's summary table for 2025 shows the redistribution it expects: out-of-pocket spending falls from $9.5 billion to $6.8 billion, private insurance from $17.3 billion to $12.5 billion, existing public plans from $18.8 billion to $13.6 billion, with pharmacare spending $8 billion [13]. Adding those four columns gives a total under the status quo of roughly $45–46 billion and under pharmacare of roughly $41 billion, a saving of around $4–5 billion. That is my own calculation from the committee's four figures; the committee does not state the total or the saving itself.

The committee's financing recommendation is the substantive one: it rejected the bilateral model outright. It rejected "the idea of a limited "fill-the-gaps" model" in favour of universal, single-payer coverage, and recommended that the federal government be solely responsible for funding the essential list [13]. That is a direct critique of the four agreements, and it was not adopted.

### Estimate 4: C.D. Howe's "$40 billion"

The C.D. Howe Institute's September 2025 conference report puts the cost of "first-dollar universal pharmacare – estimated to cost almost $40 billion annually" [21]. This is the highest figure in circulation and the least comparable to the others. It is a total-cost figure for a first-dollar program covering the full drug basket — essentially all of Canadian drug spending moved onto public books with no copayments — and $40 billion is in the same range as CIHI's estimate of total drug spending. PBO's $33.2 billion for 2024-25 is the closest analogue.

The institute's argument is not that the number is unaffordable in isolation but that it is unnecessary: "With 97 percent of Canadians already having access to some form of drug coverage," it argues for gap-filling, strengthened catastrophic coverage, or a Quebec-style mixed model instead, warning that a first-dollar plan "could disrupt coverage for the 27 million Canadians currently benefiting from private insurance" [21].

### Estimate 5: The Fraser Institute's critique of the estimates themselves

The Fraser Institute's contribution is not a competing number but a challenge to a shared assumption. Both the government and PBO "assume that nobody already covered by some type of drug insurance plan (this was 81 per cent of Canadians in 2019) will switch to the new national plan, or that no public or private insurers will adjust or renegotiate their plans" [32]. If employers drop private coverage once a public plan exists — which is exactly what happens when a public plan is first-dollar and displaces private coverage for the same drugs — the public cost rises and the private cost falls. The Fraser Institute treats this as evidence the estimates understate the true cost.

That critique cuts both ways, and the record should be clear about it. The four actual agreements are structured so that pharmacare pays first, and private plans continue to cover everything outside the basket [20]. That means displacement of private coverage is already happening for the listed drugs, and the fiscal effect of that displacement has not been published by any government. The Fraser Institute is right that the static estimates miss it. It does not follow that the program costs more than advertised in net terms, because the spending is moving from premiums to taxes, not being created. Neither PBO nor the government has published an estimate of the net effect.

### How to read the numbers together

The honest summary is a range, and the choice within it is a policy choice about what gets covered:

- **First phase as legislated** (contraception and diabetes, layered on existing coverage): $1.9 billion in federal spending over five years [6], against about $957 million actually committed across four agreements and the device fund — my arithmetic from Health Canada's transfer-payment tables [31].
- **Essential medicines list, publicly funded** (185 medicines, generics): $6 billion to $10 billion a year in total public cost [13].
- **Full single-payer with a RAMQ-length formulary:** $11.2 billion net incremental public cost in year one, rising to $13.4 billion, with economy-wide savings of $1.4 billion rising to $2.2 billion [1].
- **First-dollar universal coverage of everything:** close to $40 billion a year in total cost [21].

The spread from $6 billion to $40 billion is not disagreement about facts. It is the difference between a short generic list and the entire drug basket, and between measuring the public bill and measuring total national spending. Any claim that "pharmacare would cost $X" without specifying which of those is being described is not a cost estimate; it is a rhetorical choice.

Two things are genuinely unresolved in the estimates. No published estimate incorporates the actual negotiated prices in the four agreements, because those are confidential. And no published estimate models the cost of the essential medicines list *incremental* to existing public spending — the committee gives total cost, PBO gives incremental cost for a different formulary, and nobody has published the incremental figure for the list the Act actually requires. That is the number a government would need before funding phase two.

### 6. Where the program stands now — expiring agreements, the 2026 fiscal and political record, and what happens to coverage if deals lapse

The program is not cancelled. It is also not continuing. The Act remains in force, the four agreements remain in force, and the coverage they fund is operating in four jurisdictions. What has stopped is everything beyond that: no new agreements, no phase two, no funding after 2029.

### The 2026 fiscal record

Budget 2026, tabled 5 November 2026, contains "no new pharmacare funding" and does not mention national pharmacare at all [17]. The only drug-coverage item in the health chapter is a three-year extension of the PEI Affordable Prescription Drug Pilot at $11 million a year [17]. The budget also did not mention the $500 million a year for drugs for rare diseases that Health Minister Marjorie Michel had confirmed at the federal-provincial-territorial health ministers' meeting in Winnipeg [17].

Santis Health's budget analysis reads the fiscal tables: health agreements sit at $4.3 billion in 2026-27 and 2027-28, then drop to $2.5 billion a year as home care, mental health and long-term care funding expire. And in its timeline: "2029: The four national pharmacare agreements expire" [17].

The spending path is therefore a ramp up to 2028 and a cliff in 2029. Health Canada's planned pharmacare transfers rise from $100,939,163 in 2025-26 to $320,066,361 in 2026-27 and $477,227,188 in 2027-28 [31], with the agreements ending 31 March 2029 [31]. The CCPA's Andrew Longhurst puts the trajectory slightly differently — federal pharmacare contributions of $88.1 million in 2025-26, expected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29, with nothing after that [7].

Those two series do not reconcile, and the discrepancy is worth stating plainly: Health Canada's planned figures run to 2027-28 and peak at $477 million; Longhurst's run to 2028-29 and peak at $269.6 million. They may reflect different accounting bases (planned versus actual, or including versus excluding the devices fund), but neither document explains the difference and I could not resolve it from published sources. What both agree on is that the money stops.

### What the provinces were told

In April 2026, "P.E.I.’s health minister revealed that Ottawa will be cutting $29 million in health care funding to the province over the next three years" [7]. That is the clearest public evidence of what expiry looks like from a province's side: the federal contribution is not merely not renewed, it is being reduced before the agreements end.

The political consequence was immediate. After PEI raised the cuts publicly, Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said "The door was closed on our province" [18] — a province that had been actively seeking a deal concluded that seeking one was pointless. Nova Scotia had said five months earlier that it wanted to restart talks. Neither province has an agreement.

Michel's own framing in July 2025 was that Canada had "a new government" in "a new context," and that some provinces had not wanted the two coverages on offer at the time, and still did not. The federal position is that it remains willing to support partners, but not that it intends to expand the program.

### What the Act still requires, and what happened to it

Three statutory deliverables were due by 10 October 2025 and their status is uneven.

**The essential drugs list** was prepared by Canada's Drug Agency. Its June 2025 consultation screened 655 drugs across 14 ATC groups plus 9 related products, starting from the CLEAN Meds list of 128 medications and aligning with the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines [29]. The list was delivered. It is not funded, no province covers anything because of it, and the national formulary it was meant to inform does not exist.

**The bulk purchasing strategy** was also requested from CDA by the same deadline. There is no public evidence of a published strategy producing price effects; the committee of experts noted only that the work "may further inform the procurement strategy for the list of essential medicines that will make up the essential medicine" formulary.

**The committee of experts' report** was delivered and tabled. Its central recommendation — that Ottawa fund a national essential medicines list directly rather than through bilateral deals — was not adopted, and the bilateral model it criticised is the one that exists.

**The appropriate-use strategy** under section 10 has not been published in any form I could locate.

So the Act's machinery produced documents and no coverage. The coverage that exists comes entirely from section 6 payments under four agreements.

### What happens to coverage if the agreements lapse

This is the question the record does not answer, and it is the most consequential open item. Three scenarios are possible and none has been publicly costed.

**Renewal.** Ottawa renews the four agreements at or near current levels. Cost: roughly $477 million a year on Health Canada's own 2027-28 planning figure [31]. No government has committed to this.

**Wind-down.** The federal money stops on 31 March 2029 and each province decides whether to keep the benefit from its own revenues. BC's Plan NP is the largest exposure: it covers nearly 570,000 people with diabetes and 160,000 with menopausal symptoms [11], and BC has framed the program as federally funded [9][10]. Whether BC would absorb $670 million over three years from its own budget is unknown and unstated. Manitoba's MEPP predates the federal money for contraception (October 2024) but not for all of its categories, so its exposure differs. PEI's program began with the federal agreement. Yukon's began in April 2026.

**Partial continuation.** Provinces keep the cheapest and most politically salient element — contraception — and drop the diabetes devices and supplies, or reinstate income-tested deductibles for diabetes drugs. This is the most likely outcome on current evidence, because it is what provinces did before 2025: BC already covered diabetes medications through PharmaCare, subject to deductibles [9][11], and Manitoba already covered birth control from October 2024 [30]. In three of the four jurisdictions, the federal money did not create coverage; it removed deductibles and copayments from coverage that already existed. Removing the federal money would restore them.

That last point is the most important thing to understand about what the program delivered. In BC and Manitoba especially, the pharmacare agreements did not extend drug coverage to people who had none. They made existing coverage first-dollar. That is a real benefit — a $3,000 deductible at $100,000 of family income is a genuine barrier — but it is a different achievement from the one the Act's preamble describes, and it is far cheaper to reverse.

### The distributional consequence

Four jurisdictions with 18% of the population hold 62% of the funding envelope [24]. Four out of five Canadians live in a province or territory where the federal pharmacare program does not exist [8]. If the agreements lapse in 2029 and are not renewed, the program's lasting legacy will be the essential medicines list, the bulk purchasing request, a committee report, and a two-to-four-year window in which roughly 7.5 million people had no-cost contraception and diabetes drugs. That is not nothing. It is also not national pharmacare, and the gap between the two has widened since October 2024 rather than narrowed.

## TL;DR

## Key Findings
