## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone restrictions, and what each rule actually requires (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states, France, Sweden, and others)

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone restrictions, and what each rule actually requires

The policy wave is recent, fast and uneven. The clearest global count comes from UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report team, which began monitoring school phone bans in 2023 and now updates the tally: as of March 2026, "114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide", up from "Less than 1 in 4 countries (24%) had bans in June 2023" and 40% by early 2025 [1]. That headline number needs reading with care, because the GEM team counts very different instruments as "bans": outright prohibitions, national regulations requiring schools to write restrictive policies, and everything in between. The same article notes that Comoros, Colombia, Estonia, Lithuania, Iceland, Peru, Indonesia, Serbia, Poland and the Philippines have recently required schools to develop restricting policies without a national prohibition, and that recent national bans include Bolivia, Costa Rica, Croatia, Georgia, Maldives and Malta [1]. Federal systems produce subnational bans: in Germany, Bavaria, Saarland and Thuringia have banned smartphones in primary and special-needs schools, while Brandenburg, Bremen, Hesse and Schleswig-Holstein have tightened rules; Argentina's Buenos Aires province has banned phones in primary schools [1].

**United States.** There is no national ban. The GEM count is "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)", with most other states having bills pending [1].

**Ontario.** Ontario's rules took effect with a revised provincial Code of Conduct on 1 September 2024, issued through Policy/Program Memorandum 128. The substantive rule is age-graded rather than a blanket ban: "Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher", while students in Grade 6 and below may not use devices "at school during the school day" except at a teacher's discretion [9]. Devices may stay with students but must be turned off or silenced and stored out of view; a device seen out of storage is handed in for the class (Grades 7–12) or for the day (Kindergarten to Grade 6), and refusal escalates to the principal [9]. Boards must publish enforcement policies and send parents an annual reminder. Two features matter for evaluation: the restriction is on *use during instructional time*, not possession, and secondary students may use phones at recess and lunch [9]. Ontario's earlier attempt, in 2019, was widely judged unevenly implemented, which is one reason the 2024 version added explicit enforcement and reporting duties.

**England.** England has guidance, not statute. In February 2024 the Department for Education issued non-statutory guidance asking school leaders to prohibit mobile phone use throughout the school day, including breaks and lunch, with implementation left to individual schools and reinforced through inspection [1]. UNESCO's summary is precise about the design: "the government has issued strengthened guidance encouraging schools to prohibit mobile phones during the school day. The expectation is reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools" [1]. That design choice — a national expectation with school-level discretion — is what made the SMART Schools natural experiment possible, since English schools in 2022–23 already sorted into restrictive and permissive policies [2].

**Netherlands.** The Dutch arrangement is a national agreement between the ministry and the education organisations rather than a law. "the ban on mobile phones in the classroom was first introduced in January 2024 for secondary education, and it was extended to include primary education as of the 2024/2025 school year" [10]. Schools set the concrete rules, and there are exceptions for educational use and for students with medical or wellbeing needs; some schools extended the ban to the whole school day including breaks, others kept it to lessons [10]. The ministry said it would review with stakeholders in summer 2025 whether a statutory ban was needed [10]. That variation is itself a research finding: Dutch school boards were given autonomy, so "some schools have restricted the ban to the classroom only (i.e., a partial smartphone ban), while others extended the prohibition to the entire school grounds (i.e., a full smartphone ban)".

**Australia.** Australia is a set of state systems rather than one national rule. Victoria moved first, "banning phones in public primary and secondary schools in 2020. By term four, 2023, Western Australia Tasmania, New South Wales and South Australia had followed suit; Queensland restricted phones in term one, 2024" [11]. New South Wales's ban took effect at the start of Term 4, 2023, and requires phones to be off and out of sight during the school day. South Australia's policy, announced November 2022, applies from Term 1 2023 and requires students in government schools to keep personal devices "off and away between the start and end of each school day", with schools allowed to delay implementation until Term 3 2023 — a staggered rollout that created the comparison group for the one preregistered Australian evaluation [3].

**France and others.** France's 2018 law prohibiting phone use in primary and lower secondary schools is the most-cited early national ban; French policymakers are now considering further rules, and a proposed social media ban for under-16s was rejected by parliament [1]. Sweden is the instructive counter-case: it had no national ban, but schools adopted bans individually from the late 1990s onwards, reaching about 60% of schools by 2017, which is what made a large Swedish replication study possible [5].

**France: from a use ban to a possession ban.** France legislated first, in the 2018 law on "l'encadrement de l'utilisation du téléphone portable", which bans phone use in nursery, primary and lower-secondary schools and during any teaching activity outside them. In 2024–25 the ministry ran a "Portable en pause" experiment in about 100 collèges covering 32,000 pupils, testing lockable pouches, individual lockers and collective boxes; it was generalised to all public collèges from September 2025, and the President announced extension to lycées in November 2025 [35]. Costs fell on départements: one principal priced lockers at about €20,000 for his school, pouches at €7 each were paid for by families in another, and Départements de France put the national cost of lockers at €125 million [35]. Implementation lagged the announcement badly: in the Senate in January 2026 a senator recorded that 70% of school heads surveyed in September had not yet been able to implement it "faute de moyens adaptés" [30], and a union survey of school heads two weeks into the 2025–26 year put uptake far below that.

**Sweden: the country that reversed.** Sweden spent a decade as the international exemplar of classroom digitisation and then legislated in the other direction. From autumn 2026 it became compulsory for all schools and after-school clubs to collect students' phones and hold them until the end of the day, affecting children aged seven to 16, with 95 million kronor allocated for 2026 and 100 million the following year [29]. Most Swedish schools already confiscated phones at the start of the day, and students had learned to defeat the rule by handing in a fake handset. This matters for reading the Swedish null results discussed below: the Kessel study measures a period of voluntary school-level adoption, not the 2026 statutory regime.

**Denmark.** A broad majority of the Danish parliament agreed in late 2025 to make primary and lower-secondary schools and school-based leisure facilities mobile-free from the 2026/2027 school year, with a standard policy template, local board policies, exemptions for disability support, and accompanying content filtering of non-educational sites [32]. The stated rationale cites research that over half of students in years 6 and 8 are distracted by their own or others' screen use in lessons [32].

**Australia, nationally.** Beyond the state bans, Education Ministers agreed that phones would be banned or restricted in all public schools from Term 1 2024, so the country now has a national expectation layered over state rules [34]. Victoria is extending its ban from January 2027 to smartwatches and headphones and to Catholic and independent schools, on the strength of what the government calls an independent evaluation finding students more focused in class, more social during breaks, and fewer critical incidents involving phones [33].

**Ontario's enforcement record.** Ontario's rule has an implementation trail worth recording because it bears on every null result in this report. An independent audit of 60 English-language Ontario boards' publicly posted codes of conduct, conducted between June and August 2025, found that "55 of the 60 boards assessed (92%) failed at least one of the five mandatory requirements; five boards failed all five", with 49 boards (82%) lacking a clear reporting mechanism and 48 (80%) failing the signage requirement [31]. This audits documents rather than classrooms, and it is not a peer-reviewed study; but it shows that a provincial directive can coexist with incomplete board-level implementation for a full school year. Teacher-survey evidence from Toronto points the same way: consistent enforcement was reported by over 70% of elementary teachers but only 44% of secondary teachers [7].

The pattern across these jurisdictions is that almost none of them were designed as evaluations. The rules were announced as child-protection and classroom-order measures, on timetables set by politics. Where evaluations exist, they exist because researchers found variation — between schools in England and Sweden, between states and schools in Australia, across municipalities and cohorts in Norway — not because governments built in measurement. The GEM team's own framing concedes the point: "while limiting phone use may help reduce classroom distraction, it does not remove the need for students to learn how to navigate digital environments" [1].

### 2. What the evidence shows about learning and academic achievement: the natural experiments, the within-school studies and their numbers


The academic literature on school phone bans is now large enough to contain a clean natural experiment in disagreement. Two studies using almost the same design, on different countries, reach opposite answers, and a third generation of studies with better data has begun to adjudicate between them.

**The English result that started it.** Louis-Philippe Béland and Richard Murphy surveyed schools in four English cities about whether they banned phones and when, matched that to student exam records, and ran a difference-in-differences design: "we find that student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban", with gains "driven by the lowest-achieving students" [8]. The published headline estimate is about 0.07 standard deviations on average, driven by the lowest achievers; King and colleagues describe Béland and Murphy's estimate for low-achieving students as "the equivalent of an additional hour a week in school or five additional school days a year" [3]. The finding is intuitive and it is the one that launched the policy wave: phones distract the students least able to resist, so removing them helps most where help is needed.

**The Swedish replication that found nothing.** Dany Kessel, Hulda Lif Hardardottir and Björn Tyrefors then ran the same design on Swedish data — school-level panel data on grade-9 pupils from 1997 to 2017, covering 1,086 of 1,423 schools (about 76% response), with bans spreading from three schools in 1997 to 631 schools, roughly 60% of the sample, by 2017 [5]. Their conclusion is unambiguous: "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [5]. The precision matters more than the null. Their preferred merit-point specification gives a coefficient of −0.034 (SE 0.029), and "Focusing on the 95 % con- fidence interval in brackets, we find that effects larger than 0.024 can be rejected" [5]. In other words, the Swedish data are inconsistent with the English estimate of 0.07 SD; the two studies cannot both be right about a common underlying effect.

Why might they differ? Kessel and colleagues note that the two settings differ in what a "ban" meant, in when bans were adopted (English bans in the 2006–2010 window were early, when smartphones were still rare; Swedish bans by 2017 were adopted into a saturated smartphone environment), and in the outcome measures (high-stakes exam scores in England, teacher-set and national-test merit points in Sweden). The English study has also been criticised for relying on school leaders' retrospective reports of ban timing, which invites measurement error correlated with school improvement efforts. Neither paper resolves this; the honest reading in 2020 was that the academic effect was context-dependent and unknown in size.

**Norway: the gender and subgroup result.** Sara Abrahamsson's Norwegian study is the most-cited evidence that bans work, and its final peer-reviewed version is more careful than its reputation. Using administrative data plus survey data on middle-school phone policies and an event-study design, she reports in the *Journal of Human Resources* (online March 2026) that "banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [13]. The earlier working-paper framing put the gains in sharper terms — a ban "significantly increases girls' average grades", improves their maths test results, and raises their likelihood of attending an academic high-school track, with larger effects among low-SES girls [6]. Two cautions attach. The identifying assumption is that the timing of a school's adoption is unrelated to other determinants of its students' outcomes, which is plausible given how Norwegian schools adopted (in waves, partly imitating neighbours) but not testable. And the gender asymmetry means the headline "bans raise grades" is really "bans raise girls' grades", with the male effect near zero — a pattern that no simple distraction story explains well.

**Spain: big PISA gains, from regional aggregates.** Pilar Beneito and Óscar Vicente-Chirivella studied Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha, which banned phones in primary and secondary schools at the end of 2014 and the start of 2015, using PISA scores from 2006 to 2018 and officially reported bullying cases from 2012 to 2017 [20]. Applying the synthetic control method to Galicia, they estimate that "after less than three years since the mobile phones ban was in force (from 2015 to 2017), students’ PISA scores in Galicia improved by around 10 points in maths and 12 points in sciences as compared to a synthetic Galicia that had followed exactly the same trend in these scores before the intervention" [20]. Their preferred specification gives 10.7 points in maths and 12.7 in science by 2017, which they convert, following Woessmann, to "0.6–0.8 years of learning in maths and around 0.72 to near one year of learning in sciences" [20]. Those are enormous effects for a policy that, as the authors themselves stress, was "not a categorical prohibition" and allowed educational use. The design is aggregate: 17 Spanish regions, five PISA waves, one treated unit with complete pre-treatment data. Synthetic control with a single treated region is fragile — the estimate is only as good as the fit of the synthetic counterfactual, and here the "effect" partly reflects Galicia holding steady while the synthetic Galicia (a weighted mix of Castilla y León, the Balearics, Catalonia and Madrid) declined. The authors report placebo tests in which no other region produces a comparable gap, which is reassuring but not decisive, and the bullying outcome relies on police-reported cases, which move with reporting behaviour as well as with bullying.

**Brazil: a district-wide ban with individual data.** Allcott and colleagues summarise a newer study — Lichand, Moreno-Louzada, da Costa and Gentzkow (2026) — finding that "a district-wide ban in Rio de Janeiro led to improvements in test scores" [19]. I did not read the Rio paper itself, so it should be treated as a pointer rather than a verified result here.

**Florida: state-wide ban, individual records, phone-location data.** Umut Ozek's study of Florida's HB 379, enacted in 2023 and the first statewide US ban, is the most methodologically interesting of the American studies. It uses student-level administrative records from one of the ten largest US districts, three test administrations a year, and — crucially — commercial smartphone-location ("ping") data to measure how much phone activity actually fell at each school. Phone activity on campus "dropping to about one-third of the pre-ban levels in the first two months of the ban" confirms the policy bit [18]. Because every school was treated, Ozek compares schools with high versus low pre-ban phone activity, an exposure design he concedes "likely understates the positive effects of the ban on students, because both high effect and low effect schools are treated by the ban" [18]. The results: "student test scores improved by 0.6 percentiles, with the ban increasing spring test scores 1.1 percentiles in the second year relative to the spring test right before the ban took effect" [18]. Effects are larger for male students (1.4 percentiles on the spring test) and for middle and high school students (1.3 percentiles), and absent in elementary school and for female students. The gains come with a striking mechanism: the ban also reduced unexcused absences, and "An exploratory mediation analysis suggests that the effect of the ban on unexcused absences in middle and high schools explains nearly half of the positive effect on student test scores" [18]. The summary judgement is that the policy "apparently improved student learning climate, at least after a period of transition" [18]. Note the units: percentile points, not standard deviations. A 0.6–1.1 percentile gain is small — roughly a hundredth of a standard deviation in the metric Allcott and colleagues use for comparison — and much smaller than the Beland–Murphy or Galician estimates.

**The largest US study: pouches, nationwide, near-zero average.** The best-powered study yet is Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob's evaluation of Yondr lockable phone pouches, using administrative adoption records from the company (4,608 schools), GPS pings for 40,542 schools, a teacher survey with nearly 108,000 responses covering about half of US middle and high schools, state test data, attendance records and Panorama student surveys, in a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design [19]. It is the strongest test available of a genuinely binding restriction: teacher-reported in-class phone use for personal reasons falls "from 61 percent to 13 percent" [19]. The academic answer is essentially null: "we can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" over the first three years [19]. The heterogeneity runs the other way from the distraction story: in general, "High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects", though the gap is not statistically significant overall; in maths specifically, high-school adoption raises achievement by roughly 0.024 student-level SD — about 0.9 percentile points, or a fifth of the gain from a higher value-added teacher — while middle-school effects are negative and about half as large [19]. Allcott and colleagues note that phone activity fell more in high schools than middle schools in their data, so middle schools may have borne enforcement costs for smaller benefits. Their summary of the prior literature is the fairest short account anyone has written: Beland and Murphy found that school-level bans in England raised test scores, particularly among lower-achieving students, while Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors found no academic effects of similar bans in Sweden [19].

**Australia: one preregistered test, null on engagement.** The South Australian natural experiment by King and colleagues is the only preregistered Australian evaluation. The state's policy from Term 1 2023 required devices to be "off and away" during the school day, with schools allowed to delay implementation until Term 3 — creating a comparison group. Five metropolitan schools took part (two already banning, three delaying), with 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up [3]. The academic outcome was self-reported engagement, not test scores. The ban group's engagement rose (d = 0.28), but "there was no significant between-group difference in academic engagement at follow-up" (d = 0.03) [3]. The authors' overall verdict: "in broad terms, the present study did not detect evidence of the desired, or any undesired, effects of the phone ban over a short period of time" [3]. Five schools and one term is very little, and the authors say so.

**England again, cross-sectionally.** The SMART Schools study, the largest English study, is cross-sectional and cannot estimate a ban's effect on attainment; what it can do is compare schools that already had restrictive versus permissive policies. On attainment it found no difference, and its authors list academic attainment among the outcomes that did not differ between policy types [2].

**Where the learning evidence nets out.** Taking the studies together, three patterns hold. First, effects on average attainment are small — small enough that the best-powered study can rule out anything above about 0.007 SD [19], and the second-best finds 0.6–1.1 percentile points [18]. Second, when gains appear they cluster in older students and in specific groups: low achievers in England [8], girls in Norway [13], middle and high schoolers and boys in Florida [18], high-school maths in the pouch study [19]. Third, the two studies that look most alike on paper (England 2016, Sweden 2020) disagree in a way that cannot be explained by sampling noise, which means the effect depends on context — on what the ban replaced, how well it was enforced, and whether students had other screens to hand. The large Spanish estimates [20] are the outlier, and they come from the weakest design of the set.

### 3. Attention, distraction and classroom behaviour: what has actually been measured, and how


Attention is the outcome everyone assumes a ban will fix, and it is the one where the measurement is weakest and the evidence most interestingly split.

**The measurement problem comes first.** Attention is not observed; proxies are. Four kinds appear in the literature, and they disagree with each other in informative ways:

*Direct observation.* The Odisha trial used unannounced classroom spot checks — 7,797 visits in which a research assistant watched a classroom for under a minute through a window or doorway and coded behaviours from a checklist [21]. This is the closest thing to an objective measure in the literature, and it produced a genuine puzzle.

*Teacher and principal report.* The Dutch one-year monitoring study asked school leaders whether the national agreement had changed pupils' concentration: "Driekwart van de scholen (74,9%) ervaart een positief tot zeer positief effect van de landelijke afspraak op de concentratie en oplettendheid van leerlingen op hun school" — three-quarters of secondary schools reported a positive or very positive effect on concentration and attentiveness, and none reported a negative effect [14]. The English-language summary of the same evaluation reports the concentration figure as 75% and the "social environment was better" figure as 59% [17]. In New South Wales, the Department of Education's Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation surveyed almost 1,000 public school principals a year after the Term 4 2023 ban: 95% supported it, "81 per cent say students’ learning has improved since mobile phones were banned", 87% reported less distraction and 86% reported improved socialising [16]. These are perceptions by the adults responsible for enforcing the policy, collected by the government that introduced it. They are evidence about how schools experience the policy, not about attention.

*Student self-report.* Here the answers tend to be null. In Odisha, students assigned to phone-free classrooms reported no change in perceived distraction, and no significant change in perceived learning, subjective well-being or academic motivation [21]. In South Australia, self-reported academic engagement rose within the ban group (d = 0.28) but "there was no significant between-group difference in academic engagement at follow-up" (d = 0.03) [3].

*Behavioural and administrative records.* Phone use itself, disciplinary incidents and attendance can be measured directly, and this is where the strongest findings sit.

**Does removing phones actually reduce phone use?** Yes, sharply, where enforcement is physical. Allcott and colleagues, using Yondr pouches across thousands of US schools, find that "The share of students reported to be using their phones in class for personal reasons falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools" [19]. They corroborate this with commercial GPS ping data showing a large, persistent decline in device activity on school campuses — roughly 30% fewer pings by the third year — while cautioning that pings include adults' phones and phones that are on but not in use, so this is a conservative lower bound [19]. In Florida, phone activity on campus fell to about a third of pre-ban levels in the first two months [18]. In South Australia, 87% of students in ban schools reported complying at the first survey and 79.9% at the second [3]. The Dutch monitoring study reports that the minority of schools agreeing that non-educational phone use is a problem at their school fell to "28,8%", from "62,5%" at baseline [14]. So the first link in the causal chain — bans reduce in-school phone use — is solid when the ban is enforceable and much weaker when it is a matter of teacher discretion.

**Does less phone use mean more attention?** The evidence does not say so clearly. The Odisha spot checks found fewer instances of student chatter and disruptive behaviour, reduced phone use, and more teacher engagement in phone-ban classrooms, and observers recorded significantly fewer disruptive behaviours and less peer conversation unrelated to coursework [21]. But the same observers recorded students appearing *more* distracted: "Spot checks also revealed that students appear more distracted, possibly due to withdrawal from habitual phone checking, yet, students did not report being more distracted" [21]. The authors call this the distraction paradox and offer an attention-allocation explanation: removing the dominant source of self-distraction may make students more responsive to ambient stimuli that an outside observer can see. Teachers in phone-free rooms were "significantly busier maintaining order and student focus" [21]. In other words, a ban may convert private distraction into visible restlessness and add to the teacher's load.

The US pouch study, which has by far the best power for attention outcomes, reports the opposite of the hoped-for result: "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying or self-reported classroom attention", though the authors warn that pre-trend differences limit what can be concluded on those two outcomes specifically [19].

**The cognitive premise underneath the policy is shakier than the policy debate assumes.** The "brain drain" hypothesis — that the mere presence of a phone drains working memory even when unused — is the mechanism usually cited for why bans should help attention. The largest test of it is a four-level meta-analysis by Hartanto and colleagues: 166 effect sizes from 53 samples and 33 studies, 4,368 participants, finding that "the mere presence of smartphone had no significant effect on cognitive outcomes (d = −0.02, SE = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.01], p = .246)" [15]. Active in-class use is a different matter — a phone being scrolled is obviously not being attended to — but the widely repeated claim that a phone on the desk degrades cognition does not survive the meta-analytic evidence, and it should not be used to justify bans.

**The clearest behavioural cost is discipline.** In Florida, suspensions rose immediately: the authors estimate the ban raised suspension rates by about 12% in the first year, with in-school suspensions up about 20%, and the increases were concentrated among Black and male students — "we find that the ban increased in-school suspensions by about 30 percent among the former group" [18]. These effects largely dissipated by the second year. The US pouch study finds the same shape: disciplinary incidents rise about 0.03 student-level SD in the adoption year — roughly a 15% increase in suspension rates — and fade afterwards [19]. Allcott and colleagues are explicit that this may reflect enforcement of the new rule rather than worse behaviour, and that recorded incidents can rise simply because monitoring rises [19].

The most defensible summary is narrow: binding bans reliably cut in-school phone use; they reduce some observable off-task behaviour; they do not reliably improve self-reported or teacher-reported attention; they raise recorded discipline in the first year; and schools that adopt them overwhelmingly report that concentration improved, in surveys commissioned by the governments that adopted them.

### 4. Bullying and cyberbullying: what the evaluations find


Bullying is where the evidence most nearly supports the policy case, and where the measurement is most easily confused, because bullying and *cyber*bullying are different outcomes with different base rates and different school-hour exposure.

**Norway: the largest reduction, from survey self-reports.** Abrahamsson's event study uses the national pupil survey plus administrative health data. Her abstract states that "Post-ban bullying among both genders decreases" [22]. The magnitudes reported from the paper are substantial: girls who spent three years of middle school under a ban reported being bullied "about 46 percent less compared to when no policy was in place", and boys experienced "a decline in bullying incidents by about 43 percent" four years after a ban [23]. A scoping review of the same study puts the effect at 0.24–0.31 standard deviations, appearing after two to three years [26]. Two things should be weighed. First, the outcome is self-reported victimisation on a national school survey, which is a reasonable measure but is sensitive to reporting climate; if a ban makes a school talk more about bullying, reports can rise even as incidents fall. Second, the timing matters: effects appear only after two to three years of exposure, which is much slower than the political timetable on which these policies are sold.

**Spain: police-recorded bullying falls among teenagers, not children.** Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella used the Spanish Ministry of Education's bullying statistics, drawn from reports of bullying cases, for 2012–2017 across the regions that banned phones in 2015 and those that did not. Their results are age-specific: "They found mobile phone bans were unrelated to number of bullying cases in students under 12 years old, however bans were estimated to be linked 15% to 18% reduction in bullying among children aged 12 to 14 years, and a decline of 9.5% to 18% in 15 to 17 years age group" [26]. The age gradient is what a phone-centred mechanism predicts, since under-12s are less likely to own phones and to be on social media. But the measure is administrative cases, so it moves with reporting behaviour as well as with bullying. Their own caveat, recorded in the scoping review, is that they could not distinguish complete bans from partial ones, and that schools in banned regions could still allow phones for educational purposes [26].

**England: no difference.** The SMART Schools study found no difference in bullying or cyberbullying between schools with restrictive and permissive policies, consistent with its wider null result [2]. The study is cross-sectional and cannot rule out small effects.

**Australia: no difference, and a baseline imbalance.** In the South Australian preregistered experiment, "There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups" [3] — with no condition-by-time interaction, meaning the ban did not change the trajectory. The ban group started higher, which is a design weakness the authors acknowledge; the schools that had already adopted a ban were not randomly chosen. Overall the authors concluded that "in broad terms, the present study did not detect evidence of the desired, or any undesired, effects of the phone ban over a short period of time" [3]. With five schools and two survey waves, this is a weak test — it cannot detect anything but a large effect.

**United States: nothing measurable.** The Yondr pouch study reports "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying or self-reported classroom attention", and adds that for those two outcomes, some evidence of differential pre-trends limits the conclusions the authors can draw [19]. That is the most honest statement in the literature: the best-powered study cannot detect a bullying effect, and cannot rule one out either, because adopting schools were already on a different trajectory.

**Two counter-findings worth taking seriously.** The scoping review records that "two studies showed that incidents of online victimization and harassment was greater in schools that imposed mobile phone bans than schools that did not (Davis & Koepke, 2016; Walker, 2013)" [26]. Davis and Koepke surveyed 2,079 secondary students in Bermuda; Walker surveyed 325 students in two English schools. Both are cross-sectional, so the obvious alternative explanation is reverse causation — schools with more online victimisation may be more likely to adopt a ban, not the other way round. Davis and Koepke's own proposed mechanism is different and more interesting: punitive phone regimes may sour school climate, and poor school climate predicts more cyberbullying. Neither study can distinguish these. They should be read as a warning that the direction of the association is not settled in cross-sectional data, not as evidence that bans increase bullying.

**Why the mechanism is doubtful anyway.** Campbell and colleagues make the structural argument: "It is crucial to recognize that banning mobile phones and not banning other available internet- connected devices in schools is a simplistic solution which seems unlikely to have meaningful impact" [26]. Their reasoning is that students can cyberbully from laptops, tablets, smartwatches or library computers, and that cyberbullying usually happens outside school hours — they cite evidence that cyberbullying accounts for only about 1.1% of bullying experiences. A school-hours phone ban therefore targets a small slice of the exposure window. This is an inference from base rates rather than a tested result, and the Norwegian and Spanish findings do suggest a real if modest effect on in-school bullying; but it explains why a ban would shift bullying rather than eliminate it.

**What to conclude.** The strongest positive evidence on bullying comes from Norway (large, self-reported, slow-acting, both genders) and Spain (moderate, administrative, only in adolescents). The strongest null evidence comes from England and South Australia, both short-window. The US pouch study is inconclusive on this outcome by the authors' own account. The defensible statement is that phone bans plausibly reduce in-school bullying among adolescents by a modest amount after a year or more, that the best-powered studies have not confirmed it, and that no study has shown a ban reduces cyberbullying that occurs off school premises — which is where most of it happens.

### 5. Mental health and wellbeing: what the evaluations find, and what they cannot find


Mental health is the justification most often given for these policies and the outcome on which the evidence is weakest. The problem is not that studies disagree; it is that almost no study has the design, the sample and the follow-up needed to answer the question, and the two that come closest pull in opposite directions.

**England: the SMART Schools cross-section.** The SMART Schools study is the largest direct comparison of English schools with restrictive and permissive phone policies: 30 schools, 1,227 pupils aged 12–15, surveyed on the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale plus measures of anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep, physical activity, attainment and classroom disruption [2]. The wellbeing result is null and precisely estimated enough to be informative: mean WEMWBS score 47 (SD 9), with "no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [2]. The authors also found no differences in anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep duration or efficiency, physical activity, attainment or disruptive behaviour: "Comparing schools that restrict the daytime use of phones with schools that permit it, we observed no differences in adolescents’ self-reported mental wellbeing, anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, and their motives for using social media" [2].

The mechanism the authors identify is the important part. Restrictive policies did reduce in-school phone and social media time — by 0.67 hours and 0.54 hours a day respectively — but there was no difference in total weekday or weekend use [2]. That is, the ban moved phone time, it did not reduce it. This is the single most consequential finding in the whole literature for policy: if the harm mechanism runs through total exposure, a school-hours ban cannot do much about it. Saffer's summary of the same study puts the in-school reduction at about 40 minutes a day, offset by increases in the evenings and at weekends [27].

The SMART Schools study has real limits. It is cross-sectional: schools choose their policies, so the comparison confounds policy with school ethos, intake and leadership. Its response rate was about 10% of invited schools, and Weiss and Bonell, commenting in the same journal, note that this and the cross-sectional design limit causal conclusions [25]. They also make the broader point that the upstream evidence is thin: "the epidemiological evidence for a causal association is weak", since most studies are ecological or cross-sectional and do not adjust for confounders [25]. That matters because a school phone ban is a downstream intervention premised on an upstream causal claim that is itself contested.

**Norway: the strongest positive signal, and it is narrow.** Abrahamsson's event study is the best evidence that a ban can improve adolescent mental health, and it is specific about what improved: "banning smartphones significantly decreases the health care take-up for psychological symptoms and diseases among girls" [22]. The peer-reviewed version adds that bans "reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds", while having "no average effect on education or mental health" [13]. The reported magnitude is large: girls' consultations with a general practitioner fell by about 29% [23]. Boys showed no mental health effect at all, which Abrahamsson attributes to girls' higher baseline phone use and higher rates of adolescent mental health problems.

What this measures is health-care *utilisation*, not symptoms or diagnoses. Utilisation depends on supply, referral practice and parental behaviour as well as on need, and Abrahamsson explicitly reports no effect on whether students were diagnosed or treated for psychological conditions [23]. So the finding is consistent with a real reduction in distress, and also with a reduction in help-seeking or in GP referral. It is a strong study of a real outcome, but the outcome is one step removed from mental health.

**Netherlands: two evaluations, both null on wellbeing.** The government-commissioned monitoring study by Kohnstamm Instituut and Oberon surveyed 317 secondary school leaders, 313 primary schools and ran 12 focus groups; the reported effects are concentrated in classroom atmosphere rather than wellbeing: 75% of secondary schools said concentration improved, 59% said the social environment improved, and 28% said results improved [17]. In the full report, a small majority of schools — "58,7%" — reported a positive or very positive effect on pupil wellbeing and school or classroom climate, and only "27,7%" on learning performance, against 68.6% who had expected a learning effect at baseline [14]. Those are school leaders' perceptions and the study has no counterfactual.

The Dutch EPoSS study does have a comparison, between partial and full bans: 1,398 students in 24 secondary schools, surveyed in 2024–25. Its finding is the most troubling in the literature for the wellbeing case: "No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [12]. Both are cross-sectional comparisons, and connectedness and belonging are exactly the mediators that the developmental literature says protect adolescent mental health. A full-grounds ban, the strictest kind, was associated with *worse* relational outcomes, not better.

**United States: two national studies, both null, both underpowered.** Saffer's study is the first US causal estimate of state bans on youth mental health. It uses the National Survey of Children's Health for 2016–2024 — over 167,000 interviews with children aged 11–17 — and a synthetic difference-in-differences design across states, exploiting Florida's 2023 ban plus two states that banned in 2024 [27]. The verdict: "Overall, these preliminary results provide no evidence that the school smartphone ban policy reduces screentime nor improves the psychological wellbeing of students" [27]. Four of the five wellbeing outcomes with valid parallel trends had negative point estimates, and the bullied measure pointed toward less bullying in Florida's second year, though not significantly. The author is unusually candid about the limits: "Because the estimated 95% confidence intervals for the ban effects encompass the MDE and zero, the study lacks the statistical power to distinguish between a null effect and a small significant effect" [27]. He also offers three reasons the effect could genuinely be zero, the first being that students offset school-day reductions with evening and weekend use [27].

The Yondr pouch study gives a different and more interesting picture of dynamics. Average test scores were flat, but subjective well-being was not: "We also find suggestive evidence of a dynamic response in student-reported subjective well-being: it declines in the year of adoption and then rebounds, becoming positive by the second post-adoption year. The decline is roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations, followed by an increase of 0.16 standard deviations" [19]. If that pattern is real, it means short-run evaluations of wellbeing will systematically find harm and long-run evaluations may find benefit, and any study that measures one year post-adoption will mislead in one direction or the other. The authors themselves call the evidence suggestive.

**India (tertiary): no wellbeing change, mild fear of missing out.** The Odisha cluster-randomised trial, the only randomised test of in-class phone removal, found "Despite a mild rise in reported fear of missing out, there were no significant changes in overall student well-being, academic motivation, digital usage, or experiences of online harassment" [21]. It is a university sample, so it speaks to young adults rather than adolescents, but it is the one design that removes selection entirely, and on wellbeing it found nothing.

**Australia: nothing detectable.** The South Australian preregistered study found no condition-by-time interaction for wellbeing or belonging and concluded that it "did not detect evidence of the desired, or any undesired, effects of the phone ban over a short period of time" [3].

**Two counter-findings from the earlier literature.** The scoping review records two quasi-experimental studies with null or negative wellbeing results: Guldvik and Kvinnsland, using Norwegian register and survey data, "found a trend for mobile phone bans to negatively impact student wellbeing outcomes", while Abrahamsson found social wellbeing stable [26]. The same review notes qualitative reports of students feeling anxious without phone access and of distress after heavy reliance on devices during the pandemic [26]. These are weak designs, but they are a reminder that the direction of the effect is not guaranteed.

**What the mental health evidence can and cannot support.** What it can support: a school-hours ban does not measurably improve adolescent mental health in the short run in England, the Netherlands, South Australia or the United States, and it does not reduce total screen time. What it cannot rule out: small effects, effects that take more than two years to appear, and effects concentrated in girls, which is where the one strong positive result sits. What nobody has yet shown: that a ban reduces diagnosed anxiety, depression or self-harm, in any jurisdiction, at any follow-up length.

### 6. How strong is the evidence? Study designs, the systematic reviews, the disagreement among researchers, and what would settle it


**The design hierarchy, and where each study sits.** Nothing in this literature is a randomised trial of a school ban. The scoping review that searched 1,317 records and screened 73 full texts found "an absence of randomized controlled trials with evidence resting on a small number of studies with different designs, samples, operational definitions of mobile phone bans (i.e. partial, or complete bans) and outcome measures, making reconciliation of findings challenging" [24]. Its final sample was 22 studies, 12 of them unpublished, across 12 countries, and "We did not find research on mobile phone bans from the Oceania region" [26] — which is to say that when the review was searched in 2021 and updated in May 2023, the Australian state bans had not produced a single peer-reviewed evaluation.

Ranked by what they can support:

*Cluster-randomised trials of in-class phone removal.* One exists, in higher education: 16,955 students across 10 institutions in Odisha, randomised at the department-semester level, with an in-class deposit requirement [21]. It is the only design here that removes selection, and it is not about schools. Its GPA effect is 0.086 SD, concentrated among lower performers.

*Staggered difference-in-differences with administrative outcomes and high power.* The Yondr pouch study is the best of these: 4,608 adopting schools from company records, GPS pings covering 40,542 schools, a teacher survey of about 108,000 respondents, state test scores and Panorama surveys, pre-registered [19]. Its null on test scores is precise enough to rule out gains above 0.007 SD. Its main weakness is that Yondr adoption is not random — schools that buy pouches are plausibly more committed to the problem — but that bias runs toward finding an effect, not against it, which makes the null more informative.

*Exposure-design difference-in-differences within a treated jurisdiction.* Florida is the model: phone-location data to establish dose, student-level records, three test administrations a year, event studies showing no pre-trends [18]. Its weakness is acknowledged: with everyone treated, the comparison is between high- and low-dose schools, and the authors say the design "likely understates the positive effects of the ban on students" [18]. High- and low-phone-activity schools also differ at baseline, with the high-activity schools starting from lower mean scores, so the design leans on parallel trends in a sample that is not balanced.

*Event studies on staggered school-level adoption.* Abrahamsson's Norway and Kessel's Sweden are both of this type, and both rest on the assumption that adoption timing is unrelated to other determinants of outcomes. Kessel's case is unusually clean because adoption spread as a "bandwagon" — Swedish schools copying neighbours after 2015 — which is close to exogenous [27]. Abrahamsson's case is similar in structure but the adoption process is less well documented in the published version.

*Synthetic control on regional aggregates.* Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Spain study has one treated unit with complete pre-treatment data and 15 potential donors. The estimates are large (10.7 and 12.7 PISA points) and the placebo tests are reported as supportive, but aggregate designs of this kind are sensitive to which regions end up in the synthetic counterfactual and cannot separate a phone ban from anything else the region did.

*Cross-sectional comparisons of schools with different policies.* SMART Schools (30 English schools) and the Dutch EPoSS study (24 schools) are the two largest. Both are confounded by school choice: schools that ban phones differ from schools that do not in ethos, intake and leadership, and no covariate set fixes that.

*Perception surveys commissioned by the governments that introduced the policy.* The NSW principal survey (95% support, 81% saying learning improved) [16] and the Dutch Kohnstamm/Oberon monitoring (75% seeing better concentration) [14] are the evidence most often quoted in policy announcements, and the weakest. They measure satisfaction and institutional commitment, not outcomes, and they are collected by the implementing body. Neil Selwyn of Monash makes the point bluntly about the Australian case: the bans were not set up "with the intention of properly testing their effectiveness", and the research is "inconclusive, and … not particularly rigorous" [11].

**Where the reviews land.** Campbell and colleagues concluded that "Our consolidated findings showed little to no conclusive evidence that ‘one-size-fits-all’ mobile phone bans in schools resulted in improved academic outcomes, mental health and wellbeing and reduced cyberbullying" [26]. Their tallies are worth recording because they show how evenly the literature splits: on academic outcomes, 7 studies, 4 finding gains (Abrahamsson; Béland and Murphy; Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella; Melattinkara) and 3 finding none (Guldvik and Kvinnsland; Kessel et al.; Smith et al.) [26]; on mental health, 6 studies, none providing credible support and two quasi-experiments showing no benefit or a negative trend [26]; on bullying, 5 studies in favour and 2 cross-sectional studies finding more online victimisation in schools with restrictions [26].

Vanluydt and colleagues, writing in 2026, reach the same verdict with a blunter count: "While there are some studies that report an increase in academic performance after implementation of smartphone bans (e.g., Abrahamsson, 2024), there are almost an equal number of studies that report no differences in academic performance irrespective of bans (e.g., Kessel et al., 2020)" [12].

**The genuine disagreements, and who is more credible.**

*Béland–Murphy versus Kessel et al.* This is not sampling noise; the confidence intervals do not overlap. Kessel's study covers an entire national cohort with a longer window and a pre-registered replication logic; Béland–Murphy's covers four English cities with school-reported ban dates. On internal validity Kessel is stronger. But the settings differ in an important way: English bans arrived around 2006–2010, when phones were basic; Swedish bans arrived en masse after 2015, with smartphones. If the harm requires a smartphone in every pocket, the English study may have measured something else. The most defensible reading is that the effect is context-dependent and the Swedish null does not generalise to 2026 conditions — nor does the English positive.

*Abrahamsson versus Saffer and SMART Schools.* Abrahamsson finds mental health gains for girls; Saffer and SMART Schools find none. The differences are in outcome (health-care visits versus wellbeing scales), in setting (Norway's municipal variation versus state-level US bans with one to two post-years), and in power (Saffer concedes he cannot distinguish a null from a small effect [27]). Abrahamsson's result is more credible as a finding about girls' health-care use in Norway; it is not evidence that bans improve adolescent mental health generally.

*Florida versus the Yondr study.* Both are strong; they disagree in sign for middle schools. Florida finds gains concentrated in middle and high school; the pouch study finds high-school maths gains and middle-school losses. The likely reason is that the policies are different — Florida's district enforced a full-day ban with suspensions; pouches are bell-to-bell but the pouch study's middle schools saw smaller reductions in phone use. This is a real disagreement about implementation, not about method, and it points at dosage as the operative variable.

*Bans versus nothing.* Campbell and colleagues argue that "banning mobile phones and not banning other available internet- connected devices in schools is a simplistic solution which seems unlikely to have meaningful impact" [26]. The Dutch monitoring data give that argument empirical support: schools reported that inequality became more visible because students with their own laptops could still reach social media while others could not, and that enforcement added to teacher workload [14]. A phone ban can be a device-substitution policy rather than a screen-reduction policy.

**The one mechanism finding that most evaluations converge on.** SMART Schools found restrictive policies cut in-school phone and social media time substantially — 0.67 and 0.54 hours a day — with no difference in weekday or weekend totals [2]. Saffer's reading of that study, and his own null on screentime, support the same conclusion [27]. If total exposure is what matters for mental health, a school-hours ban is a small lever on a large quantity, and this single fact explains most of the null results better than any methodological complaint.

**What would settle it.** Five things, none of which exists:

1. *A cluster-randomised trial in schools.* Randomise schools within a district to immediate versus delayed adoption, measure outcomes for at least three years, and measure total screen time, not just in-school use. This is feasible — South Australia's staggered rollout was effectively half of it, and the researchers used the delay — but nobody has run it at scale.
2. *Total-exposure outcomes.* Every study should report weekday, evening and weekend use separately. Without that, the substitution question cannot be answered.
3. *Objective mental health endpoints.* Diagnoses, self-harm presentations, crisis contacts. Only Abrahamsson uses anything close (health-care utilisation), and only for girls.
4. *Longer follow-up.* The Yondr study's own wellbeing series suggests the sign flips between year one and year two [19]; anything shorter than three years is measuring transition costs.
5. *Independent evaluation of the perception surveys.* If governments are going to cite principal surveys, those surveys should be fielded and analysed by someone other than the department that made the policy.

Until then, the honest summary of the strength of evidence is this: on whether bans reduce in-school phone use, the evidence is strong. On whether that improves attention or learning, the evidence is weak, mixed and mostly null, with the best-powered study finding effects too small to matter. On bullying, there is modest positive evidence from two countries and null evidence from two others. On mental health, there is no credible evidence of benefit and some evidence of short-run harm to wellbeing and belonging. And on the question the policy is actually sold on — whether banning phones in schools improves adolescents' mental health — the most that can be said is that the studies capable of answering it have not found it, and that none of them was designed to be able to.
