q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad After Forty Years: What McLuhan's Laws of Media Claimed, What Scholars Made of It, and Whether Anyone Tested It
report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's four laws — every artefact enhances something, obsolesces something, retrieves something older, and reverses into something else when pushed to its limit — were presented in 1975 and again in *Laws of Media* (1988) as testable scientific laws, modelled explicitly on Popper's criterion of falsifiability. They were never tested. The one serious attempt to hold McLuhan to that claim, William Henry Venable's 1976 critique in *Technology and Culture*, produced a reply in which McLuhan abandoned logic for analogy and denied there was any "point of contact." Since 1988 the tetrad has been extended (Logan's laws of media environments and users; Levinson's tetrad wheels; Harman's object-oriented reading) and applied thousands of times, but the applications are instantiations rather than tests, and the only systematic review of them concludes that different researchers will never produce equal tetrads from the same object. The framework's own custodians now describe a method that begins with observation, admits any accurate answer, and makes no unique predictions — which is to say the McLuhan tradition has quietly answered "no" to the question of whether the laws are laws, while keeping the word.

## Key Findings

- **The four laws are clear; their status is not.** Enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, operating simultaneously, claimed to apply to every product of human effort — money, numbers, clothing, elevators, theories [2][1]. The McLuhans said Popper's falsifiability criterion "made it both possible and necessary" to formulate them [2].
- **McLuhan's own definition of "law" was confirmationist.** He called them laws because they represent "an ordering of thought and experience which has not yet been disproved" — survival, not testability [13].
- **The one test attempt produced a retreat to analogy.** Venable's 1976 critique argued the four terms presuppose a single target all inventors aimed at [13]; McLuhan replied that the tetrads are "ana_logical" with "no connections between any of them," and that there was "no point of contact whatever" with the critique [3]. By 1978 he described the method as analogical rather than logical, simultaneous rather than consecutive [3].
- **The 1988 "challenge" tests coverage, not truth.** Readers were asked to find a fifth question or a case where one of the four fails [8]; but Harman shows the tetrad rests on figure/ground, so four poles exhaust the possibilities and a fifth was never available [6]. Eric McLuhan's claim that the answers can be "checked" by anyone anywhere [1] is contradicted by the later family position that the method begins with observation rather than hypothesis [9].
- **The tetrad is unfalsifiable and coercive at once.** Tyler's double bind: too vague, because "a sufficiently creative mind" can fill any quadrant, and too rigid, because it "requires us to fill the gaps" [1]. The McLuhans themselves printed two incompatible tetrads for wine on one page [1].
- **The number four has no stated ground.** Fekete's objection, reported by Guardiani: the four is a metaphysically privileged structure asserted as "a figure minus a ground" [7]. Harman supplies the missing derivation — two crossed dualisms — and the test that goes with it [4].
- **Extensions are real but have not tested anything.** Iseri and Logan generate laws for environments and users [2]; Levinson's tetrad wheels make the four laws chain across media [6]; Harman extends the tetrad to all objects, not just artefacts [4]. Iseri and Logan concede the laws are "not strictly scientific" because they make no unique predictions [2].
- **The application literature is large, uncritical and non-reproducible.** Of 21 reviewed applications, only five discussed the tetrad as a method [5]; the questions themselves are worded differently from chapter to chapter in the primary texts [5]; and the reviewers conclude that analyses of the same object "will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [5].
- **No empirical test of the tetrad exists in the literatures searched** — English, Portuguese, Spanish, German, dissertations — despite targeted searching for coding schemes, inter-coder reliability, pre-registration or prediction scoring [5][15].
- **Adjacent McLuhan claims have been tested, with mixed results.** An eye-tracking study found a significant difference in fixation count but not fixation duration between image and text news [12]; a careful operationalisation of media temperature found a continuum, not McLuhan's binary, and its authors note the field has rarely made the concept measurable at all [11].
- **The tradition's own verdict is retrospective.** Levinson: tetradic analysis may be historically descriptive but not predictive [6]; Islas and Bernal: media ecology "does not anticipate the future" [10].

## Details

### 1. What the four laws actually say: the text of Laws of Media, McLuhan's 1975 declaration, and the claim to be a 'new science'

The laws of media exist in three printed forms before the book: an article in *Technology and Culture* in January 1975, an article in *et cetera* in 1977, and the posthumous *Laws of Media: The New Science* of 1988, assembled by Eric McLuhan from work the two had done together before Marshall's death at the end of 1980 [2]. What the four laws say is not in dispute; what they claim *to be* is.

Stated as four questions — the form McLuhan used in 1977 — they run: what does the artefact enhance; what does it obsolesce; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential [2]. Stated as four declarative laws, which is how Iseri and Logan render them: every artefact enhances some human function; in doing so it obsolesces some former medium used to achieve that function earlier; in achieving its function it retrieves some older form from the past; and when pushed far enough it reverses or flips into a complementary form [2].

The scope claimed is the whole of human making. McLuhan said the four laws could be applied to "the wheel, cable TV, the Xerox, elevators, railways, clothing, housing, money, numbers, and much more besides" [1]. Iseri and Logan put it flatly: the laws "apply with equal validity to all the artifacts of humankind, whether they are communication media, technological inventions, or scientific laws or principles" [2]. Money, on their reading, enhanced trade, obsolesced barter, retrieved the conspicuous consumption of hunting and gathering societies, and flipped into credit [2].

Three features of the framework matter for everything that follows. First, the four operate simultaneously, not in sequence; the numbering is conventional. Second, obsolescence is not extinction. Iseri and Logan insist on McLuhan's sense of the word — "obsolescence does not mean the end of something but the beginning of something new" — and give the horse and carriage surviving as a tourist attraction and the handwritten Torah surviving alongside print as the examples [2]. Third, the fourth law has a source McLuhan acknowledged: he quotes the *I Ching* to the effect that when any form reaches the end of its potential it reverses its characteristics [2].

The standard illustration is radio, in the version Paul Levinson supplied and Tom Tyler borrowed. Radio amplifies the human voice and gives "simultaneous access to the entire planet"; it obsolesces print to the extent that breaking news arrives by airwave rather than newspaper; it retrieves the town crier, the pre-literate public announcer; and pushed further it reverses into television, so the amplified town crier of the global village can be seen as well as heard [1].

The book's own most quoted self-description is not a definition of the laws but a claim about their reach: the questions, Eric McLuhan wrote, "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1]. That sentence is where the argument starts, because "checked" is doing enormous work in it, and the McLuhans did not supply the procedure by which the checking would be done. The nearest thing to a statement of the epistemological ambition is the line Logan quotes from page 93 of the book, that Popper's criterion — a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification — "made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media" [2]. "Necessary" is the tell. The laws were formulated to satisfy a criterion, not derived from data that met it.

### 2. The status-of-the-claim problem at the time: Popper, the 1976 Venable exchange, and McLuhan's retreat to analogy

The claim that the laws are science was made at the outset, in public, and in a form that invited refutation. In the January 1975 *Technology and Culture* article McLuhan wrote that he had been "experimenting" with a series of laws and offered them to historians, philosophers, economists, engineers and sociologists who, he hoped, might enjoy and profit from attempting to disprove them [13]. His stated rationale for the word "law" is where the trouble starts: he called them laws "because they represent, as do scientific ‘laws’, an ordering of thought and experience which has not yet been disproved" [13]. That is not Popper's criterion. Popper's criterion asks whether a statement *could* be refuted; McLuhan's sentence describes a statement that *has not yet been* refuted, which is the logic of survival, not of testability. The two are routinely conflated in the secondary literature and in McLuhan's own later glosses.

The 1988 book made the stronger claim. Iseri and Logan quote the McLuhans' own words on page 93 — Popper's "statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media" [2]. Eric McLuhan's preface supplied the boast that anyone could check the answers about any artefact [1], and the book's introduction issued a direct challenge to the reader: find a fifth question that applies to all media, or find a single instance in which one of the four is absent or irrelevant, because "Your answer is of the first importance as it determines the kind of our science" [8]. By Eric's account in the preface, Marshall spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law, if there were one, and trying at the same time to find a single case in which one of the first four fails [8]. This is the closest the framework ever came to a specified test, and it is worth being precise about what kind of test it is. It is a test of *coverage*, not of *truth*. A schema that can absorb any artefact without remainder passes it by construction, and as Tyler points out, the publisher's own description of the book — that anything lacking answers to the four questions is not a product of human creation — makes the tetrad definitionally unfalsifiable for anything the McLuhans would count as an artefact [1].

**The Venable exchange.** William Henry Venable, a Pittsburgh engineer and lawyer, took up the invitation. His "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" appeared in *Technology and Culture* 17:2 (April 1976), pages 256–262, and McLuhan's reply, "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws," on page 263 of the same issue [3][13]. Venable read the four laws through C. S. Peirce's logic of representation, in which a sign stands for its object not in all respects but in reference to its ground [13][3]. His objection was that the four predicates presuppose a single target that all technologists have always been aiming at: past and present inventors shooting at the same mark, with the new shot either closer (enhancement), or the old bow abandoned (obsolescence), or an old design recovered (retrieval), or a shot known to have gone the other way (reversal). That, Venable said, is the error Derek de Solla Price warned of, "in which all that happens is seen by the historian as leading with a single arrow to the present" [13]. Notably, Venable did not dispute the fourfold typology. He disputed its status, treating the laws as a symbolic or legal ordering rather than a phenomenal one [13].

McLuhan's published reply is the most revealing document in the whole affair. He complained that Venable had tried to relate his tetrads, or laws, to logic — Peirce's logic — and answered that the whole point about the tetrads is that they are *ana*logical: "there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios" [3]. He added that Venable had not read him at all and that "there is simply no point of contact whatever" [3]. So when a critic took the testability claim seriously and examined the laws as propositions, McLuhan withdrew them from propositional space and relocated them to analogy. He did the same thing in 1978, describing the approach as "a right hemisphere study which is analogical rather than logical, simultaneous rather than consecutive" [3]. The "new science" of the book's subtitle is, on the author's own later account, not a logical or propositional science at all.

**Levinson's inside account.** Paul Levinson, who knew McLuhan and organised the 1978 Tetrad Conference at Fairleigh Dickinson with him, reports the joke that fixes the tone: McLuhan said that when he came across Popper's principle that a scientific hypothesis is one capable of falsification, "I decided to hypothesize the ‘Laws of the Media’" — by which, Levinson writes, McLuhan meant that "if the laws of the media are capable of falsification, they can’t do too much damage" [6]. That is a joke about the risk of being wrong, not a research programme. Levinson's own mature verdict is that tetradic analysis may be historically descriptive but not predictive, and so escapes what Popper called the poverty of historicism [6]. The Popper who is invoked to license the laws at the front of the book is the Popper whose strictures on prediction are invoked at the back to excuse them.

**What the framework was for.** Harman's reading of Eric McLuhan's preface is that the tetrads "were meant as nothing more than a revision of the earlier book, in the face of criticisms that Understanding Media was ‘unscientific’" [4]. That is the plainest available account of the motive, and it reframes the whole question. The laws were not generated by a research question about media and then tested; they were generated by a reputational problem — a demand from critics for scientific standing — and shaped to satisfy the appearance of the demand. The strongest single piece of evidence for this reading is the sequence: a claim of falsifiability in 1975, a retreat to analogy under pressure in 1976, a restatement as "the new science" in 1988 with a challenge that tests coverage rather than truth, and an insider's joke that falsifiability was a way of limiting the damage.

None of this settles whether the tetrad is *useful*. It settles that the claim to be a science was asserted, tested once on its own terms, and abandoned by its author in favour of analogy — and that the later literature inherited the assertion while quietly dropping the test.

### 3. Applications and extensions since 1988: Logan, Levinson, media ecology, Harman, and use in game studies, design and digital media

The literature since 1988 divides into four kinds of work: extensions that add laws or change the tetrad's shape, applications that run the four questions on a new medium, philosophical reconstructions, and a large popular and professional literature that uses the tetrad as a thinking tool. Harman's observation is the right starting point for judging the proportions: "Even McLuhan’s fans rarely devote much energy to the tetrad, despite his son’s gripping narrative of how the tetrad was meant to summarize his father’s work as a whole" [4]. The tetrad is cited far more than it is used, and used far more than it is examined.

**The extensions.** Robert Logan, McLuhan's collaborator in the 1970s, is the most persistent extender. With Zeynep Merve Iseri he published a paper in *Philosophies* in 2016 that takes the four laws and generates two further sets from them: Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU) [2]. The move is systematic rather than ad hoc. If the tetrad describes what an artefact does, then there is a parallel set of questions about what the artefact's *environment* does to it, and another about what happens to its *users*. Iseri and Logan also argue that tetrads chain, each cycle linked to the previous and the next, giving the sequence of media a spiral structure [2]. The most striking feature of that paper for anyone assessing the tetrad's scientific standing is its frank concession in the middle of an otherwise confident extension: "LOMs are not strictly scientific laws." A law of media, Iseri and Logan explain, makes no unique prediction about what will be retrieved from the past or what complementary form a medium will flip into; the tetrad is an exploratory tool or probe, and there is often more than one correct answer to its four questions [2]. The man who co-authored the framework's foundational work says plainly that it does not make unique predictions. That single sentence should settle most of the argument about whether the laws are laws.

The second major extension is Levinson's tetrad wheel, proposed at the 1978 Tetrad Conference and only fully written up by Lindia and Levinson in 2021. Levinson's insight was to notice that McLuhan's claim that tetrads are "double figure/grounds" leaves open which quadrant is figure and which is ground. His answer: enhancement and retrieval are figures, obsolescence and reversal are grounds, and the grounds split by time — obsolescence is a *pre-ground* (it existed before the figure), reversal a *post-ground* (it comes after). So the four map as "A) Intensification [enhancement] = Figure; B) Obsolescence = Pre-Ground; C) Retrieval = Pre-Figure; D) Reversal = Post-Ground" [6]. The payoff is a diagram in which rotating one tetrad by 90 degrees produces the next medium's tetrad, so a chain of tetrads becomes a spiral. Lindia and Levinson are explicit that this fixes a real defect: the tetrad tends to present a medium and its effects as isolated from the rest of technological history, rather than as already intertwined with it [6]. The wheel restores sequence. It is, in their words, a shift from metaphor to chiasmus — from a snapshot to a moving picture.

Third, attempts to find the fifth law. Frank Zingrone proposed a law of syncretism in 1991; Lindia and Levinson judge that it ends up redundant to enhancement, retrieval, or both of them [6]. Duncan Echelson, Gerry Fialka and Robert Logan proposed a counterfactual fifth question: what would *not* have happened if this artefact had never been invented [8]. Harman's argument explains why all such attempts fail structurally rather than by lack of imagination: because the tetrad is built on figure/ground, and the four poles exhaust the four possible figure/ground relationships, a fifth pole is not available within the scheme [6]. That is a serious point. It means the McLuhans' own challenge — find a fifth question — could not in principle be met, so the challenge tested nothing.

Fourth, Harman's own extension, which runs the other way. Where the McLuhans confined the laws to human artefacts, Harman insists the term media "is relevant not just to paper and electric technologies, but also to trees" — and to reptiles, gases and stones — since every object is a medium transmitting the energies and broadcasts of others [4]. He is not being whimsical. The claim follows from his object-oriented metaphysics, in which every object is a fourfold of real and sensual qualities and relations, and the tetrad becomes a description of how any object withdraws from and appears to others. This is the most ambitious extension of the tetrad in the literature and the least empirical: it turns the laws from a media theory into an ontology.

**The applications.** The dominant use is the case study: take a medium, fill four quadrants, publish. Tyler's digital-games tetrad is the most methodologically careful of these. It argues that games enhance diverse modes of play, obsolesce traditional television viewing, retrieve lost means of participation, and reverse into pervasive and persistent play [1]. What distinguishes it is that each quadrant is anchored in cited research and the weak quadrant is reported as weak: on whether games displace TV, Tyler assembles the evidence (Nick Yee's MMORPG survey showing 21 hours a week of play against 7.7 hours of television, with the two adding up to about the national average of 28 hours) and concludes that existing studies are collectively uncertain, then redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction [1].

Beyond games, the applications cluster in three areas. In media ecology proper, *Explorations in Media Ecology* has carried tetrads on high heels, on screens (including animal-made and natural screens, in a 2018 piece that explicitly extends the laws to non-human artefacts), on online design studio pedagogy, and on the comparison of the tetrad with Lévi-Strauss's canonical formula. In professional and management literature, Federman and de Kerckhove's *McLuhan for Managers* (2003) packaged figure/ground and the laws of media as business thinking tools. In software, Michael Bolton's "McLuhan for Testers" (2007) and its descendants apply the tetrad to generative AI, and a 2025 position paper uses it across the stages of the software-engineering research pipeline. Since 2023 there has been a wave of tetrads on large language models — one in the *Journal of Media Literacy* argues that LLMs enhance personalised learning, obsolesce traditional assessment, retrieve transmission-model pedagogy, and risk reversing into cognitive offloading and epistemic dependency [9]. The pattern across all of these is the same: the tetrad is offered as "a heuristic to probe (as opposed to diagnose)" [9], and the claim of testability is repeated without ever being operationalised. That 2025 paper still describes the four laws as "an analogical, holistic, and testable framework" [9], which is precisely the conflation Tyler identified seventeen years earlier.

**The pattern in the applications.** Lindia and Levinson, who are sympathetic, describe what happened with unusual candour. McLuhan's original appeal to scholars was to test the laws' validity historically and empirically, and in their account scholars have mostly followed that request, at the cost of never testing the epistemological and ontological insights the tetrads imply [6]. That formulation gives the applications more credit than the record supports. What most applications do is not test the laws but *instantiate* them: the analyst assumes the four questions are exhaustive, fills them, and reports the result as an insight. That is exactly the use McLuhan wanted and exactly the use that cannot fail. Islas and Bernal, writing in the media ecology tradition, state the consequence in a sentence that ought to be better known: the tradition "does not anticipate the future" [10]. The tetrad, on its defenders' own account, is a retrospective sense-making instrument.

### 4. The criticism: the Procrustean double bind, the metaphysics objection, and the charge of technological determinism

Three objections have shaped the reception, and they operate at different levels: the tetrad is too loose and too tight at once; the number four is asserted without justification; and the framework is either determinist or evasive about causation. The first is the most damaging and the best evidenced.

**The Procrustean double bind.** Tom Tyler's 2008 *Game Studies* article is the sharpest critique in the literature, and its originality is that it refuses the standard move of calling McLuhan vague. Vagueness would be one failure. Tyler shows there are two, in opposite directions, and that the tetrad suffers from both simultaneously. On one side: "Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into" [1]. On the other: "At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps" [1]. A schema that can absorb anything and also demands four entries is unfalsifiable in the first respect and coercive in the second: the analyst cannot report that a quadrant is empty, and cannot fail.

Tyler's decisive evidence is internal to the primary text. On a single page of *Laws of Media* (p. 206) the McLuhans give two different tetrads for wine. In the first, wine enhances grape juice, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, and reverses into cooking vinegar. In the second, it enhances food and the occasion, obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult. Tyler's inference is exact: "If the authors themselves seem unsure as to the consistency of the results of the tetrad’s application, it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”" [1]. This is not a critic scoring a point; it is the framework's own authors producing incompatible outputs from the same instrument on the same page.

Tyler's verdict is worth quoting in full because it is so often softened in citation: "The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses" [1]. The concession matters. Tyler's positive proposal is that the tetrad works as a heuristic device, "a set of questions," a probe, and that its real virtue is to redirect attention from content to the operation of the artefact itself. He then demonstrates the disciplined version: every quadrant grounded in cited research, contrary evidence reported where it exists, terms defined (obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction), scope narrowed deliberately, and each quadrant aimed at overturning a named misconception. His conclusion is a defence of the method on non-scientific grounds: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive" [1].

**The number four.** The second objection is philosophical and was raised in the first wave of reviews. John Fekete, reviewing the book in *Canadian Journal of Communication* in 1990, objected to what Francesco Guardiani summarises as the "groundlessness" of the number four, "fixed by the McLuhans as a metaphysically privileged explanatory structure-in effect, as a figure minus a ground-a flaw and contradiction in their argument" [7]. That is a precise charge: McLuhan's whole method consists in showing that every figure rests on a ground, yet the tetrad itself is a figure presented without a ground. Why four? The answer in the book is inductive — twelve years of investigation found no fifth — which is a claim about the investigators' experience, not about the structure of artefacts. Harman's later reconstruction supplies the missing ground by deriving the four from the crossing of two dualisms (figure/ground and the withdrawal/appearance of objects), and he makes the requirement explicit: "The only means of obtaining a rigorous quadruple structure is to cross-breed two dualisms, yielding a world split into four distinct zones" [4]. He also names the danger: even frivolous fourfolds can be generated — his joke example being day/night crossed with eating/drinking — so any fourfold must ensure that its underlying dualisms are profound enough [4]. Whether the tetrad passes that test is a judgement, not a measurement.

Guardiani's survey of roughly thirty reviews of the book found something that bears on the whole reception: most reviewers declined to run a tetrad themselves before judging it. He defines bad reviews as those by people who avoid engaging with the text even for a first reading, and insists that this "doit-yourself kit must be tested to get a sense of what it is all about" [7]. The hostile reviews were often hostile in advance. John Sturrock, in the *New York Times*, dismissed them as "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing" [7]. That sentence is a verdict without an argument, and it is representative. The result is a reception in which neither side did the work: critics dismissed the tetrad without applying it, and admirers applied it without testing it.

**Determinism.** The third objection is that the tetrad attributes effects to media as such, independent of who uses them, how, and in what social relations. Raymond Williams's critique of McLuhan is the classic statement of the position, and Daniel Chandler's summary gives the political stake: "if technology is a cause, we can at best modify or seek to control its effects" [14]. Chandler's own catalogue of determinist sins — reductionism, reification, the assumption of technological autonomy, the technological imperative — names McLuhan among the non-Marxist theorists who adopt the stance, and offers a reductio in McLuhan's own words, that "such inventions as the horse collar quickly led to the development of the modern world" [14].

The interesting thing is that the tetrad was, in part, designed to answer this. Harman's reading makes the anti-determinist case from inside the framework: enhancement, on his account, forecloses alternatives and then presents itself as inevitable, so "An ‘extension of man’ is never a laughing matter, since it silently murders other possible worlds" [4]. The tetrad's job is to make visible the worlds that were killed, which is why "it is ironic when Marshall McLuhan is accused of ‘technological determinism’, for such determinism is accounted for and criticized by the tetrad itself" [4]. There is something to this — retrieval and reversal are both ways of showing that the present arrangement was not the only possible one — but it is a defence of the framework's *intent*, not of its execution. In practice, as the applications in the previous section show, the four quadrants are almost always filled with effects attributed to the medium, with the social arrangements that shaped the medium left in the ground where McLuhan said they belonged. Scolari's critique identifies a related failure at the level of the individual law: pushed to its extreme on its own, reversal produces an out-of-control interpretive explosion, because "the other three laws cease to function as balancing rods in the theoretical reactor, preventing it from exploding" [8]. The tetrad's four parts are supposed to constrain each other. When one is used alone — as reversal is, constantly, in commentary on digital media — the constraint disappears and anything can be called a reversal.

Taken together the three objections converge on one diagnosis. The tetrad has no ground for its number, no rule for filling its quadrants, and no account of the causal mechanism connecting a medium to its effects. Those are the three things a scientific instrument would need. What it does have is a set of questions that reliably produce observations an analyst would not otherwise have made, which is a real and unusual virtue — and a different one.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? Coding schemes, inter-coder reliability, and the scattered evidence for individual laws

The short answer is no. In everything located for this report there is no study that tests the tetrad as a whole — no pre-specified predictions, no independent coding, no comparison against rival accounts, no falsification attempt of the kind McLuhan invited in 1975. What exists instead is four things: a systematic review that documents why the tetrad resists replication, an insider tradition that denies the hypothesis-test structure, one internal-consistency check that has been proposed but not run at scale, and a handful of studies testing *adjacent* McLuhan claims (hot versus cool media, media displacement) rather than the four laws themselves.

**The systematic review.** The single most useful empirical document on the tetrad's use is Dall'Agnese, Canavilhas and Barichello's systematic review of tetrad applications in communication research in Brazil and Portugal, published in *Matrizes* in 2020 [5]. It followed a pre-registered protocol: defined research questions, inclusion and exclusion criteria, specified databases and repositories, Portuguese-language works only, 2009–2019, and — importantly — it excluded works that did not present an actual application of the tetrad, so the corpus is applications rather than commentary. The final sample was 21 works [5].

Three findings matter. First, the objects: social networks, and specifically Facebook, were the most frequent theme, followed by mobile devices and interfaces, cinema, internet memes and educational platforms [5]. This is a literature of case studies on whatever medium was current. Second, the methodological silence: "The presence of reflection on tetrad as a methodological tool in commu- nication research, or even notes about the potentialities and limits based on applications, was verified in only five of the 21 studies" [5]. Sixteen of 21 applications never discussed the instrument they were using. Third, and most damaging, the review's own conclusion: "even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads" [5]. The authors' explanation is that the researcher's theoretical background, combined with individual perception, determines what is seen and asked of the object. That is a precise statement of non-reproducibility, and it comes from sympathetic reviewers, not critics.

Two further findings from the same review show the problem is deeper than analyst variance. The primary texts themselves do not fix the instrument: "The questions used as basis for laws of the media, for example, despite maintaining the main ideas, are elaborated in different ways throughout the chapters of the two publications" [5]. If the wording of the four questions shifts from chapter to chapter in *Laws of Media* and *The Global Village*, there is no canonical formulation to code against. And the translation record shows how far interpretation is unconstrained: in the 21 Portuguese-language studies the reviewers found twelve different verbs rendering the first law's "enhances" — accentuates, amplifies, perfects, increases, extends, increments, intensifies, improves, potentiates, highlights, and more [5]. The reviewers also found at least one application that misunderstood the simultaneity of the laws, looking for separate examples for each face of the tetrad rather than analysing one object across four dimensions [5].

**Why it resists testing by design.** The framework's custodians have, in recent years, stated explicitly that the tetrad is not a hypothesis-test instrument. Eric McLuhan's instruction, quoted by the reviewers, is that there is no single correct answer to any of the four questions: "all accurate answers are correct answers. When you have a clear answer to any of the aspects, ask ‘what else?’" [5]. A method that instructs the analyst to keep generating further correct answers has no stopping rule, and therefore no point at which a prediction could fail. Andrew McLuhan, director of the McLuhan Institute, makes the contrast with science explicit: "Where the so-called ‘scientific method’ begins with hypothesis, a conclusion then proved or disproved, McLuhan’s method begins with observation" [9]. That is a coherent position, and it is a flat contradiction of the 1988 claim that the answers can be "checked" by anyone anywhere. Both cannot be true. The most defensible reading is that the later McLuhans chose the probe over the science, and the earlier claims were not withdrawn.

**The one proposed check.** Lindia and Levinson, reviving Levinson's 1978 tetrad wheels, sketch what a test would look like inside the framework. Rotate a tetrad one position and see whether the resulting analysis of the *next* medium is consistent with what is independently known about it. If it is not, then either the original tetrad or the new one is falsified — "we must conclude that either (1) we have misunderstood theeffects of McLuhan tetrads (i.e. tetrad wheel analysis falsifies tetrad analysis) or (2) we havemisunderstood the nature and effects of tetrad wheels (i.e. tetrad analysis falsifies tetrad wheelanalysis)" [6]. This is a genuine falsification proposal and it is the most rigorous thing in the literature. But it tests *internal coherence between two analyses*, not correspondence with the world, and as far as this search reached it has never been run as a systematic exercise with independent analysts. Levinson also supplies the reason the tetrad cannot predict, which undercuts the whole idea of testing its forward claims: novelty enters at reversal, the one quadrant that is not already present in the original tetrad, which makes artefacts "open, evolving systems" [6]. If the future content of the fourth quadrant is by definition new, no prediction about it can be scored.

**The adjacent empirical work.** Where McLuhan's medium claims have been operationalised, it is the hot/cool distinction rather than the tetrad that gets tested. The clearest experimental attempt located is Zhu, Kwon and Zhao's 2022 eye-tracking study: 22 subjects, a Tobii tracker, four stimuli edited into image-news and text-news versions, two parameters (fixation count and total fixation duration) analysed by area of interest [12]. The result was mixed and the authors report it as mixed — a statistically significant difference in fixation count between the two media, consistent with the hot/cool distinction, but no statistically supported difference in total fixation time [12]. Twenty-two subjects in one lab is thin evidence for a claim about media as such, and the study tests the temperature of a format, not the exhaustiveness of four laws.

The most careful recent operationalisation is Iskandar and colleagues' 2026 study of the Indonesian Parliament's Facebook, Twitter/X and YouTube accounts, which translates "media temperature" into four measurable dimensions — information richness, sensory intensity, audience participation and interaction affordances — and applies them to content from July 2020 [11]. Their own framing concedes the gap this report has been documenting: studies of McLuhan's hot–cool distinction "remain largely conceptual and have rarely translated media temperature into observable analytical dimensions suitable for empirical investigation" [11]. Their finding is that temperature behaves as a continuum rather than a binary, with Facebook coolest, YouTube hottest and Twitter/X hybrid. The study is qualitative-dominant, its engagement metrics are not comparable across platforms, and its authors say plainly that visible engagement is not evidence of how audiences interpret content [11]. It is a real attempt at measurement, and it measures a different thing from the tetrad.

Tyler's games article is the best example of a tetrad application that engages evidence honestly. On the obsolescence quadrant he assembles the displacement data — Nick Yee's MMORPG survey, in which players averaged 21.0 hours a week of play and 7.7 hours of television, the two summing to roughly the 28-hour national television average — and then declines to treat it as decisive, concluding that existing studies are collectively uncertain and redefining obsolescence as remediation instead [1]. That is what disciplined use looks like. It is also, note, an application using evidence, not a test of the tetrad.

**What a test would require, and what is missing.** To test the tetrad as a whole one would need: the four quadrants specified in advance for a named artefact by analysts blind to each other; an agreed coding rule for what counts as an instance of each; inter-coder agreement reported; rival accounts (a social-shaping explanation, a uses-and-gratifications explanation) scored against the same evidence; and a dated prediction that could fail. None of the 21 reviewed applications does this, and repeated searches for coding schemes, inter-coder reliability figures, or pre-registered tetrad studies returned nothing. That is a negative result from a bounded search, and it should be reported as such: absence of evidence here is reasonably strong evidence of absence, given how thoroughly the applied literature has been mapped in at least one language community, but a test could exist in a literature this search did not reach — Chinese, German or Spanish-language scholarship, or unpublished theses.

**Where I looked, and what was not there.** Because a negative result is only worth reporting if the search was wide, the following were checked and produced no test of the tetrad. Spanish-language scholarship: the closest thing found is Gutiérrez-Cortés, Islas-Carmona and Arribas-Urrutia's 2019 *Palabra Clave* article, which imports exaptation from evolutionary biology expressly so that it can "evaluar la pertinencia de las leyes de los medios" — assess the pertinence of the laws — and does so by theoretical review, with no data, no coding and no cases scored against predictions [15]. Portuguese: the 21-work systematic review, which maps applications and finds them non-reproducible [5]. German: the media-science literature treats McLuhan's claims as a historiographical problem rather than a testable hypothesis, with the standard verdict being that his theses are neither empirically nor otherwise scientifically verifiable — a judgement offered without an attempted test. Doctoral work: Wachs's Duquesne dissertation, *The Triptych Tetrad*, is a reconstruction of McLuhan's neo-medieval communication theory, not an empirical study. The primary documents of the dispute — Venable's 1976 critique and McLuhan's reply — are behind Project MUSE's verification wall, and the *Lost Tetrads* collection is on JSTOR without accessible text; both were used here through the secondary sources that quote them, which is a real limitation on the section 2 account of Venable's argument. Repeated searches combining tetrad terms with coding, inter-coder reliability, pre-registration, prediction and hypothesis testing returned nothing.

The honest summary is that the tetrad's empirical status is not tested-and-failed but never tested, and progressively redefined so that testing is no longer required. The claim of 1975 and 1988 was that the answers could be checked. Forty years later the framework's own defenders describe a method that begins with observation, admits any accurate answer, and makes no unique predictions. On the question of whether the laws of media are laws, the McLuhan tradition has, in effect, answered no — while continuing to use the word.


## Beyond this question

For anyone using the tetrad as a working instrument rather than a historical curiosity, the findings sort into rules that can be applied tomorrow.

**Report a blank quadrant.** Tyler's double bind is a design flaw that can be fixed at the point of use: if a quadrant has no evidence, say so. A tetrad with one evidenced quadrant and three blanks is worth more than four fluent ones, and the instruction to "ask what else?" [5] should be read as permission to keep looking, not as an obligation to fill the box.

**Produce rival tetrads, not one.** The wine page is the most instructive document in the literature because it shows the instrument's authors generating two incompatible readings and printing both [1]. Treat that as the format rather than the embarrassment: two tetrads for one artefact, with the evidence that separates them.

**State the dualisms.** Harman's requirement — a rigorous fourfold comes from crossing two dualisms, and frivolous fourfolds are easy to generate [4] — is a cheap filter. If the analyst cannot name the two distinctions that generated the four boxes, the analysis is decoration.

**Never use reversal as prediction.** Levinson's argument that novelty enters at the fourth quadrant [6], and the tradition's own conclusion that tetradic analysis is descriptive rather than predictive [6][10], together mean that any "X will reverse into Y" claim is a forecast wearing a law's clothing. Put it in a dated ledger where it can be scored.

**Cite the quadrant.** The single behavioural difference between an instantiation and a test is that each quadrant carries a source. Tyler's games tetrad is the model: every quadrant anchored, contrary evidence reported, obsolescence redefined when the data did not support displacement [1].

## Open questions

**Whether a test is possible at all.** Nobody has designed one, and the framework as its custodians now describe it may not admit one: a method that begins with observation [9], accepts any accurate answer [5] and makes no unique predictions [2] has no failing observation. The open question is whether that is a defect to be repaired or the honest description of what the tetrad always was.

**Whether the historical record supports the laws.** The McLuhans asked readers to find a case where one of the four fails [8], and nobody has systematically looked. A corpus of, say, a hundred documented media transitions, coded blind by independent analysts for enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal, would answer the coverage question the McLuhans actually posed. It has not been done. The nearest existing thing is a review that maps applications and finds them mutually inconsistent [5].

**Whether inter-coder agreement is achievable.** No study reports a reliability statistic for tetrad coding. Since the primary texts word the four questions differently from chapter to chapter [5], and since 21 Portuguese-language studies used twelve different verbs for "enhances" [5], the instrument may be too underspecified for agreement to be measurable. That is an empirical question nobody has asked.

**Whether the tetrad beats alternatives.** No study compares a tetrad analysis of an artefact against a social-shaping account, a uses-and-gratifications account, or an affordance account on the same evidence. Until one does, the claim that the tetrad produces insight the alternatives miss rests on the persuasiveness of individual essays.

**What the adjacent evidence actually shows.** The hot/cool distinction has been operationalised at least twice, with a mixed experimental result on 22 subjects [12] and a continuum finding in one parliament's social media [11]. Neither tests the tetrad, and both are single-site studies. Whether McLuhan's medium claims hold up under replication is still unknown.

**Coverage limits of this report.** Three gaps are worth naming. Venable's 1976 critique and McLuhan's reply are behind Project MUSE's verification wall; the account here rests on the secondary sources that quote and summarise them [3][13], which is adequate for the shape of the argument but not for its fine detail. The *Lost Tetrads* collection, which contains the unpublished tetrad lists, was not accessible. And the search for empirical tests, while it covered English, Portuguese, Spanish and German material plus dissertations, would not reach scholarship in Chinese, Japanese, Italian or unpublished conference work; a test could exist there. Given how thoroughly one language community's applications have been mapped [5], the absence is more likely real than an artefact of searching, but it is an absence of evidence.

q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: Rent-setting software in Canada: what RealPage and Yardi sold, who used it, and what remains unproven about rents
report.body: Rent-setting software pools landlords' private leasing data and returns a recommended rent for each unit, each day: competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations. Canada's competition regulator opened an inquiry into whether that happened here in January 2025 and closed it in November 2025 without answering the question a tenant would ask, which is whether the software raised what they paid. The established facts are narrower. Large Canadian landlords used the software from at least 2017. It is built to lift revenue per unit rather than to fill buildings. And the question of what it did to Canadian rents was never put to a test. ## The product returns a daily rent, and it is built to lift revenue per unit The recommendation is hard to ignore. Two features see to that: an "auto-accept" function and human "pricing advisors" raise compliance. In the American litigation that produced the fullest public account of how the products behave, court documents cited landlords accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time. The intent inside the largest vendor was not disguised. RealPage described its goal as driving every possible opportunity to increase price, and its own summary of the effect was a rising tide raises all ships. A Canadian landlord's executive described the same logic from the client side, optimizing net operating income rather than occupancy. That last phrase is the whole mechanism in miniature. Software aimed at occupancy cuts the rent when a unit sits empty. Software aimed at revenue per unit has a different answer to the same empty unit, because a lower rent on one lease sets the comparable for the next one. The two goals pull apart exactly when a building is hardest to fill, which is when a tenant has the most room to negotiate. The two vendors in the Canadian market sell differently designed products, and the difference matters to the legal question. ## What Canadian landlords used, sorted by how well it is documented The trail starts with the vendor's own announcement. a June 2017 RealPage press release naming GWLRA subsidiary Vertica Resident Services as a YieldStar client reporting "2%–4% revenue outperformance" is the earliest hard documentary evidence of the software in Canada, and a reminder that vendors later delete such testimonials. Below that, the confirmations come from the companies themselves. GWLRA confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar, then "terminated" it after an internal review (Oct 2024). Tricon Residential told CBC it stopped using YieldStar in summer 2024 and that it "never impacted rents." Woodbourne Capital confirmed its use publicly, through a vice-president quoted in academic research. For QuadReal, the proof is a job advertisement: a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys "(updating YieldStar)," documented in peer-reviewed research. A hiring notice is a thin document. It is also the kind that survives a vendor's cleanup, which is why it carries weight. Then comes the pleading. The November 26, 2024 statement of claim named RealPage and 14 landlord/manager groups, among them QuadReal, Westcorp, FirstService, GWLRA, CAPREIT, Dream Unlimited, Woodbourne, RioCan, Choice Properties and Tricon. Those are allegations, and the research on which this account rests is explicit that naming defendants reflects pleadings, not proven conduct. The weakest tier is a press report. The Breach described Starlight Investments, citing an unnamed market-research database, as one of at least 13 companies in Canada with more than $5 billion in revenue that have used the YieldStar software. The database was not named, and the claim has not been confirmed by the company. Several named landlords denied it. CAPREIT said We have not, are not, and will never use YieldStar. Dream Unlimited and Choice Properties said a third-party property manager had subscribed and that they told it to stop. Associated Property Management and M&R also denied use. ## The only figure about Canadian revenue comes from the company selling the software Strip out the allegations and the denials and one number remains attached to a Canadian landlord's results: the 2%–4% revenue outperformance in the 2017 press release. It was published to sell software, it measures revenue against a counterfactual the vendor chose, and it is not a rent. It is also the only quantified claim in the Canadian material about what the product did for a landlord. The other number in the file is RealPage's own estimate of its reach. A spokesperson told the *Financial Post* that the company's Canadian presence is fairly low at a one per cent penetration rate, and that its software is purposely built to be legally compliant. The research treats that figure for what it is: The 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving. The Bureau's finding is consistent with it, but the Bureau did not publish a share of its own. > **Objection: a vendor's marketing number and a landlord's denial cancel out, leaving nothing to argue about** > > They leave nothing measured, which is the point of this section rather than an answer to it. A marketing claim about revenue and a denial about rents are both statements by interested parties, and neither is a measurement of what a tenant paid. What is left is the design of the product, the acceptance rate the American court documents record, and the fact that the Canadian question was never tested. ## What is known about rents comes from the United States and a German petrol market The strongest evidence about effect sits outside Canada, and it is worth separating by what it actually shows. In the United States, RealPage's clients comprised nearly 90% of the market for multifamily rental housing units of 50 units or more. That concentration is what made an antitrust case possible, and the case produced allegations with numbers in them: prosecutors allege one landlord raised rents more than 25% within 11 months of adopting the software. An allegation in a complaint is a claim to be tested, not a finding. The settlement that ended the government's case did not test it. RealPage settled in November 2025 with no fine and no admission of wrongdoing, accepting a seven-year term and a monitor, and terms that bars use of competitors' nonpublic data, restricts geographic granularity below the state level, prohibits identical recommendations to competitors in the same market. The antitrust chief's summary was a conclusion about conduct rather than a measurement of rent: RealPage was replacing competition with coordination, and renters paid the price. Private litigation settled too, with Private multidistrict-litigation settlements total nearly US$360 million across two batches. Legislatures moved faster than courts. nine US municipalities plus two states (California, New York) have banned or restricted algorithmic rent-setting. No Canadian province or municipality has enacted or formally tabled an algorithmic-rent ban. The one clean measurement of a shared pricing algorithm in a real market is not about housing at all. A study of German petrol stations found adoption increases margins by 9%, but only in non-monopoly markets, with the effect appearing about a year after market-wide adoption, suggesting that algorithms in this market learn tacitly-collusive strategies. That timing is the interesting part: a rise that arrives a year late looks like learning rather than like a deal. How far any of this generalises is disputed. In simulation, pricing algorithms learn to charge above competitive prices without communicating at all, and later work found the result flips with the learning protocol the experiment uses. The research's instruction on the point is to present it as contested rather than proven, and the caution applies with more force to rents, where the only Canadian numbers are a vendor's. ## The Bureau closed the file on adoption, and said so in its own words The Competition Bureau opened its file in August 2024, launched a formal civil inquiry in January 2025, ran a consultation that drew 103 responses, and discontinued the inquiry into RealPage Canada and Yardi Canada on November 10, 2025. It examined three kinds of conduct: the comingling of nonpublic, competitively sensitive competitor data to generate recommendations; special rules that artificially inflate recommendations (e.g., hard price floors, inventory-limiting features); and incentives for high compliance or barriers to rejecting recommendations. It assessed abuse of dominance and anticompetitive collaboration and found neither — explicitly because adoption "did not reach the anticompetitive thresholds" and had fallen since late 2024. Those thresholds are about market share, and the gap between them and the vendor's own figure is the reason the file closed. The Bureau did not walk away satisfied. It remains concerned and issued four diagnostic compliance questions, warning that even anonymized competitor data used in back-end processes can let software "act as a means for competitors to coordinate." That warning is the part worth keeping. It says the pooling does not have to be visible in the price to do its work. > **Objection: the regulator investigated and found nothing, so there is nothing here** > > The Bureau's own account is narrower than that. The Bureau's closure is a discretionary enforcement decision on present evidence, not a ruling that the software is lawful, and the research adds that the Bureau can reopen on new and compelling evidence. What ended the inquiry was share and a retreat: A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding — a bar neither vendor met given low Canadian uptake. A case that fails on share is not a case that fails on effect. ## Concentration is what makes the tool matter, and concentration has not retreated Adoption was low and is now lower. Ownership is neither. the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates putting financialized ownership higher. A tool that returns a daily rent for every unit in a portfolio is worth more to the firm that owns more units, and it does more to a submarket when several of its users sit in the same one. The incentive to use something like it does not depend on the vendor's name. Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize. Where a sitting tenant's rent is held below the market and a new tenant's is not, the money is in the turnover, and software that prices each new lease against the market is the obvious instrument for it. Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats. ## The law needs an agreement that a shared tool never asks for The Competition Act was written for people in a room. Sections 45 (criminal conspiracy) and 90.1 (civil agreements) both require an "agreement/arrangement." An intermediary that produces parallel prices without a provable meeting of minds falls into the tacit-collusion gap that the Bureau's own June 2025 discussion paper and consultation explicitly flagged. That gap is not a Canadian peculiarity, and it is not small. The Bureau's discussion paper counted over 60 companies offering algorithmic pricing services in Canada across sectors, and its January 2026 report on what it heard recorded the complaint in the stakeholders' own terms: tacit collusion through algorithms typically falls outside existing competition law because the law requires evidence of a 'meeting of the minds.' The amendments that took effect in June 2025 help at the margin without reaching the middle of the problem. They make abuse of dominance easier to establish, widen the civil provision to some agreements between non-competitors, repeal the efficiencies defence and open private access to the Tribunal with monetary awards, but none reach genuinely autonomous tacit coordination absent an agreement. The research's summary of the Canadian position is blunt: the law is built for human agreements, and the technology routes around it. The Bureau has not lost interest in the subject, only in these two vendors. The Kalibrate inquiry (retail-gasoline data services; opened July 2024, with a July 24, 2024 court order compelling documents) remains open. If a contested decision comes out of it, it will say something about algorithmic agreement that the closed rent file never had to. ## The class action ended before anyone was examined The private route closed on the same day the public one did, and more completely. The *Cynthia Black* action, filed in Toronto on November 26, 2024, covered anyone in Canada who leased a unit from a named defendant back to 2009, and it was discontinued by court order effective April 1, 2026, before any certification motion. What that costs is not only the claim. The Canadian discontinuance leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm constitutes an "agreement." It also leaves the questions that only discovery answers. The US cases produced internal documents, sworn testimony, and evidence of RealPage-hosted "user group" meetings where competing landlords discussed pricing, a "rim" connecting the spokes that the Canadian plaintiffs never reached discovery to develop. One consequence is practical and dated. Because the action was never certified, class members' individual limitation periods (suspended under s.28(1) of the Class Proceedings Act) resumed running on April 1, 2026. ## What remains unproven about Canadian rents The central question is simple to state and has no answer in the Canadian material: were rents higher than they would have been without the software? Nobody has measured it. The class action would have had to prove it and ended before it could try. The Bureau assessed conduct against share thresholds rather than estimating a price effect. The vendor's figure is a revenue claim about one client in 2017, and the one landlord that addressed rents directly denied an effect. Reading the answer off public listings is the obvious next idea, and the research that examined the option rejected it. Synchronized-pricing detection from listing data is statistically fragile. Parallel pricing is the expected output of competitive markets, rent-control caps, and shared public benchmarks (Rentals.ca, CMHC). Rent listings in one submarket can move together for reasons that have nothing to do with coordination, and separating them requires nonpublic data. The instruction that follows is At most, present price-dispersion visualizations as hypothesis-generating, never as proof. There is a live tension in the research on this point, and it is worth naming rather than smoothing over. One document concludes that with both accountability tracks closed, any new evidence would have to come from a detection instrument built on rental-listing data. The feasibility study says the same data cannot bear that weight, and that the usable evidence lies in documents instead: securities filings that name the software, job postings that instruct staff to update it, vendor case studies captured before they are deleted, and the pleadings and position statements that already exist. Three public events would reopen the question without any of that. A contested decision in the Kalibrate inquiry would clarify what an algorithmic agreement is. A province or municipality tabling a rent-setting disclosure rule or ban would create the record Canada lacks; none has. A private applicant testing the Tribunal access the June 2025 amendments created would put a vendor or a landlord in front of a decision-maker for the first time. ## The file closed on a retreat, and the rule is unchanged The software's retreat after late 2024 is the reason the enforcement question became historical, and it is not the reason the question was answered. The retreat removed the evidence, not the incentive. Vacancy decontrol still pays for turnover, ownership is still concentrated, and the vendor products that replaced YieldStar in the sales pitch are built on the same idea of a daily recommended rent. What the Canadian episode shows is a mismatch that survives every actor in it. Competition law asks who agreed. The tool never needs anyone to agree: it takes the data, returns a number, and lets a hundred landlords arrive at the same rent without a conversation. A tenant in a building owned by one of the large financial landlords cannot tell from the rent whether a rival's asking rents set it or a model trained on rivals' private data did, and no Canadian body has been asked to find out.
