q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's National Pharmacare Since 2024: Agreements, Coverage, Uptake, and What a Full Program Would Cost
report.body:
## TL;DR

Since the *Pharmacare Act* received royal assent on October 10, 2024, what has actually been delivered is a two-category, four-jurisdiction benefit, not a national drug plan. Only British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon signed agreements (all in February–March 2025), covering listed contraception and diabetes products at no cost at the pharmacy, and they went live on four different dates from April 2025 to April 2026. Utilization is measured only piecemeal — Manitoba reports over 55,000 people and over 200,000 prescriptions, PEI over 5,000 contraception users and over 20,000 diabetes beneficiaries, and BC and Yukon have published none — and no federal or CIHI count exists. The Parliamentary Budget Officer's costing of the *full* single-payer program is an incremental $11.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 in public-sector spending, alongside economy-wide drug-spending savings of $1.4–2.2 billion; other estimates range from the Hoskins council's $15.3 billion in 2027 to the Committee of Experts' $6–10 billion for an essential-medicines list, while critics argue the real cost could reach $32.7 billion if assumed price-negotiation savings fail.

## Key Findings

- The Pharmacare Act came into force October 10, 2024 as "the first phase of a national universal pharmacare program", with coverage delivered only through bilateral agreements, not by the Act itself [4].
- Four jurisdictions signed agreements — Manitoba (February 27, 2025), British Columbia (March 6, 2025), PEI (March 7, 2025) and Yukon (March 20, 2025) — and the other nine have none [1].
- The agreements fund universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage of listed contraception and diabetes products, plus diabetes devices and supplies, and BC also funds menopausal hormone therapy [24][5].
- Benefits went live April 15, 2025 in Manitoba, May 1, 2025 in PEI, March 1, 2026 in BC and April 15, 2026 in Yukon [13][17][12][16].
- The federal contribution is $88.1 million in 2025-26, rising to a projected $269.6 million by 2028-29; the agreements expire March 31, 2029 [23][24].
- The Spring 2026 Economic Update contains no funding for new deals, and the CCPA concludes the federal government appears poised to let the four agreements lapse [23].
- The PBO's full single-payer program would cost the public sector an incremental $11.2 billion in 2024-25 and $13.4 billion in 2027-28, while saving the economy $1.4–2.2 billion in drug spending [3].
- The PBO cannot isolate the federal share of that cost because no federal–provincial cost-sharing formula exists [3].
- The PBO's own first-phase (Bill C-64) costing is $1.9 billion over five years, about $400 million above the government's $1.5 billion budget [11][9].
- The 2019 Hoskins advisory council estimated a full program at $15.3 billion by 2027; the 2025 Committee of Experts estimated $6–10 billion for an essential-medicines list; the Fraser Institute relays a $32.7 billion scenario if price savings fail [21][22][10].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64) actually did and did not do

The *Pharmacare Act* (Bill C-64, *An Act respecting pharmacare*) was introduced in the House of Commons on February 29, 2024, and received Royal Assent on October 10, 2024, coming into force immediately [4]. The Health Canada news release announcing passage is explicit about what the statute is and is not: it is "the first phase of a national universal pharmacare program", not a fully implemented national drug plan. Its mechanism is bilateralism. The Minister of Health "will continue working with provinces and territories to reach bilateral agreements to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar access to a range of contraception and diabetes medications" [4]. In other words, the Act created a legal framework and a negotiating mandate; the actual coverage exists only where a province or territory has separately signed a funding agreement with Ottawa.

The government framed the first phase around two target populations: "up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada" gaining free access to contraception, and "the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes" gaining universal access to a suite of medications [4]. The stated rationale was an insurance gap documented by Statistics Canada: "one in five adults in Canada did not have the insurance they needed to cover their medication costs" in 2021 [4].

Beyond the bilateral coverage mechanism, the Act imposes a set of preparatory obligations. It requires Canada's Drug Agency to develop a list of essential drugs and related products to inform a national formulary, a national bulk purchasing strategy to help reduce drug prices, and a pan-Canadian strategy on the appropriate use of prescription medications [4]. It also required a committee of experts to be established within thirty days of royal assent to make recommendations on the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare [4]. The Act also establishes a fund for diabetes devices and supplies, to help people "manage and monitor their diabetes and administer their medication" [4].

Several things the Act does *not* do are equally important to the question of what has actually been delivered. It does not itself list or price a single drug; coverage depends on formularies attached to each bilateral agreement. It does not create a universal entitlement that applies across Canada on the date of royal assent; residents of provinces and territories without an agreement have no pharmacare coverage under the Act. It does not set out the full cost of a national program, nor does it settle the federal–provincial division of that cost. And although it contemplates a future national formulary, bulk purchasing and appropriate-use strategy, those are advisory and preparatory work products, not benefits at the pharmacy counter. The distinction between the framework (passed in 2024) and the benefits (delivered only through the agreements signed in 2025) frames everything that follows.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed agreements, and the status of the rest

As of Health Canada's pharmacare agreements page (last updated January 26, 2026), the federal government "has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [1]. Those four are the complete list. They are, in the order the page presents them and with the date of each signing news release:

- **British Columbia** — "Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with British Columbia to improve universal access to free medications (March 6, 2025)" [1].
- **Manitoba** — "Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Manitoba to improve affordable access to medications (February 27, 2025)" [1].
- **Prince Edward Island** — "Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Prince Edward Island to improve universal access to free medications (March 7, 2025)" [1].
- **Yukon** — "Government of Canada signs pharmacare agreement with Yukon to improve universal access to free medications (March 20, 2025)" [1].

Manitoba signed first, on February 27, 2025; the other three followed within the first three weeks of March 2025. Each agreement is titled "Universal Access to Contraception and Diabetes Medications and Increased Access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies" [1].

Nine jurisdictions have no agreement. Those are the other nine provinces and territories: Newfoundland and Labrador, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec, Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut. Health Canada's "what's covered" page states the rule plainly: "Only provinces or territories that have reached an agreement with the federal government are listed. If your province or territory isn't listed, contact your provincial or territorial health ministry for information about public prescription drug coverage in your area" [2]. The practical consequence is that pharmacare's first phase is a regional program covering roughly a fifth of Canada's population, concentrated in two small Atlantic and western jurisdictions, one mid-sized Prairie province, and one large province.

The status of the remaining nine has become a live political question rather than a settled one. CBC reported in July 2025 that Health Minister Marjorie Michel, asked why negotiations were not progressing, said Canada has "a new government" and is "in a new context," raising the question of whether Ottawa would abandon further deals; her office said the government would "protect" the four existing agreements with B.C., Manitoba, P.E.I. and Yukon. The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives, writing in May 2026, reports the federal contribution in the program's first year: "In 2025-26, the federal government contributed $88.1 million to support these provinces and one territory in the expansion of public coverage of diabetes medications and contraception for all residents. The federal pharmacare contribution is expected to increase to $269.6 million by 2028-29" [23]. The same analysis reads the Spring 2026 Economic Update as the pivot: with bilateral health funding dropping from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28, and concludes the federal government "appears poised to allow existing bilateral funding agreements to expire without renewal" [23]. A detailed explainer published by Refdesk.ca, citing CBC News, The Tyee, the CCPA and the Spring 2026 Economic Update, reports the same: no new agreements, and no funding to renew the existing four past their March 31, 2029 term. Refdesk quotes Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister saying "the door was closed on our province", and reports that PEI's health minister said Ottawa is cutting roughly $29 million in health-care funding to the province over three years [6]. This is a secondary account that assembles primary reporting; the underlying figures on funding levels should be read against the Economic Update's own fiscal tables, which I did not retrieve in full. What the official record itself establishes is narrower and unambiguous: four agreements exist, signed February–March 2025, and Health Canada's own pages list no others [1][2].

One further distinction matters for accuracy. The pharmacare agreements are separate from the *National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases*, under which Ottawa reached bilateral agreements with all 13 provinces and territories. Health Canada's own news release for the Pharmacare Act lists the rare-disease strategy as a distinct program with its own funding model [4]. A reader encountering a report that all 13 provinces and territories have signed a drug agreement is looking at rare-disease funding, not pharmacare; only four jurisdictions have a pharmacare agreement.

### 3. What is covered under the agreements, and for whom

Pharmacare's first phase covers exactly two therapeutic categories — contraception and diabetes — and only the specific products listed in each agreement's annex, not a general drug benefit. Health Canada's "what's covered" page is precise: "Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee." Delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees are excluded [3]. Within a signatory jurisdiction, listed products "will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter", and patients "won't need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans" for covered products [1]. Coverage is first-dollar and single-payer for the listed items: there is no deductible and no private-insurance coordination step.

On the diabetes side, Health Canada describes "generally free access" in agreement jurisdictions to medications such as metformin, insulin, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors, and states illustrative annual costs that coverage removes: metformin about $100 per year, insulin between $900 and $1,700 per year, and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors from $100 to over $1,000 per year [5]. The agreements also fund devices and supplies — insulin pumps and syringes for administration, and glucose monitors and test strips for monitoring [5]. Health Canada puts the diagnosed diabetes population at about 3.8 million people, with 2018 health-system costs estimated at $27 billion, projected to surpass $39 billion by 2028 [5].

On the contraception side, Health Canada lists the covered "contraceptive drugs and devices" as oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, rings, implants and injections [5]. The intent is stated as reproductive freedom and choice of method; the October 2024 news release framed it as free access to contraception for "up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada" [4].

The precise drug lists live in each agreement's Annex A — the "List of prescription drugs and related products" — published separately for British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon [2]. I did not retrieve the four annexes in full, so the exact DIN-level lists are beyond what this report can state from the pages read. What can be stated is the structure: the annex is where a product is either listed or not, and unlisted products — including most medicines outside these two categories — remain with provincial plans and private insurers. Health Canada's "about" page confirms that "Private and public drug plans will still cover a range of products outside the contraceptives and diabetes medications included in pharmacare bilateral agreements" [5].

Who is covered follows from geography plus the usual residence rules of each jurisdiction's drug plan, not from any federal eligibility test. Health Canada's pages describe coverage as applying to people who "live in a province or territory with an agreement" [2][5]. There is no income test, no age limit and no employment condition attached to the pharmacare benefit itself; the single-payer, first-dollar design means the covered items are simply paid at the pharmacy for residents of the four jurisdictions. British Columbia's provincial page adds one operational detail worth noting: its Plan NP covers diabetes medications, contraceptives and menopausal hormone therapy, and a pharmacist can substitute an equally safe and effective medication with better coverage — a substitution rule that shapes which listed product a patient actually receives in practice. Residents of the other nine provinces and territories have no pharmacare benefit at all and fall back on their existing provincial or private coverage, which the government's pages direct them to consult [2].

In short: what has been delivered is not "a national drug plan" but a two-category, listed-product, four-jurisdiction benefit. The breadth of the promise — a national formulary and a broader universal plan — remains in the Act's preparatory requirements, not in anything available at a pharmacy counter today.

### 4. How many people are using it: enrolment, claims and utilization evidence

There is no single national count of pharmacare users, and Health Canada publishes no Canada-wide utilization dashboard. What exists is per-jurisdiction reporting from the four signatory governments, and it is uneven: some jurisdictions report beneficiaries, some report prescriptions, and none of the pages I read publish a single consolidated "pharmacare enrolments" figure. This section reports what each of the four governments has actually said, and flags where a number predates the federal agreement or measures something different from federal pharmacare use.

**Manitoba.** Manitoba's free prescription birth control began October 1, 2024 under the province's own program, *before* the February 27, 2025 federal pharmacare agreement; the federal agreement then carried that coverage forward into the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program (MEPP), effective April 15, 2025 [13]. The Manitoba government's March 2026 news release states the running totals: "more than 55,000 women accessing free birth control and more than 200,000 prescriptions filled since the program launched in October 2024" [14]. Both figures measure the provincial free-contraception benefit across its full run, not only the federally funded months, so they overstate what the federal pharmacare agreement alone has delivered; the government has not published a separate count for the MEPP months after April 15, 2025. On the diabetes side, the federal agreement's announcement said the funding would support "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes" [18], but that is an eligible-population estimate, not a count of users.

**British Columbia.** BC's Plan NP launched March 1, 2026 — roughly a year after the March 6, 2025 agreement was signed — providing "100% coverage of select diabetes medications, menopausal hormone therapy (MHT), and contraceptives for any B.C. resident enrolled in MSP" [12]. BC's launch release frames the eligible population rather than actual claims: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [15], with up to $670 million in federal funding over three years [15]. Because Plan NP is automatic at the pharmacy with no registration, BC does not maintain an "enrolment" list to count; the province's pages state coverage is processed in PharmaNet like all PharmaCare plans [12]. I found no BC government release reporting the number of Plan NP prescriptions dispensed since March 1, 2026.

**Prince Edward Island.** PEI's program took effect May 1, 2025. The provincial government's October 30, 2025 release is the clearest utilization report of any jurisdiction: "Since launching on May 1, 2025, over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [20]. The federal agreement's announcement states the eligible populations the same way: reproductive freedom for "over 41,000 Islanders" and essential medications for "over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes" [17]; the realized diabetes figure of over 20,000 exceeds that earlier projection, while the realized contraception figure is a small fraction of the projected eligible population.

**Yukon.** Yukon was the last to implement, launching its program April 15, 2026, administered by Pacific Blue Cross with eligible residents automatically enrolled and claims adjudicated in real time at pharmacies, acting as primary payer even for people with private insurance [16]. Because it launched most recently, no utilization figures exist yet; the signing announcement projected coverage "supporting the reproductive health of more than 12,000 Yukoners" and "more than 3,000 residents with diabetes" [16].

Assembled, the only actual-use figures published to date are Manitoba's (over 55,000 people and over 200,000 prescriptions, mostly pre-dating the federal agreement), PEI's (over 5,000 contraception users and over 20,000 diabetes beneficiaries through late October 2025), and the eligible-population estimates for BC and Yukon. Two general points follow. First, "how many people are using it" cannot yet be answered nationally: there is no federal count, three of four jurisdictions launched only in 2026, and the one with a full year of data (PEI) reports beneficiaries in the tens of thousands, against a national target population of up to nine million for contraception and 3.7 million for diabetes [4]. Second, the figures that do exist are mostly eligible-population or running-total figures from government news releases, not audited claims statistics; CIHI's prescription-drug data infrastructure, which the Committee of Experts says Canada needs to take back from private vendors, does not yet publish a pharmacare utilization series.

### 5. The Parliamentary Budget Officer's estimate of a full single-payer program

The Parliamentary Budget Officer's most recent costing of a full single-payer universal drug plan is *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan*, released October 12, 2023 — an update of its 2017 estimate, prepared in response to parliamentary interest as the Pharmacare Act was being drafted. It is a costing of the full program contemplated by the Act's framework, not of the two-category first phase, and its numbers are therefore the reference point for "what a full program would cost."

The headline estimates are two sides of one coin. On the public ledger: "we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [3]. On the economy-wide ledger: "In terms of the economy as a whole, we estimate cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28" [3]. The two figures reconcile because the plan transfers spending that is currently private (employer insurance and out-of-pocket) onto governments, while reducing total national drug spending through lower prices. The PBO estimates total drug expenditures under Pharmacare at $33.2 billion in 2024-25, rising to $38.9 billion in 2027-28 [3], with economy-wide savings growing because Pharmacare drug spending grows at 5.3 per cent a year versus 5.8 per cent under the status quo — historically, private plan spending grows faster than public plan spending [3].

The model's assumptions matter more than the headline number, because they define what "a full program" means in the PBO's terms. The PBO retained the framework given to it by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health in September 2016: Pharmacare would be a universal plan; it would replace existing public and private drug plans; it would use the Régie de l'assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary as the national formulary; and it would require a $5 co-payment for all brand-name prescriptions, with exemptions for children 15 and under, students 16–18, people 65 and over, pregnant women, the physically disabled, Employment Insurance recipients and their dependants, and welfare/social-assistance recipients and their dependants [3]. On top of that structure, the PBO assumes behavioural effects (utilization rises 13.5 per cent as out-of-pocket prices fall 47 to 100 per cent), generic substitution converging to the median provincial public-plan rate, biosimilar switching, and price effects from a single payer's negotiating power: all existing drug prices negotiated down to the lowest observable Canadian price, plus confidential-rebate discounts of 20 per cent for brand-name drugs and 25 per cent for drugs new to the Canadian market [3].

Two limits on the estimate are stated by the PBO itself and should travel with any use of the number. First, "As there is no certainty with respect to the federal and provincial shares of the cost of such a program, it is not possible to isolate federal costs" — the $11.2–13.4 billion is a combined federal–provincial figure, and the PBO cannot say how much Ottawa alone would pay [3]. Second, the incremental cost varies sharply by province, from 1.4 times projected baseline public spending in Saskatchewan to nearly three times in Prince Edward Island, because provinces start from very different baseline public plans [3].

The PBO also costed two alternative formularies, which bracket the design space. A catastrophic-drug-only plan would add $1.8 billion in 2024-25 and $2.0 billion in 2027-28 to the public sector, while *saving* the economy $2.6–3.6 billion relative to baseline. An essential-medicines list (the WHO model list adapted for Canada by St. Michael's Hospital researchers) would cost slightly *more* than the status quo — $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more in 2024-25 and 2027-28 respectively — because essential medicines are mostly generics already priced low, so the single payer's savings cannot offset the induced increase in use [3].

For completeness, the earlier 2017 PBO estimate — which some secondary sources still quote — put the *federal* cost of a national program at roughly $19.3 billion a year, a figure that differs because it isolates the federal share differently and uses older data. The 2023 report supersedes it and explicitly frames itself as an update of the first estimate, Federal Cost of a National Pharmacare Program, published in 2017. The 2023 numbers are the ones to cite for the current debate, and they are the numbers used throughout this section.

### 6. Other independent cost estimates and how they differ from the PBO

The PBO's full-program estimate is one of several. The others fall into three groups: the government's own advisory council (the 2019 "Hoskins report"), the 2025 Committee of Experts created under the Act itself, and critics who argue the official numbers understate the true taxpayer cost.

**The Hoskins advisory council (2019).** The Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare, chaired by former Ontario health minister Eric Hoskins, recommended a universal, single-payer, public plan built around an essential medicines list starting January 1, 2022 and growing to a comprehensive formulary by 2027. Its cost estimate: "it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines. As the national formulary grows to cover a comprehensive list of drugs, we estimate that annual incremental costs will reach $15.3 billion in 2027" [21]. This $15.3 billion figure is the one most commonly paired with the PBO's $13.4 billion in commentary, and the two are broadly comparable: both are incremental public-sector costs for a full single-payer program in 2027, with the difference largely reflecting the Hoskins council's slightly different formulary-growth assumptions and its own modelling of price and utilization effects. The Hoskins report also projected that by 2027 total prescription-drug spending would be $5 billion lower than without pharmacare — the same direction of economy-wide savings the PBO found, at a larger magnitude [21].

**The Committee of Experts (2025).** The committee the Act itself required to be established within thirty days reported in 2025 and reached a different, narrower costing question: what would it cost to publicly fund an *essential medicines list*, the committee's recommended first building block, rather than a comprehensive formulary. Its answer: "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars" [22]. Its Figure 3 lays out a 2025 status-quo-versus-pharmacare comparison built from IQVIA, CIHI and PBO data: out-of-pocket spending $9.5 billion falling to $6.8 billion; private insurance $17.3 billion falling to $12.5 billion; public plans $18.8 billion falling to $13.6 billion; and new pharmacare spending of $8 billion [22]. The committee also reports that total prescribed-drug spending in Canada rose from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024, and argues the status quo already carries a hidden public subsidy of about $5 billion a year through the non-taxation of employer private-plan contributions [22]. This is an advocacy document as much as a costing — the committee's own preface disclaims that its views "do not necessarily reflect the views of Health Canada" — but its $6–10 billion essential-list estimate and its redistribution table are the Act's own expert body's numbers, and they bracket a cheaper, phased program than the PBO's full single-payer model.

**Critical estimates (Fraser Institute and others).** The principal counter-argument comes from the Fraser Institute, which disputes the government's first-phase costing rather than the full-program number. The federal government's 2024 budget set aside $1.5 billion over five years for the first phase; the Fraser Institute notes the government reported the first phase of national pharmacare would cost $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024/25 [9]. The PBO's legislative costing of Bill C-64 then found a higher number: "the PBO now reports that this phase of national pharmacare will cost $1.9 billion over five years" [9] — roughly $400 million more than budgeted. The PBO's own note puts it as: "The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [11], and it is explicit about the modelling assumption that produces this figure: the program covers 100 per cent of diabetes and contraception expenses for people currently without public or private coverage and for those who do not fill prescriptions for cost reasons, the latter "assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions" [11].

On the full-program number, the Fraser Institute cites the same range as everyone else — "a fully universal single-payer (that is, paid by government) pharmacare program could cost between $13.4 billion and $15.3 billion in 2027/28" [10] — while arguing the figure is a floor, not a ceiling. It relays economist Jack Mintz's estimate that "the actual annual cost could be much higher at $32.7 billion or beyond" if the assumed price reductions from single-payer negotiation do not materialize [10]. That is the central analytical disagreement across every estimate in this report: every official figure (PBO, Hoskins, Committee of Experts) assumes that consolidating purchasing and negotiating prices — down to the lowest observable Canadian price plus confidential-rebate discounts in the PBO's model — will offset much of the new public cost. The critics' case is that those savings are assumptions, not results, and that if they fail, the incremental public cost roughly doubles. The PBO is explicit that its savings depend on negotiated price effects and confidential rebates [3]; it does not present the $32.7 billion scenario, but its own sensitivity to those assumptions is the reason the two camps' numbers differ by more than the gap between any two official estimates.


## Beyond this question

For anyone tracking or writing about Canadian pharmacare, the record supports three distinctions that most coverage blurs.

First, "pharmacare has delivered X" requires stating *which layer* is being measured, because the four layers move on different clocks: the Act passed October 2024; agreements were signed February–March 2025; benefits went live on four different dates (Manitoba April 15, 2025; PEI May 1, 2025; BC March 1, 2026; Yukon April 15, 2026); and utilization data lags further still. A claim that "pharmacare is now delivering" was false for most of 2025 in three of the four jurisdictions, and a claim that "pharmacare delivered nothing" misses that roughly two years of real claims now exist in Manitoba and PEI.

Second, the program's future is governed by a date almost nobody quotes: March 31, 2029, the expiry written into the BC agreement [24]. The Spring 2026 Economic Update contains no new money for additional deals, and the CCPA's reading — that Ottawa appears poised to let the four agreements lapse — is the single most consequential fact for the program's trajectory [23]. Anyone assessing pharmacare should be watching the 2029 renewal question and the federal contribution path ($88.1 million in 2025-26 rising to $269.6 million by 2028-29 [23]) rather than only the signing announcements.

Third, the cost debate is not really a disagreement about how much drugs cost; it is a disagreement about whether a single payer can extract the price savings every official model assumes. The PBO's incremental $11.2–13.4 billion sits between its own total-spending baseline of $33.2–38.9 billion [3] and the critics' $32.7 billion scenario [10], and the entire gap turns on negotiated-price effects and confidential rebates that have not yet been demonstrated in Canada at national scale. When someone cites "what pharmacare costs," the responsible question is which assumption about price negotiation their number is carrying.

## Open questions

**No national utilization count exists.** Neither Health Canada nor CIHI publishes a consolidated count of pharmacare users or claims. The only realized-use figures are provincial news-release numbers: Manitoba's over 55,000 people and over 200,000 prescriptions (mostly from before the federal agreement), and PEI's over 5,000 contraception users and over 20,000 diabetes beneficiaries as of late October 2025 [14][20]. BC launched March 1, 2026 and Yukon April 15, 2026, with no claims data published by either government as of the pages I read. Because BC's coverage is automatic with no registration, there is no enrolment roster to count; utilization would have to come from PharmaNet claims, which BC has not released in a pharmacare-specific form.

**The Manitoba figures overstate federal pharmacare use.** Manitoba's free birth control began October 1, 2024 under a provincial program, six months before the federal agreement's coverage began April 15, 2025, and the published counts span the combined period. The government has not separated federal-funded months.

**What happens on April 1, 2029.** The agreements expire March 31, 2029, and the current federal government has signalled no new deals and, by the CCPA's and Refdesk's reading of the Spring 2026 Economic Update, no renewal. There is no public commitment either way from the government, and the nine non-signatory provinces remain without any federal pharmacare.

**The federal–provincial split of a full program is unknowable from public estimates.** The PBO explicitly cannot isolate the federal share because no cost-sharing formula exists [3]. The 2017 PBO report's federal-only figure ($19.3 billion for 2015-16) uses a different framework and should not be mixed with the 2023 combined figure.

**Whether price-negotiation savings materialize.** Every official estimate banks on single-payer price reductions; the critics' higher numbers assume they fail. No Canadian data yet tests either assumption, because the first phase negotiated no national prices — it funds provincial coverage of already-listed products.

**Coverage thin spots in this report.** I read the BC agreement's full text and annex but not the Manitoba, PEI or Yukon agreements' annexes, so DIN-level lists for those three are stated at the category level only. I did not retrieve the Spring 2026 Economic Update's own fiscal tables, relying on the CCPA's and Refdesk's readings of them. And no source I found publishes the actual first-year claims cost against the budgeted $1.5 billion or the PBO's $1.9 billion five-year first-phase estimate.

report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have banned or restricted phones in schools, and what do the policies actually say?

Smartphone bans in schools have moved, in a few years, from isolated local rules to a near-global default. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring (GEM) Report, which has tracked this since 2023, counts 114 education systems with a national ban on mobile phones in schools as of March 2026 — 58% of countries worldwide. The same monitoring shows how fast the shift was: fewer than one in four countries (24%) had bans in June 2023, 40% by early 2025, and "almost 20 percentage point higher" by March 2026 [4]. Where there is no national ban, sub-national rules often fill the gap: UNESCO counts 39 US states with either a statewide ban (15) or a requirement that districts restrict phones in classrooms (24) [4].

The design of these policies varies more than the headlines suggest, and the variation matters for what the evaluations can measure. Four models recur:

**Legislated, device-wide bans (France).** France passed the first major national law, loi n° 2018-698 of 3 August 2018. The French Senate's annual review of the law's application records that Article 1 prohibits a pupil's use of a mobile phone "ou de tout autre équipement terminal de communications électroniques" in nursery schools, elementary schools and middle schools (collèges), and during any teaching activity outside school grounds, with an exception for pedagogical use where a school's internal rules expressly allow it; lycées (upper secondary) are given the power to prohibit phones through their internal rules rather than being subject to a national ban [13]. The law also authorises confiscation of devices, with the terms set by each school's internal rules [13].

**Non-statutory guidance with a statutory turn (England).** England's Department for Education (DfE) published non-statutory guidance in February 2024 telling schools to prohibit phone use throughout the school day, but left implementation to schools; the DfE's stated expectation is that pupils have no access "during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [7]. The guidance has since hardened: the current published guidance states that "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only." [7] This applies from the start of the 2026 school year. This matters for the evidence base because England's schools had been adopting bans autonomously for years before any central guidance — which is precisely the variation the Beland–Murphy study exploited [15].

**National agreements rather than law (the Netherlands).** The Netherlands banned phones, tablets and smartwatches in classrooms through an agreement between government, school organisations, teachers, parents and pupils, not through legislation. Eurydice records that the ban applied to secondary education from January 2024 and was extended to primary education for the 2024/2025 school year, with exceptions for educational and medical use and enforcement left to institutions [8]. The policy was framed partly around cyberbullying: "The ban aims to encourage discussions and social interactions while addressing cyberbullying, making the school a safer place for students" [8].

**State-level Australian bans with a staggered rollout.** Australia has no single national ban, but all states and territories now restrict phones, with details varying. The Guardian's October 2025 review records the sequence: Victoria moved first, banning phones in public primary and secondary schools in 2020; by term four 2023 Western Australia, Tasmania, New South Wales and South Australia had followed; Queensland restricted phones in term one 2024 [9]. South Australia's policy, which is the subject of one of the few pre-registered evaluations, requires students in all government schools to keep personal devices "off and away" between the start and end of each school day and during authorised off-site activities [17]. The staggered rollout created the natural experiment that later studies exploit.

**The US and Brazil.** In the United States, Florida passed the first statewide ban — House Bill 379 of July 2023 — prohibiting wireless communication devices including smartphones, earbuds, headphones and smartwatches during instructional time except when a teacher expressly directs educational use; the large urban district studied by Figlio and Ozek went further, requiring devices silenced and put away for the entire school day [20]. Brazil's federal law No. 15,100/2025 now prohibits smartphone use in public and private schools during class, recess and other school activities, but the first and best-evaluated Brazilian policy is Rio de Janeiro's municipal ban: non-pedagogical use was banned in classrooms from August 2023 and school-wide from February 2024 [21].

**Canadian provincial rules (Ontario, Quebec and others).** Ontario, the largest Canadian province, tightened its rules effective 1 September 2024: students in Grade 7 and above may not use phones or other mobile devices "during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher." Students in Grade 6 and below may not use them "at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher" [5]. Quebec first banned phones in classrooms from 1 January 2024, then extended the rule from the 2025–2026 school year to the entire school day including breaks and lunchtime; the Quebec ban covers cellphones and communication devices, earbuds and headphones, smartwatches with messaging or calling features, personal tablets and music players, "anywhere on school property — including classrooms, hallways, cafeterias, bathrooms, libraries, outdoor areas, and sports fields — from the first bell to the last." Phones brought to school must be locked in lockers, with exceptions only for medical reasons arranged through school administration [14]. British Columbia, Alberta, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia have introduced similar classroom restrictions for the 2024–2025 school year, meaning the large majority of Canadian students are now covered [4].

Two structural points carry into the evidence sections. First, several of these policies — England's, the Netherlands', Ontario's earlier version — restrict phones in class or during lessons, while others — Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia, Quebec's newer rule, England's default position — extend to the whole school day including breaks and lunchtime. The strictest form, requiring phones to be locked away rather than merely switched off, appears in South Australia, Quebec and (from 2026) England. Second, most of the bans were introduced as policy announcements rather than as evaluated interventions, which is why the natural-experiment evidence below comes from places where bans arrived at different times — England's schools before 2011, Spanish regions in 2015, Norwegian middle schools — and not from the newest wave of blanket national rules.

### 2. What do evaluations measure about academic outcomes — test scores, grades, attainment?

The academic-outcome evidence comes mostly from natural experiments in which bans arrived at different times in different schools, plus one large randomised trial in higher education. The oldest studies split along national lines; the newest ones, using better data and designs, have begun to converge on a modest, uneven, positive answer.

**England: the founding positive result.** Beland and Murphy (published in *Labour Economics*, 2016) surveyed schools in four English cities about when they introduced mobile-phone policies and combined this with administrative data on high-stakes exams. Using a difference-in-differences design that exploits schools' autonomous decisions to ban phones, they find that "We find that student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban, by about 0.07 standard deviations on average. These increases in performance are driven by the lowest-achieving students" [15]. The CEP working-paper version frames the same result as evidence that the "unstructured presence of phones has detrimental effects" on student achievement [3]. The published paper also reports the gains concentrated among the lowest-achieving students, with no significant effect on high achievers [15]. Their bottom line is that restricting phones is a low-cost way to reduce educational inequality.

Two features of this study deserve emphasis because later work turns on them. First, it measures a policy schools chose for themselves, not a centrally imposed ban, so the identifying variation is in timing. Second, its survey response rate was modest — the Swedish replication team put it at roughly 21% of schools contacted — which raises the question of whether the banning schools were otherwise untypical.

**Sweden: the direct failure to replicate.** Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors (*Economics of Education Review*, 2020) set out to replicate Beland–Murphy using the universe of Swedish secondary schools and a staggered difference-in-differences design. Their conclusion is flatly negative: "In Sweden, we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" [12]. They increased the survey response rate to about 75%. The authors offer two explanations for why Sweden differs from England: teachers in Sweden appear to enforce classroom phone restrictions regardless of whether a formal school policy exists, and Sweden is "the most computer-dense country in Europe," with 70% of grade-8 students having their own computers, so a phone ban may not remove the distracting device from the classroom [12]. Either way, the Swedish result shows the English finding does not generalise mechanically, and that the size of any effect is sensitive to how much the ban actually changes a school's digital environment.

**Norway: average null, large gains for girls.** Abrahamsson's Norwegian study (NHH working paper 2024; accepted at the *Journal of Human Resources*) is one of the strongest causal estimates, and the difference between its working-paper and journal framings matters. The working paper reports that bans significantly increase girls' grade point average and their likelihood of attending an academic high-school track, with larger effects for girls from low socio-economic backgrounds [6]. A US commentary summarising the working paper puts the girls' gains at "on the order of 0.22 standard deviations" in both GPA and externally graded mathematics exams, and notes that Abrahamsson benchmarks this against a class-size reduction of one student, which improves outcomes by roughly 0.00–0.05 standard deviations [18]. The peer-reviewed version states the result more carefully: banning smartphones in middle schools "has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences." [16], with bans improving "girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [16]. The phrase "no average effect" is central: the headline benefit is concentrated in girls, particularly disadvantaged girls, and there is no comparable gain for boys.

**Spain: large PISA gains in one of two regions.** Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella (published in *Applied Economic Analysis*, 2022) studied the two Spanish autonomous regions — Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha — that banned phones in schools from 2015, using a synthetic-control design against the other Spanish regions. They find that within three years, Galicia's PISA scores improved "by around 10 points in maths and 12 points in sciences" relative to a synthetic Galicia that had followed the same pre-ban trend, which they convert, using Woessmann's (2016) cross-country learning benchmarks, to the equivalent of "0.6–0.8 years of learning in maths and around 0.72 to near one year of learning in sciences" [1]. The authors are explicit that this is one region and that the effect was not observed symmetrically elsewhere; the finding's credibility rests on the synthetic control, and it has not been independently replicated.

**The United States: the first statewide and nationwide evidence.** Figlio and Ozek (NBER working paper, 2025) study Florida's July 2023 statewide ban (House Bill 379), plus one large urban district's stricter all-day enforcement, comparing schools by their pre-ban level of student phone activity measured from GPS data. They report that "student test scores improved by 0.6 percentiles, with the ban increasing spring test scores 1.1 percentiles in the second year relative to the spring test right before the ban took effect" [20], with larger gains for male students (1.4 percentiles) and middle/high schools (1.3). The benefits were not immediate: test scores were flat in year one and improved only in year two, which is also when the initial surge in suspensions receded [20]. Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob (2026) provide the largest and most rigorous US estimate, evaluating the adoption of Yondr lockable phone pouches (nearly 5,000 schools using pouches by 2026, according to the paper) with a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design that combines teacher surveys, GPS phone-location pings, test scores and administrative records. Their average academic result is near zero: "we find average effects on test scores that are close to zero over the first three years following adoption: we can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations" [19]. That average hides grade-level heterogeneity — high schools show modest positive effects, particularly in math (roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations, about 0.9 percentile points), while middle schools show small negative effects [19].

**Brazil: positive and well-identified.** Lichand, Moreno-Louzada, da Costa and Gentzkow (NBER, 2026) evaluate Rio de Janeiro's municipal ban — non-pedagogical use banned in classrooms from August 2023 and school-wide from February 2024 — by contrasting middle schools that already had strict rules (the control group) with those that did not (the treatment group). Their main result: an index of math and Portuguese standardized test scores "improved by 0.06 standard deviations in treatment schools relative to control schools after the school-wide ban" [21]. Because phone use also declined in control schools, the authors argue the reduced-form estimate understates the total effect, and a calibration based on the first-stage change in phone use suggests gains "on the order of 0.2 standard deviations" where the ban actually reduced use [21]. The design is credible — quarterly test data over two pre-ban years show flat pre-trends, and results survive matching on observable school characteristics — but the authors are explicit that it identifies a relative contrast, not ban-versus-no-ban.

**The only large randomised trial: phones out of class.** Sungu, Choudhury and Bjerre-Nielsen (*Science*, 2026) randomly assigned 16,683 higher-education students across ten institutions in Odisha, India, to hand in their phones at the start of each class or to continue as normal, for a full semester. Phone-free classes "achieved higher grades on average than the control group. The effect corresponds to an improvement of 0.073 standard deviations" [22], with the largest gains among students whose prior marks were lowest. The authors found no evidence the effect ran through attendance, inferring that freed mental capacity in class is the likely mechanism [22]. This is the cleanest causal estimate in the entire literature, but two caveats bound it: it is higher education, not schoolchildren, and an independent critical assessment notes the 95% confidence interval runs from 0.003 to 0.144 standard deviations, so the estimate is fragile at its lower bound, with an unexplained one-sided test and subgroup claims not backed by reported interaction tests [23].

**Reconciling the estimates.** Read together, the studies have begun to converge rather than contradict. The positive estimates — Beland–Murphy in England, Abrahamsson for Norwegian girls, Beneito–Vicente-Chirivella in Galicia, Figlio–Ozek in Florida, Lichand et al. in Rio, and the Sungu et al. RCT — are all consistent with a modest effect, in the rough range of 0.06 to 0.07 standard deviations for the average treated student, that is larger among low-achieving or disadvantaged students and that may take a year to appear. The null estimates — Kessel et al. in Sweden, and the US nationwide average in Allcott et al. — come from settings where devices remain in the classroom (Sweden's laptop-saturated schools) or where the treatment (a phone pouch) removes only one device among many, and even the US null average conceals positive high-school effects. The scoping review's two large-sample null studies predate the platform-era smartphone and the enforcement-based designs of the new wave. What no study has done is reconcile the size of the effect with how completely the ban removes the device from the classroom, although the Rio calibration (0.06 SD reduced-form versus roughly 0.2 SD treatment-on-complier) and the Florida timing (gains only in year two) both point in that direction.

### 3. What do evaluations measure about attention, distraction and classroom behaviour?

Attention and distraction are the outcomes politicians most often cite when introducing bans, and they are also the outcomes with the weakest direct measurement. Until 2026 no large study had measured classroom attention before and after a ban with anything other than opinion surveys, and the two studies that have now tried — one using student self-reports at national scale, one using direct classroom observation — both failed to find a clear improvement. The evidence falls into three categories: school-leader and teacher perception surveys, student self-reports in observational studies, and two newer attempts at direct measurement.

**What the perception surveys report.** The Dutch government's commissioned evaluation — carried out after the national guideline took effect in 2024 — surveyed 317 secondary school leaders and 313 primary schools, and ran 12 focus groups with teachers, teaching assistants, students and parents [11]. Its headline is that secondary schools "reported that children found it easier to concentrate (75%), the social environment was better (59%) and some said results had improved (28%)" [11]. This is the largest implementation study of any national ban to date, but its design is explicit: it measures school leaders' and teachers' perceptions of change, not change in students' measured attention, and it cannot separate the ban's effect from the general trend or from schools' broader anti-distraction measures.

The Australian states, which banned phones earlier and more comprehensively, have produced similar perception surveys rather than outcome evaluations. In New South Wales, the Department of Education's Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation surveyed almost 1,000 public school principals one year after the ban: 95% still supported it, and "Eighty-one per cent said the ban has improved students’ learning, 86% said it has improved socialisation among students and 87% believed students were less distracted in the classroom" [9]. South Australia's 2025 research found 70% of teachers reporting increased focus and engagement during learning time and 64% reporting "a lower frequency of critical incidents" related to device use [9].

These surveys are consistent with each other and with the classroom-behaviour claims of the academic literature, but they measure satisfaction and perceived change, not attention. A principal reporting that students "are less distracted" is evidence that the ban is being experienced as working; it is not evidence that measured attention or learning improved — and the two can diverge, as the two direct-measurement studies below show.

**The direct-measurement evidence is now null on attention.** Allcott et al.'s US nationwide study of Yondr pouches is the first to measure classroom attention as a primary outcome at scale, using student survey responses from Panorama Education on self-reported classroom attention. Their result: "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying or self-reported classroom attention." [19], though they note some evidence of differential pre-trends that limits conclusions for those two outcomes. This is important precisely because the same study confirms the mechanism — phone use in class fell from 61% to 13% of students by teacher report, and GPS pings on campuses fell roughly 30% by the third year [19]. Removing the phones did not move self-reported attention.

The one study to observe classrooms directly found the same tension. Sungu et al.'s randomised trial in India collected phones in class and raised grades by 0.073 standard deviations, but an independent critical assessment of the paper notes that "perceived distraction did not change and treated students appeared more distracted during spot checks." so the authors' attention-allocation explanation for the grade gains is post hoc [23]. The lesson is not that attention is unaffected by phones — laboratory work has long shown phone presence impairs cognitive performance — but that the school-level studies to date have not found an attention effect that they could measure, even when a learning effect appeared.

**What the observational studies find on behaviour and engagement.** SMART Schools, the cross-sectional English study of 1,227 pupils in 30 secondary schools, included disruptive classroom behaviour among its outcomes and found that adolescents in schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their disruptive classroom behaviour from pupils in permissive schools [4]. This is the only published measure of actual classroom behaviour from students across both policy types, and it shows no association. It is cross-sectional, so it cannot establish causation, but it directly contradicts the assumption that a restrictive policy by itself changes measured classroom behaviour.

The King et al. South Australian study measured academic engagement (motivation, concentration on studies, perceived achievement) rather than attention per se. Within the ban group, engagement improved over the study period, while the no-ban group did not change significantly; but "there was no significant between-group difference in academic engagement at follow-up" [17], so the improvement cannot be attributed to the ban. Their conclusion is that the ban showed "limited to no short-term benefits" [17].

**An inference about where attention effects should appear.** Combining the bodies of evidence produces a pattern worth stating as an inference rather than a finding. Where a ban actually removes a device from the classroom — as in Abrahamsson's Norway, where the largest effects appeared at schools that required phones to be handed in or locked away rather than merely silenced — the mechanism for improved attention is plausible and the downstream academic effects for girls are measurable. Where devices remain in the classroom or are replaced by laptops (Sweden's 70% computer ownership; English schools' one-to-one device programmes), no attention effect would be expected, and the null academic results are what the studies find. But the direct measurements to date — student self-reports at US scale and classroom observation in India — have not confirmed an attention effect even where the device was removed, which suggests either that the measures are too coarse, that attention effects are too small or too transient to capture, or that the learning gains run through a different channel than sustained classroom attention. The attention claim remains the most asserted and least evidenced element of the entire phone-ban literature.

### 4. What do evaluations measure about bullying?

Bullying is the one domain where several independent studies report reductions after bans, but the studies measure different things and disagree about cyberbullying specifically.

**The strongest positive evidence: Spain and Norway.** Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella used the two Spanish regional bans (Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha, both from 2015) and administrative data on officially reported school-bullying cases from the Spanish Ministry of Education between 2012 and 2017. Against a synthetic control, they find that "bullying incidence fell by around 9.5% to 18% over its pre-intervention levels among teenagers in the treated regions" [1]. Their companion discussion of the same study, as summarised by King et al., puts the reduction at 15–18% among 12–17-year-olds and 10–18% among 15–17-year-olds [17]. The reduction is in reported bullying incidence generally, not cyberbullying specifically.

Abrahamsson's Norway study uses administrative and survey data and reports the same direction of effect: "Post-ban bullying among both genders decreases" [6]. In the peer-reviewed version the claim is stated as bans "lower bullying for both genders" [16]. The Norwegian result is the more persuasive of the two for causal purposes because it exploits within-school timing across 477 middle schools with an event-study design, and because the outcome is measured from survey and registry data rather than only official reports, which can move with schools' reporting behaviour.

**The null and negative evidence.** The methodologically strongest recent studies find no ban-attributable effect on bullying. Allcott et al.'s US study measured students' perceived likelihood of online bullying directly and found "no measurable improvements for perceived online bullying or self-reported classroom attention." [19], with the caveat that differential pre-trends limit conclusions. This is the largest direct test of the cyberbullying claim to date, and it is null. King et al.'s pre-registered South Australian natural experiment measured bullying with the PISA seven-item index (verbal, physical, relational and extortion, plus an online/offline item). The ban and no-ban groups did not differ significantly; there was "a significant main effect of condition on bullying, indicating that, collapsed over time, the ban group had higher bullying than the no ban condition," and bullying declined significantly over time in both groups (d = 0.33), but with no condition-by-time interaction the decline cannot be attributed to the ban [17]. In other words, bullying fell in the study period, but it fell equally where phones were banned and where they were not.

Campbell and Edwards' scoping review finds the literature split. Four studies reported a small reduction in bullying after bans, especially among older students, but "the studies did not specify whether or not they were talking about cyberbullying" [10]. Two further studies reported that teachers believed phones increased cyberbullying. Against this, two studies found "the number of incidents of online victimisation and harassment was greater in schools with mobile phone bans compared with those without bans." though the data did not distinguish in-school from out-of-school hours; the authors suggested bans might be experienced as punitive and worsen school climate, which other research links to more bullying [10].

**Why the findings diverge.** Four differences explain most of the apparent contradiction. First, outcome: Spain and Norway measure bullying reported or recorded broadly; King et al. measure students' self-reported exposure on a validated index; the scoping review's negative studies measure online victimisation specifically. A ban can plausibly reduce in-person and in-school bullying while leaving, or even displacing, out-of-hours online harassment untouched — the phone is removed from the yard but not from the evening. Second, the Spanish and Norwegian effects are concentrated among teenagers, while several null studies span younger and older groups together. Third, design quality: the Spanish synthetic control and Norwegian event study are the strongest causal designs, but the Spanish result rests on two regions and official reporting, and the Norwegian result predates the widespread platform-era smartphone (its data end in 2018). No study has yet measured cyberbullying as the primary outcome in a design that can isolate the ban's causal effect, and the Australian review is explicit that there is no research evidence on whether students simply move bullying to laptops, tablets or other devices [10].

The balanced summary is that bans are associated with modest reductions in broadly measured, mostly in-school bullying among teenagers in the two best causal studies, but that the specific claim about cyberbullying — the justification several governments, including the Netherlands and South Australia, give for their policies — is now directly tested and not supported: the largest US study found no improvement in perceived online bullying, and two smaller studies found more online victimisation where phones were banned.

### 5. What do evaluations measure about mental health and wellbeing?

Mental health is where the evidence is most clearly in tension, and where the strongest causal study and the strongest descriptive study point in different directions.

**Norway: reduced psychological care for girls.** Abrahamsson's is the only study to use hard mental-health outcomes — health-care take-up — rather than self-reported wellbeing. The working paper reports that "banning smartphones significantly decreases the health care take-up for psychological symptoms and diseases among girls" [6]. A US commentary summarising the working paper gives the magnitude as a reduction of "about 2–3 visits per child, per year" for psychological symptoms [18]. The peer-reviewed version restates it as: bans "reduce psychological health care use among girls" [16]. The nuance that both framings carry is that this is a reduction in girls' use of care for psychological symptoms — the closest available proxy for reduced distress — while the average effect across boys and girls together is null [16]. The same study found no effect on the likelihood of students being diagnosed or treated for psychological conditions overall, which the Boston Globe's coverage of the working paper noted [18]. The health-care effect is therefore best read as evidence that bans reduced some measurable burden of psychological symptoms among girls, not that they changed diagnosed mental illness.

**England: no wellbeing difference, and no change in total use.** SMART Schools, the cross-sectional study of 1,227 English secondary pupils, is the largest direct comparison of restrictive and permissive school phone policies on wellbeing. Its headline is flatly null. Mean mental wellbeing on the WEMWBS measure was 47 (SD = 9), "with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [2]. The study also found no differences in anxiety, depression, problematic social media use, sleep duration or efficiency, or physical activity between restrictive and permissive schools [4]. The mechanism is illuminating: pupils in restrictive schools did use their phones less during the school day — phone use was 0.67 hours per day lower and social media use 0.54 hours per day lower during school time (both p < 0.001) — "but there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [2]. In other words, the ban shifted when pupils used their phones, not how much they used them, and total use is what associates with poorer wellbeing. The authors' interpretation is explicit and worth quoting in full: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [2].

**The scoping review: perception-based and conflicting.** Campbell and Edwards found the wellbeing literature inconclusive and, in their words, "based only on anecdotes or perceptions, rather than the recorded incidence of mental illness" [10]. Two studies in their review reported positive effects on mental health, but both used teachers' and parents' perceptions of students' wellbeing and did not ask the students. Two studies found no difference. Three studies — including a doctoral thesis conducted as students returned from pandemic lockdowns — reported more harm to students' mental health and wellbeing when they were subjected to phone bans, with students reporting they felt more anxious without their phones [10].

**The US: wellbeing dips, then recovers and improves.** Allcott et al.'s nationwide pouch study is the largest causal evidence on wellbeing dynamics. Student-reported subjective wellbeing declines in the year of adoption — roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations — "and then rebounds, becoming positive by the second post-adoption year. The decline is roughly 0.2 student-level standard deviations, followed by an increase of 0.16 standard deviations" [19]. The authors read this as short-term disruption followed by adaptation and improvement, and note for comparison that deactivating Facebook for four weeks raised wellbeing by 0.09 standard deviations in an earlier experiment [19]. The pattern matters because it implies that studies measuring only the first months after a ban — including the South Australian trial below — may catch the disruption and miss the adaptation.

**The South Australian trial: no wellbeing effect in the short window.** King et al. measured psychological distress (K10) and life satisfaction before and after the ban. There were no significant main effects of the ban condition and no condition-by-time interactions on psychological distress or life satisfaction, and neither baseline distress, life satisfaction nor socio-economic status moderated the ban's effect on any outcome [17]. Like the English study, this is a short-window result (about one month), and the authors caution against reading it as proof that longer-term effects cannot emerge.

**Reconciling the strongest studies.** Abrahamsson finds a real, gender-specific reduction in a hard outcome (girls' use of psychological care) over years; SMART Schools finds no association between restrictive policies and adolescents' own wellbeing over the school day, because total use is unchanged; Allcott et al. find wellbeing worsens in the first year then improves. These are not necessarily contradictory: they differ in country, design (event study vs. cross-section vs. staggered panel), outcome (care use vs. self-reported wellbeing vs. survey wellbeing), and in whether and how completely the ban removed the phone. The English null result has a mechanism the Norwegian study does not measure — displacement of use to the evening — and the Norwegian study has an outcome the English study does not measure — girls' clinical care. The US result adds a third ingredient the others lack: time. The honest synthesis is that bans have not been shown to improve adolescents' general wellbeing in the short term, but the best causal evidence shows they can reduce the psychological burden on girls, especially disadvantaged girls, where the ban is enforced strictly enough to change the school day, and that any wellbeing benefit may take more than a year to appear.

### 6. How strong is this evidence overall — designs, replication, and what remains unknown?

The overall strength of this evidence base is low for a policy that now covers a majority of the world's schoolchildren, and the reasons are structural as well as empirical.

**The literature is small and largely not peer-reviewed.** The most complete map is Campbell and Edwards' scoping review, which screened 1,317 articles, reports and dissertations and found only 22 studies that examined schools before and after phone bans, across every country and language they could reach [10]. Twelve of the 22 — more than half — were masters or doctoral theses rather than peer-reviewed research [10]. None examined Australian schools, even though Australia has some of the oldest and strictest bans in the world and governments there routinely cite the bans' benefits [10]. The genuinely causal studies number perhaps five: Beland–Murphy (England), Kessel et al. (Sweden), Abrahamsson (Norway), Beneito–Vicente-Chirivella (Spain), and King et al. (South Australia). Of these, only King et al. was pre-registered, and it found no ban-attributable effects on any primary outcome.

**The designs have identifiable weaknesses.** The founding English study relies on schools' self-reported ban dates from a survey with a modest response rate (about 21% of schools contacted, as the Swedish authors note), and its difference-in-differences design is vulnerable to the schools with early bans being otherwise unusual. The direct Swedish replication, with the universe of secondary schools and a 75% response rate, finds nothing and can reject small effects [12]. The Spanish result is a synthetic control over two regions with official bullying reports — a credible design for those regions, but thin on independent confirmation. The Norwegian study is the strongest: an event-study across 477 middle schools with administrative data, ban timing uncorrelated with school characteristics and prior trends [18], and now peer-reviewed at the *Journal of Human Resources*. Its own author's framing — "no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences" — is a caution against the simple "bans work" reading [16]. The South Australian study, the only pre-registered trial, found no ban effect on problematic phone use, engagement, belonging or bullying, and its authors conclude that imposing access restrictions "may not affect the underlying psychological mechanisms that drive problematic phone use" [17].

**Replication is the decisive gap.** On academic outcomes, the literature currently contains one positive result, one direct failed replication, one gender-specific positive, and one region-specific positive. There is no second independent study confirming any single positive estimate, and the two null studies the scoping review deems most trustworthy — the 30%-of-Norway thesis and the nationwide Swedish cohort — both found nothing [10]. On mental health, the two most rigorous studies measure different things and point in different directions, and no study has measured the same hard outcome in two countries. On cyberbullying — the stated justification for several bans — there is no causal evidence at all, and two studies point the wrong way [10].

**Why the newest wave of bans is the least evaluated.** The policies now in force in Ontario, Quebec, England, the Netherlands and most Australian states arrived as administrative decisions, not as trials. Neil Selwyn's assessment of Australia applies more broadly: the bans were not set up, he says, "with the intention of properly testing their effectiveness", and the concrete research is "inconclusive, and … not particularly rigorous" [9]. The studies that do exist mostly predate the platform-era smartphone and the 2020s surge in adolescent distress; Abrahamsson's Norwegian data end in 2018, Beland–Murphy's English bans were introduced around 2006–2010, and the Spanish bans date from 2015. The devices, the platforms and the adolescent mental-health baseline have all changed since, so even the well-identified historical effects may not describe what a 2024–2026 ban does.

**What the evidence can and cannot support.** The evidence can support these statements: bans reduce in-school phone use; bans are not associated with lower total daily use, because use displaces to the evening; bans may reduce broadly measured, mostly in-school bullying among teenagers in some settings; bans may improve girls' educational outcomes, especially disadvantaged girls, where enforcement is strict; and bans have not been shown to improve average wellbeing. The evidence cannot support these statements: that bans raise test scores generally; that they improve measured attention or classroom behaviour (no one has measured it); that they reduce cyberbullying; or that they improve mental health on average. A policymaker asserting any of the latter is asserting more than the studies show, however reasonable the inference may feel.
