label: ideas, scholarship
q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: McLuhan's Laws of Media (the Tetrad): The Claim, Its Scholarly Life Since 1988, and the Search for Empirical Tests
report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's "laws of media," the tetrad published posthumously with his son Eric in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988), claim that every human artefact manifests exactly four simultaneous effects, asked as four questions: what does it enhance, what does it obsolesce, what does it retrieve, and what does it reverse into when pushed to its limits — a claim the book frames as a "new science" of falsifiable laws modelled on Popper. Since 1988 scholars have applied the tetrad widely but shallowly (social networks, smartphones, GIS, software), extended it theoretically (Levinson's tetrad wheels; Logan's Laws of Media Environments and Users; Harman's metaphysical fourfold), and criticised its scientific pretensions, most influentially in Tom Tyler's "Procrustean Probe," which shows it is simultaneously too vague to be falsifiable and too rigid in forcing all four boxes to be filled. The near-consensus — reached independently by a hostile critic, a sympathetic exponent, and a systematic review — is that the tetrad is not a set of scientific laws but a useful question-generating probe whose outputs are non-unique and non-predictive. On empirical testing, the direct finding is that nobody has tested the tetrad as a law in any strong sense: what exists are data-anchored applications and post-hoc sortings, not pre-registered predictions, reliability measurements, or counterexample searches.

## Key Findings

- The 1988 book's claim is strong and specific: everything humans make "manifested the same four dimensions" — enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal — operating simultaneously, scoped to human productions, and presented as exhaustive (no fifth law found, no counterexample found) [10][1].
- The scientific framing is traceable to the 1975 *Technology and Culture* article, where McLuhan adopted Popper's falsifiability criterion and invited scholars to try to disprove the laws; but McLuhan's own 1977 joke, glossed by Paul Levinson, deflated the claim — if the laws are falsifiable, "they can't do too much damage" [2][1][9].
- Applications are numerous but unproblematized: a systematic review of Brazil and Portugal (2009–2019) found 21 studies, mostly of Facebook and mobile media, with only five reflecting on the tetrad as a method and only two adapting its structure [6].
- The applied literature is explicit that the tetrad is non-reproducible — different researchers will not produce equal tetrads for the same object — and that it works as "an opening exercise, not closing" [6].
- Extensions fall into two lines: Levinson's tetrad wheels (chaining tetrads diachronically, with the explicit caveat that tetradic analysis is historically descriptive but not predictive) and Logan's parallel Laws of Media Environments and Users; Harman re-derived the fourfold from two dualisms and argued its scope should extend beyond human artefacts to all objects [9][4][1].
- Tyler's critique is a double bind, not just "too vague": the tetrad is too loose to be falsified ("empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit") yet unrelentingly rigid because "it requires us to fill the gaps," and the authors themselves produced two different tetrads for wine on one page [5].
- Even the tetrad's strongest academic exponent concedes the point: Logan and Iseri state the laws "are not strictly scientific laws" because they make no unique predictions and admit "more than one correct answer" [4].
- Nobody has tested the tetrad empirically as a law: the closest things are Tyler's data-anchored MMORPG quadrant, Takkeci and Erdem's post-hoc sorting of 20 empirical studies into the four categories, and Thomas's 2007 "operationalization" — which is a method proposal, not a test [5][8].
- A telling asymmetry: prior research concentrates on the enhancement and obsolescence quadrants, while retrieval and reversal — the two hardest to verify or falsify — are the least studied [7].

## Details

### 1. The claim: what the 1988 tetrad actually asserts

*Laws of Media: The New Science* (University of Toronto Press, 1988), completed and edited by Eric McLuhan from his father's papers after Marshall's death in 1980, states its central claim in the preface: "We found that everything man[kind] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions" [10]. Those four dimensions, the "laws of media," are put as four simultaneous questions to be asked of any artefact: what does it enhance or intensify; what does it obsolesce or push aside; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it reverse or flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential [2][4]. McLuhan's own 1977 wording, preserved in the secondary literature, frames them as "in analogical proportion to each other" [4].

Harman's summary reproduces the book's compact statement of each law: Enhancement, "every technology extends or amplifies some organ or faculty of the user"; Obsolescence, "the attendant "closure"... when one area of experience is heightened or intensified, another is diminished or numbed"; Reversal, "every form, pushed to the limit of its potential, reverses its characteristics"; and Retrieval, "the content of any medium is an older medium" [1]. The reversal law carries an information-theory gloss in the book itself: "Any word or process or form, pushed to the limits of its potential, reverses its characteristics" [1]. And the book is explicit that retrieval is not simple revival — "Retrieval is not simply a matter of hauling the old thing back onto stage, holus-bolus. Some translation or metamorphosis is necessary to place it into relation to the new ground" — and adds that retrieval "always seems to provide the keynote or dominant mode of each tetrad," which is "why it is often the most difficult of the four to discover" [1].

Three structural commitments matter for everything that follows. First, the four laws are simultaneous, not sequential: the tetrad is a single structural snapshot, not a timeline. Second, the laws are said to be exhaustive. Eric McLuhan reports in the book that "We found these four ... and no more," and that his father spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and simultaneously for a single case in which one of the four did not apply — both efforts, Eric reports, were unsuccessful [1]. Third, the claim is scoped to human productions, not nature: Harman reports that "The McLuhans hold that their own tetrads are not universal, but apply only to the structure of language and hence only to human productions" [1]. This scope restriction — which Harman himself argues is too modest — is the load-bearing boundary of the whole book.

The book also embeds the laws in the figure/ground vocabulary McLuhan had used since the 1960s: enhancement and retrieval are the "figures," obsolescence and reversal the "grounds" of any artefact. The invitation the book extends is deliberately universal in its reach — the enhancement question, Sandstrom notes, "can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper, as well as about a proposition in Euclid or a law of physics. It can be asked about any word or phrase in any language" [10]. In short, the 1988 book makes a claim at three levels at once: a descriptive claim (these four effects actually occur for every artefact), a methodological claim (these four questions are the correct instrument for finding them), and a scientific claim (the result is a "new science" whose laws are stated so as to be capable of falsification — the subject of the next section). It is the tension among these three levels, not any single one, that the subsequent literature has spent thirty-five years working over.

### 2. Origins: the 1975 article and McLuhan's invitation to falsify

The tetrad did not first appear in the 1988 book. It first appeared in print in articles by McLuhan in the journals *Technology and Culture* (1975) and *et cetera* (1977), and only reached book form in the posthumous *Laws of Media* (1988) and *The Global Village* (1989) [2]. The 1975 article is the source of most of the tetrad's scientific self-presentation, and of the invitation to falsify that later critics took up.

In that 1975 article, "McLuhan's Laws of the Media," McLuhan described his procedure as inductive, and tied the laws to the figure/ground method he had been developing: "In formulating the Laws of the Media I have proceeded by induction, even though in the process of induction one discovers many things that could not be merely inducted. The Laws of the Media have been shaped by studying the effects of media so there is always a hidden ground upon which these effects stand, and against which they bounce" [3]. The framing was deliberately Popperian. According to the account the book itself later gives, in search of a properly scientific method to answer his critics McLuhan settled on falsifiability, and one evening he found the answer in Sir Karl Popper's *Objective Knowledge* – that a scientific statement was something stated in such a manner that it could be disproved [1]. Logan and Iseri, working from the book, quote its claim that Sir Karl Popper's statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media [4]. The subtitle chosen for the 1988 volume, *The New Science*, was, on this account, a direct claim that the project would place McLuhan's work "on a scientific basis" [4].

The origin story is more specific than a general appeal to Popper. The Brazilian–Portuguese systematic review reports that the four laws "were drafted after an intense review of *Understanding media* undertaken by Marshall and Eric McLuhan" in order "to find claims that could be tested, proven or refuted by anyone, anywhere and at any time. In other words, which could be presented as scientific principles" [6]. That is the claim Tyler later targeted directly: the idea that the tetrad's answers are checkable "by anyone, anywhere, at any time."

There is, however, a recorded counter-current to the scientific framing, and it is worth keeping in view because it explains the mixed register of the later debate. Paul Levinson — who organized the 1978 Tetrad Conference and knew McLuhan personally — reports that in the 1977 *et cetera* article McLuhan "joked that 'When I came across Karl Popper's principle that a scientific hypothesis is one that is capable of falsification, I decided to hypothesize the "Laws of the Media"'" [9]. Levinson's firsthand gloss: by which McLuhan meant that if the laws of the media are capable of falsification, they can't do too much damage — and Levinson, the paper notes, learned this in more than one in-person conversation with McLuhan [9]. So the historical record contains both a serious Popperian claim (falsifiability as the test of scientific law) and McLuhan's own off-the-record deflation of it (falsifiability as a low-cost insurance policy). Both are primary to the question of how literally the "laws" and "new science" language should be read, and both have been available to the scholars who argued over them ever since.

### 3. Applications: how scholars have run the tetrad since 1988

The most systematic picture of how the tetrad has actually been used in peer-reviewed work comes from Dall'Agnese, Canavilhas and Barichello's systematic review of applications in Brazilian and Portuguese communication research between 2009 and 2019, published in *Matrizes* in 2020 [6]. They located 21 studies, and found a varied use of the tetrad, both as a tool for analyzing technologies, platforms and media and as a tool for analyzing notions and concepts [6]. Social networks — specifically Facebook — were the most frequent object, followed by mobile devices and interfaces, cinema, internet memes, and educational platforms [6]. The list of the review's included works shows the range: television on the internet, Facebook, mobile journalism, memes, drones, live cinema, and the adaptation of the tetrad itself as a method for studying journalism's reconfiguration.

Two findings from that review are the most important for assessing the tetrad as an instrument. The first is non-reproducibility, stated as a property of the tool rather than a failure of individual authors: even if analyses of the four processes (enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, reversal) are constructed based on the same empirical objects, we will not have, in different researches, equal tetrads, and therefore the research path — from observation through theory to data collection — must be clear in the research report [6]. The second is the verdict that the tetrad functions as an opening rather than a closing device: it is an interesting way to organize perceptions about an object — as an opening exercise, not closing; useful as one component of a research's theoretical-methodological toolkit, but not enough by itself to draw conclusions in a broader investigation [6]. The review's overall assessment is blunt: adoption of the tetrad as a methodological tool seems incipient and lacking in problematization, with only two of the 21 studies proposing any adaptation of its four faces, and only five reflecting on the tetrad as a method or noting its limits [6]. In other words, the dominant pattern in the applied literature is to run the tetrad as a frame and report the results, without interrogating the frame.

Outside that corpus, the tetrad has been applied to a widening set of technological objects, almost always in the same essayistic register. Isabelle Adam's peer-reviewed 2016 essay in *Glocality* applies it to the smartphone: enhancement of accessibility and real-time communication; obsolescence of feature phones and, partially, the personal computer; retrieval of the camera and the book; reversal into augmented-reality wearables such as Google Glass, with a socio-psychological flip from facilitating communication to restricting it. Sui and Goodchild's widely cited 2003 paper in *The Canadian Geographer* runs a "tetradic analysis" of geographic information systems (GIS) as media for communicating social and environmental information — an early, influential application in a quantitative-adjacent discipline that helped the tetrad travel beyond media studies proper. In software engineering, Storey and colleagues' 2024 playbook in *ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology* adopts the tetrad as step one of a research method, noting that it "has been commonly used in recent years to evaluate technological innovations (Thomas, 2007)" [7]; their Table 1 runs the tetrad across machine languages, high-level programming languages, the internet, IDEs, and social coding, and they illustrate a full tetrad for Stack Overflow. The MDPI education paper by Takkeci and Erdem (2024) applies it to online architectural design studios. McLuhan's grandson Andrew McLuhan maintains an active public-facing account of the tetrad as a tool for exploring media effects. Across these cases the tetrad is consistently treated as a generative, four-question prompt rather than as a hypothesis to be confirmed — which is exactly the register Tyler recommends and the register the 1988 book's "new science" subtitle disclaims.

### 4. Extensions: Logan, Harman and the theoretical development of the tetrad

The theoretical development of the tetrad since 1988 runs along two main lines: an internal line that extends the tetrad's structure without leaving its assumptions (Levinson's tetrad wheels; Logan and Iseri's Laws of Media Environments and Users), and an external line that re-derives the tetrad's fourfold from more general principles and then argues its scope is too narrow (Harman).

**Levinson's tetrad wheels.** Paul Levinson proposed "tetrad wheels" at the Tetrad Conference he organized at Fairleigh Dickinson University in 1978, and the idea is reconstructed in full for the first time by Matthew Lindia and Levinson in *New Explorations* (2021) [9]. Levinson's original mapping gave each of the four laws a figure/ground position: "A) Intensification [enhancement] = Figure; B) Obsolescence = Pre-Ground; C) Retrieval = Pre-Figure; D) Reversal = Post-Ground" [9]. The wheel turns when one artefact makes way for the next: the reversal of one tetrad becomes the enhancement (figure) of the next, the old figure drops into obsolescence, and the formerly obsolesced is retrieved. The point of the device, in Lindia and Levinson's reconstruction, is to fix a shortcoming of the tetrad as McLuhan left it: the tetrad is a "snapshot" of a single medium's figure/ground relations, isolated from technological history, whereas the wheel chains tetrads diachronically, treating media evolution as a chiasmus in which figure and ground constantly reverse into one another [9]. Levinson's original formulation already contained the crucial caveat about prediction, which matters for the empirical-testing question in the next sections: tetradic analysis of culture may thus be historically descriptive but not predictive, thereby avoiding what Popper called the poverty of historicism [9]. The wheel, in other words, is a device for retrospection and inter-technology comparison, not a forecasting engine.

**Logan's threefold extension.** Robert K. Logan — McLuhan's collaborator and the most prolific contemporary exponent of the tetrad — extended the four laws into two parallel fourfolds, the Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and the Laws of Media Users (LOMU). The underlying claim, developed with Izabella Pruska-Oldenhof and others in the MDPI journal *Philosophies*, is that the ground in which an artefact operates, and the users of that artefact, undergo a parallel enhancement–obsolescence–retrieval–reversal cycle to the artefact itself [4]. LOME 1 states that every medium or technology creates a new environment or ground, and the remaining laws trace that environment's obsolescence, retrieval and flip [4]. LOMU 1 states that users of the new medium become its servomechanisms, with the user then flipping, with the medium, into the servomechanism of its successor [4]. Logan's reading also supplies the evolutionary framing: each tetrad cycle is linked to the previous one, so that the reversal of one artefact is the enhancement of the next — a continuous, spiraling emergence of new artefacts.

**Harman's re-derivation and scope objection.** Graham Harman, writing from object-oriented philosophy in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (2009), approaches the tetrad from outside media ecology. His general claim is that the only means of obtaining a rigorous quadruple structure is to cross-breed two dualisms, yielding a world split into four distinct zones, and he identifies the tetrad's two generating dualisms as figure/ground (the morphology of an artefact) and metamorphosis (how each term contains the seed of its opposite) [1]. On Harman's account the tetrad passes this test — its four poles are not arbitrary — and he reads the book as making enhancement flip into "final cause," so that a winning extension "begins to carry an air of the inevitable"; the tetrad thereby becomes, on his reading, an engine of counterfactual critique rather than a hymn to technological determinism [1]. His disagreement with the McLuhans is about scope, not validity: where the book holds that the tetrads apply only to the structure of language and hence only to human productions, Harman contends that the tetrads transform not just the philosophy of technology, but metaphysics as a whole, because every object, not only every artefact, is a medium [1]. Eric McLuhan's preface claim — that the tetrad is "the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of our time, but of at least the last couple of centuries" — is Harman's warrant for taking the tetrad seriously at all, and Harman is effectively its most ambitious philosophical endorser [1].

A smaller comparative thread treats the tetrad as an answer to an ancient fourfold. Sandstrom records that McLuhan prescribed the Four Effects as a complementary method to Aristotle's well-known Four Causes — material, efficient, formal and final — and quotes William Sheridan's 1990 judgment that the combination of the four causes and the four effects is the most comprehensive and capable framework developed so far for evaluating the impacts and implications of new technologies [10]. This positions the tetrad as completing, rather than replacing, the classical causal vocabulary — an extension of a different kind, one that later critics of the tetrad's scientific pretensions rarely engage.

### 5. Criticisms: Tyler's double bind and the status of the "laws"

The strongest and most influential criticism of the tetrad is Tom Tyler's "A Procrustean Probe," published in *Game Studies* in 2008. Tyler's title names the precise objection: Procrustes is the mythic bandit who stretched or cut his guests to fit an iron bed, and Tyler warns the tetrad is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles, hammering or shearing inconvenient empirical details to make them fit. His article is the clearest statement of why the tetrad fails as science and how it can nonetheless be used well.

Tyler quotes the book's own universal checkability claim — Eric McLuhan's statement that the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" — and replies: this is not, in fact, the case, as one of the McLuhans' own examples illustrates [5]. The example is wine. On a single page of *Laws of Media*, the authors give two different tetrads for the same artefact: in one, wine enhances grape juice, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, and reverses into cooking vinegar; in the alternative on the same page, it enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces inhibition, retrieves festive spontaneity of speech and gesture, and reverses into hangover and insult [5]. If the authors themselves cannot agree, Tyler reasons, the promise that anyone, anywhere will reach the same checked answer cannot hold.

From this he develops a double objection, which is the heart of the article. The tetrad is too loose: conceived as a universal "scientific method", the tetrad is far too vague — a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into; the laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit. And simultaneously too rigid: just like Procrustes' bed, McLuhan's tetrad is unrelentingly rigid — it requires us to fill the gaps [5]. His verdict on the scientific claim is the most-quoted sentence in the debate: the idea that these are "scientific laws" in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous [5].

Yet Tyler's conclusion is not that the tetrad should be abandoned. "And yet the tetrad has its uses," he writes, best conceived as a set of questions — what does a technology enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into — in the exploratory register McLuhan himself often used [5]. The key concession: the diversity of responses to its application need not be a problem — once we lose the cod-scientific rhetoric — so long as these provide illuminating insights [5]. Tyler then demonstrates the disciplined use of the probe on digital games, anchoring each quadrant in cited empirical research rather than free association — for example, he supports the obsolescence quadrant for MMORPGs with Yee's survey numbers, that gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing and 7.7 hours watching television, against a national television average of about 28, which lends support to the claim that time spent watching TV has been displaced by MMORPG playing [5]. His closing sentence states the general principle: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us" [5].

Three other strands complete the critical picture. First, McLuhan's own response to an early tester. When William Henry Venable, writing in *Technology and Culture* in 1976, took the invitation to falsify seriously and tried to relate the tetrads to Peirce's logic of signs, McLuhan replied that this was a category error: "The whole point about my tetrads is that they are _ana_logical. That is, there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios" [3]. When pressed on the testability claim, in other words, McLuhan retreated from logic to analogy — a move Tyler and later critics treat as the tell that the "laws" were never meant as laws in the ordinary sense. Second, even the tetrad's strongest academic exponents concede the point from inside. Logan and Iseri write that the laws of media "are not strictly scientific laws," because a law of media "does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into"; it is "more of an exploratory tool or probe," and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions" [4]. Third, the Brazilian–Portuguese review reaches the same verdict independently from the applied side: despite dozens of worked examples, "the four media laws are theoretically poorly developed," which hampers their identification in use [6]. And Levinson's own tetrad-wheel work had already stated the consequence in 1978 terms: tetradic analysis is historically descriptive but not predictive, sidestepping Popper's poverty of historicism rather than claiming predictive power [9].

The upshot is a near-consensus in the scholarly literature, reached from three different directions — a hostile critic (Tyler), a sympathetic exponent (Logan), and a neutral systematic review — that the tetrad is not a set of scientific laws in any falsifiable sense, and that its value lies elsewhere: as a question-generating probe whose outputs are illuminating but non-unique and non-predictive.

### 6. Empirical testing: what has actually been tried

The direct answer to the empirical-testing question is that no one has tested the tetrad as a set of falsifiable laws in anything like the way a scientific law is tested — no experimental manipulation, no systematic attempt to find counterexamples against a pre-registered prediction, no measurement of inter-rater agreement across coders, no test of whether the tetrad predicts outcomes better than chance. What exists instead is a spectrum of weaker engagements, and it is worth being precise about each rung.

**Historical and empirical checking, in McLuhan's own loose sense.** Lindia and Levinson, looking back from 2021, observe that for the most part, scholars have followed McLuhan's request to test the laws' validity historically and empirically, but that this activity eclipsed the philosophical evaluation of the tetrad [9]. What this means in practice is that the applied literature (section 3) is full of examples where a tetrad's individual quadrants are checked against historical or observational facts: the smartphone demonstrably obsolesced the feature phone's market; the MMORPG time-use numbers Tyler cites are consistent with games displacing television. That is evidence for individual instances of individual quadrants, not a test of the general claim that every artefact exhibits all four effects, and not a test of the "laws" as laws.

**Tyler's MMORPG quadrant is the closest thing to a check in the literature.** In his own disciplined application, Tyler anchors the obsolescence quadrant to survey data rather than intuition: MMORPG players report 21.0 hours per week of play and 7.7 hours of television, which together approach the national television average of roughly 28 hours — "this lends support to the claim that time that was spent watching TV has been displaced by MMORPG playing" [5]. Note the epistemic modesty: the finding "lends support" to one quadrant of one artefact. Tyler draws no conclusion about the other three quadrants from that data, and no conclusion about the tetrad as a whole. This is checking a local empirical claim, not testing a law.

**Thomas's operationalization (2007) is a methodological proposal, not a test.** The one work whose stated purpose is "operationalizing" the tetrad is John Charles Thomas's 2007 conference paper and Iowa State thesis, Operationalizing McLuhan's Tetrad to Focus on Innovation Effects. Its abstract states the aim precisely: to operationalize the tetrad and demonstrate that it can also be used as an investigative research tool for new product innovation. That is an argument for transplanting the four questions from media to product design, with a structured study design (its Figure 3 is reproduced as "Tetrad study design"), not an empirical test of whether the four effects occur. Storey and colleagues' 2024 playbook, which cites Thomas, treats the tetrad exactly this way: as step one of a research method for disruptive innovations, an instrument for generating and organizing observations rather than a hypothesis to confirm [7].

**The nearest approximation to a test of coverage: Takkeci and Erdem (2024).** The MDPI higher-education paper on online design studios runs the closest thing to an empirical procedure with the tetrad as an explicit analytic frame. Its method is a systematic review: the authors "identified 176 records of peer-reviewed empirical studies for further analysis and 20 papers were read and included in the review, defining repeating topics/themes and organized under four categories" — the four tetrad categories [8]. The result is a demonstration that findings from independent empirical studies can be sorted into enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval and reversal without remainder, which the authors take as evidence that the tetrad "revolves around four questions based on empirical observation" rather than theory [8]. But sorting post hoc is not the same as predicting: the test would require that the four categories be specified in advance and shown to exhaust the observed effects better than an alternative taxonomy, which this paper does not attempt. The authors themselves describe the tetrad as a hermeneutic tool for critical interpretation, not as a falsifiable law [8].

**A revealing asymmetry: which quadrants get studied.** Storey et al. note, in passing, that in the prior research they survey, most research focuses on the enhances dimension, with some research on what it made obsolete, while less research so far has considered McLuhan's retrieve and reverse dimensions [7]. This is the empirical-testing situation in miniature: the quadrants that are easiest to observe (enhancement, obsolescence) attract the most evidence, while the two quadrants that would be hardest to verify or falsify — retrieval and reversal — are the least studied. A genuine test of the tetrad would need all four, and the two hardest are the least touched.

The overall finding, then, is that the tetrad has been *applied* to empirical material and *used* to organize empirical findings, but has not been *tested* in any strong sense. The reasons are not mysterious: as section 5 documents, the tetrad's own exponents concede it makes no unique predictions and permits multiple correct answers, which removes the property — unique, checkable predictions — that would make a decisive empirical test possible. Levinson's formulation, that tetradic analysis is historically descriptive but not predictive, is the field's own acknowledgment of why this is so [9]. Any future empirical test would have to settle, first, what claim exactly is being tested: the weak claim (these four questions are a useful way to organize observations) is already amply supported by the applied literature; the strong claim (every artefact necessarily exhibits all four effects, and the answers are checkable by anyone, anywhere, at any time) has never been operationalized in a way that could fail.


## Beyond this question

The most practically useful thing the literature yields is a specification for how to use the tetrad without reproducing its failure mode. Tyler's article, read carefully, is not a dismissal but a design brief, and the applied review's findings corroborate it. A defensible tetrad application names a concrete artefact and concrete practices (not abstractions like "ritual"); anchors each quadrant in cited evidence or reports a genuinely empty quadrant rather than filling it; defines obsolescence as displacement, not extinction, and reversal as an already-observable potential rather than futurology; states the two dualisms that generate the fourfold (Harman's test); and — most importantly — generates at least two rival tetrads for the same artefact and publishes the disagreement, converting the wine problem from a hidden flaw into a visible feature. Levinson's caveat supplies the boundary: the tetrad describes what has happened, it does not predict what will happen, so any forecast attached to a tetrad must carry a separate, dated, checkable stake. These are the conditions under which a generative instrument whose outputs are hypotheses can be used honestly; they follow directly from Tyler [5], Logan and Iseri [4], the Brazilian–Portuguese review [6], and Harman [1], and they are what a research practice that wants the tetrad's diagnostic reach without its scientific pretensions should adopt.

## Open questions

The genuine open questions, stated plainly:

- **No strong empirical test exists.** After searching the applied and theoretical literature, I found no study that tests the tetrad as a set of falsifiable laws: no pre-registered prediction, no inter-rater reliability measurement across independent coders applying it to the same artefact, no systematic search for a counterexample to the claim that every artefact exhibits all four effects. The nearest engagements — Tyler's data-anchored quadrant [5], Takkeci and Erdem's post-hoc sorting of 20 empirical studies into the four categories [8], and Thomas's operationalization proposal — are applications, not tests. Anyone claiming the tetrad has been "empirically validated" is overstating what the literature contains.
- **Whether the four categories are exhaustive.** The book's claim that every human production manifests exactly these four dimensions, and no fifth, has never been tested against an alternative taxonomy. Takkeci and Erdem's sort shows the categories can absorb findings post hoc; it does not show they do so better than, say, a cost/benefit, intended/unintended, or short/long-term scheme, because no comparison was run.
- **The two hard quadrants are unoperationalized.** Retrieval and reversal are, by the field's own account, the least studied and the hardest to verify — Storey et al. note that prior work concentrates on enhancement and obsolescence [7], and the book itself calls retrieval "often the most difficult of the four to discover" [1]. No one has published a workable operational definition of retrieval or reversal that would let two independent researchers agree on whether a given instance has occurred.
- **What "law" means is still unsettled.** The literature has converged on the negative claim — the tetrad is not a law in the scientific sense — but has not settled the positive one. Tyler says "probe" or "set of questions"; Logan and Iseri say "exploratory tool"; Harman treats it as a metaphysical fourfold with real philosophical content. These are different claims about the same object, and no one has adjudicated them.
- **The fifth-law search remains open on the book's own terms.** The McLuhans reported that Marshall spent his last years looking for a fifth law and for a single case where one of the four did not apply, without success; Lindia and Levinson record later attempts (for example, Frank Zingrone's proposed law of syncretism) and their failure to stick. Whether that failure reflects the fourfold's genuine completeness or, as Harman argues, the fact that it is built from two dualisms and therefore cannot have a fifth pole, is a live philosophical question, not an empirical one.

Coverage note: this report rests on the primary statements of the tetrad (the 1975 and 1977 articles as quoted in the secondary literature, and the 1988 book as quoted by Harman, Sandstrom, Logan and Iseri), on Tyler's critique read in full, on the one systematic review of applications, on Logan and Iseri's and Lindia–Levinson's extensions, and on representative applied papers. I could not read the 1988 book's own full text in a machine-readable form (the accessible scans have no text layer), so every quotation from the book is as reproduced in the scholarly sources named; where the exact wording of the book matters most — the preface's "five laws" account and the four questions — I have relied on Harman's and Sandstrom's reproductions, which agree with each other.

label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Canada's National Pharmacare Since 2024: Agreements, Coverage, Uptake, and the Cost Estimates
report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act did and the first-phase scope

The *Pharmacare Act* (Bill C-64, "An Act respecting pharmacare") received royal assent on October 10, 2024, and — per Health Canada's own announcement the same day — "immediately came into force" [7][21]. It is important to be precise about what the Act is and is not. It does not create a single national drug plan, and it does not itself deliver coverage to any Canadian. Its operative funding clause is conditional and narrow: the Minister "must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [7]. In other words, the Act's first phase is a federal transfer program that only turns on where a province or territory signs a bilateral agreement, and it is scoped to two therapeutic categories — contraception and diabetes — not to prescription drugs generally.

The framing at launch was national in ambition. Health Canada said the agreements "will support reproductive freedom by providing up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada free access to contraception" and that "the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes will have universal access to a suite of medications" [21]. (Health Canada's own website later rounds the diabetes figure up slightly, as "About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes" [5].) But those are the populations who *would* be covered *if* every jurisdiction signed and implemented; the Act itself does not guarantee that outcome, which is why the actual delivery record, set out in the following sections, is much smaller.

The Act also created a set of institutions and deliverables. Health Canada's release states that the Act "will also establish a fund for diabetes devices and supplies to help Canadians manage and monitor their diabetes and administer their medication" and that it requires Canada's Drug Agency develop a list of essential drugs and related products to inform the development of a national formulary, "a national bulk purchasing strategy to help further reduce drug prices," and a pan-Canadian strategy on the appropriate use of prescription medications, plus that "a committee of experts be established within thirty days to make recommendations on the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [21]. These have all been produced: the Committee of Experts delivered its final report (tabled late 2025), and Canada's Drug Agency delivered advice on bulk purchasing, an essential-medicines list, and an appropriate-use strategy [5]. None of these, however, is coverage; they are planning instruments toward a full national formulary that does not yet exist.

One threshold fact matters for everything that follows. The Act contemplates a first phase, not the full program. Health Canada's phrasing is explicit that the contraception-and-diabetes coverage is "the first phase of a national universal pharmacare program" [21]. The "full program" — a single-payer plan covering a comprehensive list of drugs for all Canadians — remains legislative intent and planning advice, not law. The cost estimates for that full program (Section 5) are therefore estimates of something that has not been built and, as of late 2026, is not being funded toward.

### 2. Which provinces and territories signed agreements, when, and what each covers

As of the most recent update of Health Canada's own "National pharmacare bilateral agreements" page (dated January 26, 2026), exactly four jurisdictions have signed: "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free" [1]. They are, in order of signing, Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Yukon. Nine provinces and territories — Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut — had no agreement as of that date [10][22].

**Manitoba (first to sign, February 27, 2025).** Manitoba signed the first agreement. Health Canada's release: "Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [2]. The same release said the deal would support the reproductive freedom of "nearly 350,000 Manitobans" and that "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes" could access the medications [2]. Manitoba delivered the coverage through a new provincial vehicle, the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program (MEPP), which took effect April 15, 2025 [12]. Two details distinguish Manitoba's implementation. First, the federal funding also covered diabetes devices and supplies through a separate stream. Second, Manitoba added coverage beyond the two federal categories — including hormone replacement therapy (HRT) and HIV prevention and treatment — a point returned to in Section 3.

**British Columbia (March 6, 2025).** Health Canada announced BC's agreement the next week: an investment of "more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [3]. The actual funding agreement is more granular and slightly different from the news-release framing. The scheduled Stream 1 transfers are $17,406,567 in fiscal 2025-26 and $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29, plus a one-time Stream 2 payment of $37,839,549 in 2026-27 for diabetes devices and supplies; the agreement runs to March 31, 2029, and BC's "Implementation Date will be March 1, 2026" [23]. There is a small discrepancy worth flagging: BC's own news release describes the federal money as "up to $670 million in funding over three years" [11], while Health Canada's release says "over four years" [3]. The four scheduled Stream 1 transfers ($17,406,567, $204,948,289, $204,948,289 and $204,948,289) plus the $37,839,549 Stream 2 payment add up, on my own arithmetic, to about $670 million — essentially the round figure both governments cite [23]. The agreement's term spans four fiscal years of drug funding (2025-26 through 2028-29) plus the device payment, so whether one describes the deal as "three years" (BC's release) or "four years" (Health Canada's release) is a matter of what one counts; the agreement text is the controlling document [11][3]. BC's agreement also committed the province, at its own cost, to "provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies identified by British Columbia to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents" effective March 1, 2026 [23] — an add-on beyond the federal list, parallel to Manitoba's HRT add-on.

**Prince Edward Island (March 7, 2025).** PEI signed third, "more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents" [24] (the same figure was confirmed in CBC and Canadian Press coverage). Health Canada's release said the deal would "support the reproductive freedom of over 41,000 Islanders" and ensure "over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes can access essential medications" [24]. PEI coverage began May 1, 2025 — the fastest implementation of the four — and included diabetes devices and supplies from that date [16].

**Yukon (announced March 2025; program launched April 15, 2026).** Yukon was the only territory to sign. Health Canada's release said the agreement would invest "up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon" [25]. The executed agreement specifies Stream 1 maximums of $2,548,410 (2026-27), $2,650,056 (2027-28) and $2,650,056 (2028-29), plus a one-time $306,143 Stream 2 payment for diabetes devices, ending March 31, 2029 [17]. Yukon's program launched April 15, 2026, making it the last of the four to go live and the only jurisdiction whose coverage began after the federal election that replaced the government that had signed the deals [19][26].

A consistent theme across all four: the money is modest relative to the full-program costings discussed in Section 5. The four agreements' combined federal envelope is on the order of $930 million over four years — roughly $219 million (Manitoba) plus roughly $670 million (BC) plus roughly $30 million (PEI) plus roughly $9.5 million (Yukon). The actual federal cash flowed so far is smaller still: $88.1 million in 2025-26, per the CCPA's reading of the Spring 2026 Economic Update [10].

The political turn is as important as the signatures. By July 2025, Health Minister Marjorie Michel (of the government elected that spring) told reporters that "this is a new government in a new context," and her office said the government would "protect the four signed pharmacare agreements" but would not say whether new ones were planned [27][28]. The Canadian Press reported at the time that the minister was "not committing to sign pharmacare funding deals with all provinces and territories" [27]. That framing — reflected in CBC's contemporaneous observation that national pharmacare may become a regional privilege afforded to only four of Canada's 13 provinces and territories — proved accurate: no further agreements were signed through late 2026 [27].

### 3. Coverage details: drugs, devices and who is eligible

The first-phase benefit is deliberately narrow, and Health Canada's own guidance is explicit about its limits. The "What's covered" page states that pharmacare covers only the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee, and does not cover delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees [4]. Coverage is defined by the Annex A lists in each bilateral agreement, not by diagnosis: a product is covered only if it appears on the agreed list, regardless of why it was prescribed.

**Contraception.** The covered categories span both drugs and devices. Health Canada's summary lists oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal intrauterine devices (IUDs), vaginal rings, implants (the etonogestrel implant) and injectable contraceptives (medroxyprogesterone), plus emergency contraception (levonorgestrel) [5]. BC's agreement Annex A makes the granularity visible: specific combination oral contraceptives by active ingredient (levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol, desogestrel/ethinyl estradiol, drospirenone/ethinyl estradiol, norethindrone/ethinyl estradiol, norgestimate/ethinyl estradiol), progestin-only pills (norethindrone, drospirenone), injectable medroxyprogesterone, the etonogestrel implant, emergency levonorgestrel, copper IUDs, progestogen IUDs and the etonogestrel/ethinyl estradiol vaginal ring [23]. A "Low Cost Alternative" policy applies to several brand-name products in BC — for example, a resident choosing Alesse or Min-Ovral over a generic pays the difference, while "other free options are available" [23]. This means "free" in practice means free at the lowest-cost interchangeable version, not free for any brand on the list.

**Diabetes.** The covered drug classes are metformin, insulins, sulfonylureas, SGLT-2 inhibitors and (in BC's case) DPP-4 inhibitors and pioglitazone [5][11]. BC's list details porcine, human and analogue insulins (including lispro, aspart, glulisine, glargine and their blends), metformin, glyburide, gliclazide, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin, saxagliptin, linagliptin and pioglitazone [11][23]. The glaring omission, noted in Manitoba's own documentation, is semaglutide: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [12]. GLP-1 receptor agonists — the most talked-about diabetes drug class of the decade — are therefore not part of first-phase pharmacare, and private insurers continue to cover them (the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association confirms the Act bars insurers from covering drugs the single-payer plan covers, but GLP-1s are not covered in the signed provinces, so insurers keep paying) [16]. Health Canada gives a sense of the costs at stake: typical annual drug costs run about $100 for metformin, $900 to $1,700 for insulin, and $100 to more than $1,000 for sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors [5].

**Devices and supplies (Stream 2).** Each agreement has a separate one-time envelope for diabetes devices and supplies, funded and reported apart from the drug list. Health Canada says the agreements "will also help you access the supplies you need" — insulin pumps, syringes, glucose monitors and test strips [5]. BC's Stream 2 is a one-time $37,839,549 payment (2026-27) to expand hybrid closed-loop glucose-monitor and insulin-delivery systems, add lancets, and add supplies for pump and glucose-monitor users [23]; BC devices/supplies coverage began April 1, 2026 [11]. Manitoba and PEI likewise covered devices/supplies through their own provincial programs, though in Manitoba the supplies remained in the existing deductible-based Manitoba Pharmacare Program rather than the new no-deductible MEPP [12].

**Provincial add-ons beyond the federal list.** Two provinces extended coverage past the two federal categories at their own initiative. Manitoba's MEPP covers, at no cost with no deductibles, birth control, diabetes, HIV prevention and treatment, and hormone replacement therapy [12] — that is, free HIV prevention/treatment and HRT are provincial additions on top of what Ottawa funds. BC added free menopausal hormone therapy from March 1, 2026 under its agreement's "additional coverage improvements" clause [23]. These add-ons matter for the uptake figures below: some of the "pharmacare" claims and prescriptions being counted (Manitoba's HRT and HIV medications, BC's menopause therapies) are provincial programs riding on the federal agreements, not the federal benefit itself.

**Who is eligible.** Eligibility is residency-based and universal, not income- or age-tested. Health Canada: "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your" income, age, or whether you have private insurance; you qualify if you live in a province or territory with an agreement, are eligible for provincial/territorial health insurance, and have a valid prescription [6]. Private insurance status is irrelevant — the program is single-payer and first-dollar, meaning it pays before private plans, which are barred from covering the same products [16][6]. Members of federal drug plans (Non-Insured Health Benefits, veterans, Canadian Forces, RCMP, corrections, refugees) keep their existing coverage rather than moving to provincial pharmacare [6][23]. In Yukon the program is administered by Pacific Blue Cross, requires a valid Yukon health card, and pays upfront "including for residents with private insurance" [26].

Two structural caveats are worth stating plainly. First, because eligibility is tied to provincial health insurance, anyone not enrolled in provincial/territorial health insurance — a meaningful population that includes people with precarious immigration status and some unhoused people — is outside the program even in the four signed jurisdictions. Second, "universal, single-payer, first-dollar" describes the design of the benefit in the four signed provinces, not the state of the country: roughly three-quarters of Canadians, living in the nine unsigned jurisdictions, have no federal pharmacare coverage at all.

### 4. How many people are using it: enrolment, claims and uptake

The honest answer to "how many people are using it" is that there is no single national count, and the federal government has not published one. What exists is a patchwork of provincial announcements, each counting different things over different periods, and several of the headline numbers conflate the federal pharmacare benefit with provincial programs that predate or go beyond it. This section separates what each jurisdiction has actually reported.

**Manitoba — the largest and longest-running uptake, but mostly provincial.** Manitoba's free birth control actually began October 1, 2024, under a provincial program, before the federal agreement was signed in February 2025 and before the federal-funded MEPP launched April 15, 2025 [18]. The province's March 2026 update reported "more than 55,000 women accessing free birth control and more than 200,000 prescriptions filled since the program launched in October 2024," plus more than 36,000 women saving monthly on free HRT [18]. The key caveat: the October 2024 birth-control launch predates federal funding, so a large share of these prescriptions were Manitoba dollars, not federal pharmacare dollars. Diabetes uptake under MEPP specifically has not been published as a clean figure; what is documented is that Ozempic (semaglutide) is expressly not covered by the federal list [12]. Health Canada's own planning numbers were that the deal would support nearly 350,000 Manitobans' reproductive freedom and 149,000 with diabetes [2].

**Prince Edward Island — the cleanest uptake figure.** PEI launched May 1, 2025, and its Department of Health and Wellness has reported actual use: "Over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [16]. Health Canada's planning estimates for PEI were over 41,000 Islanders for reproductive freedom and over 16,000 for diabetes [24]. The contrast between the ~20,000 diabetes users reported and the ~16,000 planning estimate is not a contradiction: the province counted people using covered diabetes medications and supplies, while the federal estimate counted people with diabetes who could benefit.

**British Columbia — the largest eligible population, launch too recent for a user count.** BC's Plan NP launched March 1, 2026, the last big launch and only weeks before the federal government signalled it would not expand further. The province has published eligibility-scale estimates rather than actual users: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [11]. As of the sources available for this report, no BC count of people actually claiming the new coverage had been published. BC also already had free prescription contraception before Plan NP, so the marginal population newly covered is smaller than the headline would suggest [11].

**Yukon — smallest, latest, no usage data yet.** Yukon's program launched April 15, 2026, and the territory's own communications frame it in terms of who is expected to be supported: "more than 12,000 Yukoners" for contraceptives "in addition to more than 3,000 Yukoners" for diabetes medications [19]. No actual claims or user counts had been published in the sources reviewed, which is unsurprising given the April 15 launch date.

Two things about these numbers need emphasis. First, they are not comparable: Manitoba counts prescriptions and people under a program that started before federal funding and includes provincial add-ons (HRT, HIV); PEI counts people who have actually accessed free contraception and diabetes drugs/supplies since May 1, 2025; BC and Yukon report eligible-population estimates, not users. Summing them would be misleading, and this report does not do so. Second, even the largest numbers are a small fraction of the population the Act was framed around. Health Canada said the first phase would support "up to nine million women and gender diverse people" for contraception and "3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes" for medications [21]; in practice, only residents of Manitoba, BC, PEI and Yukon — roughly 15 per cent of Canada's population — have any access, and within those four, the measured use to date is on the order of tens of thousands of people per jurisdiction, not millions. The gap between the legislative framing and the delivery record is the single most important fact about the program's first two years.

### 5. What the PBO and other independent estimates say the full program would cost

Cost estimates for "the full program" come in two families: estimates of a *comprehensive single-payer national pharmacare* (the original 2019–2023 debate, covering all or most drugs for all Canadians), and estimates of the *first phase* actually legislated in 2024 (contraception and diabetes only). The question asks about the full program, but the full program was never built; the most useful numbers are therefore the comprehensive-plan estimates, with the first-phase numbers as a reality check on what the Act itself would have cost.

**The PBO's comprehensive single-payer estimate (2023).** The Parliamentary Budget Officer's October 2023 report, *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan*, is the reference independent costing. Modelled on Quebec's RAMQ formulary as the baseline national list, the PBO estimated the incremental cost to the public sector (federal and provincial governments combined) at "$11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [9]. The gross incremental cost was higher — "$14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28" — with the difference explained by savings to public plans from renegotiated prices and reduced private-plan overhead [9]. Critically, the PBO found the plan would be net *cheaper* for the economy as a whole: cost savings on drug expenditures of $1.4 billion in 2024-25, rising to $2.2 billion in 2027-28, because the single-payer plan's expenditure growth (5.3 per cent a year) runs below the baseline (5.8 per cent) [9]. In other words, the PBO's headline is that a full single-payer plan costs governments roughly $11–13 billion a year more, while saving the country $1.4–2.2 billion a year in total drug spending — the classic "public cost up, economy cost down" finding.

The PBO also ran alternative formulary scenarios, which matter because they show how sensitive the answer is to what "full" means. A catastrophic-coverage formulary (covering only very high drug costs) would cost the public sector just $1.8 billion (2024-25) and $2.0 billion (2027-28); an essential-medicines formulary would cost only $0.4 billion and $0.3 billion more than baseline in those two years [9]. A comprehensive list is the expensive end; the narrower the formulary, the smaller the incremental public cost.

**The PBO's earlier estimate (2017).** In its September 2017 report *Federal Cost of a National Pharmacare Program*, the PBO costed the then-current framework differently — net cost *to the federal government alone*, not the combined public sector. The 2017 report put the net federal cost at "$19.3 billion," based on total prescription drug spending of roughly $28.5 billion in 2015-16 ($13.1 billion public, $10.7 billion private, $4.7 billion out-of-pocket), with an additional gross public-sector cost of $7.3 billion [20]. The two PBO numbers are not in conflict: the 2017 figure is a gross federal transfer figure in 2015-16 dollars under an immediate-implementation scenario; the 2023 figure is a combined-government incremental figure in 2024-25 dollars. Both are cited in the public debate, and it is easy to misread them as the "same" cost; they are different scopes, years and baselines.

**The Hoskins Advisory Council (2019).** The federal government's own advisory council, chaired by Dr. Eric Hoskins, estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines, rising to annual incremental costs of $15.3 billion in 2027 as the formulary grew to a comprehensive list [15]. The same report projected that by 2027 Canada "would spend $5 billion less on prescription drugs while at the same time improving access for all" — the economy-wide savings claim that the PBO's 2023 work independently reproduced at a smaller scale [10][9]. The $15.3 billion is the number most often quoted as "what full pharmacare would cost," and it is defensible, but it is the *incremental public cost in 2027 of a comprehensive formulary*, not an annual cost of the first phase.

**The Committee of Experts (2025).** The committee the Act itself created delivered the most recent independent estimate. It reported that total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in five years, from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024, and concluded that the total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars [14]. This is a narrower scope than Hoskins's comprehensive formulary — an essential-medicines list — and lands between the PBO's essential-medicines scenario and its comprehensive scenario. The committee also flagged that the non-taxation of employer-paid private drug-plan premiums is a roughly $5 billion-a-year public subsidy embedded in the current system, a point that matters for any cost comparison between private and public financing [14].

**The first phase, for contrast.** The numbers above are for the full program. The first phase actually legislated was much cheaper — and even then the estimates were contested. The government said the contraception-and-diabetes first phase would cost $1.5 billion over five years; the PBO's costing of Bill C-64 put it at "$1.9 billion over five years," $400 million higher [8]. The Fraser Institute argued both figures understate the true cost, because they assume nobody with existing private or provincial coverage switches plans, when in fact the Act's single-payer design displaces private coverage for the listed products [13]. The actual cash spent to date is far below all of these: $88.1 million in 2025-26, projected to rise to $269.6 million by 2028-29 under the four signed agreements [10].

**How to read these numbers together.** For the full comprehensive program, the defensible range is roughly $11–15 billion a year in incremental public cost (PBO 2023's $11.2–13.4 billion and Hoskins's $15.3 billion by 2027), against economy-wide savings of $1.4–2.2 billion a year (PBO) or $5 billion a year (Hoskins). For an essential-medicines-only plan, the Committee of Experts put it at $6–10 billion a year. For the first phase that actually became law, the estimate was $1.5–1.9 billion over five years, and actual spending has been a fraction of even that. The single most important caveat: every one of these is a modelling estimate of a program that, as of late 2026, has not been built past four jurisdictions and two drug categories, and none of the independent estimates includes the cost of the federal government's decision not to fund expansion.

### 6. What has not been delivered and where the program stands now

The gap between what the *Pharmacare Act* promised and what has been delivered is wide, and it widened rather than narrowed in 2026.

**Nine provinces and territories have nothing.** Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut — home to roughly 85 per cent of Canada's population — have no federal pharmacare agreement [1][22]. Their residents continue to rely on their own provincial/territorial drug plans, private insurance, or out-of-pocket payment. New Brunswick is the clearest case of a jurisdiction that wanted *something* but not *this*: its Liberal government told reporters it had not made progress on a deal and had not heard from Ottawa since the April 2025 election, and that it supports the principle but not the federal design, instead asking Ottawa to fund contraception access as a first step and put any further money toward making its existing plans more affordable [28]. Saskatchewan said it would "engage constructively" but needed to know whether the program would enhance its existing coverage [28]. The absence is not just federal reluctance; it is also provincial ambivalence about a single-payer design that displaces private coverage.

**The federal government stopped expanding, then signalled non-renewal.** The sequence is documented. In July 2025, Health Minister Marjorie Michel said Canada has "a new government in a new context" and her office would "protect the four signed pharmacare agreements" without committing to new ones [27][28]. The Spring 2026 Economic Update then contained no new pharmacare funding, and its fiscal projections reportedly did not include renewal of the four agreements past their March 2029 expiry [10]. The CCPA's analysis put the arithmetic plainly: bilateral health funding falls from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28, while the pharmacare line item rises from $88.1 million in 2025-26 to $269.6 million in 2028-29 before the existing agreements lapse [10]. In April 2026, PEI's health minister said Ottawa would cut $29 million in health funding to the province over three years [10]. Newfoundland and Labrador's health minister said "the door was closed" [10]. Budget 2026 (tabled November 5, 2026) confirmed the direction: it did not boost health transfers, and the Canada Health Transfer's guaranteed minimum annual growth rate is slated to fall from 5 per cent to 3 per cent in 2028 [22]. NDP Leader Avi Lewis called for deals with the nine unsigned jurisdictions ahead of the budget; the policy was "absent from Thursday's document" [22].

**What the four signed provinces have is time-limited.** Every agreement ends March 31, 2029 [23][26]. Yukon's own communications are explicit that the program's "future beyond that" depends on renewed federal funding [26]. So even the delivered pharmacare — contraception and diabetes drugs free at the counter for residents of Manitoba, BC, PEI and Yukon — is a four-year bridge with no committed continuation.

**What has not been delivered, specifically.** Beyond the nine unsigned jurisdictions: no national formulary (the essential-drugs list is advisory work product, not coverage); no bulk-purchasing agreement binding the country (the strategy exists as advice); no single-payer coverage for any drug outside the contraception/diabetes lists; no federal coverage of GLP-1 diabetes drugs such as semaglutide, the largest-ticket diabetes item [12]; and no path to the "comprehensive" or even "essential-medicines" formulary that the independent costings in Section 5 priced [14][15]. The diabetes device fund was paid in modest one-time Stream 2 amounts to BC and Yukon (and delivered through provincial programs in Manitoba and PEI), but it is not an ongoing national benefit.

**The political stakes.** The program's architects framed pharmacare as the unfinished business of medicare, and the Act's own purpose clause commits Canada to "continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" [23]. The record since October 2024 shows the opposite trajectory: a first phase signed with four willing jurisdictions in early 2025, then a change of government, then an explicit halt. The honest summary is that the *Pharmacare Act* delivered a small, regional, time-limited first phase — free contraception and a subset of diabetes drugs for about 15 per cent of Canadians — and, as of late 2026, the federal government is not expanding it and is not committing to renew it. Everything beyond that remains a cost estimate and a set of expert recommendations, not a program.
