report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. The policy landscape: which jurisdictions have adopted bans or restrictions and what they actually require

School phone restrictions have moved from a handful of national initiatives to a mainstream policy in a few years. UNESCO's Global Education Monitoring Report tracks national bans: by March 2026, "114 education systems now have a national ban on mobile phones in schools, representing 58% of countries worldwide. The expansion has been rapid. Less than 1 in 4 countries (24%) had bans in June 2023, when it was first monitored in the 2023 GEM Report. By early 2025 this had risen to 40%" [24]. A parallel count cited in the Florida evaluation puts a quarter of countries with a ban in 2023, rising to 31% in 2024 [4]. The two counts differ in definition — UNESCO counts education systems with a *national* ban, the Florida paper counts countries with a ban "through a law or policy" — but the trajectory is the same.

Beneath the headline numbers, jurisdictions differ sharply in what "ban" means, in three dimensions: legal force (statute versus guidance versus agreement), scope (class time only versus the whole day including breaks), and where the phone must be (out of sight in a bag versus locked away versus handed in).

**France is the canonical legislated ban.** A 2010 law already barred use in class; the 2018 "detox" law extended this so pupils are "banned from using mobile phones anywhere on school grounds" in nursery, primary and middle schools (collèges, to about age 15), including "in school playgrounds, at breaktimes and anywhere on school premises" [23]. High schools were not covered by the 2018 law. Enforcement detail was deliberately left open, and some schools argued lockers were costly and that schools lacked the legal right to confiscate phones [23].

**England uses guidance, not statute.** The Department for Education's guidance, updated 19 January 2026, states that "All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only" [18]. It requires schools to prohibit phones and functionally similar devices (smartwatches and anything that can send notifications or record audio/video) "throughout the school day, including during lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime" [18]. But the document itself is labelled "non-statutory guidance," and UNESCO's description is accurate: the expectation "is reinforced through school inspection frameworks, yet the policy leaves implementation decisions to individual schools" [24]. The policy model is therefore guidance plus inspection pressure, not a law. What England's schools actually do falls short of the guidance's ambition: a 2024 classification of secondary schools found 11% with an "effective ban" (phones not allowed in school, or stored at the start of the day), 52% "ban, but phone present" (in bags), 36% "partial ban" (class only), and none with no ban at all [33].

**The Netherlands uses a national agreement.** A ban on phones in the classroom "was first introduced in January 2024 for secondary education, and it was extended to include primary education as of the 2024/2025 school year" [19]. It covers the classroom, and by the 2024/25 year also primary schools. Critically, "While the measure is government promoted, it is up to the individual education institutions to provide concrete rules and to determine what the policy will look like in practice" [19]. The Dutch monitor found almost all secondary schools had complied, with close to two-thirds requiring phones to be left at home or in lockers and about one in five collecting them at the start of lessons [20].

**Ontario is a restriction, not a confiscation regime.** Under rules that took effect 1 September 2024 through the provincial Code of Conduct, "Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher. Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher" [17]. Phones stay with students, silent and out of view: "If an educator sees a mobile device that is not stored out of view, they will ask it to be handed in for the class (Grades 7-12) or for the day (Grades k-6)" [17]. So Ontario bars use during class for older students and during the whole day for younger ones, but does not collect or lock devices as a default.

**Australian states run the full-day model, applied to government schools.** Victoria was first, banning phones in government schools from 2020 with phones switched off and stored securely during the day [26]. South Australia bans phones in all public schools throughout the day "from the first bell to the last," including recess and lunch [26]. Western Australia bans them in public schools — kindergarten to year 6 phones are stored with teachers, years 7–12 must be off and out of sight [26]. Tasmania bans them during school hours including recess and lunch; the Northern Territory bans phones in primary schools and requires secondary students to be "off and away all day" [26]. New South Wales banned phones in public primary schools earlier and extended the ban to public high schools from the start of Term 4 2023 (9 October 2023): phones "turned off and out of sight" during class, recess and lunch, with students still permitted to carry them to and from school, and schools choosing among off-and-away, lockers, locked pouches or front-office collection [28]. Queensland was last, banning phones and smartwatches in all state schools during school hours including breaks from Term 1 2024 [27]. Queensland's announcement illustrates how much of the policy was codifying practice: over 95% of its state schools already had a classroom ban, but about 15% did not extend it to break times, and students could still bring phones for travel before and after school [27].

**The United States is a patchwork of state policy.** There is no nationwide ban. By late 2026, per UNESCO, "39 states now have statewide bans (15) or regulations requiring school districts to adopt policies restricting phone use in classrooms (24)" [24]. Florida's July 2023 HB 379, the most studied, prohibits students from using wireless devices at school during instructional time, except when expressly directed by a teacher solely for educational purposes, covering smartphones, earbuds, headphones and smartwatches [4]. The US also illustrates the strictest end of the implementation spectrum: lockable pouch (Yondr) adoption, where phones are magnetically sealed on arrival and inaccessible until dismissal [11].

Two general points emerge. First, most bans are "use" bans rather than "possession" bans — the phone may be on the student, just off and away; the strict physical binding of pouches or central collection is the exception. Second, the policy question is rarely binary. UNESCO's own monitoring stresses that "while limiting phone use may help reduce classroom distraction, it does not remove the need for students to learn how to navigate digital environments." It also notes a parallel movement of countries requiring schools to develop restrictive policies rather than imposing blanket prohibitions [24]. The policy landscape is better described as a spectrum of restrictions than a set of uniform bans.

### 2. Learning and academic achievement: what the evaluations measure and find

The learning question is the most-studied dimension of school phone bans, and the results are split between an older European literature finding real gains and newer, larger US studies finding close to zero.

**The founding positive result is English.** Beland and Murphy's study (published in *Labour Economics*, 2016) surveyed schools in four English cities about when they banned phones and linked that to national pupil data. Using a difference-in-differences design exploiting schools' staggered, autonomous decisions to ban, they found "student performance in high stakes exams significantly increases post ban" [9]. The gain was about 0.07 standard deviations on average, and it was "driven by the lowest-achieving students" [9]. The authors' interpretation is that phones distract, and the students with the least existing academic capital lose the most attention.

**The Scandinavian replication found nothing.** Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors (*Economics of Education Review*, 2020) replicated the design in Sweden — where a 2018 law lifted a prior ban on phones in secondary schools, creating policy variation in both directions — and found "we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" of about 0.024 standard deviations [10]. The contradiction is direct: the same empirical strategy, applied in a similar country, produced a null where England produced 0.07 SD.

**The largest and most recent US studies find near-zero average effects.** The nationwide lockable-pouch study (Allcott et al., NBER working paper 35132, April 2026, revised September 2026) covers 4,608 US public schools that adopted Yondr pouches, estimated with a staggered difference-in-differences design against matched never-treated schools. On achievement, the average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero, and the authors can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations over the first three years [6]. That average hides heterogeneity: "high schools see modest positive effects while middle schools see small negative effects," and for math specifically, "adoption in high schools increases student achievement by roughly 0.024 student-level standard deviations" — about a 0.9 percentile-point gain — while middle schools show small negative effects [6]. Attendance effects are also precisely null: improvements larger than 0.189 percentage points can be ruled out, trivial against a 93% mean attendance rate [6].

**Florida's statewide ban shows a small, delayed gain with a first-year cost.** The Florida study (Figlio and Ozek, NBER working paper 34388) evaluates the July 2023 HB 379 ban in a large urban district. Student test scores improved by "0.6 percentiles" overall, with spring test scores up "1.1 percentiles in the second year relative to the spring test right before the ban took effect" [4]. The dynamics matter: the gain appears in year two, "which is also when disciplinary incidents began to decline after an initial surge following the cellphone ban" [4]. The first-year cost was real and unequally distributed: suspensions up 12% relative to the comparison-group mean, in-school suspensions up roughly 20%, and in-school suspensions up about 30% among Black students, before dissipating [4]. A striking mechanistic finding: "nearly half of the test score effects of the ban in middle and high schools in the first two years can be explained by the effect of the ban on unexcused absences" [4] — meaning much of the Florida learning gain may run through attendance and engagement rather than through restored attention in class.

**Brazil and Spain find larger positive effects outside the Anglosphere.** In Rio de Janeiro, a municipal ban on non-pedagogical phone use (August 2023 classrooms, February 2024 school-wide) improved an index of math and Portuguese standardized test scores by 0.06 standard deviations in treatment schools relative to control [25]. Because phone use also fell in control schools, the authors estimate the total gain where the ban actually changed usage could be on the order of 0.2 standard deviations. Effects were positive for both subjects, somewhat larger and more precise in math [25]. In Spain, Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's synthetic-control study of the two regions that banned phones from 2015 found Galicia's PISA scores rose by around 10 points in maths and 12 in sciences relative to a synthetic control — "equivalent to 0.6–0.8 years of learning in maths and around 0.72 to near one year of learning in sciences" [14]. These are large effects by education-policy standards, but they rest on two treated regions and a synthetic-control design, and the authors frame them as effects of enforcing use-for-learning-only rather than of categorical prohibition [14].

**The only English individual-level evaluation finds no attainment difference.** The SMART Schools study (Goodyear et al., *Lancet Regional Health – Europe*, 2025), comparing 20 restrictive and 10 permissive English secondary schools with 1,227 students, found no differences in academic attainment in English or maths between the two groups [21]. This is cross-sectional rather than a causal design, but it is the closest England has to a direct test of the current policy, and it found nothing on learning.

The one randomised controlled trial on the learning question is recent, large, and college-level rather than school-level. Sungu, Choudhury and Bjerre-Nielsen (*Science*, 2026) randomly assigned 420 department-grade units — 16,683 students across 10 higher-education institutions in Odisha, India — to mandatory in-class phone collection or business-as-usual for one semester. The intent-to-treat effect on GPA was 0.073 standard deviations (95% CI 0.003 to 0.144), with 60–80% of grades coming from externally set, off-site, blinded exams, and the largest gains among lower-performing and first-year students [29]. An independent assessment flags the estimate as "borderline, with a confidence interval beginning at 0.003 and an unexplained one-sided test" [29]. It is the cleanest causal evidence that removing phones from a room improves grades, but it tests a lecture-time collection policy in Indian colleges, not a whole-day school policy for adolescents.

Reconciling the literature: the studies that find learning gains (England 2016, Spain, Brazil, Florida's year-two effect, India's college RCT) tend to be older, smaller, or from settings where phones were newly and sharply removed; the studies that find nothing on average (Sweden 2020, the US pouch study, SMART Schools) tend to be newer, larger, or to measure the policy as actually implemented. The honest reading is not that one side is right and the other wrong, but that the effect of a phone ban on learning is heterogeneous — positive for some schools, grades, subjects and students, and absent or slightly negative for others — and that the average effect in the most rigorous large-scale estimates is small and frequently indistinguishable from zero.

### 3. Attention, distraction and classroom behaviour

The starting point for any attention claim is how much distraction there is to reduce. The best cross-national baseline is OECD's PISA 2022, reported in *PISA in Focus*: "Nearly one in three students, on average across OECD countries, reported that students in their classes are distracted by using digital devices in most or every mathematics lesson." Roughly one in four report being distracted by *other students'* devices [16]. That is a large pool of classroom distraction, and it is the pool the ban advocates are responding to.

The causal chain the bans rest on has three links: phones cause in-class distraction, bans cut phone use, and less phone use restores attention. The evidence is strongest on the middle link and weakest on the first and last.

**The middle link holds.** The US lockable-pouch study (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow and Jacob, NBER working paper, April 2026) covers 4,608 US schools that adopted Yondr-style phone pouches, estimated with staggered difference-in-differences. The share of students reported to be using their phones in class for personal reasons "falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools" [6]. In other words, strict bans do sharply cut in-class personal phone use.

**The last link does not clearly hold.** The same study finds "little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [6]. That is the single most important finding for this section: a policy that reduced in-class phone use by roughly 80 percent produced no clear measured improvement in attention. The authors add a caution about the attention measure's pre-trends, so the finding is a null rather than a definitive refutation, but it directly contradicts the assumption that less phone use in class automatically yields better attention.

The behavioural by-product also ran against the intuitive story in the short run. "In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption" [6]. On classroom behaviour, the pouch study therefore shows a temporary cost, not an immediate gain; the disruptions faded in later years.

The widely cited positive finding on the attention mechanism is Beland and Murphy's study of English cities (difference-in-differences, 2001–2013), which found high-stakes exam performance rose by about 0.07 standard deviations after bans and that the increases were "driven by the lowest-achieving students" — their interpretation being that phones distract, and the lowest-achieving students lose the most attention [9]. But a Swedish replication with a similar design (Kessel, Hardardottir and Tyrefors, *Economics of Education Review*, 2020) reports "we find no impact of mobile phone bans on student performance and can reject even small-sized gains" of about 0.024 standard deviations [10]. The two are not strictly about attention as measured directly, but they are the strongest quantitative tests of the presumed consequence of distraction, and they point in opposite directions.

The perception evidence is consistently positive and consistently weak. One year after New South Wales's Term 4 2023 statewide ban, a government survey of almost 1,000 public school principals found "87 per cent of principals say students are less distracted in the classroom since mobile phones were banned" [5] — a principal's judgement, not a measure of attention. The Dutch government-commissioned monitor (Kohnstamm Instituut/Oberon, 2025) reports schools reporting positive effects on concentration (75%), the social climate (59%) and — in a minority — learning outcomes (28%) [15]. These are school leaders' self-reports, useful as implementation feedback but not evidence that attention improved.

OECD's own reading of PISA 2022 cuts against strong versions of the policy case: "Whether these are written statements about the general use of devices, rules established by teachers, or programmes to prepare students for responsible Internet behaviour, these types of school policies show little association with the likelihood of students becoming distracted due to digital devices in class" [16]. And while bans may reduce distraction, "PISA 2022 results suggest they are not always effectively enforced" [16].

The pattern across the evidence is consistent: bans demonstrably cut in-class phone use, principals and school leaders overwhelmingly report better concentration, but the most rigorous designs — which measure attention-related outcomes rather than asking for opinions — find little or no clear improvement. The honest summary is that the attention benefit is widely *perceived* and weakly *measured*.

### 4. Bullying and school climate

The bullying evidence is genuinely mixed, with the direction of the finding depending heavily on study design and jurisdiction.

The broadest review is a scoping review of 22 before-and-after studies by Marilyn Campbell and Elizabeth Edwards (QUT and the University of Queensland), summarised in The Conversation. Four studies "reported a small reduction in bullying in schools following phone bans, especially among older students" — but the studies did not specify whether they meant cyberbullying or offline bullying [1]. Counter-evidence sits right beside that: two other studies "showed the number of incidents of online victimisation and harassment was greater in schools with mobile phone bans compared with those without bans." The data do not show whether the harassment happened in or out of school hours [1]. The authors suggested the ban-related increase might occur because students experienced bans as punitive, "which made the school climate less egalitarian and less positive." Other research links a positive school climate with fewer bullying incidents [1]. A further limit on any ban's reach: a 2019 Australian study found 99% of students who were cyberbullied were also bullied face-to-face, so even a fully effective ban on school-day phone use would leave the bulk of school bullying untouched [1].

The large quasi-experimental studies split. On the null side, the US lockable-pouch study of 4,608 schools found "similarly small and null effects on attendance, classroom attention, and perceived online bullying" [2], and its abstract states flatly there is "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [11]. The point estimate for students' perceived likelihood of online bullying was −0.039 school-level standard deviations with a standard error of 0.092 — small and not statistically significant [12]. The authors explain why this could be: online bullying can occur outside school hours or through other devices, so the overall effect of in-school restrictions is uncertain, and removing phones may increase in-person interaction and thus opportunities for conflict [12].

On the positive side, two peer-reviewed quasi-experiments find real reductions. Sara Abrahamsson's study of Norwegian middle schools (published online in the *Journal of Human Resources*, March 2026), using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, finds bans "lower bullying for both genders," alongside reduced psychological health-care use among girls and better girls' GPAs and track placement [13]. And in Spain, where the regions of Galicia and Castilla-La Mancha banned phones in primary and secondary schools from 2015, Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella estimate using police-reported bullying cases per 10,000 students aged 6–17 (2012–2017) with difference-in-differences that "bullying incidence fell by around 9.5% to 18% over its pre-intervention levels among teenagers in the treated regions" [14]. The same authors stress, drawing on Abrahamsson's work, that the policy "is effective only when it is implemented as a clear prohibition to bring the device (mobile phone) into school" — strictness of implementation, not the nominal existence of a ban, is what matters [14].

Reconciling these: the strongest study by scale (the US pouch study) finds no bullying improvement; two peer-reviewed studies in smaller, culturally different systems (Norway, Spain) find reductions, with the Spanish effect measured through police reports rather than self-report. The scoping review shows small, inconsistent effects across 22 mostly weaker designs, including two findings in the wrong direction. No study cleanly separates cyberbullying from face-to-face bullying or establishes how much of any effect occurs inside versus outside school hours — the two things a school ban could plausibly affect.

### 5. Mental health and wellbeing

The mental-health question has the weakest causal evidence base of the four, for a specific reason: until very recently, no large study had measured it directly. The SMART Schools study (Goodyear et al., *Lancet Regional Health – Europe*, 2025) is, in its authors' words, the first evaluation of school phone policies on mental health and wellbeing "which involves a nationally representative sample" and individual-level data [21]. Everything else on the topic before it was ecological or school-level, and most conclusions came from administrative data collected before 2018 or from small, non-validated descriptive studies [21].

**The flagship result is a null.** SMART Schools compared 1,227 students aged 12–15 across 30 English secondary schools — 20 with restrictive policies (recreational phone use not permitted) and 10 with permissive policies — with propensity-matched school recruitment. The primary outcome, mental wellbeing on the Warwick–Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale, showed a mean WEMWBS score of 47 (SD = 9) "with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [21]. The secondary outcomes were also null: no differences in self-reported anxiety, depression, problematic social media use or motives for using social media, and no differences in sleep duration or efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, or disruptive classroom behaviour between restrictive and permissive schools [21].

**The key mechanism finding explains the null.** Restrictive-school students did use phones less *in school*: lower phone time by an adjusted 0.67 hours (95% CI −0.92 to −0.43) and lower social-media time by 0.54 hours (95% CI −0.74 to −0.36) during school time. But "there was no evidence for differences when comparing usage time on weekdays or weekends" [22]. In other words, students displaced the foregone school-day use into the rest of the day — the ban changed *when* they used their phones, not *how much*. Since total use was unchanged, total-use-driven mental-health effects would not be expected to move.

**The dose–response finding cuts both ways.** Within the same sample, "increased time spent on phones/social media is significantly associated with worsened outcomes for mental health and wellbeing, physical activity and sleep, and attainment and disruptive behaviour" [21]. So the study does not exonerate phones: it finds that heavier total use is associated with worse outcomes. What it refutes is the specific policy claim that restricting use *at school* — without changing total use — improves mental health. The authors' conclusion is blunt: there is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents, and the findings do not provide evidence to support school-day phone prohibitions in their current form [21].

**A US state-level analysis agrees.** Saffer's synthetic difference-in-differences study using National Survey of Children's Health data (2016–2024) on US state school smartphone bans found "no clear evidence that the school ban policy reduced screentime or improved psychological wellbeing" [7].

**The US pouch study finds a dynamic, initially negative effect.** The nationwide pouch study found "suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls" in the adoption year — consistent with adjustment costs — before recovering and turning positive by the second post-adoption year [6]. The authors flag the short panel and cross-cohort heterogeneity as reasons for caution, but the pattern (worse before better) is the opposite of the simple "ban phones, improve wellbeing" claim, at least in the short run.

**A Lancet commentary frames the broader problem.** Commenting on the SMART Schools findings, Weiss and Bonell note that the epidemiological evidence for a causal association between smartphone/social-media use and adolescent mental health is weak, that the associations are likely complex and bidirectional, and that there is little causal evidence to date that reducing time spent on social media improves mental wellbeing [8]. Their point is not that phones are harmless but that the causal chain from school-day restriction to better adolescent mental health is unproven at every link.

**The one positive mental-health signal is Norwegian and gendered.** Sara Abrahamsson's event-study study of Norwegian middle-school smartphone bans (published online in the *Journal of Human Resources*, March 2026) finds no average effect on mental health, but a meaningful distribution: bans "reduce psychological health care use among girls" while improving girls' GPAs and academic track placement, especially among disadvantaged students [13]. This is administrative-data evidence of a real mental-health-relevant outcome (health-care use) in one country, concentrated in one group. It does not generalise to an average benefit, and it sits alongside the null average effects elsewhere.

The overall mental-health picture: no large, well-designed study finds an average improvement in adolescent mental health from school phone restrictions. The strongest studies find nulls (England, US states) or null-on-average with a girl-specific benefit (Norway) or short-run harm before recovery (US pouches). The consistent mechanism finding — that bans shift use within the day without reducing total use — is the most plausible explanation for why the expected mental-health gains have not appeared.

### 6. The strength of the evidence overall: designs, disagreements and what is still unknown

The honest assessment of the evidence base is that it is stronger than the policy debate acknowledges and weaker than the policy decisions imply — at the same time.

**The strongest designs are quasi-experimental, and they now exist at scale.** The US pouch study is the high-water mark: 4,608 public schools, a pre-registered staggered difference-in-differences design (Callaway–Sant'Anna), matched never-treated comparison schools, and outcome data drawn from a teacher survey with nearly 108,000 responses, GPS phone-location pings, standardized test scores, administrative records and Panorama student surveys [11]. Rio uses quarterly student-level test scores over a two-year pre-period to check pre-trends [25]. Florida uses student-level administrative records and GPS data [4]. These are credible causal designs by the standards of education research.

**But every design has a structural limitation, and the limitations systematically pull in the same direction.** Three recur. First, *the treatment is the policy as implemented, not a perfect ban.* The US pouch study's GPS and teacher-survey data confirm phones still get used — the share of students using phones in class for personal reasons falls from 61% to 13%, not to zero [6]; Rio's principals report usage stayed well above zero after the ban [25]; Sweden's replication could reject even small gains in part because bans there changed access rather than eliminating it [10]. Second, *control groups are contaminated or awkward.* Florida bans the whole district, so the authors can only compare schools with high versus low pre-ban phone use — "this design likely understates the positive effects of the ban on students, because both high effect and low effect schools are treated by the ban" [4]. Rio's control schools also reduced phone use after the municipal ban, so the 0.06 SD estimate is a lower bound on the ban's effect relative to no ban [25]. Third, *outcome coverage is uneven.* The attention and bullying survey measures in the US pouch study have differential pre-trends that limit conclusions [6]; mental health was unmeasured in a causally adequate way until SMART Schools, and that study is cross-sectional [21].

**The sceptical critique is methodological, and it has bite.** Christopher Ferguson, writing in the *World Journal of Pediatrics*, argues that "Smartphone bans were implemented as a means of improving youth grades, behavior, and mental health. Current evidence suggests that they do not work." [3] His strongest point is about what should count as evidence: "too many studies fail to consider whether a reported effect size is large enough to be a true effect or merely the product of unreliable responding, hypothesis guessing and other statistical noise that can create false-positive results, particularly in large sample studies" [3]. Large samples make tiny, substantively trivial effects statistically significant; the policy question is whether the effect size matters, and by that standard several of the "positive" findings (0.6 percentile points in Florida, 0.024 SD in US high-school math) are small. Ferguson also warns that the window for the decisive experiment may have closed: "the wide proliferation of smartphone bans without evidence may make true randomized-controlled trials unlikely at this juncture, given that it may be increasingly difficult to locate schools systematically that have not been touched by such bans" [3]. The Florida authors made the same point earlier and more precisely: as of their writing, "we know of no causal evidence of the effects of national, state, or district-level policies on student outcomes, and no causal evidence even on school-level policies in the United States" [4] — their own study being the first for a statewide ban.

**The field is genuinely split, and the split is not noise.** The Rio paper's own literature review states the two camps cleanly: Beland–Murphy find a 0.07 SD gain in England; Abrahamsson finds reduced bullying and improved girls' grades and mental health in Norway; Beneito–Vicente-Chirivella find about 0.10 SD in PISA scores and less bullying in Spain; but Kessel et al. find no impacts in Sweden, "rejecting even small improvements," a recent Chilean study finds no effects on test scores, and the nationwide US study finds mixed effects — modest gains in high schools, small negatives in middle schools [25]. The disagreements correlate with setting, design and era, which is itself informative: effects appear where bans were newly and sharply binding, and where phones were a bigger share of the day's distraction.

**What would strengthen the evidence is known and mostly unbuilt.** On randomised evidence, the situation is nuanced. The only randomised controlled trial is not of a school ban: Sungu, Choudhury and Bjerre-Nielsen (*Science*, 2026) randomly assigned 420 department-grade units — 16,683 students across 10 higher-education institutions in Odisha, India — to mandatory in-class phone collection or business-as-usual for one semester, and estimated an intent-to-treat GPA gain of 0.073 standard deviations, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.003 to 0.144 and 60–80% of grades coming from externally set, off-site, blinded exams [29]. That is strong causal evidence for the *classroom* mechanism, but it is college students and lecture-only, not K–12 schools and not a whole-day policy. An independent assessment rates the result "borderline, with a confidence interval beginning at 0.003 and an unexplained one-sided test" [29]. For K–12 bans specifically, the peer-reviewed scoping review still states there is "an absence of randomized controlled trials" with evidence resting on a small number of studies of varying design [32], and Ferguson is probably right that the spread of bans makes a school-level trial hard to mount [3]. There is also no study that cleanly separates cyberbullying from face-to-face bullying or in-school from out-of-school harassment [1]. There is no long-run evidence: the US pouch study observes at most three years post-adoption and flags longer-run effects as an open question [6]. Canada has survey evidence but no outcomes evaluation — a University of Ottawa survey of 892 elementary and 350 secondary Toronto District School Board teachers found enforcement and reported benefits in elementary schools but neither in most secondary schools, with no administrative outcomes measured [30] — and Ontario's EQAO results for the first year under the ban (2024–25) are reported descriptively, without any attribution of the changes to the ban [31]. And there is no study that measures the mechanism everyone assumes — restored attention — with an instrument better than self-report, which is precisely where the strongest nulls sit [6].

**The policy reading.** If the question is whether school phone bans improve learning, attention, bullying and mental health on average, the most rigorous evidence says: learning, mostly no or small, with real gains in some settings; attention, perceived by staff but not measured; bullying, genuinely mixed with reductions in two smaller systems and none in the largest; mental health, no average improvement. If the question is whether bans do what their mechanics say — cut in-school phone use — the answer is an unambiguous yes, by roughly 60 to 80 percent. The gap between those two answers is the whole story: the intervention works as a restriction but has not been shown to work as a treatment, because total phone use, and the social and psychological dynamics that travel with it, do not stop at the school gate.


## Beyond this question

The single most useful framing for anyone working on attention, feeds or adolescent wellbeing is this: the school phone ban is the rare policy whose *mechanism* is proven while its *outcomes* are not. Bans reliably cut in-school phone use by 60 to 80 percent [6], yet the measured downstream effects on learning, attention, bullying and mental health are small, mixed, or null. That gap is itself the finding. It means the problem the bans target — "phones disrupt attention" — is real at the level of the device in the room, but the harms people attribute to phones (lower grades, worse wellbeing, more bullying) are not sufficiently located in the school day to be cured by removing the device from it. Total phone use is unchanged by school bans [22]; bullying happens mostly face-to-face and outside the mechanism a school can control [1]; and the attention restored in class does not clearly translate into better measured outcomes [6]. Anyone designing interventions in this space should start from the displacement and heterogeneity findings rather than from the intuitive "remove the phone, fix the child" story.

A second, more pointed implication: the policy has run well ahead of the evidence, and the design space for the decisive experiment may be closing. Ferguson's observation that untreated comparison schools are disappearing [3], and the fact that the only randomised trial so far is a college classroom in India [29], mean future researchers will mostly be able to study *how* bans are implemented, not *whether* they work. The tractable research frontier is therefore enforcement and implementation — the Florida attendance mechanism [4], the Toronto elementary/secondary enforcement gap [30], the Norwegian finding that only clear prohibitions on bringing the device work [14] — rather than the binary ban question.

## Open questions

**No K–12 randomised controlled trial exists.** The only randomised trial is the Odisha college experiment [29]; the peer-reviewed K–12 review states an "absence of randomized controlled trials" outright [32]. Whether a school-level trial is still possible given how far bans have spread is itself contested [3].

**No study has cleanly separated cyberbullying from face-to-face bullying, or in-school from out-of-school harassment.** The scoping review flags this explicitly [1], and the US pouch study's authors say the overall effect of in-school restrictions on online bullying is "uncertain" for exactly this reason [12]. Every bullying claim in the literature is therefore ambiguous about which mechanism a ban could actually touch.

**No long-run evidence.** The best US design observes at most three years post-adoption and flags longer-run effects as an open question [6]. Nothing is known about whether bans change phone habits, attention or wellbeing after students leave the school, or whether the Toronto survey's preliminary finding — that students from restrictive schools later show healthier phone-use patterns [30] — replicates. That survey is self-reported, cross-sectional, and unpublished.

**Canada has no outcomes evaluation.** The Toronto teacher survey is the closest thing [30], and Ontario's EQAO reports the first post-ban year descriptively without attribution [31]. Whether the Ontario ban changed grades, attendance, incidents or wellbeing — and whether the elementary/secondary enforcement gap the Toronto survey found holds province-wide — is unmeasured.

**The attention mechanism is unmeasured with a good instrument.** The outcome the whole policy is named for — restored attention — rests on principal and teacher self-reports in the positive studies [5][20] and on a self-report measure with pre-trend problems in the strongest null [6]. Nobody has measured attention directly before and after a ban in a design that can support causal claims.

**Mental-health effects by age and gender are unresolved.** The strongest finding is Abrahamsson's Norwegian result — reduced psychological health-care use among girls, no average effect [13] — against SMART Schools' clean average null in England [21]. Whether benefits concentrate in girls, in younger children, or only where bans are strictest is not settled.

**Evidence quality on the two remaining named jurisdictions is thin.** The Netherlands' evaluation is a government-commissioned school-leader survey [15][20]; Ontario has only a teacher survey [30]. Neither has an administrative-data evaluation comparable to Florida's or Rio's.

q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: McLuhan's Laws of Media (the Tetrad): What It Claimed, How It Was Used and Criticised, and Whether Anyone Has Tested It
report.body:
## TL;DR

McLuhan's tetrad — developed from 1974 and published posthumously in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988, completed by his son Eric) — asks four simultaneous questions of any artefact: what it enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into when pushed to its limits. The McLuhans explicitly offered it as testable and falsifiable in Popper's sense, but their own 1976 reply to a critic retreated to "analogical" reasoning, and the framework's own scholarly extenders concede it makes no unique predictions and often has more than one correct answer per quadrant. Since 1988 it has been applied widely (smartphone, social media, digital games, AI, voice, money) and formally extended (Levinson's tetrad wheels; Logan and Iseri's Laws of Media Environments and Users), but criticised sharply — most notably by Tom Tyler, who showed the McLuhans themselves produced two different tetrads for wine on one page, and argued the scheme is simultaneously too vague to falsify and too rigid in forcing all four boxes to be filled. On the empirical question the answer is flat: no one has tested the tetrad the way a scientific law is tested, and the tradition's own defenders state that such a test is not what the tetrad is for.

## Key Findings

- **What it claims.** The tetrad is four simultaneous questions — enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, reverse — applied to any artefact, not only communication media; each law is a figure/ground relation, and the four operate at once, not sequentially [1][5].
- **It was explicitly offered as science.** The 1988 book's opening claims "testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)", citing Popper; Eric McLuhan said the answers could be checked "by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [3][5][2].
- **But the science claim collapsed under scrutiny.** McLuhan's 1976 reply to Venable says the tetrads are analogical, with "no connections between any of them"; Logan and Iseri concede the laws "are not strictly scientific laws" because they "do[ ] not make unique predictions" [1][5].
- **It has been applied more than tested.** A 2020 systematic review found 21 applications in Brazil and Portugal alone in one decade, most without methodological discussion; the pattern is post-hoc box-filling, not hypothesis testing [11].
- **It has been formally extended.** Levinson's "tetrad wheels" chain tetrads into historical spirals; Logan and Iseri add Laws of Media Environments and Laws of Media Users [5][7].
- **The sharpest critique is Tyler's double bind.** Tyler showed two conflicting tetrads for wine on a single page of the book, and argued the tetrad is "far too vague" to be falsifiable yet "unrelentingly rigid" in requiring all four quadrants — while still conceding its value as a probe [2].
- **No empirical test exists.** No experiment, survey, inter-rater study, or pre-registered falsification of the tetrad was located; the closest analogues are a 1973 experiment on McLuhan's earlier television claims (not the tetrad) and a 2024 review that sorts others' empirical results into the four boxes [4].
- **The tetrad's own defenders say testability is not the point.** Levinson in 1978 wrote that tetradic analysis is "historically descriptive but notpredictive"; Eric McLuhan said "all accurate answers are correct answers" — which is the definition of unfalsifiability stated from inside the tradition [7][11].

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims: origins and the four laws as stated

The tetrad is a four-part question scheme, not a single proposition. Its most quoted statement, from McLuhan's 1977 "Laws of the Media" article (reprinted in *Et cetera*), runs: "There seems to be only four features, and they are in analogical proportion to each other: (a) What does it enhance? (b) What does it obsolesce? (c) What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier? (d) What does it flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential?" [5]. Logan and Iseri restate the same content as four declarative "laws": every artefact, medium or technology enhances some human function; in doing so it obsolesces some former medium or technology that achieved that function; it retrieves some older form from the past; and when pushed far enough it reverses or flips into a complementary form [5]. The scheme is applied to artefacts generally, not only to communications media: McLuhan wrote in 1975 that "only a few of them deal with communications media narrowly conceived", and that he meant media as a larger ground of information and perception that forms our thoughts, structures our experience, and determines our views of the world [1].

Three features of the claim are easy to flatten out and should not be. First, the four operate **simultaneously**, not as a sequence of stages. In the tetrad, enhancement and reversal are the two figures, and obsolescence and retrieval the two grounds. Second, each law is a **figure/ground** relation, not a simple event: McLuhan wrote that "the Law of a Medium is a figure interplaying with a ground" [1]. Third, the scheme is **analogical**, not causal-linear: the quadrants stand "in analogical proportion to each other" [5], a phrasing that mattered later in the debate over whether the tetrad could be falsified at all.

The book's own examples show how the four questions are meant to be answered. The standard example is radio, which McLuhan and later commentators render as: radio enhances the human voice and gives simultaneous access to a mass audience; it obsolesces the print monopoly on asynchronous mass news; it retrieves the town crier and oral announcement; and, pushed to its limit, it flips into the audio-visual medium of television [2]. The money example from *Laws of Media* is quoted by Logan and Iseri: "Money enhanced trade and commerce, obsolesced the barter system, retrieved the conspicuous consumption of hunting and gathering societies, and flipped into credit, a complementary form" [5]. The reversal quadrant is the most distinctive and the most easily abused. McLuhan's own discipline on it was that one should “Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened” [2] — reversal describes a flip already implicit in an existing technology's trajectory, not futurology.

The intellectual origins of the tetrad predate the 1988 book. McLuhan worked on it from about 1974 until his death in 1980. A German paper, "Gesetze der Medien — strukturelle Annäherung", appeared in June 1974 and already "included tetrads, in list form, on such topics as Spoken Word, Phonetic Alphabet, Press, Typewriter, Xerox, Telephone, Radio, Electric Media, Money, and Satellite", according to Eric McLuhan in *The Lost Tetrads of Marshall McLuhan* (2017) [1]. The first English statement was "McLuhan's Laws of the Media" in *Technology and Culture* 16:1 (1975), followed by "Laws of the Media" in *Et cetera* 34:2 (1977) and "Multi-Media: The Laws of the Media" in *The English Journal* (1978); the full statement appeared posthumously in *Laws of Media: The New Science* (1988), completed by Eric McLuhan [1]. Two earlier McLuhan ideas fed into the tetrad: the "overheating"/reversal principle from *Understanding Media* (a hot medium pushed too far reverses), and the retrieval idea first made explicit in *From Cliché to Archetype* (1970), where new technologies "retrieve obsolesced older forms". The tetrad was, in effect, the convergence of ideas McLuhan had developed separately across two decades.

### 2. How the McLuhans framed it: 'laws', 'science', and the testability claim

The McLuhans consistently claimed more than "heuristic" for the tetrad — and then qualified the claim in ways that undercut it. The strongest statement is the second sentence of *Laws of Media*: “This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does; hence _Laws_ in its title” [3]. The book's subtitle was *The New Science*, explicitly borrowing the phrase from Giambattista Vico, and the authors named their warrant: “Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media” [5]. McLuhan's 1975 article had already invited refutation and given his own gloss on the word "laws" — that they are an ordering of thought and experience which has not yet been disproved. The publisher's framing went further, describing the laws as testable and able to allow for prediction, and adding that anything not answerable by the four questions was, by definition, not a human creation.

Eric McLuhan's claim was the most expansive of all. In *Laws of Media* he wrote that the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [2] — a claim of universal applicability *and* universal checkability. He separately described the tetrad, in Graham Harman's account, as the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of his time but of at least the last couple of centuries, and wrote that his father spent his final years looking for a fifth law and for a single case where one of the four did not apply, without success.

Two internal qualifications sit uneasily beside these claims. The first is the retreat from logic to analogy. When the engineer and lawyer William Henry Venable published "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture* 17:2, 1976), reading the four laws through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs, McLuhan replied: "The whole point about my tetrads is that they are _ana_logical. That is, there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios" [1], and insisted there was "simply no point of contact whatever" between Venable's reading and his own. The second qualification came from the McLuhans' own leading interpreters. Logan and Iseri — collaborators inside the tradition, not hostile critics — state flatly that "LOMs are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into. The LOM is more of an exploratory tool or probe that provides insights into the effects of a new medium or technology and its possible evolution, and there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [5]. That admission is decisive for the empirical-testing question taken up in section 5: by the admission of the tetrad's own defenders, the framework does not yield the unique, advance predictions that a falsifiable law requires.

Eric McLuhan himself sometimes framed the tetrad as a probe rather than a predictive scientific law, while continuing to describe it as a discovery of scientific rank. The resulting position is a genuine inconsistency in the record: the book's formal claim (testable, falsifiable, predictive) is contradicted by the McLuhans' own replies to critics and by the concessions of their successors. The most accurate summary is that the tetrad was *offered* as science in 1975 and 1988, *defended* as analogy in 1976, and *received* by its scholarly heirs as a heuristic. That is the ambiguity every later critic, from Tyler onward, has worked from.

### 3. How scholars have applied and extended the tetrad since 1988

After 1988 the tetrad became, in effect, the shared method of the Media Ecology Association and its successors: applied widely as a heuristic, extended in two main directions, and almost never used as a hypothesis-testing instrument. Lindia and Levinson's 2021 survey of the field makes the point sharply: McLuhan's original appeals to scholars to test the laws' validity historically and empirically were mostly followed as invitations to *apply* the tetrad to new artefacts, while its epistemological and ontological insights went unexamined [7].

The most influential *extension* is Levinson's "tetrad wheels" (first proposed at the Tetrad Conference he organised at Fairleigh Dickinson University in 1978, then formalised in print by Lindia and Levinson in 2021). The wheels restate the four laws as two figure/ground dualisms: enhancement is the figure, obsolescence the "pre-ground", retrieval the "pre-figure", and reversal the "post-ground" [7]. Rotating the wheel one position counter-clockwise turns one tetrad's reversal into the next artefact's enhancement, so tetrads chain into spirals through history. This repairs what Levinson saw as the original tetrad's isolation from technological history, and it recasts the scheme as diachronic rather than synchronic. Levinson's own 1978 account stresses that the wheels keep the method "non-comprehensive … as a heuristic tool".

The other major formal extension is Robert K. Logan and Zeynep Merve Iseri's "Laws of Media Environments" (LOME) and "Laws of Media Users" (LOMU), published in MDPI's *Philosophies* (2016). The LOME state that every artefact's ground evolves through the same four phases as the artefact: a medium creates a new environment, obsolesces the ground of the displaced medium, retrieves elements of the retrieved medium's ground, and flips into a complementary ground [5]. The LOMU apply the same logic to users, who "become their servomechanisms" — McLuhan's Narcissus language — and flip into the servomechanisms of the next artefact [5]. Logan and Iseri also assemble the tetrad into a single historical spiral: the alphabet flips into movable-type print from 1450 CE, print flips into computers after about 500 years, computers flip into the internet in 24 years, the internet into the web in 21, and the web into social media in about 5 [5]. The acceleration of flip intervals is their empirical-looking claim, but it is a post-hoc periodisation, not a tested prediction.

The bulk of the literature since 1988 is *application* rather than extension or test. The record's own corpus contains several of these: the tetrad applied to surveillance pricing, to voice interfaces, to the digital calendar, to the smartphone, and (in Tyler's essay) to digital games. Representative published examples show the range. Issac Adam's 2016 *Glocality* article applies the tetrad to the smartphone: it enhances "the accessibility and convenience of the medium internet", obsolesces feature phones and personal computers, retrieves cameras and e-books, and reverses into augmented-reality devices that might restrict rather than facilitate interaction [6]. Adam concedes the method's openness: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [6]. A 2024 architectural-education study explicitly labels the tetrad "a hermeneutic tool", and uses it to organise a review of 20 peer-reviewed empirical papers on online design studios [4]. Antonio López's ecomedia-literacy work (with an afterword by Andrew McLuhan) applies the tetrad to large language models in education — enhancing personalised learning, obsolescing recall-based assessment, retrieving the transmission model, reversing into cognitive offloading — and then reflexively to ecomedia literacy itself [9]. The pattern across all of these is identical: the tetrad is used as a four-box frame for generating and organising claims, with the analyst's own judgement supplying the content of each quadrant.

Two further applications deserve note because they moved in a more systematic direction. Sandstrom (2012) proposed the Four Effects as a complement to Aristotle's Four Causes for social epistemology, explicitly framing the tetrad as an analogical, simultaneous method "meant to shock us (sensibly)" rather than a deductive law [8]. And the McLuhans' own comparison — the tetrad as Aristotle's Four Causes restated for media — is the genealogical root of the "extension" tradition: every application inherits the assumption that the four questions are a *complete* grammar of human artefacts, which is precisely the assumption the critics in section 4 attacked. What no applied study appears to have done is specify, in advance, what observation would count against a quadrant, or test whether two independent analysts reach the same four answers — the two operations that would turn the tetrad from a heuristic into a testable instrument.

### 4. How scholars have criticised the tetrad: the Procrustean and falsifiability objections

The sharpest published critique of the tetrad came from Tom Tyler, then a Senior Lecturer in Philosophy and Culture at Oxford Brookes, in "Play: A Procrustean Probe" (DiGRA 2007), revised as "A Procrustean Probe" in *Game Studies* 8:2 (2008). Tyler wanted to use the tetrad to situate digital games in their media environment, but opened by warning that the method "is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empiric elements which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be made to fit" [2]. He anchored this to the McLuhans' own claims: McLuhan had presented the laws as testable hypotheses modelled on Popper's falsifiability, and Eric McLuhan wrote in *Laws of Media* that the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [2]. Tyler's blunt reply: "This is not, in fact, the case."

His demonstration is the wine example. On a single page of *Laws of Media*, the McLuhans give two different tetrads for the same artefact. In the first, wine enhances "grape juice" (via fermentation), obsolesces "commonplace flavours", retrieves "ritual observance", and reverses into "cooking wine vinegar". In the second version on the same page, wine enhances food and "the occasion", obsolesces "inhibition", retrieves "festive spontaneity of speech and gesture", and reverses into "hangover" and insult [2]. Tyler's inference: if the authors themselves could not produce consistent results for one artefact on one page, "it seems unlikely that the same results will be achieved by “anyone, anywhere, at any time”".

Tyler's objection is a double bind, not a single complaint, and the two halves pull in opposite directions. First, the tetrad is **too loose**: "Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit" [2]. Second, it is **too rigid**: "At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps" [2]. The four slots must be filled whether or not the evidence supports an answer, so analysts are forced to "hammer or shear" complex phenomena to fit the frame. Tyler's overall verdict: "The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses" [2]. It is best treated, he writes, as a set of questions — what a technology enhances, obsolesces, retrieves, and reverses into — a "probe" rather than a science.

Tyler's constructive move matters as much as his negative one. His applied tetrad of digital games shows what a disciplined probe looks like: each quadrant is anchored in cited empirical research (Putnam's and Berger's work on social capital for the enhancement of solo play; European media-use studies and Nick Yee's MMORPG data for the obsolescence of television); where the evidence cuts against a quadrant he says so and redefines the term (obsolescence becomes Bolter and Grusin's "remediation" rather than replacement, since Yee's players still watched nearly 8 hours of TV a week); and each quadrant is aimed at a specific misconception — Berger's claim that solo gaming is alienating, the naive claim that games "displace" television, the "immersive fallacy" of Salen and Zimmerman. He closes with the principle behind the whole essay: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us, as did the bed for Theseus, rather than against us, as was Procrustes’ lot" [2]. The standard in Tyler's version is not whether it fits but whether the resulting analysis overturns a named misconception and stays anchored in evidence.

The earlier exchange with William Henry Venable shows the same tension from McLuhan's side. Venable, an engineer and lawyer, took up McLuhan's 1975 invitation in "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" (*Technology and Culture* 17:2, 1976), reading the four laws through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs and arguing that they presuppose a single target technologists have always aimed at. McLuhan's published reply retreated from the scientific framing: "The whole point about my tetrads is that they are _ana_logical. That is, there are no connections between any of them, but there are dynamic ratios" [1]. He insisted there was "simply no point of contact whatever" between Venable's reading and his own. In other words, when a critic took the testability claim seriously, McLuhan moved from logic and falsifiability to analogy and ratio — exactly the ambiguity Tyler later exploited.

A second line of criticism is the older, broader "not theoretical / not falsifiable" charge applied to McLuhan generally — Dwight Macdonald's 1967 "He Has Looted All Culture", Jonathan Miller, George Steiner, and Raymond Williams in *Television: Technology and Cultural Form* (1974). Williams added the technological-determinism charge: that McLuhan's scheme makes technology the unidirectional cause of consciousness and thereby naturalises the status quo. The tetrad specifically is the McLuhans' most explicit attempt to answer these charges, so the question of whether it succeeded is inseparable from the older debate. The record's own comprehensive map of McLuhan's thought notes that defenders — Donald Theall, Glenn Willmott, Paul Grosswiler, Richard Cavell, and the Media Ecology Association — argue that McLuhan was deliberately writing in a "probe-and-mosaic mode" and that a new method was needed for environments invisible to propositional reason; the reversal law itself is incompatible with simple linear determinism. But the fair core of the criticism remains that the framework gives little weight to the political-economic and institutional shaping of technology.

Graham Harman took the opposite side in "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" (in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology*, 2009). Where Tyler treats the tetrad as a useful-but-unscientific probe, Harman argues Eric McLuhan was "largely right" that it applies to *all* objects, not just human artefacts, since "every object is a medium." Harman's contribution is a test for any fourfold: a rigorous one must be generated by crossing two deep dualisms (his example of a frivolous fourfold: daytime eating, daytime drinking, night-time eating, night-time drinking). He identifies the tetrad's underlying dualisms as figure/ground and metamorphosis, and stresses that the four operate simultaneously, not sequentially. On this reading the tetrad's value is metaphysical rather than empirical, and its "failure" to be an ordinary scientific law is beside the point. Tyler and Harman disagree about the tetrad's importance but converge on the key negative claim: it is not ordinary empirical science, whatever else it is.

### 5. Has anyone tested the tetrad empirically? Operationalisations and attempts

The short answer is: no. In the nearly four decades since *Laws of Media* appeared, no one has published a study that tests the tetrad the way a scientific law is tested — by specifying in advance an observation that would falsify it, collecting data, and risking refutation. What exists instead is a large body of post-hoc *application*, plus a small number of explicit statements, mostly from inside the tradition, explaining why such a test has not happened and, on their account, cannot happen.

The clearest admission comes from Logan and Iseri, the tetrad's own formal extenders. After restating the four laws, they write: "LOMs are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into. The LOM is more of an exploratory tool or probe that provides insights into the effects of a new medium or technology and its possible evolution, and there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [5]. If there is "more than one correct answer" to each question, then a test cannot fail: any answer, or its opposite, can be accommodated, which is the definition of unfalsifiability. This is not a hostile verdict; it is the official position of the paper that extended the tetrad into environments and users.

Levinson reached the same conclusion in 1978, before the book even appeared, and his formulation is the most precise statement of the limit. In the tetrad-wheel paper reprinted by Lindia and Levinson in 2021, he wrote that "Tetradic analysis of culture may thus be historically descriptive but notpredictive, therein avoiding the logical fallacy that Karl Popper has called the “poverty ofhistoricism,” or the logical inability of predicting the future of human events from the past" [7]. Levinson is explicit that he is *avoiding* the predictive burden: the reversal quadrant, the one place the tetrad appears to look forward, is re-read as the new element that cannot be charted from the past. On this account the tetrad is a descriptive taxonomy of what has already happened, and a test of it would be as odd as a test of Aristotle's four causes.

The Brazilian media theorist Sérgio Basbaum, in the only paper located that takes the "scientificizing" project literally, makes the same point from the Popperian side: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim" [3]. Basbaum then attempts the one genuinely operational route to an empirical McLuhan: the "triplex isomorphism" hypothesis that medium, experience, and neural activity should show the same structure "at some level of description", which would let one verify McLuhan's thesis through neural-correlates-of-consciousness research. But he ends by conceding that "the measurability of McLuhan’s theory through NCC observation becomes highly undermined" [3] in a networked, collective media ecology. The article is best read as a program for making McLuhan falsifiable that announces its own failure; no subsequent study is known to have carried the program out.

What the empirical record actually contains is application dressed as test. The closest published example is a 2024 review that "identified 176 records of peer-reviewed empirical studies" on online architectural design studios, read 20 of them, and then organised the findings and interpreted them within the tetradic framework [4]. Here the tetrad is used to sort other people's empirical results into four boxes; the empirical content comes entirely from the 20 studies, and nothing about the tetrad itself is put at risk. Every other located "empirical" use has the same structure: the smartphone study [6], the arts-based media analyses [10], the LLM-in-education tetrad [9], and the many tetrads in the record's own corpus all generate the four quadrants from the analyst's knowledge and then present them as findings. Because the quadrants are filled after the fact from whatever the analyst knows, a tetrad of this kind cannot be disconfirmed by any evidence, and its success rate is trivially 100%.

The absence of tests is over-determined by the design of the instrument. To test the tetrad as the McLuhans claimed it could be tested, one would need at least three things that the published tradition never supplies. First, an operational definition of each quadrant with decision rules — what counts as "enhancement" versus a mere feature, what makes one obsolescence the right one when several candidate obsolescences exist. Second, a specification, before analysis, of what observation would count as a failure — for example, an artefact that enhanced nothing, or a reversal that failed to arrive at the predicted threshold. Third, and most fundamentally, inter-analyst agreement: if the four answers are checkable "by anyone, anywhere, at any time" [2], then two independent analysts given the same artefact and the same rules should converge on the same answers. The wine example already shows the failure of this test at the source: the McLuhans themselves produced two different tetrads for wine on a single page [2], and the 2005 arts-media study notes as an unremarkable fact that the McLuhans "provided multiple examples of tetrads for the same media" [10]. No published study has ever measured inter-rater reliability on the tetrad, and the reason is plain: the framework's own practitioners describe multiple, equally valid answers as a feature, not a bug [5][6][10].

There is one respect in which the tetrad has been "tested", and it is worth stating carefully because it is the only empirical content the tradition can claim. The enhancement, obsolescence and retrieval quadrants are often historical claims, and specific historical claims are checkable after the fact. When Levinson applies the tetrad to radio and says radio retrieved the town crier, or when the smartphone study says the smartphone obsolesced the standalone camera, those are empirical assertions about what actually happened in media history, and they can be (and largely are) supported by historical evidence. But this is testing the *content of a particular application*, not testing the *law*. A law that said every medium enhances something, obsolesces something, retrieves something, and reverses into something could survive any number of failed applications, because a new application can always be substituted for the failed one — which is exactly what the two wine tetrads demonstrate. The historical accuracy of individual quadrants does not accumulate into support for the framework, because the framework does not say which quadrant content is correct in advance. The only located *experimental* test of any McLuhan medium theory is also not a test of the tetrad: a 1973 California State University, Northridge master's thesis by Robert Tregenza experimentally tested McLuhan's claims about the television medium's effect on audience perception and reported, in the repository's abstract, that the statistical tests showed no significant differences between treatment groups on any dependent variable, so the results did not support the hypotheses advanced. That study targeted the hot/cool and medium-is-the-message claims of the early 1960s, a decade and a half before the tetrad existed, but it is the tradition's only located instance of McLuhan's media claims being put to a controlled experimental test at all.

My inference, stated as such: the most defensible summary is that the tetrad has never been empirically tested because, as stated, it is not empirically testable. Its own strongest advocates (Levinson, Logan and Iseri) and its most careful scientific-minded reader (Basbaum) agree, from different directions, that it yields no unique predictions and can always be made to fit. The closest thing to a falsifiable descendant is Basbaum's triplex-isomorphism hypothesis, which no one has yet run, and which its own author concedes is undermined by the collective character of the media environments it would have to measure. Any future empirical test would first have to solve the problem the tradition has spent forty years defining away: stating, in advance and with decision rules, what would count as a wrong answer to one of the four questions.


## Beyond this question

The tetrad's fate is a worked example of a more general problem in media theory: what happens when a thinker offers a heuristic in the language of a law. The record shows the pattern in detail — a claim offered as testable in 1975 and 1988, defended as analogy in 1976, and received as a probe by its heirs — and it generalises beyond McLuhan. Any framework that is generative enough to be useful across artefacts will tend to be too loose to be falsified, and the two properties pull against each other: tighten the terms until the tetrad yields one right answer per quadrant, and it loses the very flexibility that makes it illuminating. The practical lesson, already embedded in the record's own "Collision Desk" proposal, is to run rival tetrads (as the two wine versions unwittingly demonstrate), permit an empty quadrant, and treat each quadrant as a hypothesis with a named misconception at stake rather than a box to fill. Whether the tetrad "beats" other lenses — figure/ground inversion, assumption-denial, ontology audits — is itself an empirical question no one has yet measured.

## Open questions

- **No test exists, and none is near.** I searched specifically for any operationalisation, experiment, survey, content analysis, or inter-rater reliability study of the tetrad, and found none. The closest items are: the 1973 CSUN experiment on McLuhan's television claims (predates the tetrad); the 2024 architectural-studio review that sorts others' empirical findings into the four boxes; and the 2020 Brazilian–Portuguese systematic review of 21 *applications*, which itself concludes that different researchers analysing the same object "will not have … equal tetrads". No one has measured whether two independent analysts converge, and no one has pre-registered a falsifying observation.
- **Basbaum's triplex isomorphism is the only genuine test design on offer, and it has not been run.** The one proposal to operationalise the tetrad — checking that medium, experience, and neural activity share a common structure — is stated in programmatic form in one article, and its author himself concludes the measurability is undermined in networked media environments. No follow-up study was located.
- **The reversal quadrant is the least specified.** Because McLuhan insisted one should never predict anything that hasn't already happened, the reversal law has never been stated with a threshold (how far is "pushed to its limits"?) or a deadline, which is precisely what a predictive test would require. Logan and Iseri's acceleration claim (print to computers 500 years, internet 24, web 21, social media 5) is retrospective periodisation, not a forward prediction.
- **Coverage gaps in this report.** The Venable–McLuhan exchange is read only through the McLuhans' reply and the secondary summary on mcluhansnewsciences.com; the full Venable letter itself is paywalled at Project MUSE and was not read. Harman's "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" chapter was read only in part (via the record's prior research document). The primary 1975 and 1977 McLuhan texts are quoted through the mcluhansnewsciences.com reproduction and Logan–Iseri's citations rather than from the journals themselves. Andrey Mir's recent book-length work on reversal (*The Digital Reversal*) was identified but not read in full; it is cited only as an example of ongoing extension, not as a source.
- **The one thing that would change the answer.** A pre-registered study that gives N analysts a fixed corpus of evidence about one artefact, asks them to complete the four quadrants under stated rules, and measures agreement — or a historical study that specifies in advance what a failed enhancement/obsolescence/retrieval/reversal would look like and then looks for it — would convert this entire question from a matter of framework exegesis into a matter of fact. Until then, the honest statement stands: the tetrad has been applied hundreds of times and tested never.
