label: policy, numbers
q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

report.title: Pharmacare After the Act: the four agreements, the drugs actually covered, who is enrolled, and what a full program would cost
report.body:
## TL;DR

Two years after Royal Assent, Canada's national pharmacare program consists of four bilateral agreements — Manitoba, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island and Yukon — worth about $928 million over four years and covering roughly 7.5 million people, about 17 per cent of the population. All four were signed in a five-week window in early 2025; nothing has been signed since, no new money has been budgeted, and the agreements expire on 31 March 2029. Coverage is narrower than the federal communications imply: first-dollar drug coverage for a negotiated list of contraceptives and diabetes drugs, with devices and supplies funded through one-off transfers and delivered via deductible-based provincial programs. No one can say how many Canadians are using it, because the agreements require no such reporting — while the federal government's parallel rare-disease drug program, with all thirteen jurisdictions, requires outcome reporting and published a count of 632 patients reached. A full single-payer program would cost the public sector $11.2 billion in 2024-25 rising to $13.4 billion in 2027-28 on the PBO's estimate, against an implemented first phase costed at $1.9 billion over five years.

## Key Findings

- **Four of thirteen signed, and none since March 2025.** Manitoba (27 Feb 2025, $219M+), British Columbia (6 Mar 2025, $670M+), PEI (7 Mar 2025, $30M+) and Yukon (21 Mar 2025, $9.5M) total about $928 million over four years — roughly 62 per cent of the $1.5 billion set aside in Budget 2024 [14][20][21][22][23][25]. Nine jurisdictions are outside, covering about 83 per cent of the population [25].
- **The Act creates no entitlement.** Section 6(1) obliges the Minister to pay only "if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory" [1]. The Act sets deadlines for studies, not for coverage; the government's own expert committee called the bilateral model a drawback and recommended full federal funding of an essential medicines list instead [10].
- **"First-dollar" means the drug and the dispensing fee, not everything.** Health Canada excludes delivery and pharmacist prescribing fees [33]; PEI charges them [31], BC's Full Payment Policy forbids them [36]. Diabetes supplies are not first-dollar in any jurisdiction: Manitoba leaves them under deductible-based provincial Pharmacare [19], PEI excludes syringes and pen needles and co-pays test strips [24], BC funds them through Fair PharmaCare and Plans C, F and W [36].
- **Devices were funded by a one-time payment.** Manitoba's Stream 2 is $9,945,348 in a single fiscal year, against Stream 1's $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each following year [40]. BC used the money to list the mylife Ypsopump (Dec 2025) and Omnipod 5 (Apr 2026) and to cover lancets, ketone strips and alcohol wipes [36].
- **Ozempic is not covered** — "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [19].
- **Hormone replacement therapy was a federal requirement written into the contracts**, not provincial discretion: Manitoba's agreement section 5 obliges free HRT for all residents [40].
- **Utilisation is unreported by design.** Manitoba's agreement requires annual financial statements and, for devices only, "the amount of Savings delivered" [40]; evaluation "rests with Manitoba" [40]. The only published user counts are PEI's (over 5,000 for contraception, over 20,000 for diabetes) [27] and Manitoba's provincial program (12,436 in month one at $743,528; over 53,000 people and 190,000 prescriptions in year one) [38][42].
- **Health Canada publishes what it is required to publish.** The rare-disease strategy requires outcome reporting from all provinces except Quebec and produced a published figure: "Over 632 people living in Canada got new access to drugs for their rare condition due to strategy funding" [41]. Pharmacare has no equivalent.
- **The program stopped expanding, and the money is winding down.** Health Minister Michel says Ottawa is not in active discussions [25]; the November 2025 budget added nothing and mentioned pharmacare once [25]; Budget 2026 (Nov 2026) had "no new pharmacare funding" [28]; the federal contribution runs to $269.6 million by 2028-29 before the agreements expire [16][28].
- **Cost: $11.2B rising to $13.4B a year** in incremental public-sector cost for a full single-payer plan on the RAMQ formulary, with economy-wide savings of $1.4B–$2.2B [2]. The 2019 Hoskins council put it at $15.3B a year by 2027 [8]; the 2025 expert committee put an essential medicines list at $6.0–$9.8B for 2025-26 [10]. The first phase as legislated was costed at $1.9B over five years [6].

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually requires, and what "first phase" was defined to be

The Pharmacare Act received Royal Assent on 10 October 2024 and came into force immediately [12]. Understanding what it has delivered since requires reading what it actually obliges, because the gap between the statute's ambition and its operative machinery explains almost everything that follows.

The Act does not create a benefit. Its coverage provision is conditional on a second, separate legal instrument — a bilateral funding agreement with a province or territory. Section 6(1) reads: "The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes" [1]. The condition is doing all the work. A House of Commons committee amended the clause so that the Minister "must" rather than "may" pay where conditions are met [3], which sounds like a strengthening but is not one in practice: the mandatory duty only bites once a province or territory has signed, and nothing in the Act obliges the Minister to secure a signature, or requires any province to sign. The Library of Parliament's summary describes the same structure neutrally: the Act "requires the Minister, if certain conditions are met, to make payments to provinces and territories to cover specific prescription drugs and related products for contraception or diabetes" [3].

Two consequences follow. First, the Act creates no individual entitlement: no Canadian can point to the statute and demand a covered drug. Second, the Act's purpose clause commits the government only to "continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare" [1] — a direction of travel, not a destination with a date.

### What "first phase" means, and what it does not

The phrase "first phase" appears throughout government communications but is not statutory language. Health Canada used it as an administrative label: "The Minister of Health will continue working with provinces and territories to reach bilateral agreements to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar access to a range of contraception and diabetes medications as the first phase of a national universal pharmacare program" [12]. When the bill was introduced in February 2024, the government described it as proposing "the foundational principles for first phase of national universal pharmacare in Canada and describes the Government of Canada’s intent to work with provinces and territories (PTs) to provide universal, single-payer coverage for a number of contraception and diabetes medications" [4] — the language of intent, not of obligation.

The scope was narrow and itemised. Health Canada's contraception backgrounder named a specific list rather than a category: "This includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills" [5]. And that list was explicitly a negotiating position, not a guaranteed benefit: "The Government of Canada will be launching discussions with PTs on providing universal, single-payer coverage based on the list of contraceptive drugs and devices attached to this backgrounder" [5].

Devices sat outside the statute altogether. Diabetes supplies — syringes, test strips, insulin pumps, glucose monitors — were announced as a separate fund: "Separate from Bill C-64, the federal government is announcing its intention to establish a fund to support access to diabetes devices and supplies. Further details regarding this fund will be provided following discussions with PT partners, who will be essential partners to its roll out" [7]. The Act's first phase therefore covered drugs; devices arrived later through the agreements, not through the legislation.

First-dollar coverage is the defining feature of what the Act funds, and it is written in: "For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients" [1]. Patients pay nothing at the counter for listed products.

### The Act's other obligations, none of which deliver coverage

Beyond payments, the Act imposes a set of procedural duties with one-year deadlines. Section 8(1) requires the Minister to ask the Canadian Drug Agency to prepare, within one year of Royal Assent, a list of essential prescription drugs and related products to inform a national formulary setting the scope of drugs Canadians should have access to under national universal pharmacare [1]. Section 11(1) requires a committee of experts, established within 30 days, "to make recommendations respecting options for the operation and financing of national, universal, single-payer pharmacare" [1]. A national bulk purchasing strategy and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy were also due within a year [1]. All of these were done — but none of them puts a drug in anyone's hands.

The formulary track is worth noting for scale. The advisory panel produced "a proposed list of 513 drugs and 6 related products across 14 therapeutic areas" [13] — a package roughly two orders of magnitude broader than the contraception-and-diabetes first phase. That contrast is the clearest measure of how deliberately partial the implemented program is.

The Act's long-term funding commitment also begins somewhere other than the first phase: "The Government of Canada commits to maintaining long-term funding for the provinces, territories and Indigenous peoples to improve the accessibility and affordability of pharmaceutical products, beginning with those for rare diseases" [1]. The first phase sits alongside a separate rare-disease stream rather than being the whole of the Act's funding promise.

### The government's own expert committee criticised the delivery mechanism

The committee the Act created did not endorse the bilateral-agreement model. Its 2025 report recommended full federal funding of an essential medicines list, arguing that a single-payer approach "avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements, enshrines universal access and strengthens the ability to negotiate drug prices with drug companies" [10]. It also described the Act's achievement in modest terms: "The act laid the legal and policy groundwork for a universal pharmacare system, starting with contraceptives and diabetes medications and working towards a more comprehensive formulary" [10]. That is the government's own appointed body saying the statute was groundwork, and that the agreement-by-agreement route it mandates was a weakness rather than a design feature.

**Inference (mine, not a source's):** the Act was drafted to be unfalsifiable on delivery. It legislates a funding mechanism that activates only on provincial consent, sets deadlines for studies rather than for coverage, and defines no benefit package that a citizen could be denied. That structure means a government can comply fully with the statute while covering nobody — which is precisely the question the rest of this report has to answer with counts rather than intentions.

### 2. Which provinces and territories signed, for how much, and which are excluded

Four jurisdictions signed, all within a five-week window in early 2025, and all before the April 2025 federal election. Nothing has been signed since. Health Canada's national pharmacare page, updated 26 January 2026, still says: "We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter" [31].

### The four agreements

**Manitoba — 27 February 2025.** The first agreement, announced as "the first-ever national pharmacare agreement": "the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans" [21]. Coverage was to begin for the majority of products in June 2025. Manitoba's own program, the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program, took effect slightly earlier, on 15 April 2025 [19]. The federal announcement framed the reach as nearly 350,000 Manitobans for contraception and over 149,000 with diabetes [21].

**British Columbia — 6 March 2025.** Health Canada's release: the agreement would "invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC" [14]. The federal framing of reach was more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [14].

**Prince Edward Island — 7 March 2025.** "Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them" [22]. The pharmacare money was part of a larger package — PEI's release describes more than $40 million over four years across two agreements. Coverage began 1 May 2025. Reach: over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes [22].

**Yukon — 21 March 2025.** The smallest agreement: up to $9.5 million over four years [23]. The federal release said Yukoners could anticipate coverage "no later than January 2026." Reach: more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes [23].

### The totals, and the discrepancy inside them

The four agreements commit roughly $928 million over four years — about 62 per cent of the $1.5 billion the 2024 budget set aside for pharmacare over five years [20][25]. The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives and the Canadian Health Coalition both use the $928 million figure.

There is a discrepancy in the public record on the largest agreement. Health Canada describes BC's deal as more than $670 million over four years [14]. The Government of British Columbia describes the same agreement as "up to $670 million in funding over three years" [18]. Both cannot be right, and the difference matters for per-capita comparisons: a three-year denominator raises BC's annual value by a third. I could not resolve which is correct from the agreement text itself; the federal figure is repeated consistently across two Health Canada pages, while the provincial figure appears in BC's own news release. Anyone quoting BC's per-capita number should state which term they assume.

Per-capita funding is not uniform, which is itself a finding. CCPA calculated: "The per capita funding of the four participating jurisdictions varies widely, from $117 per resident for British Columbia to $198 per resident for Yukon. The average per capita amount of $156 was applied to non-participating jurisdictions to calculate likely amounts they would be eligible to receive in federal funding" [20]. On that basis CCPA estimated forgone funding of roughly $2.5 billion for Ontario, $171 million for Nova Scotia and $136 million for New Brunswick over four years [20].

### Who is outside

Nine jurisdictions have no agreement: Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, the Northwest Territories and Nunavut. The population consequence is stark. CBC reported: "With just four pharmacare deals, only about 17 per cent of the Canadian population is covered" [25]. CCPA put the covered population at "nearly 7.5 million people" [20].

The reasons for non-participation differ by province, and the record is more informative than the usual "provinces refused" framing. CBC surveyed every non-signatory: no jurisdiction said it was in talks; Saskatchewan and New Brunswick both said they were ready to speak with Ottawa; Quebec and Alberta said they were waiting to hear back from the federal government; Nova Scotia said it had wanted to restart talks five months earlier and had not heard back [25]. Alberta added that it had "serious concerns" about long-term sustainability and wanted to decide what medications were covered [25]. Health Minister Marjorie Michel's own account of the obstacle was that some provinces did not want the two categories on offer: "When the pharmacare agreement happened last time, some provinces or territories didn't want to have the two coverages that we offered at that time. And it's still true" [25].

**Inference (mine):** the pattern is not simply provinces declining free money. At least three provinces say they are willing or waiting, and the federal side is not negotiating. The binding constraint since spring 2025 has been federal willingness and federal money, not provincial refusal — a distinction the "most provinces are refusing" framing in advocacy material obscures.

### The anti-substitution clause, and what the baseline reveals

The agreement text contains a protection the press releases do not mention. Canada may withhold or reduce payments if Manitoba's 2022-23 Stream 1 spending reported in Annex B is greater than the amount reported for a given year, in which case "Canada will withhold or reduce an amount equivalent to the difference between these two amounts" [40]. In other words, federal pharmacare money must sit on top of a fixed provincial baseline; a province cannot use it to replace its own spending and book the difference.

Annex B discloses what that baseline was: Manitoba spent $23,195,236 on the diabetes products on the list and $750,746 on the contraception products in 2022-23, for a total of $23,945,982, plus $1,449,593 on insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors [40]. Set that against Stream 1 funding of $52,509,230 in 2025-26 rising to $54,603,615 [40]. The federal transfer is roughly double what Manitoba was already spending on the same drug categories — which is a genuine expansion of public spending, not a relabelling.

It also tells you where the money goes. Manitoba was already paying for most of these drugs; the change is that patients stopped paying deductibles and copays on them. The federal money largely replaced household and third-party spending on drugs the province was already subsidising, which is exactly the mechanism PBO modelled when it found higher public cost alongside lower economy-wide cost [2].

### What the provinces got, in federal money per resident

The per-capita spread ($117 in BC to $198 in Yukon) reflects neither need nor population alone; it reflects bilateral negotiation. There is no formula in the Act, no published allocation rule, and no requirement that funding track diabetes prevalence or uninsured rates. That is a design feature of the agreement-by-agreement model the Act mandates, and it is the mechanism by which the same federal program delivers materially different value per resident depending on which province they live in.

### 3. What is covered in practice: the drug lists, devices and supplies, and how it interacts with private insurance

The gap between the federal description of coverage and what provincial programs actually pay for is the most under-reported fact about the program. Health Canada's page tells Canadians: "Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee." It then excludes "delivery fees" and "pharmacist prescribing fees" [33]. It also warns, on the "about" page, that "You may still have to pay other fees, like delivery fees or prescribing fees" [31]. First-dollar coverage, in other words, attaches to the drug cost and the dispensing fee and nothing else.

### The contraception list

The covered list is broad within a defined clinical range but stops well short of all contraception. PEI's resident guide, published for the 1 May 2025 launch, enumerates it: "The program covers some oral contraceptives (i.e. birth control medication), hormonal intrauterine devices (IUD), copper IUDs, contraceptive implants, contraceptive injections, vaginal rings, and emergency contraceptives" [24]. And explicitly not others: "No, non-hormonal contraceptives, such as condoms, cervical caps, diaphragms, and sponges are not covered under the National Pharmacare Program. Copper IUDs (a non-hormonal contraceptive) are available at no cost with a prescription through the National Pharmacare Program" [24]. Generics are fully covered; choosing a brand where a generic exists means paying the difference [24].

The design choice here — devices yes, barrier methods no — is not explained anywhere in the federal materials. It is a defensible clinical decision (LARCs and oral contraceptives are the methods with the strongest evidence base for effectiveness) but it does mean that the cheapest and most accessible methods are outside the program.

### The diabetes list, and where devices actually stand

This is where the federal and provincial accounts diverge most sharply. Health Canada states: "The pharmacare agreements we've signed with provinces and territories will also help you access the supplies you need to: administer your medication, such as insulin pumps and syringes manage and monitor your condition, such as glucose monitors and test strips" [31].

The provinces' own documents do not support that as a description of the pharmacare program. Manitoba is explicit: "Diabetes supplies remain as benefits under the Manitoba Pharmacare Program (where deductibles apply), and other provincial programs such as Employment and Income Assistance" [19] — that is, supplies are not part of the federal-funded program at all and remain subject to income-based deductibles. PEI is similarly specific: "The National Pharmacare Program in Prince Edward Island does not cover the cost of insulin syringes or insulin pen needles" [24], and blood glucose test strips carry an $11 co-pay per 100 strips for non-insulin patients (reducible to $2.20 with private insurance) [24]. PEI also states that its Insulin Pump Program and Glucose Sensor Program criteria are unchanged by pharmacare [24].

The most defensible reading is that devices and supplies were addressed in the agreements through adjacent provincial programs and incremental funding, not through a new first-dollar benefit — and that the federal page describes the aspiration rather than the delivered benefit. Health Canada's own 2024 backgrounder had already placed devices outside the legislation entirely, in a fund to be detailed later [7].

### Ozempic and the boundaries of the list

The covered list is a negotiated document, not a clinical guideline, and its exclusions are consequential. Manitoba: "Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories" [19]. Semaglutide is the highest-profile diabetes drug of the decade and it is outside the program — which produces the unusual situation where a person with diabetes can receive insulin free and pay out of pocket for the drug their physician might otherwise prefer.

This exclusion has a second-order effect on private insurance. The Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association told a reporter: "The Pharmacare Act is clear that insurers cannot cover any drugs that are covered by single-payer government pharmacare" — adding that "in provinces that have signed deals with the Federal government to date, GLP-1 drugs are not covered by pharmacare. As such, insurers will continue to cover these drugs in all provinces and territories, including those with federal pharmacare" [27]. Note that the industry association asserts a legal prohibition on private coverage of pharmacare-listed drugs; the Act's text as I read it does not plainly say that, and the association is describing an interpretation rather than quoting a provision.

### The displacement question

Whether pharmacare adds to private coverage or replaces it is the single biggest unknown in the cost estimates, and the one real-world signal is alarming in a specific way. New Brunswick's health minister told campaigners that private insurers might respond to pharmacare by dropping Ozempic coverage, pushing those costs onto the provincial plan — a potential $60 million in additional cost. The department did not explain where the figure came from [27].

PEI's design confirms the mechanism is live: "Yes, PEI residents with private insurance are still eligible for the National Pharmacare Program. The costs of contraceptives and diabetes medications included in the National Pharmacare Program will be paid publicly.This means you won’t need to coordinate benefits for covered products with your private insurance plans" [24]. The public plan pays first, and private plans are not expected to top up. That is the correct policy choice for access — nobody should face a deductible for a covered drug — but it means that for the covered categories, employers and employees are paying premiums for coverage that no longer pays out. Whether insurers rebate those premiums or bank them is not measured anywhere in the public record.

### Universality, portability, and the Canada Health Act claim

Eligibility within a participating province is genuinely universal. Health Canada states that you are "covered under pharmacare no matter your" age, income, or private or workplace health insurance status [32]. Those on federal plans (NIHB, CAF, VAC, CSC, IFH) keep their existing coverage [32], and Manitoba excludes people with 100 per cent coverage through NIHB or EIA from its program [19].

Portability — a Canada Health Act principle the Act invokes — is not delivered. PEI's guide states that medications "will not be eligible for coverage if they are filled at an out-of-province pharmacy", and that eligibility "will end the day you leave PEI" [24]. Students studying out of province must have prescriptions filled by a PEI pharmacy [24]. A person in Vancouver can fill a pharmacare prescription in Seattle's suburbs and pay full price; a person in Charlottetown cannot fill one in Moncton. That is a meaningful divergence from the portability standard applied to hospital and physician services, and it exists because pharmacare was built outside the Canada Health Act rather than inside it.

### Hormone therapy: an obligation, not provincial discretion

BC's Plan NP covers menopausal hormone therapy at 100 per cent [15] — a category nowhere in the federal first phase as legislated. I initially read this as provincial discretion expanding the benefit. The agreement text corrects that: HRT was written into the bilateral deal as a federal-side requirement. Manitoba's agreement contains a standalone clause — section 5, "Additional coverage improvements" — stating: "Manitoba will provide free public coverage of hormone replacement therapies specified by Manitoba to treat menopausal symptoms for all Residents" [40]. BC's agreement contains an equivalent. So HRT is part of the federal template, negotiated into the agreements rather than legislated in the Act, and the four jurisdictions that signed got it while the nine that did not sign got nothing. That is a real coverage expansion delivered entirely outside the statute — and it is the clearest illustration of how much of this program exists in contracts rather than in law.

### How devices were actually funded: a one-off, not a benefit

The Manitoba agreement shows the structure precisely. It has two streams: "Stream 1" is universal first-dollar coverage of the drug list; "Stream 2" is to "Increase access to insulin pumps and advanced glucose monitors (AGM) by expanding eligibility for public coverage of these products" [40]. Stream 1 pays Manitoba $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years. Stream 2 is a single payment: "The amount of $9,945,348 is to be transferred to Manitoba in Fiscal Year 2025-2026" [40].

That is the answer to the devices question, and it is not the answer the federal communications imply. Device access was funded by a one-time transfer in a single fiscal year, not by an ongoing first-dollar benefit. In BC the same pattern holds: federal pharmacare money let PharmaCare expand coverage of "alcohol wipes, lancets and blood and urine ketone strips" and list the mylife Ypsopump (17 December 2025) and the Omnipod 5 automated insulin delivery system (1 April 2026) [36] — genuine improvements, delivered through existing provincial device programs. But BC confirms the funding route: "Coverage for diabetes supplies is through Fair PharmaCare, Plan C, Plan F and Plan W. Coverage for insulin pumps is through these plans as well as Plan B" [36]. Those are deductible-based and income-tested plans. Plan NP, the first-dollar plan, covers drugs. So a British Columbian with diabetes gets insulin free at the counter and still meets a Fair PharmaCare deductible before their lancets and test strips are covered.

BC does apply a stronger patient protection than PEI on the drug side: "PharmaCare's Full Payment Policy applies to Plan NP benefits with 100% coverage. This means pharmacies cannot charge a client for the medication or any service associated with the dispense" [36]. PEI, by contrast, allows delivery and prescribing fees to be charged on top [31]. Two provinces, two different answers to what "first-dollar" means in practice.

### 4. How many people are actually using it, and what the government does and does not publish

I searched hard for utilisation numbers — provincial news releases, annual reports, program pages, legislature statements, CIHI metadata, Health Canada's departmental results reports — and the finding is not simply that the data is missing. It is that no reporting obligation exists that would produce it, and the federal government demonstrably knows how to impose one.

### What has actually been published

Two jurisdictions have published counts of people reached, and both counts concern programs that began before federal pharmacare money arrived.

**Prince Edward Island.** PEI's Department of Health and Wellness, on the program's first anniversary: "Over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [27].

**Manitoba.** Manitoba's free birth control program began 1 October 2024 — five months before the federal agreement — under provincial funding, covering about 60 methods including the pill, IUDs and hormone injections, with the morning-after pill excluded because it is available without prescription [37]. Its first-month figure was reported in the legislature: "In one month, 12,436 Manitobans signed up for free birth control with many more accessing it each and every day," at a cost of $743,528 in that month against an expected $11 million a year [38]. By the end of the first year the province reported the fuller picture: "Between Oct. 2, 2024, and Oct. 21, 2025, more than 53,000 people got free birth control through the program," and "Over that period, 190,000 prescriptions were dispensed across all types of contraceptives," with "Nearly nine in 10 of those prescriptions were for oral birth control" [42].

Manitoba's first month is the single most useful data point in the entire record, because it is the only place where a cost and a user count appear together: $743,528 for 12,436 people, or about $60 per person in the first month (my division). Manitoba's 190,000 prescriptions for 53,000 people works out to roughly 3.6 prescriptions per user over the year, consistent with monthly dispensing of oral contraceptives (my division). Both show that when a province funds and administers free contraception itself, it can report people, prescriptions and dollars together.

**British Columbia.** BC's provincial free-contraception program, running since 1 April 2023 and budgeted at $119 million over three years, reported "166,000 women were prescribed free contraceptives" in its first six months, rising to 188,000 after eight [38]. For 2024 alone the federal release gives about 227,000 people, and more than 306,000 since the program began [14].

These are the only utilisation figures I could find for any of the four jurisdictions, and none of them is a federal pharmacare utilisation count. BC's 227,000 figure predates Plan NP (launched March 2026) and describes a provincially funded program [18]. Manitoba's 53,000 is a provincial program. Only PEI's numbers describe the federally funded program, and PEI's contraception element — over 5,000 people — is modest against a stated eligible pool of over 41,000 Islanders [22], roughly one in eight.

### What the agreements require provinces to report

The reason there is no national number is in the contracts. Manitoba's funding agreement sets out, in section 4.9, a detailed annual financial statement: total funding received, funding spent on Stream 1 and Stream 2 product costs and eligible expenditures, and spending "from sources other than Canada" [40]. That is accounting, not outcomes.

The only results-reporting clause in the agreement concerns devices: "Beginning in Fiscal Year 2026-27, as a condition of annual funding under this Agreement, by October 1 of each Fiscal Year, Manitoba agrees to report to Canada the amount of Savings delivered to Manitoba Residents as a result of the measures taken to improve access to Diabetes Devices and Supplies under this Agreement" [40]. "Savings" is defined in the agreement as what residents would otherwise have paid out of pocket [40].

There is no clause requiring a count of people covered, prescriptions filled, or patients reached for the drug program. And evaluation is devolved entirely: "Responsibility for evaluating the Initiative rests with Manitoba in accordance with its own evaluation policies and practices" [40]. Canada's role is passive — section 6.6 gives it the right, with prior notice, to incorporate provincial data into reports it "may prepare for its own purposes" [40]. Nothing requires it to prepare one.

### The comparison that settles it

The federal government runs a second, contemporaneous drug-funding program with all thirteen provinces and territories: the National Strategy for Drugs for Rare Diseases, $1.4 billion over three years. Its reporting requirements are different and the difference is decisive. "As part of these agreements, all provinces and territories, except Quebec, must submit annual financial statements and report on outcomes and results achieved collaboratively with the Government of Canada. This supports transparent use of strategy funds" [41]. And Health Canada publishes the result: "Over 632 people living in Canada got new access to drugs for their rare condition due to strategy funding" [41], alongside the share of funding spent (88 per cent), the split across categories, and a drug-by-drug table of how many jurisdictions cover each product [41].

**Inference (mine):** this is not a capability problem, a privacy problem, or a data-system problem. In the same department, in the same period, with the same provinces, a drug-funding program with outcome-reporting obligations produced a published count of people reached. The pharmacare agreements were drafted without that obligation. The absence of a utilisation number is therefore a drafting choice made in early 2025, and it is reversible by amendment under section 8 of the agreement.

### What the federal government does report instead

Health Canada's 2024-25 Departmental Results Report confirms the agreements were signed and gives no utilisation data: "Health Canada signed national pharmacare bilateral agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon to provide free or low-cost coverage for contraceptives and diabetes medications" [30]. The nearest performance indicator in the same report is a population-level survey measure — the share of Canadians aged 12 and over who "did not fill a prescription for medicine or skipped doses of medicine because of the cost" — against a target of at most 8.0 per cent, with an actual of 5.1 per cent in both 2023-24 and 2024-25 [30]. That indicator is national, survey-based, and cannot attribute change to pharmacare; it also did not move between the two years reported.

What is published instead is eligible population. BC's launch release: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [18]. The federal BC release: more than 1.3 million for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes [14]. Manitoba: nearly 350,000 and over 149,000 [21]. PEI: over 41,000 and over 16,000 [22]. Yukon: more than 12,000 and more than 3,000 [23]. These sum to roughly the 7.5 million people CCPA describes as covered [20] — but "covered" means eligible to walk into a pharmacy, not having done so.

One caution on comparing these numbers: PEI's diabetes count (over 20,000 users) exceeds the eligible-population estimate given at signing (over 16,000 with diabetes) [22], because the province expanded blood glucose test strip access to people on non-insulin diabetes drugs at the same time [24]. The federal eligible-population figures are not a clean denominator.

### Why automatic enrolment forecloses the obvious metric

BC's program is structured so that an enrolment count cannot exist: "Coverage is automatic at the pharmacy. You do not need to register or submit receipts" [15], and all MSP enrollees are automatically enrolled [15]. Manitoba's and Yukon's work the same way, with Pacific Blue Cross adjudicating Yukon claims in real time at pharmacies [34]. Automatic enrolment is the right policy — it removes the application barrier that suppresses take-up in every benefits program — but it means the only measurable quantity is prescriptions dispensed, and dispensing counts are not published.

The claims data that would produce those counts exists. CIHI's NPDUIS holds claims and formulary data from ten provincial and territorial public drug programs, with client identifiers [35]; all four participating jurisdictions submit. But CIHI's most recent available year is 2025-26, with 2026 calendar-year data not available until June 2027 [35], and no CIHI product separates pharmacare-listed drugs into their own reporting category. That is a timing and categorisation limit, not a prohibition — and the fact that Health Canada extracted a 632-person count from thirteen jurisdictions for rare diseases shows what could be assembled if it were asked for.

### The number that matters is the one nobody has

Because the program pays first and covers people who already had private insurance — PEI confirms the public plan pays and "you won’t need to coordinate benefits for covered products with your private insurance plans" [24]; Yukon confirms first-dollar payment "including for residents with private insurance" [39] — some share of every user count would have obtained the same drug anyway. The measure that matters for access is the marginal one: people who obtained a drug they would not otherwise have obtained. No government has published that, and with automatic enrolment it cannot be read off claims data alone, since claims record dispensing but not the counterfactual.

**Inference (mine):** the honest summary is that roughly 7.5 million people are eligible, something in the low tens of thousands have demonstrably used the federally funded contraception benefit in the two jurisdictions that report (over 5,000 in PEI, over 53,000 in Manitoba under a program Manitoba started itself), and no one can state the national number because no one was required to count it.

### What is actually published

Only one jurisdiction has published utilisation figures, and they came out through a provincial news release and a reporter's email, not through the program's own reporting. PEI's Department of Health and Wellness: "Over 5,000 Islanders have accessed free contraception, saving more than $500,000 in out-of-pocket costs, while over 20,000 people with diabetes have benefited from covered medications and supplies, saving more than $200,000 in out-of-pocket costs" [27].

Those are the only hard utilisation numbers in the record for any of the four jurisdictions. Three things follow from them.

First, the diabetes figure (over 20,000) exceeds the eligible-population estimate given when the agreement was signed (over 16,000 with diabetes) [22]. That is not necessarily an error: the federal estimate was of people with diabetes, while the provincial figure counts people who benefited from covered medications and supplies, and PEI expanded blood glucose test strip access to people on non-insulin diabetes drugs at the same time [24]. But it means the eligible-population numbers used in federal announcements are not a reliable denominator and should not be compared with utilisation counts without care.

Second, the money is small. More than $500,000 in out-of-pocket savings for contraception across a year and more than $200,000 for diabetes, against a federal commitment of more than $30 million over four years [22], implies out-of-pocket savings are a very small fraction of program cost — which is what you would expect when the program is paying pharmacies for drugs that were previously paid for by insurers, households, or not purchased at all.

Third, the contraception uptake is modest relative to the eligible population. Over 5,000 people against a stated eligible pool of over 41,000 Islanders [22] is roughly one in eight. That is not a failure — a first year of a new program, with no registration required, will not reach everyone — but it does not support claims of transformative take-up either.

### Why there is no national number

BC's program is structured so that an enrolment count cannot exist. "Coverage is automatic at the pharmacy. You do not need to register or submit receipts" [15]. All MSP enrollees are automatically enrolled in Plan NP [15]. Manitoba's program is similarly automatic for anyone eligible for provincial Pharmacare [19]. Yukon's is automatic too, with Pacific Blue Cross adjudicating claims in real time [34]. Automatic enrolment is good policy — it removes the application barrier that suppresses take-up in every benefits program — but it means the only measurable quantity is prescriptions dispensed, not people covered.

And the federal government does not publish dispensing counts. Health Canada's 2024-25 Departmental Results Report, the department's own annual accounting to Parliament, confirms the agreements were signed and offers no utilisation data whatsoever: "Health Canada signed national pharmacare bilateral agreements with British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island and Yukon to provide free or low-cost coverage for contraceptives and diabetes medications" [30]. The nearest performance indicator in the same report is a population-level survey measure — the share of Canadians aged 12 and over who "did not fill a prescription for medicine or skipped doses of medicine because of the cost" — against a target of at most 8.0 per cent, with an actual of 5.1 per cent in both 2023-24 and 2024-25 [30]. That indicator is national, survey-based, biennial, and cannot attribute any change to pharmacare — and it did not change between the two years reported.

### What could produce a number, and does not yet

The claims data exists. CIHI's National Prescription Drug Utilization Information System holds "claims and formulary data for public drug programs from 10 provinces/territories" and captures a unique client identifier, client age, client gender, pharmacy province, prescriber identifiers and plan-paid amounts [35]. BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon all submit claims. The data could in principle produce a count of distinct people who received a pharmacare-listed drug.

It has not been released for that purpose. CIHI's most recent available year is 2025-26, with the next annual release in June 2027, and 2026 calendar-year claims data available only in June 2027 [35]. No CIHI product I could find separates pharmacare-listed drugs from the rest of public plan spending. CIHI's metadata describes NPDUIS as holding claims from ten provincial and territorial public drug programs, without any separate pharmacare reporting category [35].

**Inference (mine):** the absence of a published utilisation count is a choice, not a technical limitation. The federal government committed $1.5 billion and has spent roughly $88 million of it in 2025-26 [16]; it reports the signing of agreements as the achievement and does not report whether anyone got a drug. For a program whose stated purpose is improving access, the metric that would demonstrate success — the number of people who obtained a covered product who would not otherwise have obtained it — has not been defined, let alone measured.

### The one number that is genuinely large

The figures that do get published are eligible populations, not users, and they are consistently reported as if they were reach. BC's launch release: "Nearly 570,000 British Columbians living with diabetes will be supported, as well as approximately 160,000 people with menopausal symptoms" [18]. The federal BC announcement: support for "more than 1.3 million British Columbians" for contraception and "nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes" [14]. Manitoba: "nearly 350,000 Manitobans" and "over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes" [21]. PEI: "over 41,000 Islanders" and "over 16,000 people who have diabetes" [22]. Yukon: "more than 12,000 Yukoners" and "more than 3,000" [23].

These add up to roughly the 7.5 million people CCPA describes as covered [20] — but "covered" in that sentence means eligible to walk into a pharmacy, not having done so. The gap between eligibility and use is the entire question, and only PEI has answered any part of it.

### The BC case is the most informative, because BC had a program first

BC already provided free contraceptives before the federal agreement: "The Province already provides free contraceptives, and the same contraceptives will continue to be free under national pharmacare" [18]. And the province published results for that pre-existing program: "In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted" [14].

This is the most useful utilisation evidence in the entire record, and it is not about the federal program at all. BC's provincial free-contraception program, running since April 2023 without federal money, reached about 227,000 people in 2024 — against an eligible population of more than 1.3 million, or roughly one in six. That is the best available estimate of what a well-run, no-registration, first-dollar contraception benefit actually achieves in a Canadian province after two years. It is a meaningful number and it is nowhere near universal take-up.

It also means the federal contribution to BC did not create contraception coverage. BC's own framing is that the federal-funded Plan NP changed cost-sharing, not the drug list: "BC PharmaCare has long covered diabetes medications and menopausal hormone therapies, but people often had to meet deductible requirements based on income before receiving full coverage" [18]. The federal money removed the deductible and added HRT. That is a real benefit to real people — but it is not new coverage of new drugs, and any claim that pharmacare extended contraception coverage to 1.3 million British Columbians misdescribes what happened.

### What "using it" would even mean

There is a conceptual problem underneath the missing data. Because the program pays first and covers people who already had private insurance [24], some share of the 20,000 PEI diabetes users and the 227,000 BC contraception users would have obtained the same drugs anyway — paid by an insurer, or out of pocket. The number that matters for access is the marginal one: people who obtained a drug they would not otherwise have obtained. Nobody has published that, and with automatic enrolment and no registration it may be difficult to construct from claims data alone, since claims record dispensing but not the counterfactual.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say a full program would cost

Cost estimates for Canadian pharmacare span a very wide range — from $1.9 billion over five years for the implemented first phase to $13.4 billion a year for a full single-payer plan — and the range is not evidence of disagreement about arithmetic. It reflects four different questions being answered: what is covered, who pays, whether existing private spending is counted as a saving or merely transferred, and what happens to drug prices and utilisation when coverage becomes universal.

### The PBO's full single-payer estimate (October 2023)

The benchmark figure is the Parliamentary Budget Officer's October 2023 report, *Cost Estimate of a Single-payer Universal Drug Plan*, prepared in response to parliamentary interest. PBO modelled a plan based on Quebec's formulary: "Upon the implementation of a single-payer universal drug plan based on Quebec's Régie de l'assurance maladie du Québec (RAMQ) formulary— "Pharmacare"—we estimate the incremental cost to the public sector (that is federal and provincial governments combined) to be $11.2 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $13.4 billion in 2027-28" [2].

Those figures are the *incremental public-sector* cost — the additional burden on government, net of what private insurers and households were already paying. Three other numbers in the same report matter for anyone quoting it:

- Gross total drug expenditure under the plan: "PBO estimates total drug expenditures under Pharmacare to be $33.2 billion in 2024-25" [2].
- Gross cost incremental to existing public drug plans, before copayment revenue and offsetting federal savings: "PBO estimates the gross cost incremental to that of public drug plans will be $14.8 billion in 2024-25, increasing to $17.3 billion in 2027-28" [2].
- Economy-wide savings: "While there are incremental costs to the public sector resulting from the transfer of expenditures currently covered by the private insurance and out-of-pocket outlays, economy-wide spending on the drugs listed on the formulary is estimated to be lower. The economy-wide savings are projected to increase from $1.4 billion in 2024-25 to $2.2 billion in 2027-28" [2].

The mechanism behind the simultaneous higher public cost and lower total spending is straightforward: PBO assumed the public plan would pay prices lower than private plans pay, and that private plans' per-capita spending was growing faster than the public system's. Money moves onto the public ledger; the total shrinks slightly. Both halves of that finding get quoted selectively — the $13.4 billion by opponents of pharmacare, the $2.2 billion in savings by supporters — and each is only half the PBO's result.

### The PBO's costing of the Act itself (2024)

PBO also costed Bill C-64 as introduced, and the contrast with the full-plan figure is stark: "The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years" [6]. That is roughly one-seventieth of the annual incremental cost of the full plan, because the first phase covers two drug categories for a subset of the population and is designed to top up existing coverage rather than replace private insurance.

PBO was unusually explicit about the fragility of this estimate: "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage. Drug expenditures have several cost drivers and the projections are highly sensitive to the projected growth rate of those cost drivers, and the determinants of those cost factors" [6]. The report also noted that because the program was designed to expand rather than replace coverage, no new federal confidential rebates were assumed — meaning negotiated discounts, if achieved, would push actual cost below the estimate [6].

### The 2019 Advisory Council (Hoskins) estimate

The government's own pre-legislative Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare, chaired by Eric Hoskins, produced the estimate that framed the political debate: "We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines. As the national formulary grows to cover a comprehensive list of drugs, we estimate that annual incremental costs will reach $15.3 billion in 2027" [8]. Its savings projection was of the same order as PBO's: "As early as 2022, when national pharmacare would cover essential medications, total spending on prescription drugs would be $300 million lower than without pharmacare. By 2027, total spending on prescription drugs would be $5 billion lower than it would be without national pharmacare" [8]. The Hoskins $15.3 billion for 2027 lands close to PBO's $13.4 billion for 2027-28 — a genuine convergence from two different modelling teams, on the comprehensive-formulary scenario.

### The 2025 National Pharmacare Committee of Experts: $6–10 billion for an essential medicines list

The committee created by the Act produced a lower estimate, because it costed a narrower benefit — a defined essential medicines list, publicly funded, rather than the full RAMQ formulary: "The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2)" [10]. Its appendix gives the precise band: "The approach explained below yielded a range in costs for pharmacare from **$6.0 to $9.8 billion** in 2025 to 26" [10].

Crucially, the committee built its upper bound directly from PBO's 2023 work, and disagreed with one of PBO's assumptions: "We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature" [10]. That is the most useful single sentence in the cost literature, because it locates the disagreement precisely: not on whether pharmacare raises public cost (everyone agrees it does) or on whether it lowers total cost (everyone agrees it does, modestly), but on how much additional consumption universal coverage induces. The choice between the two assumptions — 5% versus 13.5% — moves the estimate by billions.

### The earlier PBO estimate, and why it is not comparable

PBO's first pharmacare costing, a September 2017 report prepared for the House of Commons Standing Committee on Health, produced much larger federal-only numbers: "Accounting for the estimated $645 million the federal government already spends in direct drug spending to certain populations, as well as the estimated $398 million in net revenues from co-payments, the net cost to the federal government would be $19.3 billion" for 2015-16, rising to $22.6 billion by 2020-21 [9]. Its gross public-sector incremental cost was lower: "With provincial public plans currently paying $13.1 billion for prescription drugs, the additional gross cost of Pharmacare to the public sector would be $7.3 billion" [9]. Its economy-wide saving was about $4.2 billion, with total drug spending under the program at $20.4 billion versus a $24.6 billion baseline [9].

The 2017 and 2023 reports are not contradictory but they are not comparable either. The 2017 model was a fully federal program absorbing the entire cost; the 2023 model split cost between federal and provincial governments and netted out transfers. Anyone citing "$19.3 billion" and "$11.2 billion" as a trend is comparing a federal-only gross figure with a combined net figure.

### The Fraser Institute's objection

The Fraser Institute's critique is not that the estimates are arithmetically wrong but that they are behaviourally naive: "Crucially, the cost estimates by both the federal government and the PBO fail to account for how Canadians and insurance organizations might respond to national pharmacare" [11]. Its specific claim is that both the federal government's $1.5 billion and PBO's $1.9 billion five-year first-phase figures assume nobody already insured switches to the new plan and no insurer renegotiates its offerings — so if employers drop private drug coverage once a public plan exists, actual public cost rises. The institute points back to PBO's own $13.4 billion annual full-program figure as the more realistic anchor [11]. This is a legitimate structural criticism of first-phase costing, and it cuts in one direction only: it implies the $1.9 billion understates, not overstates, cost.

**Inference (mine):** the defensible summary is that a full single-payer program on a comprehensive formulary costs the public sector roughly $11–15 billion a year more than current arrangements, reduces total national drug spending by a low single-digit percentage, and that an essential-medicines-first version costs $6–10 billion a year. The first phase actually implemented was costed at $1.9 billion over five years, or about $380 million a year (my division), a rounding error against any of these, which is the honest measure of how much of the program has been built.

### 6. The 2026 turn: has the program expanded, stalled or been wound down?

The honest answer to "has it expanded or stalled" is that implementation continued through 2026 while policy stopped in 2025. Those are different curves and they are routinely conflated.

### Implementation did advance, and later than promised

All four jurisdictions now have operating programs, but three of the four arrived well after the agreements were signed.

- **Manitoba:** program effective 15 April 2025 [19], about seven weeks after signature.
- **PEI:** coverage began 1 May 2025 [24], about eight weeks after signature.
- **British Columbia:** Plan NP launched 1 March 2026 [15] — nearly twelve months after the 6 March 2025 agreement.
- **Yukon:** launched 15 April 2026 [34] — thirteen months after signature, and against a federal commitment that coverage would begin "no later than January 2026" [23].

Yukon's slippage is the clearest single measure of the gap between announcement and delivery. In March 2025 the federal release said Yukoners could expect coverage by January 2026 [23]. By late 2025 a territorial spokesperson was saying the program was "on track" to start in March 2026, and it actually started in April. A three-to-four month delay is not scandalous, but it means that for the whole of the 2025-26 fiscal year, two of the four participating jurisdictions had no operating program at all — which is consistent with the federal pharmacare contribution being only $88.1 million in 2025-26 [16] against a four-year commitment of $928 million.

### Policy stopped

No agreement has been signed since 21 March 2025. The evidence that this is a deliberate stop rather than a pause is now substantial and comes from three independent directions.

**The minister.** Health Minister Marjorie Michel told CBC her department is not in active discussions to sign any others: "For now, we have the four provinces with this coverage" [25].

**The budgets.** The November 2025 budget set aside no additional money for pharmacare, with 60 per cent of the original $1.5 billion already committed by the four agreements [25]. In over 400 pages it mentioned pharmacare once, in a line about "protecting the vital social programs Canadians rely on, from child care to dental care to pharmacare" [25]. The Spring Economic Update 2026 repeated the same framing and nothing more: "That's why the government is protecting the essential social programs that give Canadians a fair chance to get ahead—child care, dental care, and pharmacare" [29]. Budget 2026, released 5 November 2026, contained "no new pharmacare funding" and did not mention national pharmacare at all; the only drug-coverage item was a three-year extension of the PEI Affordable Prescription Drug Pilot at $11 million a year from previously provisioned funds [28].

**The department's own page.** Health Canada's national pharmacare page, updated 26 January 2026, describes the forward plan as learning "by doing" in a Canadian context, basing "discussions about the future on what we learn as we implement existing pharmacare agreements" [31]. That is a description of a pilot, not of a national rollout.

### The money is being withdrawn, not just withheld

CCPA's account is that the federal contribution is not merely frozen but scheduled to fall away, and that provincial transfers are shrinking at the same time: "In 2025-26, the federal government contributed $88.1 million to support these provinces and one territory in the expansion of public coverage of diabetes medications and contraception for all residents. The federal pharmacare contribution is expected to increase to $269.6 million by 2028-29" [16] — against bilateral health funding falling from $4.3 billion in 2025-26 to $3.1 billion in 2027-28 [16]. CCPA also reports that PEI's health minister disclosed Ottawa would cut $29 million in health funding to the province over three years [16].

The expiry date is the hard fact in all of this, and it is written into the contracts, not just reported: "This Agreement will come into effect on the date the last party has signed and will end on March 31, 2029, unless terminated earlier" [40]. The four pharmacare agreements expire in 2029 [28]. Santis Health's budget analysis lists it as the last item in its timeline: "2029: The four national pharmacare agreements expire" [28]. No renewal has been announced, no successor framework exists, and no money has been set aside for one.

### The committee the Act created has been ignored

The National Pharmacare Committee of Experts, which the Act required to be struck within 30 days and to report within a year, submitted its final report in November 2025. Benefits Canada's expert panel: "The 2024 federal budget committed $1.5 billion in funding over five years but there has been no new funding since" [17], and the committee's report "was submitted in November 2025 but no action has been taken" [17]. Its central recommendation — full federal funding of an essential medicines list, precisely to escape the bilateral-agreement model — has not been adopted, and the government has not formally responded.

### What the provinces say, and why "refusal" is the wrong word

CBC's survey of non-signatories is the most useful primary reporting on the stall. No jurisdiction said it was in talks. Saskatchewan and New Brunswick said they were ready to speak with Ottawa. Quebec and Alberta said they were waiting to hear back from the federal government. Nova Scotia said it had wanted to restart talks five months earlier and had not heard back [25]. Alberta said it had "serious concerns" about the program's long-term sustainability and wanted to decide what medications were covered [25]. Michel's own explanation was that some provinces did not want the two categories on offer [25].

**Inference (mine):** the record supports a specific causal account. The first phase was designed as a two-category offer with no room for provincial variation, funded from an envelope too small to interest Ontario or Quebec, and administered through a negotiation the federal government stopped conducting after March 2025. Provinces that wanted in were left waiting. That is a federal supply-side failure as much as a provincial demand-side one, and it is not the story either the government ("protecting pharmacare") or its critics ("provinces refusing money") tell.

### What would count as evidence of revival

Three observable things: a signed agreement with any of Ontario, Quebec, Alberta or BC-adjacent large jurisdictions; new money in a federal budget rather than a reallocation of the 2024 envelope; and any federal publication of utilisation. As of the 2026 budget, none of the three has happened. The next plausible windows are the Spring Economic Update 2027 and the fall 2027 budget, after which the agreements run toward expiry with no renewal mechanism in place.


## Beyond this question

Three things follow for anyone tracking this file.

**Watch the contracts, not the announcements.** Every substantive fact in this report came from the agreement text or a provincial program document, not from a press release. The Manitoba agreement disclosed the 2022-23 baseline spending, the anti-substitution clause, the one-off device payment and the expiry date — none of which appeared in the announcement. The four agreements are public and comparable; the BC agreement in particular should be read against Manitoba's to resolve the three-versus-four-year discrepancy in its stated value.

**The reporting gap is the lever.** Because the agreements are amendable by mutual consent under section 8, a utilisation-reporting requirement could be added without legislation. The rare-disease precedent shows the federal government can design and publish this within one year. Anyone arguing about whether pharmacare is working is currently arguing without a denominator.

**Expiry is the real deadline.** The agreements end 31 March 2029 and the federal contribution is scheduled to peak at $269.6 million in 2028-29, immediately before that. A province deciding whether to sign, or whether to keep funding a program it inherited, faces a cliff with no announced renewal. The political question from 2027 onward will not be whether to expand pharmacare but whether the four existing programs survive their funding agreements.

## Open questions

**How many people actually use it.** No national figure exists and none can be constructed from published sources. PEI and Manitoba have published counts for their own programs; BC and Yukon have published none. The 2025-26 and 2026-27 financial statements due to Health Canada under section 4.9 would show spending but not patient counts, and they are not published. CIHI's claims data could produce a count but is not organised to separate pharmacare benefits and will not cover calendar 2026 until June 2027.

**The marginal patient.** Even with full claims data, nobody has measured the number of people who obtained a drug they would not otherwise have obtained. Because the program pays first and covers people with private insurance, some unknown share of every user count is displacement rather than new access. The New Brunswick estimate of $60 million in shifted Ozempic costs is the only attempt in the record to quantify displacement, and the department did not explain the figure.

**Whether private premiums fell.** Employers and employees continue paying premiums for drug coverage that no longer pays out on the covered categories, since the public plan pays first with no coordination of benefits. No source I found measures whether insurers rebated those premiums. This is the missing half of the PBO's economy-wide savings finding, and it determines whether the $1.4–$2.2 billion in savings reaches households or stays with insurers.

**The three-versus-four-year discrepancy in BC's agreement.** Health Canada says more than $670 million over four years; BC says up to $670 million over three years. I could not resolve it from the agreement text. Every per-capita comparison involving BC depends on which is right.

**What "diabetes devices and supplies" actually delivered.** Federal releases claim improved access to insulin pumps, syringes, glucose monitors and test strips. Manitoba's and PEI's documents exclude syringes and pen needles and leave supplies under deductible-based programs. Whether the one-off Stream 2 transfers expanded access, and for how many people, is unmeasured — and the device "Savings" reports due 1 October 2027 are the only place it might appear.

**Why nine jurisdictions are out, definitively.** CBC's reporting establishes that several provinces say they are willing or waiting and that the federal side is not negotiating, which contradicts the "provinces refusing money" framing. But no government has published its negotiating position, so the relative weight of federal supply-side reluctance and provincial demand-side conditions remains an inference.

**Coverage of the estimate literature.** The PBO's October 2023 full-plan estimate is the benchmark, and I found no PBO update reflecting 2026 prices, the expert committee's essential-medicines scenario, or the possibility of provincial non-participation. A costing of a four-province program — the thing that actually exists — has not been published by anyone.
