q: What does the evidence say about school smartphone bans: which jurisdictions (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states and others) have adopted them, what have evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong is that evidence?

report.title: School smartphone bans: which jurisdictions adopted them, what evaluations measured, and how strong the evidence is
report.body:
## TL;DR

School phone restrictions are now near-universal across rich anglophone and western European jurisdictions — 46 US states, every Australian state and territory, every Canadian province, England, France, the Netherlands, and Denmark and Sweden from 2026/27 — but they restrict four different things under one name, and most were adopted before any evaluation of their own policy existed. The evaluations that do exist find that bans reliably cut in-school phone use where enforced, reduce bullying modestly in the two countries with credible natural experiments, and produce average achievement and wellbeing effects that are close to zero. The strongest studies — a three-year national US pouch study and an English comparison of 30 schools — found nothing on attainment, attention or mental wellbeing despite verifying that phone use fell sharply. There is no randomised trial in schools, the most-cited meta-analysis pools five studies with inputs read off graphs, and the compliance rate in ban countries is roughly two-thirds.

## Key Findings

- **The policy spread faster than the evidence.** Ballotpedia records 46 US states with laws or policies as of 29 October 2026 [20]; England made guidance statutory in June 2026 having found 99.8% of primaries and 90% of secondaries already restricted phones [2][9]; France legislated in 2018 and moved to a possession ban in 2025 [22]; Denmark and Sweden legislate for 2026/27 [28][29]. A 2023 UNESCO count found fewer than a quarter of countries with a ban before the wave [19]. Sweden legislated the strictest version in 2025 despite having produced the clearest null result in 2020 [17][29].

- **"Ban" covers four different policies.** Classroom-time only with phones carried (Ontario grades 7–12, Florida's original law) [1][20]; whole-day use bans with phones carried (England, most Australian states) [5][9]; possession bans with surrender at the gate (France's "Portable en pause", Sweden) [22][29]; and delegated duties to have some policy (California, the Netherlands) [4][20]. RAND found 67% of US principals reporting bell-to-bell policies in 2024–25, but only 23% of high schools against 82% of elementary schools [27].

- **Achievement effects average close to zero.** The US pouch study: "average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero" — with modest high-school math gains and small negative middle-school effects [11]. The most-cited meta-analysis's pooled performance effect is d = 0.05, 95% CI [−0.04; 0.14], p = 0.30, and its authors rejected their own academic hypothesis [19]. Beland and Murphy's England estimate is +0.07 SD, concentrated among low achievers [14][16]; Sweden found no benefit [17]; Rio's relative estimate is +0.06 SD, calibrated to ~0.2 SD where phone use actually fell [18].

- **Where gains appear, the mechanism is attendance and compliance, not attention.** Figlio and Özek find Florida's test-score gains come from year two and that reduced unexcused absences "may explain a large fraction of the test score gains" — while enforcement raised suspensions in year one, concentrated among Black students [10]. Beland and Murphy: "there are no significant gains in student performance if a ban is not widely complied with" [16]. The US study found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention" despite a 30% fall in pings [11].

- **Bullying is the one domain with replicated positive findings, and it is modest.** Abrahamsson's Norwegian event study finds bans "lower bullying for both genders" with no average effect on education or mental health [15]; the pooled social-wellbeing effect is d = 0.22 [19]. Against that, the US pouch study found no clear reduction in perceived online bullying [11] and the Dutch full-versus-partial comparison found none either [7].

- **Mental health: the best-controlled studies are null.** SMART Schools (1,227 pupils, 30 English schools) found no difference in wellbeing — adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62 — and its authors state the findings do not support bans "in their current form" [13]. Dutch full bans showed no wellbeing differences and were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and lower school belonging for girls [7]. Weekly phone and social media use did not differ between restrictive and permissive English schools [13].

- **Compliance is the binding constraint.** 29% of pupils report using phones at school despite a ban [19]; 19% of previously permissive Rio schools still reported most or all students on phones in class after the school-wide ban [18]; Swedish pupils evaded school-level confiscation with fake or "broken" phones [29].

- **Perception surveys carry the public case and cannot bear it.** NSW: 95% principal support, 81% saying learning improved, 87% less distraction [24]. Netherlands: 75% concentration, 59% social climate, but only 28% attainment [26]. Dutch primary schools, where phones were rare anyway, mostly saw no effect at all [26]. Neil Selwyn: "We need to do a lot better than simply asking principals whether they think students’ learning has improved." [25]

- **Students and principals want different policies.** 60% of US youth supported some in-class restriction but only 11% supported a bell-to-bell ban; 81% of opponents cited parents' ability to reach them; students' own top reason for supporting restrictions was distraction (88%), with bullying at 27% [27].

- **Exemptions are rights, not favours, and are untested.** Ontario obliges schools to grant medical exceptions [3]; England carries an Equality Act 2010 reasonable-adjustments duty [9]; Denmark permits justified disability exceptions [28]. No study counts how many pupils use them.

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone bans, and what do the policies actually require?

The striking fact about school phone bans in 2026 is that the policy has spread far faster than the evidence about it. Almost every jurisdiction discussed below adopted its rule between 2023 and 2026, and most of them adopted it before any evaluation of their own policy existed. The question "which jurisdictions have bans" therefore has a short answer — most of the rich anglophone and western European world, in some form — and a more useful one: what each of them actually banned differs so much that cross-jurisdiction comparison of "bans" is close to meaningless without reading the text.

### Ontario: a tiered rule inside instructional time only

Ontario's restrictions were issued as Policy/Program Memorandum 128 on 27 June 2024 and took effect on 1 September 2024, replacing a weaker 2019 version [1]. The policy is a provincial code-of-conduct directive that requires every school board to write a local policy; the province sets the floor. For grades 7 to 12, the floor is that for grades 7 to 12, devices "are stored out of view and powered off or set to silent mode during instructional time" [1]. For grade 6 and below, the requirement runs through "the full instructional day" [1].

Three things about the Ontario design matter for the evidence. First, it is not a ban on possession and not a bell-to-bell ban: phones may be carried, and may be used at breaks and lunch. Second, it contains explicit carve-outs — devices may be used "for educational purposes, as directed by an educator", "for health and medical purposes", and "to support special education needs", with a further duty under the Human Rights Code to accommodate [1]. Third, the provincial government's own parent-facing page states the medical exception as an obligation on the school rather than a discretionary favour: "Your school must provide an exception if your child needs to use a mobile device to support, monitor or regulate their health or medical condition" [3]. That phrasing is a useful marker of how far the Ontario policy is from the "phone-free school" model: it is a classroom-attention rule with a rights architecture built into it.

### England: from guidance nobody had to follow to statute, 2024–2026

England's path is the clearest example of policy running ahead of evaluation, and then being hardened regardless. In February 2024 the Department for Education issued non-statutory guidance telling schools to prohibit phone use across the school day. By the time the government moved to make it binding, the Children's Commissioner had found that "99.8% of primary schools and 90% of secondary schools already had policies in place that limited or restricted the use of mobile phones during the school day" [2] — that is, the guidance largely ratified existing practice rather than changing it.

The hardening came in two steps. In April 2026 the government tabled an amendment to the children's wellbeing and schools bill in the House of Lords, after the bill had been held up, "make existing guidance on mobile phone bans in schools statutory, a move that ministers have resisted until now" [2]. The statutory guidance was published on 29 June 2026 and applies from 1 September 2026 [9]. It sets a default of a phone-free environment for every school, with anything else permitted by exception only, and it extends the prohibition across the whole school day — lessons, the time between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime [9].

England's version is the most complete of the major jurisdictions in scope — it covers breaks and lunch, not just lessons — but it is deliberately non-prescriptive about mechanism. How the phone-free state is achieved (lockers, collection at the gate, secure storage) is left to headteachers [9]. Enforcement runs through ordinary school sanctions, "including confiscation and detentions," not through any new offence [9], and through the inspectorate: Ofsted has said that where a school declines to follow the guidance, inspectors will examine whether phones contribute to disruption, bullying or mental-health harm, and that "Evidence of one or more of these points may indicate that leaders are not taking effective action", making it "likely that the ‘expected standard’ for attendance and behaviour will not be met" [21]. The statutory guidance also carries an Equality Act 2010 duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled pupils — glucose monitoring is the example given — and contemplates limited access for sixth-formers [9].

### The Netherlands: a sector agreement, not a law

The Netherlands did not legislate. Its ban is a government-promoted agreement with the education sector, introduced for secondary education in January 2024 and extended to primary education from the 2024/25 school year [4]. "While the measure is government promoted, it is up to the individual education institutions to provide concrete rules and to determine what the policy will look like in practice" [4]. Exceptions are made "for educational use of mobile devices and for students with specific (medical) well-being needs" [4], and the ministry was to assess by summer 2025 whether a legal ban was needed.

That design choice turns out to be a natural experiment. Because schools wrote their own rules, Dutch secondary schools split into partial bans (classroom only) and full bans (whole site) — which is precisely the comparison the Dutch evaluation exploited, and which no legislated national ban would have permitted [7].

### Australia: eight jurisdictions, eight rules

Australia has no national school phone policy; the states and territories legislated separately, and the rules differ in ways that matter. As the ABC's survey of the state rules sets out: "Western Australia: Years K–6 in public schools may not have a phone in their possession, while years 7–12 may, but it must be turned off and put away", with smart watches required to be in aeroplane mode [5]. South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Victoria require phones to be off and stored; the ACT restricts from preschool to year 10 but allows years 11–12 to keep phones, restricted only during class [5]. All of these apply to government schools: "Private schools across the country are still free to make their own rules about mobile phone use on campus" [5]. Every state scheme carries exceptions for medical and educational use.

The Australian case is the clearest illustration of a general problem: within one country, "has a ban" can mean four different things, applied to different year levels, covering roughly 60–65% of enrolments (the government sector), with the strictest version reserved for the youngest children.

### Canada: provincial, tiered, and incomplete

Canada is the same story at a smaller scale. "Starting in September, governments in almost every province in Canada will enact policies that restrict phone use in the classroom – with rules varying for elementary schools and high schools" [12]. Manitoba's rule is typical of the tiering: "There will be a ban for students in kindergarten to Grade 8, while those in high school will be restricted from using their devices during class time but are free to use them during breaks and lunch" [12]. Coverage is not universal even at the provincial level: the territories lagged — there was, for instance, no territory-wide school phone policy in the Northwest Territories, where it was left to district education bodies [12], with Yukon and Nunavut similarly leaving it to schools or district education bodies.

### The United States: the fastest and loosest wave

The US is where the 2023–2026 wave started and where it has gone furthest in raw count. Florida's HB 379, signed 9 May 2023, was first, and it was a classroom rule rather than a bell-to-bell ban: "a student may not use a wireless communications device during instructional time, except when expressly directed by a teacher solely for educational purposes" [20]. Ballotpedia's tracker, which is the most complete public count, records that, as of 29 October 2026, "46 states had enacted laws or policies on K-12 classroom or school cellphone usage" [20]. That headline overstates uniformity considerably. Within the 46, 37 "ban or limit cellphones in classrooms"; five — Alaska, Colorado, Maryland, Minnesota and New Mexico — merely "require K-12 public school districts to adopt policies around student cellphone use, though the laws don't specify the form those policies should take"; and four — Connecticut, Washington, Idaho and Montana — only "adopted policies encouraging districts to limit cellphone usage in classrooms" [20]. Ballotpedia also records the intellectual provenance plainly: "Beginning with Florida in 2023, states began enacting laws or policies regulating student cellphone usage in public schools. Lawmakers cited the work of writers like psychologist Jean Twinge and New York University social psychology professor Jonathan Haidt" [20].

RAND's nationally representative principal surveys show what this adds up to in practice during the 2024–25 school year: 67% of principals reported a bell-to-bell policy, but that average conceals a steep age gradient — 82% of elementary and 78% of middle schools had one, against 23% of high schools, where 49% allowed phone use in non-class time and 24% left it to teacher discretion [27]. The US "ban" is therefore mostly a ban on younger children.

Subsequent laws have tightened toward bell-to-bell. Georgia's HB 1009 (May 2026) extends a K–8 ban to high schools from July 2027; Maine's LD 2212 (April 2026) requires policies "from starting bell to dismissal bell"; Virginia expanded to bell-to-bell in April 2026; Kansas's HB 2299 requires devices "turned off and securely stored away from the student's person in an inaccessible location during the school day" [20]. California took the delegation route: AB 3216 (2024) required every district, county office of education and charter school to adopt a policy limiting or prohibiting smartphone use by 1 July 2026, without specifying content [20].

### France and the earlier European adopters

France is the oldest of the current regimes and the one that has moved furthest in stages. The law of 3 August 2018 (n° 2018-698) wrote into the education code that "l'usage des téléphones portables et des objets connectés est interdit dans les écoles et les collèges, sauf exceptions prévues par les règlements intérieurs" [22]. That was a ban on use with school-level exceptions. In 2025 the government converted it into a ban on possession during the school day — the "Portable en pause" scheme, requiring collégiens to deposit phones on arrival in lockers, secure pouches or collection boxes — generalised to all public collèges from September 2025, after a pilot year in a subset of schools [22]. As of 31 August 2026, official guidance states that phone use is forbidden in lycées as well, subject to derogations written into each school's internal rules, with an exemption for pupils with a disability or debilitating health condition [23].

Spain and Switzerland were earlier adopters in the same European cohort, and a 2024 review treats them alongside France as established cases [19]. The diffusion baseline before the current wave was low: a 2023 UNESCO report found that, of more than 200 countries, fewer than a quarter had such a ban, and "The OECD speaks of more than a dozen countries with a smartphone ban" [19].

### The Nordics: the last major adopters, and the strictest

Denmark legislated mobile-free schools. A broad parliamentary majority agreed in late 2025 that primary and lower-secondary schools and school-based leisure facilities become mobile-free "starting from the 2026/2027 school year" [28], with the Ministry of Children and Education issuing "a standard policy template for schools to adopt", and school boards and parent groups required to write local policies [28]. The regulation covers smartphones and private internet-connected devices but explicitly not computers and tablets used in instruction, and boards may write justified exceptions "such as allowing electronic device use to support students with disabilities" [28]. Denmark's stated rationale is a measured distraction rate rather than an attainment claim: "Research indicates that over half of students in the 6th and 8th year are distracted by their own or others' screen use during lessons" [28].

Sweden's rule is a possession ban with state funding attached. "From the next school year, starting in autumn 2026, it will be compulsory for all schools and after-school clubs to collect students’ phones and hold them until the end of the day", covering ages 7 to 16, with 95m kronor allocated for 2026 and 100m for the following year [29]. Sweden is also the country whose earlier evidence was most null [17] — the same jurisdiction that produced the 2020 study finding no academic or behavioural benefits is now legislating the strictest version, which is a useful reminder that these laws are not being driven by the evaluations.

### What the map actually shows

Read together, the jurisdictions fall into four design families rather than one policy: (a) bans on use during instructional time only, with phones carried (Ontario grades 7–12, Florida's original law, many US states); (b) bans on use across the whole school day, phones carried (England from 2026, Ontario K–6, most Australian states, most Canadian provinces); (c) bans on possession, phones surrendered at the gate (France's "Portable en pause", WA K–6, some US districts with pouches); and (d) delegation — a statutory duty to have a policy, with content left local (California, Colorado, the Netherlands). Denmark from 2026/27 sits in category (c) with a national template, and Sweden in category (c) with state funding for the collection infrastructure [28][29]. Almost all include medical, disability and educator-directed exceptions, and almost all exempt private or independent schools. Any evaluation described as testing "the effect of a ban" is testing one of these four things, in one country, at one point in its implementation.

### 2. What have evaluations measured about attention, classroom disruption and learning?


Four evaluations dominate the achievement question, and they do not agree.

**England (Beland & Murphy, 2016).** The study that launched the field surveyed schools in four English cities — Birmingham, Leicester, London and Manchester — about their phone policies, obtained complete answers from 90 schools, and combined that with the National Pupil Database. Of the 90, 68 had a strict ban and 22 a weaker policy, and most adopted theirs between 2006 and 2010 [31]. Student performance in high-stakes exams rose by about 0.07 standard deviations on average, and "These increases in performance are driven by the lowest-achieving students" [14]. In percentage terms the published paper reports test scores improving 6.41%, with the gain largest for low achievers at 14.23% and no significant effect for high achievers [16].

Two details from the primary paper matter more than the headline. First, the contrast is between strict bans and everything else: in the working-paper version, a strict ban raised the share of pupils gaining five GCSEs at A*–C by 4.31%, significant at the 1% level, while weaker policies had a positive but non-significant coefficient — "only strict ban have a significant impact on Student performance" [31]. A study comparing "schools that ban" with "schools that don't" is therefore comparing a real treatment with a partial one, which compresses the estimated effect. Second, the authors measured compliance rather than assuming it: their school survey asked heads to rate out of 7 "to what extent would you say the policy is adhered to by students" [31]. That is what licenses the compliance caveat they drew from the results — that there are no significant gains where a ban is not widely complied with [16] — and it is the single sentence that explains most of the heterogeneity in the later literature.

**Sweden (Kessel et al.).** A Swedish study in 2020 found no academic or behavioural benefits [17]. The Hechinger synthesis attributes the null partly to context: Swedish classrooms were already saturated with laptops, and phones tended to be used between tasks rather than during instruction [17].

**Florida (Figlio & Özek, NBER Working Paper 34388, October 2025).** This is the most methodologically careful US study and its findings are more interesting than a headline effect size. Three results, in the authors' own ordering: enforcement of the bans "led to a significant increase in student suspensions in the short-term, especially among Black students, but disciplinary actions began to dissipate after the first year"; test-score improvements appeared only "in the second year of the ban after that initial adjustment period"; and the gains seem to run through attendance rather than attention — "cellphone bans in schools significantly reduce student unexcused absences, an effect that may explain a large fraction of the test score gains" [10]. The Hechinger synthesis puts the size of the eventual gain in context: it amounted to less than one percentile point [17].

**The national US pouch study (Allcott, Baron, Dee, Duckworth, Gentzkow & Jacob, NBER Working Paper 35132).** This is the largest and most direct test: districts that adopted lockable phone pouches, compared with those that did not. The result is close to a clean null on achievement: "average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [11]. What makes this study the most important in the literature is that the manipulation worked. Cellphone pings from school grounds fell by 30 percent, and teachers reported far less nonacademic phone use in class. Yet the study found effects on test scores, attendance and online bullying that were close to zero, even three years after schools adopted the pouches" [17]. The mechanism was engaged; the outcome did not move.

**Rio de Janeiro (Bruhn, Ferman, Ferreira, de Souza & Gentzkow, Stanford working paper).** Rio ran a two-stage policy — a classroom-only ban in August 2023, then a school-wide ban in February 2024 — which allows a comparison between schools that had previously been permissive and those already restrictive. The main estimate: "an index of math and Portuguese standardized test scores improved by 0.06 standard deviations in treatment schools relative to control schools after the school-wide ban" [18]. The authors then do something most papers in this literature do not: they calibrate. Because compliance was imperfect, the 0.06 average understates the effect where the ban actually bit; their calibration implies total gains of about 0.2 standard deviations where the ban reduced in-class phone use, roughly one fifth of a year's typical learning progression [18].

### Attention and classroom disruption: mostly self-report, and it points the same way

Almost no evaluation measures attention directly. What exists falls into three tiers.

The weakest tier is ministerial and inspectoral impression, and it is uniformly positive. The French minister told the Senate that the 2024–25 pilot showed improvement in school climate, calmer relations within the school, better pupil attention in class and more social interaction, with nearly 80% of participating collèges favourable [22]. This is not measurement; it is the report of participants who volunteered for a pilot.

The middle tier is teacher and principal report, which is where the largest and most-quoted numbers in this literature live — and where they should be handled most carefully.

New South Wales published the first of these a year after its ban took effect in Term 4, 2023. The Centre for Education Statistics and Evaluation surveyed almost 1,000 public school principals and found 95% support for the ban; 81% said students' learning had improved, 87% said students were less distracted, and 86% said socialising had improved [24]. South Australian research released in March 2025 found 70% of teachers reported increased focus and engagement during learning time, and 64% reported "a lower frequency of critical incidents" at school as a result of device use [25].

The Dutch government-commissioned evaluation, by the Kohnstamm Instituut and Oberon and delivered to parliament on 3 July 2025, is the most informative of this type because it reports the weak category alongside the strong ones. Secondary schools reported positive effects on concentration (75%) and the social climate (59%) and — "in mindere mate", to a lesser degree — on learning performance (28%) [26]. That ordering is the finding: the closer the outcome gets to measured attainment, the smaller the share of schools claiming an effect.

Canada's first-year review is the weakest of these and shows what "evaluation" often means in practice. As provinces wrapped their first year in June 2025, "education ministries across Canada say there have been overall positive results from banning cellphones", with no outcome data behind the claim; Ontario's ministry said only that "parents and teachers find the ban has created a better learning environment" and that it would "continue gathering input" [30]. Manitoba's minister offered an anecdote instead of a measure — before the ban, students sat in the library in silence on their phones; now "they’re sitting, they’re talking, they’re laughing" [30].

The Dutch primary-school results make the point even more sharply. Because few primary pupils brought phones to class before the agreement, "de meeste basisscholen dan ook géén effecten van de afspraak op concentratie en leerprestaties" — most saw no effect on concentration or attainment at all, with 23% seeing a positive effect on wellbeing and school climate [26]. Where there was little phone exposure to remove, removing it changed nothing. That is a clean natural demonstration that the effect is proportional to the dose.

These are real perceptions and they are consistent across countries, which makes them worth something. They are also exactly what one would expect from removing a visible distractor, whether or not learning improves — and the Australian evaluations have drawn a direct methodological objection on this point. Neil Selwyn of Monash University: "We need to do a lot better than simply asking principals whether they think students’ learning has improved." [25]

The strongest tier — direct measurement of attention or phone use — tends to dissolve the effect. The US study found "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention" despite the 30% fall in pings [11]. The English SMART Schools study measured in-school phone time directly and found restrictive schools did cut it — by about 50 minutes a day (60 minutes versus 10.2 minutes) — but found no significant improvement in classroom behaviour [8]. So the honest summary on attention is: bans reliably reduce phone use in school, teachers report calmer classrooms, and no study has shown that this translates into measurably better sustained attention.

### Where the achievement gains, such as they are, might come from

Two mechanisms are on the table and they are not the ones the policy rhetoric assumes.

The first is **attendance and discipline**, not cognition. Figlio and Özek's finding that unexcused absences fall, and that this "may explain a large fraction of the test score gains", reframes the intervention: a phone ban may work as a school-climate and attendance measure whose academic payoff is indirect [10]. It also comes with a cost — the short-term rise in suspensions, concentrated among Black students, which the authors read as an adjustment period that fades [10]. A jurisdiction that adopts a ban without planning for that first-year spike is importing a known equity problem.

The second is **displacement and out-of-school exposure**. Figlio's own hypothesis, as reported, is that "the academic harms of modern technology aren’t primarily caused by classroom distraction itself", adding that phones may affect sleep, study habits, sustained attention and reading stamina outside school hours "in ways that a seven-hour school day ban cannot easily reverse" [17]. A related possibility is substitution: students move to laptops and tablets, which many bans do not cover [17]. If either is right, the ceiling on what a school-day ban can achieve is set outside the school gates, and the null results are not failures of implementation but correct estimates of a small intervention.

### The synthesis literature, and why its numbers should be handled carefully

Two reviews are routinely cited on both sides, and both are weaker than their citation frequency implies.

Böttger and Zierer's rapid review pooled five studies into a meta-analysis with an overall effect of d = 0.162 [19]. When split by domain, the performance effect was d = 0.05 and not significant, while the social well-being effect was d = 0.22 and significant [19]. That split is the single most useful number in the policy debate: whatever bans do, they do not do it to test scores. But the pool itself is fragile. The authors began with 3,241 articles, narrowed to 310, then 26 for full-text analysis, and ended with five — partly because studies without reportable statistics were dropped: "no standard deviations were reported in Guldvik andKvinnsland" [19]. A five-study meta-analysis selected on reporting completeness is not a representative estimate of a literature; it is a summary of the five studies that happened to be summarisable.

Campbell and colleagues' scoping review of 22 studies concluded that the evidence is "inconclusive" on whether bans improve academic outcomes or wellbeing, or reduce cyberbullying [18]. The Rio authors, who are sympathetic to bans, report this characterisation without disputing it [18]. The absence of randomised trials is the structural reason: the Hechinger synthesis notes there is only one RCT in the literature, and it concerns college students in India, not schoolchildren [17].

### The pattern that survives

Across these evaluations the heterogeneity is the finding, not noise around a true effect. "Some studies suggest benefits for low-achieving students, others for girls, and still others for boys. In some places, attendance or student well-being improved. In others, they didn’t." [17] The specific subgroup findings are inconsistent enough that no single mechanism story holds across jurisdictions: England found gains concentrated among low achievers [14][16]; Norway found gains for girls; Florida found them for boys; the US pouch study found modest high-school math gains alongside small negative middle-school effects [11][17].

What can be said with confidence is narrower than any advocate's position. Bans reliably reduce phone use during the school day, by a measurable amount, in schools that enforce them. Test-score effects average close to zero and are positive in perhaps half the studies, at magnitudes of roughly 0.05–0.07 standard deviations or less. Where effects are larger — Rio's calibrated 0.2 standard deviations — they depend on the ban actually displacing substantial in-class use, which is a compliance story, not a policy story. And the one consistent, large, policy-relevant finding in this literature is not about learning at all: it is that the first year of enforcement is disruptive, and that the disruption falls unevenly.

### 3. What have evaluations measured about bullying, social connection and mental health?


The SMART Schools study is the closest thing this literature has to a decisive test of the mental-health claim, and it came out null. Goodyear and colleagues surveyed 1,227 pupils aged 12–15 across 30 English secondary schools — 20 with restrictive phone policies and 10 permissive — and measured mental wellbeing with the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Wellbeing Scale. Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) "with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62)" [13]. There was no difference in anxiety or depression either.

The manipulation was real: restrictive schools cut in-school phone time by about 0.67 hours a day, and the Cyberbullying Research Center's summary of the study puts the gap at 50 fewer minutes of daily in-school phone use (60 minutes in permissive schools versus 10.2 in restrictive ones) [8]. But overall weekly phone and social media use did not differ between the groups, which is the mechanism problem in miniature: a school-day ban moves where the phone is used, not how much [13].

The authors' conclusion is unusually direct for a published paper and worth quoting because it is frequently softened in secondary coverage: "There is no evidence that restrictive school policies are associated with overall phone and social media use or better mental wellbeing in adolescents. The findings do not provide evidence to support the use of school policies that prohibit phone use during the school day in their current form, and indicate that these policies require further development" [13]. The Cyberbullying Research Center's summary reaches the same verdict — no significant improvements in anxiety or depression, academic performance or classroom behaviour [8].

Two limits on this study matter. It is cross-sectional in policy exposure — it compares schools with different rules rather than following a school before and after it changed — so it cannot rule out that restrictive schools differ in unmeasured ways. And it measured wellbeing at one point, so it cannot speak to cumulative exposure over years.

### The Dutch comparison: full bans did not beat partial bans, and may have cost something

The Netherlands produced a genuinely novel design because Dutch schools set their own rules. Vanluydt and colleagues surveyed 1,398 students in 24 Dutch secondary schools — 9 with partial bans (classroom only) and 15 with full bans (whole site) — between September 2024 and February 2025 [7]. The comparison is between two degrees of restriction within one national policy, which removes some of the confounding in cross-country work.

The result: "No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [7]. The null covers life satisfaction, loneliness, psychosomatic complaints, problematic social media use, bullying at school and cyberbullying — every outcome the policy is supposed to improve [7]. The negative finding on belonging is the one that should give legislators pause, and it is the mirror image of the impressionistic reports from France and the Dutch ministry's own survey, which were positive. The difference is that this study had a comparison group.

### Bullying: the one place a positive effect shows up, and it is conditional

Bullying is where the evidence is least null, and it is also where the mechanism is most obvious: if phones are removed from the site for seven hours, in-school cyberbullying has less opportunity.

Norway provides the strongest evidence. Abrahamsson's study, published in the Journal of Human Resources in March 2026, uses an event-study design on Norwegian middle schools adopting bans at different times, with administrative and survey data. The finding is a masked average: "banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds" [15]. Note what is doing the work here: bullying falls for both genders, and the mental-health benefit — reduced psychological health care use — appears only for girls. This is the most credible evidence in the literature that a ban can affect a mental-health-adjacent outcome, and it is a service-use measure, not a wellbeing scale.

The pooled meta-analytic estimate points the same way, weakly. Böttger and Zierer found the social well-being domain (bullying, satisfaction, conflict, competition) significant at d = 0.22 while performance was not significant at d = 0.05 [19]. Their bullying effects came from Abrahamsson's Norwegian data (d = 0.36) and from Beneito and Vicente-Chirivella's Spanish comparison (d = 0.36 at ages 12–14; d = 0.47 at 15–17) [19]. So the "bans reduce bullying" claim has two independent natural experiments behind it, in two countries, plus a modest pooled estimate.

The perception data point the same way, and they are the largest samples available. In RAND's nationally representative US principal survey, 54% of principals in schools with a policy said it had reduced cyberbullying from inside the school building — rising to 78% in middle schools — alongside 70% reporting a positive effect on school climate and 67% a reduction in inappropriate phone use [27].

Against that: the two studies that measured bullying directly and contemporaneously found nothing. The US pouch study reported "no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying" [11], and the Dutch full-versus-partial comparison found no difference in bullying at school or cyberbullying [7]. There is also a signal pointing the other way that no one has followed up. In the Dutch evaluation, some teachers reported an increase in physical bullying and disruptive behaviour alongside the concentration gains [26] — the plausible mechanism being that pupils who were bullying by message now do it in the corridor. That is teacher report from focus groups, not a measured outcome, but it is the one piece of evidence consistent with the null results in the two contemporaneous studies, and it should be tested rather than dismissed.

The most likely reconciliation is that the Norwegian and Spanish effects run through school-level climate and are detectable in administrative or survey measures over years, while self-reported bullying in a single wave is too noisy and too dominated by out-of-school conduct to move. That is an inference, not a finding — no study has tested it directly.

### Loneliness, connection and the belonging cost

The social-connection question is where policy intent and measurement diverge most sharply. The stated rationale for bans is often that phones displace face-to-face interaction and that removing them will restore it. The French ministerial account claims exactly this, listing "une augmentation des interactions sociales" among the pilot's benefits [22], and the Dutch government-commissioned evaluation reports 59% of secondary schools seeing a better social climate [26], with the researcher Alexander Krepel arguing the biggest change was in pupil interaction: because a pupil can no longer secretly photograph a classmate and spread it in a WhatsApp group, there is more social safety, and in the breaks "students would be on their phones and now they’re forced to talk" [6].

The one study that measured connection with a comparison group found the opposite direction of effect for the strictest version: full Dutch bans were "associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging" [7]. This is correlational and could reflect selection — schools that adopt full bans may be schools with more conflict to begin with. But it is the only comparative evidence on the question, and it points away from the connection story rather than toward it.

There is also a measurement gap that no study has closed: nobody in this literature has measured out-of-school social interaction, which is where the displacement hypothesis actually lives. A ban that increases in-school talk and decreases after-school meetups would show up as a win on school-climate surveys and a loss on nothing measured here.

### Mental health overall: what the nulls mean

Three of the four best-designed studies find no average mental-health benefit — SMART Schools on wellbeing, anxiety and depression [13]; the US pouch study on perceived online bullying and (by implication) the attention and climate pathways [11]; the Dutch comparison on life satisfaction, loneliness and psychosomatic complaints [7]. One finds a gender-specific benefit on health-care use and a bullying reduction [15].

That pattern is consistent with a small, real effect concentrated in the domains where school is the exposure site — in-school bullying, in-school conflict, girls' help-seeking — and absent in the domains where school is not the exposure site — sleep, evening social media, family conflict, loneliness. It is also consistent with there being no effect at all and the Norwegian result being one of several subgroup estimates. Distinguishing those two readings requires a study that measures exposure hours outside school, and none exists.

One further caution on the mental-health literature specifically: the policy case for bans is heavily driven by the Haidt/Twenge cohort narrative about smartphones and adolescent mental health, which Ballotpedia records as the explicit motivation for the US state laws [20]. But the causal evidence for that narrative is contested and is not the same evidence as the school-ban evidence. A jurisdiction can believe the cohort story and still be wrong that a seven-hour school-day restriction is the lever that acts on it — indeed the null results are exactly what that distinction predicts.

### 4. How strong is the evidence? Study designs, compliance, effect sizes and the limits of what can be concluded


The structural weakness of this literature is easy to state. Bans are adopted by governments at a date, for a jurisdiction, all at once; there is no randomisation and rarely a comparison group that was not self-selected. The Hechinger synthesis puts the count plainly: the first wave of rigorous research "does not point neatly in one direction," and the single RCT in the literature concerns college students in India, not schoolchildren [17]. Everything else is a natural experiment of some kind, and the quality of the counterfactual varies enormously.

That matters more here than in most policy areas because the outcome being debated — adolescent mental health, or exam attainment — is subject to strong secular trends running in the same period as the bans. Any study without a credible control group will pick up the trend and call it a policy effect.

The Australian case makes the problem concrete. Neil Selwyn of Monash University, reviewing the first two years of the state bans, says they were not set up "with the intention of properly testing their effectiveness" and that concrete research in the area is "inconclusive, and … not particularly rigorous" [25]. He is blunt about the government surveys that supply the headline numbers: "We need to do a lot better than simply asking principals whether they think students’ learning has improved." [25]

### The four design families, ranked

**Difference-in-differences across schools adopting at different times.** This is the workhorse, used by Beland and Murphy in England [14][31] and by Abrahamsson in Norway [15]. Its strength is that it nets out common trends; its weakness is that adoption timing is not random. Schools that ban phones may be schools with worse behaviour problems, more affluent intakes, or more assertive leadership — and in England, Beland and Murphy were estimating across four cities, not a national rollout.

**Rollout designs with staged intensity.** Rio de Janeiro's two-stage policy is the best of these, because the classroom-only phase provides a within-city comparison for the school-wide phase [18]. The authors are unusually honest about what their estimate means: "Our design does not identify the effect of a phone ban relative to no ban. Instead, it identifies a relative contrast in the effects of the municipal ban across schools with different baseline ex- posure to the policy" [18]. That sentence applies to most of the literature, and it is the reason the word "effect" in these papers should be read as an effect of moving from one policy regime to another.

**Voluntary-adoption comparisons.** The US pouch study compares districts that chose to buy pouches with those that did not [11]. This is the weakest identification of the group in principle — districts that adopt are different — but the study is strengthened by the fact that it verified the manipulation with objective ping data and followed schools for three years. A null result from a design with imperfect identification is more informative than a null from a design with none, but it is still not a randomised estimate.

**Cross-sectional policy comparisons.** SMART Schools compares 20 restrictive and 10 permissive schools in one wave [13]; the Dutch comparison sets 15 full bans against 9 partial ones [7]. These can describe associations well and cannot identify causal effects. Notably, these are the two studies with the most negative findings, which is a reminder that study quality and direction of result are not correlated in this literature — the nulls are not obviously the weaker studies.

There is a fifth category that dominates public discussion and should be ranked last: **satisfaction surveys of the people who implemented the policy**. NSW's 95% principal support, 81% "learning improved" and 87% "less distracted" [24]; South Australia's 70% of teachers reporting more focus [25]; the Dutch 75% concentration and 28% attainment figures [26]. These are useful for legitimacy and useless for effect size, and they have been doing most of the work in ministerial announcements.

### Compliance is the binding constraint, and it is measured badly

A ban that is not enforced is not a treatment, and enforcement is where these policies fail most visibly.

The OECD data cited in Böttger and Zierer's review is the bluntest single number: "According to feedback from pupils, 29% use their smartphone at school despite a smartphone ban" [19]. That is roughly one pupil in three admitting to violating the rule in a survey of ban countries.

The Rio study measured compliance directly and found it mediocre throughout: "Compliance with stated phone policies was imperfect both before and after the ban. Before the ban, 40% of control schools reported that most or all students were on their phones during class across grades 6 to 9, compared with 52% of treatment schools" — and after the school-wide ban, 19% of previously permissive schools still reported most or all students using phones in class [18]. The intervention reduced phone use substantially without eliminating it, and the outcome effect is scaled to the actual change in behaviour, not to the policy on paper.

Sweden's experience explains why its government moved from school-level practice to a statutory rule: "Most schools in Sweden already confiscate mobile phones at the start of the school day, but students have found ways to get around the ban such as handing in a fake phone or saying that they have forgotten their phone or that it is broken" [29]. Evasion of this kind is not a marginal problem; it is what determines whether the treatment exists at all.

Beland and Murphy's compliance finding is the most policy-relevant result in the whole literature: "there are no significant gains in student performance if a ban is not widely complied with" [16]. It rests on their own measurement of adherence — school heads rating compliance out of 7 in their policy survey — rather than on an assumption about implementation [31]. That is the explanation for the cross-country heterogeneity that does not require any country to be exceptional. England in 2016 had low baseline phone saturation and uneven but real enforcement; Sweden in 2020 had laptop-saturated classrooms where a phone ban changed little [17]; the US pouch districts enforced hard and got a 30% reduction in pings [17]; Florida's enforcement produced a measurable short-run discipline cost before settling [10].

### The meta-analysis everyone cites does not support the claim it is cited for

Böttger and Zierer's review is the most-cited quantitative synthesis in the policy debate, and reading its results table changes what it can be used to say.

They identified 3,241 articles, narrowed to 310, then to 26 for full-text analysis, and ended with five — partly because studies without reportable statistics were dropped: "no standard deviations were reported in Guldvik andKvinnsland" [19]. The pooled overall effect was d = 0.162 [19]. But the performance subgroup was d = 0.05, 95% CI [−0.04; 0.14], p = 0.30 [19] — and the authors say so themselves: "hypothesis H1 must be rejected" [19].

The individual inputs are even more fragile than the pooled figure suggests. Beland and Murphy's estimate enters the meta-analysis as d = 0.06 with a standard error of 1.00 and a 95% confidence interval running from −1.90 to 2.02 [19]; the Norwegian bullying estimate enters as d = 0.36 with a confidence interval of −0.19 to 0.91, which is not distinguishable from zero [19]. And some effect sizes were not reported at all in the source papers: "In such cases, effect sizes and standard errors had to be inferred from graphicalrepresentations, which may affect the precision of the calculated effects" [19].

A five-study meta-analysis, selected partly on reporting completeness, with inputs read off graphs, cannot bear the weight placed on it. Its defensible conclusion is narrow and is the one its authors state: the social-wellbeing effect is larger than the performance effect, and the performance effect is not significant.

Campbell and colleagues' scoping review of 22 studies concluded that the evidence is "inconclusive" on whether bans improve academic outcomes or wellbeing, or reduce cyberbullying [18]. The Rio authors, who are sympathetic to bans, report this characterisation without disputing it [18].

### What the null results can and cannot mean

The near-zero average achievement effects in the US pouch study [11] and the null wellbeing effects in SMART Schools [13] admit three readings, and the literature has not separated them.

1. **The effect is genuinely small.** Plausible on its face: a phone ban is a seven-hour intervention on one device in an environment with laptops, tablets, home broadband and evenings. The expected effect size on a standardised test, if it operates only through reduced in-class distraction, should be small.
2. **The effect is displaced, not removed.** Students switch to laptops and tablets [17], and total weekly phone and social media use did not differ between restrictive and permissive English schools [13]. Under this reading the treatment is weaker than it looks.
3. **The effect operates on a channel the studies do not measure.** Figlio's hypothesis is that phones affect sleep, study habits and reading stamina outside school, which a school-day ban cannot reach [17]. Under this reading the null is a correct estimate of the wrong intervention.

Only reading 3 is compatible with the policy being worth doing — and reading 3 is precisely the reading for which the direct evidence is thinnest.

There is a fourth possibility that the Dutch and French data force into view: the ban produces both gains and losses that partly cancel. The Dutch evaluation records teachers reporting increased workload from enforcement and "Toename fysiek pest- en verstorend gedrag" — an increase in physical bullying and disruptive behaviour [26] — alongside the concentration gains. Böttger and Zierer note that 43% of students in France report feeling nervous and anxious without their phone, and conclude that a ban "cannot be effective if it is only limited to taking away students’ devices" [19]. A policy that removes a coping mechanism from some pupils while removing a distraction from others should be expected to average near zero, and that is what several studies found.

### What would settle it

Three designs would, and none has been run. A cluster-randomised trial with districts randomised to pouch adoption, measuring attainment, wellbeing and out-of-school phone use at multiple waves, would settle the average effect. A natural experiment exploiting a discontinuously enforced rule — a school with a strict ban next to one without, with identical intakes — would help on identification. And a study that measures exposure hours outside school, alongside in-school phone use, would separate displacement from genuine reduction; no study in this literature measures the total dose, and the one that came closest found the school-day reduction did not change weekly totals [13].

The honest position is that the policy has outrun the evidence by a wide margin. Forty-six US states, all Australian states and territories, every Canadian province, England, France, the Netherlands, Denmark from 2026/27 and Sweden from autumn 2026 have adopted restrictions in under four years, and the total stock of credible causal evidence consists of roughly half a dozen natural experiments with inconsistent results and no randomised trial in schools. Bans are not therefore wrong — the bullying and attendance findings are real, and the first-year discipline cost is a manageable planning problem. But the claim that they improve learning or mental health on average is not established, and the two best-controlled studies in the literature found nothing on the outcomes their advocates emphasise most.
