| Abrahamsson, Norway 2026 | Event study | GPA, mental health, bullying | No average effect; bullying down both genders; girls' GPA up, psychological care use down [15] |
| Goodyear et al., England 2025 | Cross-sectional, 30 schools | Mental wellbeing (WEMWBS) | −0.48 adjusted mean difference, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06 [13] |
| Vanluydt et al., Netherlands 2026 | Full vs partial bans, 24 schools | Wellbeing, bullying, belonging | No significant differences; lower connectedness, lower girls' belonging [7] |
| Böttger & Zierer 2024 | Meta-analysis, 5 studies | Pooled | d = 0.162 overall; performance d = 0.05, CI [−0.04; 0.14]; social wellbeing d = 0.22 [19] |
| NSW CESE 2024 | Principal survey, ~1,000 schools | Perceived learning, distraction | 81% learning improved, 87% less distracted [24] |
| Kohnstamm/Oberon 2025 | School-leader survey, 317 secondary | Perceived effects | 75% concentration, 59% social climate, 28% attainment [26] |

The magnitudes cluster below 0.1 standard deviations for achievement and below 0.25 for social outcomes. For scale, the effect of a ban in Beland and Murphy's England — the study most cited by advocates — is roughly a tenth of the effect of having a better teacher, and less than a tenth of the black-white achievement gap.

### What would settle it

Three designs would, and none has been run. A cluster-randomised trial with districts randomised to pouch adoption, measuring attainment, wellbeing and out-of-school phone use at multiple waves, would settle the average effect. A natural experiment exploiting a discontinuously enforced rule — a school with a strict ban next to one without, with identical intakes — would help on identification. And a study that measures exposure hours outside school, alongside in-school phone use, would separate displacement from genuine reduction; no study in this literature measures the total dose, and the one that came closest found the school-day reduction did not change weekly totals [13].

The honest position is that the policy has outrun the evidence by a wide margin. Forty-six US states, all Australian states and territories, every Canadian province, England, France, the Netherlands, Denmark from 2026/27 and Sweden from autumn 2026 have adopted restrictions in under four years, and the total stock of credible causal evidence consists of roughly half a dozen natural experiments with inconsistent results and no randomised trial in schools. Bans are not therefore wrong — the bullying and attendance findings are real, and the first-year discipline cost is a manageable planning problem. But the claim that they improve learning or mental health on average is not established, and the two best-controlled studies in the literature found nothing on the outcomes their advocates emphasise most.

### The four design families, ranked

**Difference-in-differences across schools adopting at different times.** This is the workhorse, used by Beland and Murphy in England [14] and by Abrahamsson in Norway [15]. Its strength is that it nets out common trends; its weakness is that adoption timing is not random. Schools that ban phones may be schools with worse behaviour problems, more affluent intakes, or more assertive leadership — and in England, Beland and Murphy were estimating across four cities, not a national rollout.

**Rollout designs with staged intensity.** Rio de Janeiro's two-stage policy is the best of these, because the classroom-only phase provides a within-city comparison for the school-wide phase [18]. The authors are unusually honest about what their estimate means: "Our design does not identify the effect of a phone ban relative to no ban. Instead, it identifies a relative contrast in the effects of the municipal ban across schools with different baseline ex- posure to the policy" [18]. That sentence applies to most of the literature, and it is the reason the word "effect" in these papers should be read as an effect of moving from one policy regime to another.

**Voluntary-adoption comparisons.** The US pouch study compares districts that chose to buy pouches with those that did not [11]. This is the weakest identification of the group in principle — districts that adopt are different — but the study is strengthened by the fact that it verified the manipulation with objective ping data and followed schools for three years. A null result from a design with imperfect identification is more informative than a null from a design with none, but it is still not a randomised estimate.

**Cross-sectional policy comparisons.** SMART Schools compares 20 restrictive and 10 permissive schools in one wave [13]; the Dutch comparison sets 15 full bans against 9 partial ones [7]. These can describe associations well and cannot identify causal effects. Notably, these are the two studies with the most negative findings, which is a reminder that study quality and direction of result are not correlated in this literature — the nulls are not obviously the weaker studies.

### Compliance is the binding constraint, and it is measured badly

A ban that is not enforced is not a treatment, and enforcement is where these policies fail most visibly.

The OECD data cited in Böttger and Zierer's review is the bluntest single number: "According to feedback from pupils, 29% use their smartphone at school despite a smartphone ban" [19]. That is roughly one pupil in three admitting to violating the rule in a survey of ban countries.

The Rio study measured compliance directly and found it mediocre throughout: "Compliance with stated phone policies was imperfect both before and after the ban. Before the ban, 40% of control schools reported that most or all students were on their phones during class across grades 6 to 9, compared with 52% of treatment schools" — and after the school-wide ban, 19% of previously permissive schools still reported most or all students using phones in class [18]. The intervention reduced phone use substantially without eliminating it, and the outcome effect is scaled to the actual change in behaviour, not to the policy on paper.

Beland and Murphy's compliance finding is the most policy-relevant result in the whole literature: "there are no significant gains in student performance if a ban is not widely complied with" [16]. That is the explanation for the cross-country heterogeneity that does not require any country to be exceptional. England in 2016 had low baseline phone saturation and uneven but real enforcement; Sweden in 2020 had laptop-saturated classrooms where a phone ban changed little [17]; the US pouch districts enforced hard and got a 30% reduction in pings [17]; Florida's enforcement produced a measurable short-run discipline cost before settling [10].

### What the null results can and cannot mean

The near-zero average achievement effects in the US pouch study [11] and the null wellbeing effects in SMART Schools [13] admit three readings, and the literature has not separated them.

1. **The effect is genuinely small.** Plausible on its face: a phone ban is a seven-hour intervention on one device in an environment with laptops, tablets, home broadband and evenings. The expected effect size on a standardised test, if it operates only through reduced in-class distraction, should be small.
2. **The effect is displaced, not removed.** Students switch to laptops and tablets [17], and total weekly phone and social media use did not differ between restrictive and permissive English schools [13]. Under this reading the treatment is weaker than it looks.
3. **The effect operates on a channel the studies do not measure.** Figlio's hypothesis is that phones affect sleep, study habits and reading stamina outside school, which a school-day ban cannot reach [17]. Under this reading the null is a correct estimate of the wrong intervention.

Only reading 3 is compatible with the policy being worth doing — and reading 3 is precisely the reading for which the direct evidence is thinnest.

The magnitudes cluster below 0.1 standard deviations for achievement and below 0.25 for social outcomes. For scale, the effect of a ban in Beland and Murphy's England — the study most cited by advocates — is roughly a tenth of the effect of having a better teacher, and less than a tenth of the black-white achievement gap.

### 5. Exemptions, enforcement and uneven effects: disabled and neurodivergent students, student voice, and implementation failure


Every jurisdiction examined here carves out exceptions, and in most of them the exceptions are framed as rights rather than concessions.

Ontario's provincial policy writes two exemptions directly into the classroom restriction — devices may be used during learning time when they are needed for a health or medical reason, or where use supports special education needs — and the government's parent-facing guidance is categorical that this is not discretionary: "Your school must provide an exception if your child needs to use a mobile device to support, monitor or regulate their health or medical condition" [3]. The 2024 memorandum lists the same three categories: educator-directed educational use, health and medical purposes, and support for special education needs, plus the Human Rights Code duty [1].

England's statutory guidance carries an Equality Act 2010 duty: "Schools have a duty under the Equality Act 2010 to take such steps as is reasonable to avoid substantial disadvantage to a disabled pupil caused by the school’s policies or practices" [9]. Glucose monitoring is the example given. Ofsted's inspection guidance reinforces it — allowing a disabled pupil access to their phone "where it is necessary due to the nature of their disability, may be considered a reasonable adjustment that the school has a duty to make" [21]. France's rules exempt pupils with a disability or a debilitating health condition from the lycée prohibition [23]. The Netherlands exempts "students with specific (medical) well-being needs" alongside educational use [4].

Denmark's framework is the most explicit on how exceptions are meant to work in practice: school and parental boards "can include justified exceptions in their policies, such as allowing electronic device use to support students with disabilities." The national regulation excludes computers and tablets used as part of instruction entirely [28]. The Dutch monitoring report adds the operational detail that matters: most special-education schools make exceptions for medical or support use — hearing aids linked to mobile devices, reading software — that this is "maatwerk voor elke leerling," tailored to each pupil, and that the exceptions "lijken niet vaak nodig," appear rarely necessary [26]. That last finding is worth weighing against fears that exemptions will hollow out the policy: in the Dutch special sector they did not, and 93% of those schools were enforcing a policy [26].

The design question this raises is not whether exemptions exist but whether they are usable. A pupil with type 1 diabetes, an anxiety disorder, or a communication difference must typically disclose to staff and carry an authorisation; the policy protects the right and leaves the social cost with the child. No study in this literature measures how many pupils use the exemptions they are entitled to, and that is a real gap — the population most likely to need a phone is also the population for whom the ban's social costs are highest.

### Neurodivergent students: the sharpest evidence of uneven effect

The most concrete evidence on uneven effects comes from the Dutch special-school comparison. In special schools, where exceptions can be granted for learning-support devices, only about half reported that the ban had had a positive or very positive effect — a smaller share than the 75% concentration gains reported by mainstream secondary schools [6]. The interpretation is not that the ban failed in special schools; it is that the exemptions did what they were designed to do and softened the measured effect. That is the correct behaviour of a policy with a carve-out, and it means any evaluation that pools special and mainstream schools will understate the mainstream effect and overstate the special-school one.

The other side of the coin is the one Böttger and Zierer flag in their recommendations: phones enable disabled pupils to participate better in lessons — and a ban implemented as confiscation rather than as a managed rule can remove an accommodation [19]. Their recommendation is for the ban to be paired with professional development and media education rather than operating as a pure prohibition.

### Student voice: the evidence that students who helped write the rules liked them more

The Dutch student-voice research (Brummer and Achterberg, Erasmus University, 2025) is the only study in this literature that treats students as policy participants rather than as subjects. Its finding is straightforward and unsurprising: satisfaction with a school's smartphone policy is closely tied to how much input students had in making it. The 26 students involved in shaping the policy rated it higher than the 102 who were not [8]. The report's recommendation is to adjust policy based on evaluation and to keep students in the process.

The American data is a much larger sample and it shows the same gap from the other direction. RAND's nationally representative survey of youth aged 12–21 found that 60 percent of youth enrolled in K–12 schools supported some cell phone use restrictions during the school day, but "Only 11 percent of youth said that cell phone use should be prohibited bell to bell" [27]. Among those who opposed in-class bans, 81% said the reason was that parents should be able to reach them [27]. Students' own reason for supporting in-class restrictions was overwhelmingly distraction (88%), with reducing bullying a distant fourth at 27% [27] — so students and the principals enforcing the policy do not even agree on what the policy is for.

This is a small study and it is a public report rather than a peer-reviewed paper, so it should not carry much weight on outcomes. But it bears on a question the outcome studies cannot answer: whether the same rule, implemented with and without student buy-in, produces the same result. Nothing in the literature tests that, and the implementation evidence below suggests it should.

### Implementation failure is the dominant real-world mode

The French experience is the clearest documented case of a policy that was correct on paper and unimplementable in practice. When the "Portable en pause" scheme was generalised to all public collèges in September 2025, requiring pupils to deposit phones on arrival in lockers, secure pouches or collection boxes, the government's own answer in the Senate recorded that "en septembre dernier, 70 % des chefs d'établissement interrogés n'avaient pas encore pu mettre en oeuvre cette interdiction, faute de moyens adaptés" — 70% of surveyed school heads had not been able to implement it for want of suitable means [22]. The binding constraint was not the rule, or teacher will, but physical infrastructure and money. The senator's reply noted the same thing from the other side: compliance requires capital spending on lockers by local authorities, and the state needs to help pay for it [22].

The Dutch monitoring report also supplies the demand-side finding on the instrument itself: only 51% of secondary schools were satisfied with the national agreement as a policy instrument, and 33% wanted stronger legislation [26]. Schools did not experience the voluntary route as sufficient — which is why the ministry's promised summer 2025 review of whether a legal ban was needed pointed toward legislation rather than away from it.

The Dutch experience shows the earlier phase of the same curve. There was substantial initial resistance — "There was quite a lot of protest at first from schools, teachers, students, parents, questions about how it would all work" — and near-universal compliance only came after that [6]. Florida's data shows the third phase, the cost of enforcement: suspensions rose in the short term, concentrated among Black students, and faded after the first year as a new steady state established [10].

Student testimony is the only direct evidence on how enforcement feels, and it is uniform across countries. A Calgary Grade 11 student, sceptical at the start, reported after a year that the ban helped some pupils focus but that "Some have just become more sneaky" — one classmate hid a phone behind a textbook and watched YouTube Shorts through the lesson — and that she herself sometimes used her phone during work time with an earbud under her hijab [30]. That is not an argument against the policy; it is a measurement of its dose, and it suggests the real-world treatment is weaker than the policy text in every jurisdiction studied.

Put together, the implementation sequence in every jurisdiction that has done this looks the same: protest and non-compliance, then infrastructure spending, then a transitional spike in discipline referrals concentrated among the most policed students, then normalisation. The evaluations that find effects tend to be measuring the post-normalisation steady state; the evaluations that find nulls are often measuring a period when the policy was not yet operating as written. This is a plausible reconciliation of the literature's disagreements and, again, an inference rather than something any study has tested.

### The enforcement architecture matters as much as the rule

Two mechanisms are doing the enforcement work across these jurisdictions, and they are not equivalent.

The first is **confiscation and sanction** — ordinary school discipline. England's guidance lists "confiscation and detentions" as the available sanctions and creates no new offence [9]; France's rules provide for confiscation with procedures set in each school's internal rules [23]. This works where staff capacity exists, which is exactly what the French 70% figure shows cannot be assumed.

The second is **inspection and grading**. Ofsted's approach makes phone policy a matter of judgement about leadership rather than a compliance checklist: inspectors ask whether staff and pupils understand the expectations, whether the policy is followed consistently, and what its impact is on "pupils’ learning, behaviour and wellbeing" [21]. Where a school declines to follow the guidance, the inspectorate will explore whether phones contribute to disruption, bullying or mental-health harm, and if they do, the school is likely to fall short of the expected standard for attendance and behaviour [21]. This is a softer lever than statute and a stronger one than advice, and it is the mechanism that will determine whether England's 2026 statutory default actually changes practice in the schools that had not already banned phones — which, on the Children's Commissioner's figures, was about one in ten secondaries and a handful of primaries [2].

The third mechanism, used in the US pouch districts, is **physical prevention**: a locked pouch removes the enforcement discretion from the teacher entirely. That is why the US study could verify a 30% reduction in pings [17], and it is probably why it is the only study with a cleanly measured manipulation. It is also the most expensive and the most visible, and it makes the policy legible to students as a restriction on their property rather than a rule about attention.


## Beyond this question

The most useful thing this evidence does is break the policy question into three separate ones that were being argued as one.

**If the goal is attainment, the honest case is weak and the mechanism is not the one advertised.** The pooled performance effect in the most-cited meta-analysis is d = 0.05 with a confidence interval spanning zero [19]; the largest and best-instrumented US study found "close to zero" effects despite verifying a 30% drop in pings [11][17]; and where gains do appear — Florida, Rio — they run partly through attendance and compliance rather than attention [10][18]. Anyone building an argument for bans on learning grounds should lead with Beland and Murphy's low-achiever result [14][16] and Rio's calibrated 0.2 standard deviations [18], and should say out loud that both depend on enforcement that most jurisdictions have not achieved.

**If the goal is bullying and school climate, the case is real but modest and the mechanism is in-school opportunity.** Two independent natural experiments find bullying reductions [15][19], the pooled social-wellbeing effect is significant at d = 0.22 [19], and principals and students both report calmer schools [24][27]. The complication worth taking seriously is that full bans in the Netherlands were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and lower school belonging for girls [7], and some Dutch teachers reported more physical bullying after the ban [26]. A policy justified by belonging that may reduce belonging for some pupils needs its own measurement, not a survey of headteachers.

**If the goal is mental health, the school-day ban is close to the wrong instrument.** Weekly phone and social media use did not differ between restrictive and permissive English schools [13]; the Dutch comparison found no difference on any wellbeing outcome [7]; the Norwegian benefit is gender-specific and shows up in health-care utilisation [15]. The exposure that matters most plausibly happens at 9pm, not at 11am, and no evaluation in this literature measures the total dose.

For anyone writing on this — and this bears directly on the argument in the record's own paper on the computing environment — the practical implication is that "school phone bans" is now a policy fact with a thin evidence base, and the defensible sentence is narrower than either camp wants: bans reliably reduce in-school phone use where enforced, they modestly reduce in-school bullying, they do not measurably improve average attainment or wellbeing, and their first year costs disruption that falls unevenly on the most-policed students.

## Open questions

**No randomised trial in schools exists.** The only RCT in the literature is with college students in India [17]. Until districts are randomised to pouch adoption with attainment, wellbeing and out-of-school exposure measured at multiple waves, every estimate here is a natural experiment on self-selected adoption.

**No study measures total exposure.** The one that came closest found the school-day reduction did not change weekly totals [13]. Nobody has measured out-of-school social interaction, evening phone use, or sleep in a ban-versus-no-ban comparison with a credible counterfactual. This is the single largest hole, because it is where the displacement and out-of-school mechanisms live [17].

**Nothing is known about exemption take-up.** Every jurisdiction examined writes medical, disability and special-education exceptions into its rules [1][3][9][23][26][28], and the Dutch special-education monitoring suggests the exceptions are rarely needed in practice [26] — but no study counts how many pupils are entitled to an exemption, how many use it, or what the disclosure costs are. The population most likely to need a phone is the population for whom a ban's social costs are highest, and it is invisible in every evaluation reviewed here.

**Bullying measurement disagrees with itself.** Administrative and survey measures over years find reductions [15][19]; contemporaneous self-report finds none [7][11]; teachers in one country report an increase in physical bullying [26]. Whether this is a substitution effect, a measurement artefact, or both has not been tested.

**Ontario and most of Australia have not been evaluated at all.** Ontario's first-year "review" was a ministry statement that parents and teachers find the ban has created a better learning environment, with a commitment to keep gathering input and no outcome data [30]. NSW and South Australia published principal and teacher perception surveys [24][25], which Neil Selwyn describes as not "particularly rigorous" [25]. The jurisdictions that moved earliest and most confidently have the least evidence about their own policies.

**Long-term and cohort effects are unmeasured.** Böttger and Zierer note that most included studies examined only short-term effects [19]. Whether a ban sustained for a decade changes cohort-level attention norms, or merely moves phone use outside the gates, cannot be answered from any data currently collected.

**Coverage note.** The English-language evidence base is dominated by England, Norway, the US and the Netherlands, plus perception surveys from Australia and Canada. I found no peer-reviewed evaluation of the French, Spanish, Swiss, Danish or Swedish regimes; France's own account of its pilot is ministerial impression [22], and Denmark's and Sweden's laws take effect in 2026/27 [28][29], so no evaluation of either yet exists. The claim that these policies are "evidence-based" is, at the time of writing, unsupported for most of the countries that have adopted them.
