q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: RealPage and Yardi in Canada: YieldStar's documented users, the closed Competition Bureau inquiry, and the rent effect left unmeasured
report.body: ## The product pools private lease data and returns a daily price Algorithmic rent-setting software takes the operating data of apartment buildings — the rents actually signed, lease terms, occupancy, what is coming vacant — and returns a recommended rent for each unit, day by day. The version at issue in the American and Canadian litigation pooled that data across competing landlords: competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations. The pleading describes an auto-accept function and human pricing advisers, both of which raise the share of recommendations a landlord follows. RealPage described the goal of the exercise internally as driving every possible opportunity to increase price, and reached for a metaphor about what happens when every landlord in a market runs the same tool. In the United States the adoption was broad enough for that metaphor to be tested. RealPage's clients comprised nearly 90% of the market for multifamily rental housing units of 50 units or more, and court documents cited landlords accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time. The two vendors do not describe the same product. Yardi's product in Canada is Revenue IQ, formerly RENTmaximizer. Yardi maintains that it uses only the client's own property data plus publicly available asking rents, and never confidential competitor pricing data, and a California state court (Oct 2025) accepted Yardi's design defence. A federal judge in *Duffy v. Yardi* declined to dismiss the American case, observing that putting an intermediary between competitors does not by itself rule out an agreement. RealPage told the *Financial Post* that its Canadian presence was low and that its software is purposely built to be legally compliant. What a Canadian landlord actually ran is a narrower question than what the software can do, and the Canadian documents answer the narrower one. ## Canadian use is documented from a 2017 press release to a 2024 job advertisement CBC's reporting found YieldStar has been used in Canada since at least 2017. The earliest hard document is a June 2017 RealPage press release naming GWLRA subsidiary Vertica Resident Services as a YieldStar client, which reported 2%–4% revenue outperformance for that client. The number describes a landlord's revenue, it comes from the company selling the software, and it is the only Canadian figure anywhere in this research for what the software achieved; the study adds that vendors later delete such testimonials. GWL Realty Advisors confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar and said it ended the contract after an internal review in October 2024. Tricon Residential told CBC it stopped using YieldStar in summer 2024. Woodbourne Capital confirmed use publicly, and its vice-president described the aim as optimising net operating income rather than occupancy. QuadReal left a trace in a hiring notice: a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys, with the software named in the same instruction. The lawsuit went further than the confirmations. The statement of claim named RealPage plus 14 landlord/manager groups: QuadReal, Westcorp, FirstService, Associated Property Management (2001), GWLRA, M&R, Rhapsody, Hollyburn, CAPREIT, Dream Unlimited, Woodbourne, RioCan, Choice Properties and Tricon. The denials are part of the file too. CAPREIT's answer to CBC was "We have not, are not, and will never use" YieldStar. Dream Unlimited and Choice Properties said they had never subscribed directly, that a third-party property manager had, and that they asked it to stop. Associated Property Management and M&R denied use. Starlight Investments was reported, on the strength of an unnamed market-research database, as one of at least 13 companies in Canada with more than $5 billion in revenue that have used the YieldStar software, and nobody has confirmed that. The class-action allegations were never tested and are now discontinued; naming defendants reflects pleadings, not proven conduct. ## Both Canadian tracks ended without a finding about rents The Competition Bureau opened its file in August 2024, launched a formal civil inquiry in January 2025, ran its algorithmic-pricing consultation June 10–August 4, 2025 (103 responses), and discontinued the RealPage/Yardi inquiry on November 10, 2025. It assessed abuse of dominance and anticompetitive collaboration and found neither, because adoption did not reach the anticompetitive thresholds and had fallen since late 2024. The threshold is the thing to hold on to. A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding — a bar neither vendor met given low Canadian uptake. The Bureau still remains concerned, issued four diagnostic compliance questions, and warned that even anonymised competitor data used behind the scenes can let software act as a means for competitors to coordinate. > **Objection: the Bureau looked at the software and cleared it** > > The Bureau's closure is a discretionary enforcement decision on present evidence, not a ruling that the software is lawful, and it can reopen on new and compelling evidence. The test it applied was how much of the market the vendors held, not what the rents did in the buildings that used the product. A closure on share is a statement about adoption. The class action ended differently and for a different reason. Filed on November 26, 2024, it proposed a class of all persons in Canada who leased a unit owned, operated, or managed by any defendant between November 26, 2009 and the present. It was discontinued by court order effective April 1, 2026, before any certification motion, and because it was never certified, tenants' limitation periods resumed running on April 1, 2026. The ending leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm counts as the agreement the Act requires. What the Canadian plaintiffs never got was the material that carried the American cases: internal documents, sworn testimony, and evidence of RealPage-hosted meetings where competing landlords discussed pricing, a rim connecting the spokes that the Canadian plaintiffs never reached discovery to develop. Without it, the Canadian theory rested on a pleading. ## The American record is allegations, settlements without admissions, and a study of petrol The Justice Department sued RealPage in August 2024, added six landlords in January 2025, and settled with the company on November 24, 2025, on terms that carried no financial penalty, no admission of wrongdoing and a seven-year monitor, with the pooling of competitors' private data barred and geographic modelling restricted below the state level. Prosecutors allege one landlord raised rents more than 25% within 11 months of adopting the software. The department's antitrust chief put the case in one line: RealPage was replacing competition with coordination, and renters paid the price. Private settlements in the American litigation total nearly US$360 million, and nine US municipalities plus two states (California, New York) have banned or restricted algorithmic rent-setting. The nearest thing to a measured effect comes from somewhere else entirely: German retail petrol stations, where adoption increases margins by 9%, but only in non-monopoly markets, and margins increase by 28% in markets where both [duopolists] adopt, with the effect appearing about a year after market-wide adoption, suggesting that algorithms in this market learn tacitly-collusive strategies. The authors stress they observe outcomes, not proof of intent. In simulation, learning algorithms consistently learn to charge supracompetitive prices, without communicating with one another, though later work showed that the outcome flips with the learning protocol. > **Objection: the American case shows the software raised rents** > > It shows that the government alleged it and that the company settled without admitting it. The market-share and acceptance figures come from American litigation about buildings of 50 units or more. The one estimate of a measured price effect is about petrol, in a market where two stations can watch each other's signs, and its authors describe an observed margin, not an intent. Housing is a different market with a different product, and Yardi's version of the product, which a California court accepted as a design that does not pool private competitor data, is not the one the American case was built around. ## What the Canadian file cannot say is what happened to rents RealPage told CBC its revenue management software has never served more than 1% of the rental market in Canada. That 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving, and the Bureau did not publish a precise share of its own. So the size of the Canadian footprint rests on the seller's own arithmetic. > **Objection: a one per cent share means the software cannot have mattered** > > The figure is a national share, offered by the vendor, in a market the vendor measures nationally. The product prices individual buildings, and the American settlement restricts geographic granularity below the state level. Whether one per cent nationally amounts to a cluster of buildings inside one submarket is among the things the Canadian file does not say. On the effect on rents, the Canadian file is silent. The Bureau's finding was about adoption thresholds. The class action ended before discovery. Nothing in this research compares rents in Canadian buildings that ran the software with rents in buildings that did not. The only Canadian number about an outcome is the 2017 press release's revenue outperformance, which measures a landlord's revenue rather than a tenant's rent, and which the study describes as a testimonial that vendors later remove. Even a pattern would not settle the question. Parallel pricing is what competitive markets, rent caps and shared public benchmarks already produce, so a claim of collusion drawn from synchronized rents is exactly the inference the Bureau itself declined to draw. ## The law asks for an agreement, and the software never needs one Canada's criminal conspiracy provision, section 45, requires proof of an agreement beyond a reasonable doubt, and the civil provision asks for an agreement as well. Neither reaches *tacit* algorithmic coordination, and conscious parallelism is not illegal in Canada. the law is built for human agreements, and the technology routes around it. The amendments of June 2025 changed a good deal around the edges. They make abuse of dominance easier to establish, expand the civil provision to non-competitor agreements on a significant-purpose test, repeal the efficiencies defence, and open private access to the Tribunal with disgorgement-style awards, but none reach genuinely autonomous tacit coordination absent an agreement. A shared algorithmic intermediary that produces parallel pricing without a provable meeting of competitor minds falls into the tacit-collusion gap that the Bureau's own June 2025 discussion paper and consultation explicitly flagged. The Bureau knows this. Its January 2026 report on the consultation recorded stakeholder concern that tacit collusion through algorithms typically falls outside existing competition law because the law requires evidence of a 'meeting of the minds.' Its separate inquiry into Kalibrate Canada, over retail-gasoline pricing data, remains open. Canada has over 60 companies offering algorithmic pricing services, so the question is not confined to apartments. No Canadian province or municipality has enacted or formally tabled an algorithmic-rent ban. Ontario's Bill 60 moves tenant protections the other way, loosening fixed-term leases and easing evictions. The realistic route to a Canadian answer runs through the Bureau's compliance guidance and the new private access to the Tribunal, not through legislation. ## What is left is a concentration that did not retreat The tool was built for a market with few enough owners that each one's decisions show up in the others' numbers. Canada has that market. the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates of 30% financialized. Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize. Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats. That is the shape of what happened. A pricing tool arrived in Canadian apartment buildings, was named by reporters, was withdrawn by landlords who had used it, and then passed through every institution that could have found out what it did. The vendor's share stayed under the threshold that triggers a dominance finding. The class action stopped before it could obtain the internal documents that carried the American cases. No province or city wrote a disclosure rule that would make the next adoption visible. What the Canadian file establishes is adoption, retreat and two closures, with no measurement of rent. The only Canadian number about what the software achieved was published by the company selling it, in a release that has since come down, while the ownership structure the software was designed for kept consolidating. The gap the Bureau described is the part that survives all three endings: the law asks competitors for an agreement, and a shared algorithm lets them price in parallel without ever needing one.
